  • Bitwise reproducibility is cheap to lose and expensive to want: atomics, split-K and collective-algorithm selection make reduction order non-deterministic, a one-ulp divergence becomes an $O(1)$ loss difference within a few hundred steps, and whether that costs final quality — as opposed to costing debuggability, which it certainly does — is not settled by any published paired-run study at scale. Contested
Part II

Classical Machine Learning

Deep learning did not replace classical machine learning; it absorbed some of it and lost to the rest. This part builds linear models — the atom every neural layer is made of — then kernels, whose theory turns out to predict the behaviour of infinitely wide networks, then gradient-boosted trees, which still win on tabular data and deserve an explanation rather than an excuse, and finally the classical unsupervised objectives that reappear almost verbatim as modern self-supervision.
Chapter 6

Linear and Logistic Regression: the Atom

Learning Objectives
  • Derive the OLS normal equations $X^{\top}Xw = X^{\top}y$ and their ridge-regularized form, and explain ridge as MAP estimation under a Gaussian prior with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$.
  • Derive the logistic loss from the Bernoulli likelihood and show its gradient is $X^{\top}(\sigma(Xw) - y)$ — the identical form taken by the final layer of every classifier in this book.
  • Prove the logistic loss is convex but has no closed-form minimizer, and explain why linearly separable data drives $\|w\|_2 \to \infty$ while the decision boundary converges.
  • Generalize to softmax regression and to generalized linear models, identifying the link function — not the loss — as the actual design choice.
  • Implement logistic regression with both IRLS and gradient descent in working code, verified against finite differences and a reference solver.
Read alongside — Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, for the shrinkage and subset-selection material: its treatment of ridge in the SVD basis and of the lasso solution path is the reference version. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, for the probabilistic derivation of logistic regression and for IRLS presented as Newton’s method on the Bernoulli likelihood. Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics (2023), for exponential families, canonical links, and the calibration material, which it states more carefully than most textbooks.

A transformer is a stack of logistic regressions with learned features. The last layer of GPT-scale models — the unembedding in Chapter 23, the classification head in Chapter 20 — is a multinomial logistic regression on the residual stream, and its gradient is literally $(P - Y)^{\top}X$; everything before it exists to make that regression easy. This chapter is not a warm-up. It is where the gradient forms, the conditioning pathologies, and the calibration failures you will meet in Parts III–VII first appear with closed-form answers attached. It uses cross-entropy as negative log-likelihood from Chapter 2, conditioning from Chapter 1 and floating point from Chapter 5, and the convergence-rate vocabulary of Chapter 4. Chapter 7 replaces $x$ with $\phi(x)$ and finds the margin story here returning as the SVM; Chapter 39 returns to the sigmoid as the thing homomorphic encryption cannot evaluate.

6.1 Least Squares, Geometrically and Probabilistically

Fix a design matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ whose rows are $x_i^{\top}$, a target $y \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and weights $w \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Ordinary least squares minimizes $\mathcal{L}(w) = \|y - Xw\|_2^2$. This is a quadratic in $w$, so its gradient is affine and stationarity is a linear system — the single structural fact that separates this section from every other section in the chapter.

Theorem 6.1 (Normal equations and orthogonal projection)

$\hat{w}$ minimizes $\|y - Xw\|_2^2$ if and only if $X^{\top}X\hat{w} = X^{\top}y$. If $X$ has full column rank, $\hat{w} = (X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}y$ is unique and $X\hat{w} = Hy$ with $H = X(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}$ the orthogonal projector onto $\mathrm{col}(X)$.

Proof. Expand $\mathcal{L}(w) = y^{\top}y - 2w^{\top}X^{\top}y + w^{\top}X^{\top}Xw$. Then $\nabla \mathcal{L} = 2(X^{\top}Xw - X^{\top}y)$ and $\nabla^2 \mathcal{L} = 2X^{\top}X \succeq 0$, so $\mathcal{L}$ is convex and stationarity is necessary and sufficient. Setting $\nabla\mathcal{L} = 0$ gives the normal equations. Their content is $X^{\top}(y - X\hat{w}) = 0$: the residual is orthogonal to every column of $X$, which is exactly the statement that $X\hat{w}$ is the orthogonal projection of $y$ onto $\mathrm{col}(X)$. For $H$: $H^{\top} = H$ and $H^2 = X(X^{\top}X)^{-1}(X^{\top}X)(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top} = H$, and $Hv = v$ for $v \in \mathrm{col}(X)$, which characterizes the orthogonal projector. $\blacksquare$

Example 6.1 (Three points, by hand)

Take $X = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 1 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ (intercept plus one feature) and $y = (1, 3, 2)^{\top}$. Then $X^{\top}X = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 3\\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $6$, and $X^{\top}y = (6, 7)^{\top}$. So $\hat{w} = \tfrac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix}5 & -3\\ -3 & 3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}6\\7\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{6}(9, 3)^{\top} = (1.5,\, 0.5)^{\top}$. Fitted values $(1.5, 2.0, 2.5)$, residuals $r = (-0.5, 1.0, -0.5)$. Check orthogonality directly: $\sum_i r_i = 0$ (residual $\perp$ intercept column) and $\sum_i x_i r_i = 0\cdot(-0.5) + 1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot(-0.5) = 0$ (residual $\perp$ feature column). $\mathrm{SSE} = 1.5$. The first identity is why an intercept guarantees the residuals average to zero — a fact we reuse in Section 6.7 for calibration.

6.1.1 The probabilistic reading

Model $y = Xw + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I_n)$. The log-likelihood is $$\log p(y \mid X, w) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - Xw\|_2^2,$$ so maximizing likelihood over $w$ is minimizing squared error, exactly, for every $\sigma$. Squared loss is not a neutral default; it is the assertion that the noise is additive, homoscedastic, and Gaussian. Certain When that assertion is wrong — count data, binary data, heavy tails — least squares is the wrong estimator, and Section 6.6 says precisely what to replace it with.

Common Pitfall

Forming $X^{\top}X$ and calling a linear solver squares the condition number: $\kappa_2(X^{\top}X) = \kappa_2(X)^2$. A design with $\kappa_2(X) = 10^8$ — ordinary once you add polynomial features or one-hot columns that nearly co-occur — gives a Gram matrix with $\kappa_2 = 10^{16}$, numerically singular in float64 (machine epsilon $2.2\times10^{-16}$, Chapter 5), and the solver returns garbage without raising. Factor $X$ by QR ($\approx 2nd^2$ flops) or SVD ($\approx 6nd^2$) instead of forming the $nd^2 + d^3/3$ normal equations: a constant-factor price for halving the exponent of your error. numpy.linalg.lstsq does the right thing; numpy.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) does not.

6.2 Ridge, Lasso, and Sparsity

Definition 6.1 (Ridge estimator)

For $\lambda > 0$, $\hat{w}_{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_w \|y - Xw\|_2^2 + \lambda\|w\|_2^2 = (X^{\top}X + \lambda I_d)^{-1}X^{\top}y$. The inverse always exists: $X^{\top}X \succeq 0$, so every eigenvalue of $X^{\top}X + \lambda I$ is at least $\lambda > 0$.

Theorem 6.2 (Ridge is MAP under a Gaussian prior)

Under the likelihood $y \mid w \sim \mathcal{N}(Xw, \sigma^2 I)$ and the prior $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2 I_d)$, the posterior mode is $\hat{w}_{\text{ridge}}$ with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$.

Proof. By Bayes, $-\log p(w \mid y) = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|y - Xw\|_2^2 + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|w\|_2^2 + \text{const}$, where the constant collects the evidence and the normalizers, neither depending on $w$. Multiply by $2\sigma^2$ — a positive constant, so the argmin is unchanged — to obtain $\|y - Xw\|_2^2 + (\sigma^2/\tau^2)\|w\|_2^2$. This is the ridge objective with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$. Because the posterior is Gaussian (a quadratic exponent), the mode is also the mean. $\blacksquare$

The identification $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$ is not decoration: regularization strength is a noise-to-prior-variance ratio, so doubling the noise doubles $\lambda$ and a prior admitting large weights drives it to zero. It also explains why weight decay in Chapter 14 must be re-tuned whenever you change batch size or switch the loss from a sum to a mean — both silently move $\sigma^2$ or the effective sample count.

6.2.1 Ridge in the SVD basis

Write $X = U\Sigma V^{\top}$ with singular values $s_1 \ge \cdots \ge s_d > 0$. Substituting and using $V^{\top}V = I$, $$\hat{w}_{\text{ridge}} = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{s_j}{s_j^2 + \lambda}\,(u_j^{\top}y)\,v_j, \qquad \hat{w}_{\text{OLS}} = \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{1}{s_j}\,(u_j^{\top}y)\,v_j.$$ Ridge multiplies the OLS coefficient along $v_j$ by the shrinkage factor $s_j^2/(s_j^2 + \lambda) \in (0,1)$: directions the data explores strongly ($s_j^2 \gg \lambda$) pass through nearly untouched, directions it barely explores are crushed. The sum $\sum_j s_j^2/(s_j^2+\lambda)$ is the effective degrees of freedom, a continuous parameter count running from $d$ at $\lambda = 0$ to $0$ as $\lambda \to \infty$.

Example 6.2 (Shrinkage across three decades of spectrum)

Let $X$ have singular values $s = (10, 1, 0.1)$ and take $\lambda = 1$. The shrinkage factors are $100/101 = 0.990099$, $1/2 = 0.5$, and $0.01/1.01 = 0.009901$. The top direction survives with a $1\%$ haircut; the bottom direction — the one whose OLS coefficient would have been inflated by $1/s_3 = 10$ — is reduced by a factor of $101$. The effective degrees of freedom is $0.990099 + 0.5 + 0.009901 = 1.5$: three nominal parameters, one and a half real ones.

6.2.2 Lasso and why $\ell_1$ produces exact zeros

The lasso replaces the penalty with $\lambda\|w\|_1$. It has no closed form in general — the objective is nondifferentiable at every coordinate hyperplane — but the orthonormal case ($X^{\top}X = I$) is solvable and explains everything. There the objective separates into $(\hat{w}^{\text{OLS}}_j - w_j)^2 + \lambda|w_j|$, and the subdifferential condition $-2(\hat{w}^{\text{OLS}}_j - w_j) + \lambda\,\partial|w_j| \ni 0$ gives the soft-threshold operator $$\hat{w}_j = \mathrm{sign}(\hat{w}^{\text{OLS}}_j)\max\!\left(|\hat{w}^{\text{OLS}}_j| - \tfrac{\lambda}{2},\, 0\right),$$ against ridge's $\hat{w}_j = \hat{w}^{\text{OLS}}_j/(1+\lambda)$. With $\hat{w}^{\text{OLS}} = (2.0, -0.3, 0.6)$ and $\lambda = 1$, lasso returns $(1.5, 0, 0.1)$ — the second coordinate exactly zero in floating point, not merely small — while ridge returns $(1.0, -0.15, 0.3)$, shrinking everything and zeroing nothing. The $\ell_1$ ball has vertices on the coordinate axes and a smooth level set generically touches a convex body at a vertex; the $\ell_2$ ball has no such preferred points.

Whether $\ell_1$ is the right instrument in deep learning is genuinely disputed. Contested One camp holds it is useless at scale: unstructured sparsity buys no wall-clock speedup on dense GPU kernels (Chapter 30), and magnitude pruning after dense training reaches the same accuracy–sparsity frontier without the optimization damage. The other holds that $\ell_1$-style penalties remain correct where the pattern is structured and therefore cashable — whole heads, channels, experts (Chapter 22) — so the failure is of unstructured $\ell_1$, not of $\ell_1$. What would settle it: a comparison at fixed inference FLOPs, not fixed parameter count, on hardware that exploits the pattern produced. Our position: structured penalties earn their place, unstructured $\ell_1$ does not.

6.3 Logistic Regression and the Bernoulli Likelihood

Now $y_i \in \{0,1\}$. Model $y_i \mid x_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i)$ with $p_i = \sigma(z_i)$, $z_i = x_i^{\top}w$, and $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$. Nothing here is a choice about the loss; the loss is forced by the likelihood.

The likelihood is $\prod_i p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}$, so the negative log-likelihood is $-\sum_i [y_i \log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]$ — the binary cross-entropy of Chapter 2, arrived at from a modeling assumption rather than from an information-theoretic axiom. Substitute the sigmoid. Since $\log \sigma(z) = -\log(1+e^{-z})$ and $\log(1-\sigma(z)) = \log\sigma(-z) = -z - \log(1+e^{-z}) = -\log(1+e^{z})$, the sum collapses into the form worth memorizing: $$\mathcal{L}(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big[\log\!\big(1 + e^{z_i}\big) - y_i z_i\Big], \qquad z = Xw.$$ This form has one exponential per row, no logarithm of a possibly-underflowed probability, and is what the artifact computes via np.logaddexp(0, z).

Theorem 6.3 (Gradient, Hessian, and convexity)

With $s = \sigma(Xw)$ and $S = \mathrm{diag}(s \odot (1-s))$, $$\nabla \mathcal{L}(w) = X^{\top}(s - y), \qquad \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}(w) = X^{\top} S X \succeq 0.$$ $\mathcal{L}$ is convex, and strictly convex if and only if $X$ has full column rank.

Proof. Differentiate a single term: $\frac{\partial}{\partial w}\log(1+e^{z_i}) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{1+e^{z_i}}x_i = \sigma(z_i)x_i$, and $\frac{\partial}{\partial w}(-y_i z_i) = -y_i x_i$. Summing gives $\sum_i (\sigma(z_i) - y_i)x_i = X^{\top}(s-y)$. Differentiating again and using $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$ gives $\sum_i s_i(1-s_i)x_i x_i^{\top} = X^{\top}SX$. For any $v \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $v^{\top}\nabla^2\mathcal{L}\,v = \sum_i s_i(1-s_i)(x_i^{\top}v)^2 \ge 0$, since $s_i \in (0,1)$ strictly for finite $z_i$. It vanishes only if $x_i^{\top}v = 0$ for all $i$, i.e. $Xv = 0$; so the Hessian is positive definite exactly when $\mathrm{null}(X) = \{0\}$. $\blacksquare$

Compare the gradients: OLS gives $X^{\top}(Xw - y)$, logistic gives $X^{\top}(\sigma(Xw) - y)$. Both are prediction minus target, back-projected through the inputs — not a coincidence but a theorem about canonical links (Section 6.6), and the same expression you will write by hand for a transformer's output layer in Chapter 11. Certain Note what the Hessian does not contain: $y$. Logistic curvature depends only on the model's own confidence, which is what makes Newton's method here well behaved and the IRLS derivation possible.

Example 6.3 (One Newton step by hand)

One feature, no intercept: $x = (-1, 1, 2)$, $y = (0, 1, 1)$. At $w = 0$ every $\sigma(z_i) = 0.5$, so $\mathcal{L}(0) = 3\log 2 = 2.0794$, the gradient is $\sum_i (0.5 - y_i)x_i = (0.5)(-1) + (-0.5)(1) + (-0.5)(2) = -2.0$, and the Hessian is $\sum_i 0.25\,x_i^2 = 0.25(1+1+4) = 1.5$. The Newton step is $w \leftarrow 0 - (-2.0)/1.5 = 4/3$. Evaluate there: $\sigma(-4/3) = 0.208609$, $\sigma(4/3) = 0.791391$, $\sigma(8/3) = 0.935031$, giving $\mathcal{L} = 0.5351$ and gradient $-0.5472$. The loss fell by a factor of $3.9$ in one step, but the gradient is still strictly negative — and it will stay strictly negative forever, because this data is separable through the origin. Section 6.4 is that observation taken seriously.

6.4 Convexity, Separability, and Implicit Bias

The logistic loss is convex, its Hessian is available in closed form, and it has no closed-form minimizer. The reason is structural: OLS is solvable because $\nabla\mathcal{L}$ is affine in $w$, so stationarity is a linear system. The logistic score equations $X^{\top}\sigma(Xw) = X^{\top}y$ are $d$ transcendental equations in $d$ unknowns mixing exponentials of linear forms, and outside degenerate cases they admit no solution in elementary functions. Certain This is the first place in the book where iteration is a necessity rather than a convenience, and Chapters 4 and 13 follow from that.

Definition 6.2 (Linear separability)

With $\tilde{y}_i = 2y_i - 1 \in \{-1, +1\}$, the data $\{(x_i, y_i)\}$ is linearly separable through the origin if there exists $u \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\tilde{y}_i\, x_i^{\top}u > 0$ for every $i$. The max-margin direction is the unit $u^{\star}$ maximizing $\min_i \tilde{y}_i\,x_i^{\top}u$, equivalently the hard-margin SVM solution $\arg\min \tfrac12\|u\|^2$ subject to $\tilde{y}_i x_i^{\top}u \ge 1$, rescaled.

Theorem 6.4 (Separability destroys the minimizer)

If the data is linearly separable and $\lambda = 0$, then $\inf_w \mathcal{L}(w) = 0$ and the infimum is not attained; consequently any algorithm driving $\mathcal{L} \to 0$ has $\|w\|_2 \to \infty$.

Proof. Rewrite the loss in margin form: $\mathcal{L}(w) = \sum_i \log(1 + e^{-\tilde{y}_i x_i^{\top} w})$, which is verified by checking the two cases $y_i \in \{0,1\}$ against $\log(1+e^{z}) - y z$. Every term is strictly positive for finite $w$, so $\mathcal{L}(w) > 0$ everywhere. Take a separator $u$ and set $m = \min_i \tilde{y}_i x_i^{\top}u > 0$. Then $\mathcal{L}(cu) \le n\log(1 + e^{-cm}) \le n e^{-cm} \to 0$ as $c \to \infty$. So the infimum is $0$, unattained, and any minimizing sequence must have $\|w\| \to \infty$ since $\mathcal{L}$ is bounded below by $\log(1+e^{-\max_i \|x_i\|\|w\|}) > 0$ on any bounded set. $\blacksquare$

The naive reading — "the optimizer diverges, the model is broken" — is wrong, and the correction is one of the most useful results in modern optimization theory. The direction converges, and it converges to something specific.

Theorem 6.5 (Implicit bias of gradient descent, Soudry et al. 2018)

On separable data with the logistic loss and any fixed step size below the smoothness threshold $\eta < 2/L$, $L = \tfrac14\lambda_{\max}(X^{\top}X)$, gradient descent from any initialization satisfies $\|w(t)\| \sim \log t$ and $w(t)/\|w(t)\| \to u^{\star}$, the $\ell_2$ max-margin direction, at rate $O(1/\log t)$.

Proof sketch. In margin form the gradient is $-\sum_i \frac{e^{-\tilde{y}_i x_i^{\top}w}}{1 + e^{-\tilde{y}_i x_i^{\top}w}}\,\tilde{y}_i x_i$. Once every margin is large the weights are $\approx e^{-\tilde{y}_i x_i^{\top}w}$, which is exponentially dominated by the points of smallest margin. So asymptotically the update direction is a nonnegative combination of the minimum-margin points alone, and for $w/\|w\|$ to stop rotating, $w$ must be parallel to that combination: $w \propto \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} \alpha_i \tilde{y}_i x_i$ with $\alpha_i \ge 0$ supported on the active set. That is precisely the KKT stationarity condition of the hard-margin SVM. Writing $w(t) = \hat{w}\log t + \rho(t)$ with $\hat{w} = u^{\star}/m^{\star}$ and showing $\rho(t)$ bounded gives both the $\log t$ norm growth and the $1/\log t$ angle rate; the logarithm in the denominator is what makes the convergence so slow in practice. $\blacksquare$

The artifact measures all three claims. Over three decades of steps ($t = 10^3$ to $10^6$) the weight norm grows $6.34 \to 23.13$, an increment of $2.67$ per $e$-fold of $t$ against the theoretical $1/m^{\star} = 2.789$ — a $4\%$ gap, which is the bounded residual $\rho(t)$ still bleeding off. The cosine gap $1 - \cos(w, u^{\star})$ falls $6.04\times10^{-3} \to 1.01\times10^{-4}$; that is the angle itself going from $0.110$ to $0.0142$ radians. Read that carefully, because it is easy to over-claim: a factor of $7.8$ in angle is faster than the theorem's $O(1/\log t)$, which across these three decades would buy only $\log(10^6)/\log(10^3) = 2$. The theorem is an upper bound, and this design has just two support vectors, so the residual settles quickly. What survives either way is the practical verdict — a factor of $7.8$ for a thousandfold increase in steps is hopeless as a way to actually compute a max-margin classifier; use an SVM solver, as the artifact does. The other consequences are practical too. Weight norm is a useless convergence diagnostic on near-separable data, and early stopping is a regularizer with a known bias. Most importantly for Part III: overparameterized networks interpolate their training data and are therefore separable in the relevant sense, so gradient descent is never merely minimizing the loss — it is selecting among infinitely many zero-loss solutions, and the selection rule is what Chapter 3 is about. Likely

Any $\lambda > 0$ removes the pathology outright: the objective becomes $\lambda$-strongly convex and coercive, so a unique finite minimizer exists. This is why the artifact's IRLS routine carries $\lambda = 10^{-8}$ even when nominally unregularized — not to change the answer, which it moves by $O(10^{-8})$, but to keep $X^{\top}SX + \lambda I$ invertible when the computed $s_i(1-s_i)$ collapses to zero on confident points.

Common Pitfall

Three failures that cost real debugging hours, all downstream of separability driving $|z|$ up. First: computing the loss as -y*np.log(p) - (1-y)*np.log(1-p) after p = 1/(1+np.exp(-z)). At $z = 40$, p rounds to exactly $1.0$ in float64, so log(1-p) is $-\infty$ and one mislabeled confident point yields nan gradients that propagate everywhere. Use np.logaddexp(0, z) - y*z, exact for all $z$. Second: overflow in whichever branch you did not think about. np.exp(z)/(1 + np.exp(z)) at $z = 800$ is inf/inf, which is nan; the mirror form 1/(1 + np.exp(-z)) at $z = -800$ raises an overflow warning and returns $0$ by luck rather than by design. The artifact's sigmoid selects the branch, evaluating $e^{-z}$ only where $z \ge 0$ and $e^{z}$ only where $z < 0$, so the exponent is never positive and neither failure is reachable. Third: in IRLS, $s_i$ rounds to exactly $1$ once $|z_i| \gtrsim 37$ — that is where $e^{-|z|}$ falls below the float64 unit roundoff $1.1\times10^{-16}$ — so the computed $s_i(1-s_i)$ is exactly $0$. Note the mechanism: cancellation in $1 - s_i$, not underflow of the product, which would need $|z_i| \gtrsim 744$. Once enough rows do this the Hessian loses rank and np.linalg.solve either raises or silently returns an enormous step. A ridge of $10^{-8}$, or a trust region, fixes it.

6.5 Softmax and Multinomial Regression

With $K$ classes, $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d}$, logits $z = Wx \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$, and $$p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}}, \qquad \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i} \left[ z_{i,y_i} - \log\!\sum_j e^{z_{i,j}} \right].$$ The Jacobian of the softmax is $\partial p/\partial z = \mathrm{diag}(p) - pp^{\top}$. Composing it with the derivative of the log term collapses everything: with $Y$ the one-hot target matrix and $P$ the matrix of predicted probabilities, $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial Z = P - Y$ and $\nabla_W \mathcal{L} = (P - Y)^{\top}X$. Third time, same shape.

Example 6.4 (Softmax on three logits)

$z = (2.0,\, 1.0,\, 0.1)$. Then $e^{z} = (7.38906,\, 2.71828,\, 1.10517)$, summing to $11.21251$, so $p = (0.659001,\, 0.242433,\, 0.098566)$. If the true class is the middle one, the loss is $-\log 0.242433 = 1.41703$ nats and the gradient with respect to the logits is $p - (0,1,0) = (0.659001,\, -0.757567,\, 0.098566)$, which sums to zero. It always sums to zero, because softmax is shift-invariant: $z \mapsto z + c\mathbf{1}$ leaves $p$ unchanged. The parameterization is therefore overcomplete by exactly $d$ parameters, the Hessian has a $d$-dimensional null space, and unregularized multinomial MLE has a continuum of solutions. Adding any $\lambda > 0$ selects the zero-sum representative $\sum_k W_k = 0$. For $K = 2$ the model reduces to binary logistic regression with $w = W_1 - W_0$, which is why the binary case is not a special case worth separate code.

Always subtract $\max_k z_k$ before exponentiating; by the same shift-invariance this is exact, not an approximation (Chapter 5). At $K = 128{,}000$ — a current LLM vocabulary size (Chapter 23) Verify — be precise about where the cost actually is, because the usual claim that "the softmax is the bottleneck" misplaces it. The exponentials are $O(K)$ per token and cost nothing; the unembedding matmul that produces the logits is $2dK \approx 1.0$ GFLOP per token at $d = 4096$, which is the FLOP cost. The memory is worse than the FLOPs: a batch of $8{,}192$ tokens times $128{,}000$ classes in fp32 is $4.2$ GB of logits for one layer that has no parameters of its own. That is why Chapter 33 covers never materializing the full logit vector at inference.

6.6 GLMs and Link Functions

Definition 6.3 (Generalized linear model)

A GLM has three parts: (i) a response distribution in the one-parameter exponential family, $p(y \mid \theta) = h(y)\exp(\theta y - A(\theta))$; (ii) a linear predictor $\eta = x^{\top}w$; (iii) a link function $g$ relating the mean to the predictor, $g(\mu) = \eta$ with $\mu = \mathbb{E}[y]$. The link is canonical when $\theta = \eta$, i.e. $g = (A')^{-1}$.

Two facts about $A$, the log-partition function, do all the work. Differentiating $\int h(y)e^{\theta y - A(\theta)}dy = 1$ once gives $\mathbb{E}[y] = A'(\theta)$; differentiating twice gives $\mathrm{Var}[y] = A''(\theta) \ge 0$, so $A$ is convex. Now the payoff.

Theorem 6.6 (Canonical-link gradient)

For any GLM with the canonical link, $\nabla_w \mathcal{L}(w) = X^{\top}(\mu - y)$ where $\mu_i = A'(x_i^{\top}w)$, and $\nabla^2_w \mathcal{L}(w) = X^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(A''(\eta))X \succeq 0$, so the negative log-likelihood is convex in $w$.

Proof. Under the canonical link $\theta_i = \eta_i = x_i^{\top}w$, so the per-observation negative log-likelihood is $A(x_i^{\top}w) - y_i\,x_i^{\top}w - \log h(y_i)$. Differentiate: $(A'(x_i^{\top}w) - y_i)x_i = (\mu_i - y_i)x_i$. Sum over $i$. Differentiate again: $A''(x_i^{\top}w)\,x_ix_i^{\top}$, and $A'' = \mathrm{Var}[y] \ge 0$. $\blacksquare$

That one line proves the OLS, logistic, softmax, and Poisson gradients simultaneously. Read the table right to left: the loss is not the design choice, the response distribution is, and the link is the interface.

Response$A(\theta)$$\mu = A'(\theta)$Canonical link $g(\mu)$Loss
Gaussian ($\sigma^2{=}1$)$\theta^2/2$$\theta$identitysquared error
Bernoulli$\log(1+e^{\theta})$$\sigma(\theta)$$\log\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ (logit)binary cross-entropy
Categorical$\log\sum_k e^{\theta_k}$$\mathrm{softmax}(\theta)$$\log \mu_k + c$cross-entropy
Poisson$e^{\theta}$$e^{\theta}$$\log\mu$Poisson deviance

Choosing a non-canonical link is legitimate and changes the estimator. Probit uses $g = \Phi^{-1}$, a latent Gaussian threshold model; its gradient acquires a factor $\phi(\eta)/[\Phi(\eta)(1-\Phi(\eta))]$ and its Hessian depends on $y$, so IRLS is less stable. Fitted probit and logit coefficients differ by roughly $1.6$–$1.8\times$, since the logistic distribution has standard deviation $\pi/\sqrt{3} = 1.8138$ against the standard normal's $1$. Likely The logit wins because it is canonical — buying convexity, a $y$-free Hessian, clean IRLS — and because its coefficients read as log-odds: a coefficient of $0.693$ means the feature doubles the odds.

6.6.1 IRLS is Newton in disguise

Take the Newton step for a canonical GLM, with $S = \mathrm{diag}(A''(\eta))$: $$w^{+} = w - (X^{\top}SX)^{-1}X^{\top}(\mu - y) = (X^{\top}SX)^{-1}\big[X^{\top}SXw + X^{\top}(y - \mu)\big] = (X^{\top}SX)^{-1}X^{\top}S\,\underbrace{\big[Xw + S^{-1}(y-\mu)\big]}_{\text{working response } \tilde{z}}.$$ That is the weighted least-squares solution of $\tilde{z}$ on $X$ with weights $S$. Hence the name: each Newton iteration is a reweighted least-squares fit, so every OLS solver you have is a GLM solver. The cost is $O(nd^2 + d^3)$ per iteration against $O(nd)$ for a gradient step, buying local quadratic convergence — the artifact reaches a squared Newton decrement $g^{\top}H^{-1}g = 8.7\times10^{-22}$ (gradient norm $8.5\times10^{-15}$) in $6$ iterations where gradient descent needs $6\times10^{4}$. The tradeoff flips hard with $d$: at $d = 10^4$ the Hessian alone is $8\times10^8$ bytes and a Cholesky solve is $d^3/3 \approx 3\times10^{11}$ flops, and at the $d = 10^{9}$ of Part V second-order methods survive only in heavily structured form (Chapter 13's Shampoo and Muon are attempts to keep a usable fraction of this information).

6.7 Calibration: probabilities that mean something

Definition 6.4 (Calibration and ECE)

A predictor $f$ is calibrated if $\mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid f(x) = p) = p$ for every $p$ in its range. The expected calibration error partitions the predictions into $M$ bins $B_m$ and reports $\mathrm{ECE} = \sum_{m} \frac{|B_m|}{n}\,\big|\,\overline{y}_{B_m} - \overline{p}_{B_m}\,\big|$, the sample-weighted gap between empirical frequency and mean predicted probability.

Calibration is a different axis from accuracy. A model predicting the base rate $0.7$ for every input is perfectly calibrated and useless; one that always outputs $0.999$ for the correct class is perfectly accurate and badly calibrated.

Theorem 6.7 (MLE is calibrated in-sample along every feature)

If $\hat{w}$ satisfies $\nabla\mathcal{L}(\hat{w}) = 0$ with $\lambda = 0$, then $X^{\top}(\hat{p} - y) = 0$; in particular, if $X$ contains an intercept column of ones, $\sum_i \hat{p}_i = \sum_i y_i$ exactly, and for every feature $j$, $\sum_i x_{ij}\hat{p}_i = \sum_i x_{ij}y_i$.

Proof. Immediate from Theorem 6.3: stationarity is the moment-matching condition $X^{\top}\hat{p} = X^{\top}y$; reading off the coordinate corresponding to the intercept column gives the base-rate identity. $\blacksquare$

Two widely misunderstood consequences. First, in-sample calibration of a logistic MLE is no evidence the model is good — it is an algebraic identity that holds for a model fit to pure noise, so calibration must be measured out of sample. Second, regularization breaks the identity on purpose: with $\lambda > 0$ stationarity becomes $X^{\top}(\hat{p} - y) = -\lambda\hat{w}$, so predicted positives no longer sum to observed positives and heavy ridge yields systematically under-confident probabilities. The artifact quantifies it: a well-specified fit on $n = 20{,}000$ gives $\mathrm{ECE} = 0.00447$ over ten equal-mass bins, no bin off by more than $1.46$ binomial standard errors; scaling those same logits by $0.4$ drives the ECE to $0.13554$, $30\times$ worse, without changing a single predicted label.

That last observation is the basis of temperature scaling: fit a single scalar $T$ on held-out data and report $\sigma(z/T)$. Because it is a monotone transform it cannot change any argmax, so accuracy is untouched and only the probabilities move; it is the cheapest correct fix available, and it is a one-parameter logistic regression on the logits, which is to say this chapter again. Deep networks are typically over-confident ($T > 1$), a finding usually attributed to Guo et al. (2017). Verify

For large language models the picture is contested. Contested One position: base models are well calibrated because next-token likelihood training at scale makes them so, the evidence being the GPT-4 system card's MMLU reliability diagram, where the pre-RLHF model tracks the diagonal and the post-RLHF model does not. The opposing position: that measures token-level probability on a multiple-choice format, a narrow proxy, and free-form verbalized confidence is poorly calibrated regardless of alignment stage — so "RLHF destroys calibration" over-reads a format-specific result. The settling experiment is a matched comparison of token-level and verbalized confidence on open-ended generation, before and after preference optimization, at fixed sampling temperature; Chapters 27 and 29 return to it. Our position: the RLHF effect on token-level calibration is real and reproducible; the leap to "aligned models don't know what they know" is not yet supported.

Artifact 6.1 — Logistic regression from scratch: IRLS and gradient descent

Pure-NumPy logistic regression with four independent self-checks: analytic gradient against central finite differences of the objective, and analytic Hessian against central differences of the analytic gradient; IRLS and gradient-descent fits against sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression with regularization matched through $\lambda = 1/C$; $10^6$ gradient steps on separable data, tracking the weight norm and the angle to a max-margin direction obtained from an independent SLSQP solve of the hard-margin SVM; and a decile calibration table checked against binomial standard errors. Every cross-check import is guarded. Runtime: 24 s on one CPU core, dominated by the $10^6$ gradient steps.

"""
Artifact 6.1 -- Logistic regression from scratch: IRLS (Newton) and gradient descent.

Self-verifying. Everything numerical is checked against an independent computation:
  (1) analytic gradient  vs central finite differences of the objective
  (2) analytic Hessian   vs central finite differences of the analytic gradient
  (3) IRLS and GD solutions vs sklearn.linear_model.LogisticRegression, regularization matched
  (4) separable data: ||w|| grows without bound while w/||w|| -> the max-margin direction
  (5) calibration: on a well-specified model, binned empirical frequency ~ mean predicted prob

Core math is pure NumPy. sklearn and scipy are cross-checks only and are import-guarded.
"""

import numpy as np

try:
    from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
except ImportError:
    LogisticRegression = None

try:
    from scipy.optimize import minimize
except ImportError:
    minimize = None

RNG = np.random.default_rng(0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- core model
def sigmoid(z):
    """Numerically stable logistic sigmoid: no exp() of a large positive number."""
    out = np.empty_like(z, dtype=float)
    pos = z >= 0
    out[pos] = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z[pos]))
    ez = np.exp(z[~pos])                      # z < 0, so exp(z) in (0, 1)
    out[~pos] = ez / (1.0 + ez)
    return out


def nll(w, X, y, lam=0.0):
    """Penalized negative log-likelihood, summed (not averaged) over the n rows.

    L(w) = sum_i [ log(1 + exp(z_i)) - y_i z_i ] + (lam/2)||w||^2,  z = Xw.
    logaddexp(0, z) is log(1+e^z) computed without overflow.
    """
    z = X @ w
    return float(np.sum(np.logaddexp(0.0, z) - y * z) + 0.5 * lam * w @ w)


def grad(w, X, y, lam=0.0):
    """X^T (sigma(Xw) - y) + lam*w  -- the residual form used by every classifier head."""
    return X.T @ (sigmoid(X @ w) - y) + lam * w


def hess(w, X, y, lam=0.0):
    """X^T diag(s(1-s)) X + lam*I, with s = sigma(Xw). Independent of y."""
    s = sigmoid(X @ w)
    return (X * (s * (1.0 - s))[:, None]).T @ X + lam * np.eye(X.shape[1])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- optimizers
def fit_irls(X, y, lam=1e-8, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100):
    """Newton / IRLS. Each step solves (X^T S X + lam I) delta = grad, a weighted least squares.

    A ridge of lam keeps the Hessian invertible when s(1-s) underflows on confident points.
    """
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        g = grad(w, X, y, lam)
        H = hess(w, X, y, lam)
        delta = np.linalg.solve(H, g)
        # Newton decrement squared: g^T H^-1 g, a bound on 2*(L(w) - L*) near the optimum.
        decrement = float(g @ delta)
        w = w - delta
        if decrement < tol:
            return w, it, decrement
    return w, max_iter, decrement


def fit_gd(X, y, lam=0.0, eta=None, n_steps=20000, track=None):
    """Plain full-batch gradient descent. eta defaults to 1/L with L the exact smoothness
    constant of the logistic loss: L = (1/4) * lambda_max(X^T X) + lam."""
    n, d = X.shape
    if eta is None:
        eta = 1.0 / (0.25 * np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X)[-1] + lam)
    w = np.zeros(d)
    log = []
    for t in range(1, n_steps + 1):
        w -= eta * grad(w, X, y, lam)
        if track is not None and t in track:
            log.append((t, w.copy()))
    return w, log


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- experiments
def check_derivatives():
    """Central differences: f'(x) ~ (f(x+h)-f(x-h))/2h, error O(h^2) + O(eps/h)."""
    n, d, lam = 200, 5, 0.7
    X = RNG.normal(size=(n, d))
    y = (RNG.random(n) < sigmoid(X @ RNG.normal(size=d))).astype(float)
    w = RNG.normal(size=d) * 0.5
    h = 1e-5

    g_fd = np.zeros(d)
    H_fd = np.zeros((d, d))
    for j in range(d):
        e = np.zeros(d)
        e[j] = h
        g_fd[j] = (nll(w + e, X, y, lam) - nll(w - e, X, y, lam)) / (2 * h)
        H_fd[:, j] = (grad(w + e, X, y, lam) - grad(w - e, X, y, lam)) / (2 * h)

    g_err = np.max(np.abs(grad(w, X, y, lam) - g_fd))
    H_err = np.max(np.abs(hess(w, X, y, lam) - H_fd))
    print(f"  max |analytic grad - central FD|    = {g_err:.3e}")
    print(f"  max |analytic Hess - central FD|    = {H_err:.3e}")
    print(f"  Hessian symmetry ||H - H^T||_max    = {np.max(np.abs(hess(w, X, y, lam) - hess(w, X, y, lam).T)):.3e}")
    print(f"  min eigenvalue of Hessian           = {np.linalg.eigvalsh(hess(w, X, y, lam))[0]:.6f}  (>0 => strictly convex)")
    assert g_err < 1e-6 and H_err < 1e-6


def check_against_sklearn():
    """sklearn minimizes 0.5||w||^2 + C * sum_i loss_i. Dividing by C, that is our objective
    with lam = 1/C. So C = 1/lam is the matched setting (fit_intercept=False; sklearn does
    not penalize an intercept, our objective would)."""
    n, d, lam = 500, 6, 2.0
    X = RNG.normal(size=(n, d))
    w_true = RNG.normal(size=d)
    y = (RNG.random(n) < sigmoid(X @ w_true)).astype(float)

    w_n, iters, dec = fit_irls(X, y, lam)
    w_g, _ = fit_gd(X, y, lam, n_steps=60000)
    print(f"  IRLS converged in {iters} Newton steps, final Newton decrement^2 = {dec:.3e}")
    print(f"  ||grad at IRLS solution||_2         = {np.linalg.norm(grad(w_n, X, y, lam)):.3e}")
    print(f"  ||w_IRLS - w_GD||_inf               = {np.max(np.abs(w_n - w_g)):.3e}")

    if LogisticRegression is None:
        print("  [skipped: sklearn not installed]")
        return
    sk = LogisticRegression(C=1.0 / lam, fit_intercept=False, tol=1e-10, max_iter=5000)
    sk.fit(X, y)
    w_sk = sk.coef_.ravel()
    err = np.max(np.abs(w_n - w_sk))
    print(f"  ||w_IRLS - w_sklearn||_inf          = {err:.3e}")
    print(f"  objective ours {nll(w_n, X, y, lam):.9f}  vs sklearn {nll(w_sk, X, y, lam):.9f}")
    assert err < 1e-5


def separable_run():
    """Separable through the origin: the minimizer is at infinity, but the *direction*
    converges to the hard-margin SVM solution (Soudry et al., 2018)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)            # own stream, so this run is reproducible alone
    n, d = 40, 2
    w_star = np.array([1.0, -0.6])
    scale = np.array([3.0, 1.0])              # anisotropy: the centroid-difference direction
    Xs = []                                   # (which GD chases first) is NOT the max-margin one
    while len(Xs) < n:                        # reject points inside the margin band
        x = rng.normal(size=d) * scale
        if abs(x @ w_star) > 0.35:
            Xs.append(x)
    X = np.array(Xs)
    s = np.sign(X @ w_star)                   # labels in {-1,+1}
    y = (s > 0).astype(float)                 # labels in {0,1} for the logistic fit

    # Hard-margin SVM (no intercept): min 0.5||u||^2 s.t. s_i x_i^T u >= 1.
    if minimize is None:
        print("  [skipped: scipy not installed]")
        return
    con = {"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda u: s * (X @ u) - 1.0}
    res = minimize(lambda u: 0.5 * u @ u, np.zeros(d), jac=lambda u: u,
                   constraints=[con], method="SLSQP", options={"maxiter": 500, "ftol": 1e-14})
    u_mm = res.x / np.linalg.norm(res.x)
    margin = float(np.min(s * (X @ u_mm)))
    n_sv = int(np.sum(s * (X @ res.x) < 1.0 + 1e-6))
    print(f"  max-margin direction {np.round(u_mm, 6)}, margin = {margin:.6f}, {n_sv} support vectors")

    ckpts = [10**k for k in range(3, 7)]
    _, log = fit_gd(X, y, lam=0.0, n_steps=ckpts[-1], track=set(ckpts))
    print("       step        ||w||     loss        cos(w, w_mm)     1 - cos")
    for t, w in log:
        c = float(w @ u_mm / np.linalg.norm(w))
        print(f"   {t:>9d}   {np.linalg.norm(w):8.3f}  {nll(w, X, y):.3e}   {c:.9f}   {1-c:.3e}")
    norms = [np.linalg.norm(w) for _, w in log]
    coss = [float(w @ u_mm / np.linalg.norm(w)) for _, w in log]
    assert all(np.diff(norms) > 0), "weight norm must grow monotonically"
    assert all(np.diff(coss) > 0) and coss[-1] > 0.999, "direction must converge to max margin"
    print(f"  ||w|| grew {norms[0]:.3f} -> {norms[-1]:.3f}; angle gap fell {1-coss[0]:.2e} -> {1-coss[-1]:.2e}")
    # Theory (Soudry et al.): w(t) ~ (u_mm/margin) * log t, so d||w||/d log t -> 1/margin.
    slope = (norms[-1] - norms[-2]) / np.log(ckpts[-1] / ckpts[-2])
    print(f"  measured d||w||/d log t = {slope:.3f};  predicted 1/margin = {1/margin:.3f}")


def calibration():
    """Well-specified logistic model => the fitted probabilities should be calibrated.
    Bin the predictions into deciles and compare mean predicted prob vs empirical frequency."""
    n, d = 20000, 4
    X = RNG.normal(size=(n, d))
    w_true = RNG.normal(size=d)
    y = (RNG.random(n) < sigmoid(X @ w_true)).astype(float)
    w_hat, _, _ = fit_irls(X, y, lam=1e-8)

    p = sigmoid(X @ w_hat)
    edges = np.quantile(p, np.linspace(0, 1, 11))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    idx = np.digitize(p, edges[1:-1])
    print("    bin     count   mean p_hat   empirical      gap     gap/SE")
    ece, worst_z = 0.0, 0.0
    for b in range(10):
        m = idx == b
        cnt, pm, fm = int(m.sum()), float(p[m].mean()), float(y[m].mean())
        se = np.sqrt(max(pm * (1 - pm), 1e-12) / cnt)
        z = abs(fm - pm) / se
        ece += cnt / n * abs(fm - pm)
        worst_z = max(worst_z, z)
        print(f"     {b:>2d}   {cnt:>6d}    {pm:9.5f}   {fm:9.5f}  {fm-pm:+8.5f}   {z:6.2f}")
    print(f"  ECE (10 equal-mass bins) = {ece:.5f};  worst bin |gap|/SE = {worst_z:.2f}")

    # A deliberately miscalibrated model: shrink the logits (over-regularized => under-confident).
    p_bad = sigmoid(0.4 * (X @ w_hat))
    idxb = np.digitize(p_bad, np.quantile(p_bad, np.linspace(0, 1, 11))[1:-1])
    ece_bad = sum(np.mean(idxb == b) * abs(y[idxb == b].mean() - p_bad[idxb == b].mean()) for b in range(10))
    print(f"  ECE of the same model with logits scaled by 0.4 = {ece_bad:.5f}  ({ece_bad/ece:.1f}x worse)")
    assert ece < 0.01 and worst_z < 4.0 and ece_bad > 10 * ece


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=" * 78)
    print("[1] gradient and Hessian vs central finite differences")
    check_derivatives()
    print("\n[2] IRLS vs gradient descent vs sklearn (matched regularization lam = 1/C)")
    check_against_sklearn()
    print("\n[3] separable data: norm diverges, direction converges to max margin")
    separable_run()
    print("\n[4] calibration of a well-specified logistic model (n = 20000)")
    calibration()
    print("\nall assertions passed")
    print("=" * 78)

Running it prints, in order: max |analytic grad - central FD| = 9.512e-10 and max |analytic Hess - central FD| = 6.645e-10, both at step $h = 10^{-5}$, with the Hessian's minimum eigenvalue $21.433852 > 0$ confirming strict convexity on that design. IRLS converges in $6$ Newton steps to a final squared Newton decrement of $8.706\times10^{-22}$ and a gradient norm of $8.477\times10^{-15}$; gradient descent lands on the identical answer to $2.220\times10^{-16}$ in the infinity norm, and sklearn agrees to $1.653\times10^{-9}$, with both objectives printing $253.694627461$. On the separable set the hard-margin direction is $(0.848672, -0.528919)$ with margin $0.358562$ supported by $2$ points, and gradient descent walks $\|w\| = 6.342 \to 11.133 \to 16.975 \to 23.129$ across steps $10^3$ to $10^6$ while the angle gap $1 - \cos$ falls $6.037\times10^{-3} \to 1.639\times10^{-3} \to 3.661\times10^{-4} \to 1.006\times10^{-4}$; the measured $d\|w\|/d\log t = 2.673$ against the predicted $1/m^{\star} = 2.789$. The loss at $10^6$ steps is $6.332\times10^{-4}$ and still falling like $1/t$. The calibration table shows the worst decile off by $1.46$ standard errors, $\mathrm{ECE} = 0.00447$, rising to $0.13554$ under the $0.4\times$ logit scaling.

Under Encryption

The linear part of logistic regression is the one thing homomorphic encryption does well. Under CKKS, $Xw$ with a plaintext model and encrypted features (or the reverse) is one ciphertext–plaintext multiplication plus a rotate-and-sum reduction, consuming exactly one level of multiplicative depth, and SIMD packing puts thousands of slots in one ciphertext, so a batch costs roughly what one record costs. This is why encrypted logistic regression on genomic and clinical data — the iDASH secure-genome-analysis track, and the encrypted GWAS pipelines built on HEAAN and SEAL — is the most mature real deployment of FHE in machine learning, not a toy. Likely

The sigmoid is the entire problem. $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ is neither polynomial nor rational in a way CKKS can evaluate; it requires a division and a transcendental. The standard move is a low-degree polynomial approximation on a bounded domain, and the accuracy is worse than the literature's summaries suggest. The degree-3 least-squares fit that the CKKS logistic-regression work standardized on, $\sigma(z) \approx 0.5 + 0.15012\,z - 0.001593\,z^3$ on $z \in [-8,8]$ (Kim et al., 2018), has maximum error $0.114$ and RMS error $0.060$ — roughly $10^{-1}$, not $10^{-2}$. Raising the degree pays slowly: degree $7$ reaches $0.032$, degree $15$ reaches $2.1\times10^{-3}$. Narrowing the window is the better lever — the same degree-3 fit on $[-4,4]$ has maximum error $0.038$, a $3\times$ gain for no extra depth. Depth is $\lceil \log_2(\deg+1)\rceil$ levels, so $2$ for degree 3 and $3$ for degree 7, but only under a balanced Paterson–Stockmeyer schedule; plain Horner chains the multiplications and burns $3$ levels on the degree-3 polynomial for the identical answer. Every one of those levels is scarce: the budget is fixed at key generation, and refreshing it means bootstrapping, which for CKKS costs seconds per ciphertext rather than milliseconds. Verify

What makes the approximation safe is the linear predictor's boundedness. If features are standardized and $\|w\|$ is controlled — which ridge does, and which Section 6.4 says is exactly what fails on separable data — then $|z| \le \|x\|\|w\|$ stays inside the window with high probability. Outside it a degree-3 fit does not merely lose accuracy: the cubic term takes over and it runs off to $\pm\infty$ with the wrong sign. The fit above returns $-0.45$ at $z = 12$, where the truth is $0.99999$ — a confident positive read as a confident negative — and because the computation is encrypted nothing downstream can detect it. That is the pattern Part VIII generalizes — keep the linear algebra exact, approximate the nonlinearity, control the input range so the approximation stays valid. Chapter 39 takes up the approximation problem in detail, and Chapter 38 shows what breaks when the same recipe is aimed at softmax and layer normalization rather than a single sigmoid.

Key Takeaways
  • Squared loss is the Gaussian likelihood and cross-entropy is the Bernoulli likelihood; the loss is never the design choice, the response distribution and link are. Certain
  • Every canonical-link GLM has gradient $X^{\top}(\mu - y)$ — prediction minus target, back-projected through the inputs — which is why the last layer of every classifier in this book has the same backward pass. Certain
  • Ridge is MAP under $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2 I)$ with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$, and in the SVD basis it shrinks direction $j$ by $s_j^2/(s_j^2+\lambda)$; the effective degrees of freedom is the sum of those factors. Certain
  • On separable data the unregularized logistic minimizer does not exist, $\|w\|$ grows like $\log t$, and the direction converges to the max-margin separator at the glacial worst-case rate $O(1/\log t)$ — measured here as a cosine gap falling only $60\times$ across three decades of steps. Likely
  • MLE with an intercept is calibrated in-sample by algebra alone, so calibration claims mean nothing off held-out data; regularization and shrunk logits break calibration without touching accuracy, which is why temperature scaling works. Certain
Chapter 7

Kernels, Margins, and the Bridge to Infinite-Width Networks

Learning Objectives
  • State Mercer's theorem and the representer theorem, and explain why together they collapse an infinite-dimensional optimization onto $n$ coefficients — what makes the dual tractable.
  • Derive the hard-margin and soft-margin SVM duals from the Lagrangian, and identify support vectors as exactly the training points whose KKT inequality constraints are active.
  • Explain the $\Theta(n^2d)$ Gram construction and $\Theta(n^3)$ exact solve, and compute the sample count $n^\star$ at which an $N$-parameter model trained by SGD becomes cheaper.
  • Derive the Neural Tangent Kernel of a two-layer ReLU network and state precisely where it holds — infinite width, lazy training, bounded learning rate — and where it fails.
  • Implement SMO and an empirical NTK in working code, verifying both against reference implementations.
Read alongside — Bishop, PRML, for the cleanest treatment of kernels, RKHS, and the SVM dual including the sparsity argument. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, ESL, for the complementary view of the SVM as penalized hinge-loss regression, the framing that ties this chapter to Chapter 6. Murphy, Advanced Topics, for the Gaussian-process side of the same mathematics and the infinite-width limits.

Chapter 6 established that a linear model is fully determined by inner products of feature vectors, and that logistic regression is convex because its loss is. This chapter takes both facts seriously. If only inner products matter, the feature map need never be built: it can be specified implicitly by a kernel, and the resulting optimization stays convex and finite-dimensional no matter how large the implicit feature space is. That is the classical story, and it ends badly — the cost of an exact solve grows as the cube of the sample count, which is why kernel machines lost to neural networks somewhere around $10^4$–$10^5$ examples. The story then restarts. An infinitely wide network trained with small steps from a random initialization is a kernel machine, with a kernel determined by the architecture. Chapters 10 and 15 return to what finite width buys; Chapter 24 uses the same flop accounting used in Section 7.5.

7.1 Feature Maps and the Kernel Trick

A linear predictor separates only what is linearly separable. The standard repair is a feature map $\phi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{F}$ and a linear predictor $f(x)=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle + b$ there. Taken literally the repair is ruinous: for degree-$p$ polynomial features on $d$ inputs, $\dim\mathcal{F} = \binom{d+p}{p}$, which at $d=100$, $p=5$ is $96{,}560{,}646$ coordinates. What rescues it is that most linear methods touch the data only through inner products $\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle$; if that scalar has a closed form computable in the input dimension, $\phi$ need never be materialized.

Definition 7.1 (Positive semi-definite kernel)

A symmetric function $k : \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a positive semi-definite kernel if for every finite set $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in \mathcal{X}$ the Gram matrix $K$ with $K_{ij} = k(x_i,x_j)$ satisfies $c^\top K c \ge 0$ for all $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$. Equivalently — and this equivalence is the content of Section 7.2 — there is a Hilbert space $\mathcal{F}$ and a map $\phi$ with $k(x,z) = \langle \phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal{F}}$.

Example 7.1 (The quadratic kernel, computed both ways)

Take $d = 2$, $k(x,z) = (\langle x,z\rangle + 1)^2$, and the explicit map $\phi(x) = (1,\ \sqrt2 x_1,\ \sqrt2 x_2,\ x_1^2,\ \sqrt2 x_1x_2,\ x_2^2)$. With $x = (1,2)$ and $z = (3,-1)$: $\langle x,z\rangle = 3 - 2 = 1$, so $k(x,z) = (1+1)^2 = 4$. The explicit route gives $\phi(x) = (1, \sqrt2, 2\sqrt2, 1, 2\sqrt2, 4)$ and $\phi(z) = (1, 3\sqrt2, -\sqrt2, 9, -3\sqrt2, 1)$, whose inner product is $1 + 6 - 4 + 9 - 12 + 4 = 4$. Same number. The kernel route used $3$ multiply-adds, the explicit route about $18$. At $d=100$, $p=5$ it is $101$ operations against $9.7\times10^7$ — a factor of $10^6$, with no allocation.

The RBF kernel $k(x,z) = \exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$ pushes this to the limit: its feature space is infinite-dimensional (expand the exponential of the cross term as a power series, and every polynomial degree appears with a positive coefficient), yet each entry costs $O(d)$. An algorithm expressed purely in Gram-matrix terms therefore runs in an infinite-dimensional feature space at finite cost. Certain

7.2 RKHS, Mercer, and the Representer Theorem

Two results turn the trick into a method. Mercer's theorem says the implicit feature space exists; the representer theorem says the optimization over it is finite-dimensional.

Definition 7.2 (Reproducing kernel Hilbert space)

A Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of functions $\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ is an RKHS with kernel $k$ if $k(\cdot,x)\in\mathcal{H}$ for every $x$ and the reproducing property $f(x) = \langle f, k(\cdot,x)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$ holds for all $f\in\mathcal{H}$. Setting $f = k(\cdot,z)$ recovers $\langle k(\cdot,z),k(\cdot,x)\rangle = k(x,z)$, so $\phi(x)=k(\cdot,x)$ is a feature map. Pointwise evaluation is a bounded functional here — the property $L^2$ lacks, and the one that makes interpolation constraints meaningful.

Theorem 7.1 (Mercer)

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be compact and $k$ continuous, symmetric, and positive semi-definite. Define the integral operator $(T_k f)(x) = \int_{\mathcal{X}} k(x,z) f(z)\,d\mu(z)$ on $L^2(\mu)$. Then $T_k$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $\{\psi_i\}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i \ge 0$, and $k(x,z) = \sum_{i\ge1} \lambda_i \psi_i(x)\psi_i(z)$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}$.

Proof sketch. Continuity on a compact set makes $k$ square-integrable, so $T_k$ is Hilbert–Schmidt, hence compact; symmetry makes it self-adjoint. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators gives the eigenbasis and a spectrum accumulating only at $0$. Positive semi-definiteness of the Gram matrices forces $\lambda_i = \langle \psi_i, T_k\psi_i\rangle \ge 0$: approximate the integral by Riemann sums, each of which is a quadratic form $c^\top K c \ge 0$. The partial sums $k_M(x,z) = \sum_{i\le M}\lambda_i\psi_i(x)\psi_i(z)$ are continuous, increase monotonically on the diagonal, and converge pointwise to the continuous limit $k(x,x)$, so Dini's theorem upgrades diagonal convergence to uniform; Cauchy–Schwarz then transfers uniformity off the diagonal. Taking $\phi(x) = (\sqrt{\lambda_i}\,\psi_i(x))_{i\ge1}$ gives $k(x,z) = \langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\ell^2}$. $\blacksquare$

Mercer supplies the space. It does not by itself help, because $w \in \mathcal{F}$ may have infinitely many coordinates. The representer theorem removes that problem completely.

Theorem 7.2 (Representer theorem, Schölkopf–Herbrich–Smola form)

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the RKHS of $k$, let $\mathcal{L}$ be any loss depending on $f$ only through the values $f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n)$, and let $\Omega:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be strictly increasing. Then every minimizer of $$J(f) \;=\; \mathcal{L}\big(y_1,\ldots,y_n,\, f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_n)\big) \;+\; \Omega\big(\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}\big)$$ admits the representation $f^\star(\cdot) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\, k(\cdot,x_i)$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Proof. Let $\mathcal{S} = \mathrm{span}\{k(\cdot,x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ and decompose any $f\in\mathcal{H}$ orthogonally as $f = f_\parallel + f_\perp$ with $f_\parallel\in\mathcal{S}$ and $f_\perp \perp \mathcal{S}$. By the reproducing property, for each training point $f(x_i) = \langle f, k(\cdot,x_i)\rangle = \langle f_\parallel, k(\cdot,x_i)\rangle + 0 = f_\parallel(x_i)$. So $\mathcal{L}$ is blind to $f_\perp$. By Pythagoras $\|f\|^2 = \|f_\parallel\|^2 + \|f_\perp\|^2 \ge \|f_\parallel\|^2$, with equality iff $f_\perp = 0$, and $\Omega$ strictly increasing turns this into $\Omega(\|f\|) \ge \Omega(\|f_\parallel\|)$ with equality iff $f_\perp = 0$. Hence $J(f_\parallel) \le J(f)$, strictly unless $f_\perp = 0$. Any minimizer therefore has $f_\perp = 0$. $\blacksquare$

Together: Mercer supplies a feature space of arbitrary dimension, and the representer theorem confines the optimum to an $n$-dimensional slice of it. Every kernel algorithm here is an instance — SVMs, kernel ridge regression, kernel PCA (Chapter 9), Gaussian processes. The price is in the theorem itself: the solution has $n$ parameters, not $d$. Section 7.5 collects the bill. Certain

7.3 Maximum-Margin Classification

For a separating hyperplane $\{x:\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle + b = 0\}$, the signed distance from $\phi(x_i)$ is $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)/\|w\|$: numerator the functional margin, ratio the geometric margin. Rescaling $(w,b)$ inflates the functional margin while changing nothing geometrically, so fix the scale by $\min_i y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)=1$. The geometric margin is then $1/\|w\|$ and the slab has width $2/\|w\|$, so margin maximization is

$$\min_{w,b}\ \tfrac12\|w\|^2 \quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle + b) \ge 1,\quad i=1,\ldots,n.$$

This is the hard-margin problem: a convex quadratic objective with linear constraints, infeasible the moment the data are not separable in $\mathcal{F}$. Introducing slacks $\xi_i \ge 0$ and paying $C$ per unit of violation gives the soft-margin problem of Cortes and Vapnik (1995), which is what “SVM” has meant ever since

$$\min_{w,b,\xi}\ \tfrac12\|w\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^n \xi_i \quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle + b) \ge 1-\xi_i,\ \ \xi_i\ge0.$$

At the optimum $\xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i))$, so the soft-margin SVM is exactly hinge-loss empirical risk minimization with an $\ell_2$ penalty: $\min_f \sum_i \max(0,1-y_if(x_i)) + \tfrac{1}{2C}\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2$. That is a representer-theorem objective with $\Omega(t)=t^2/2C$, so Theorem 7.2 already guarantees $f^\star = \sum_i c_i k(\cdot,x_i)$. The dual derivation below identifies the $c_i$ and, crucially, shows most of them are zero.

7.3.1 The Dual and KKT Conditions

Attach multipliers $\alpha_i \ge 0$ to the margin constraints and $\mu_i \ge 0$ to $\xi_i \ge 0$, and write $\Lambda$ for the Lagrangian ($\mathcal{L}$ stays reserved for losses):

$$\Lambda = \tfrac12\|w\|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i - \sum_i \alpha_i\big[y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b) - 1 + \xi_i\big] - \sum_i \mu_i\xi_i.$$

Stationarity in the primal variables gives three identities. From $\partial\Lambda/\partial w = w - \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\phi(x_i) = 0$ we get $w = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \phi(x_i)$ — the representer expansion, derived rather than assumed, with $c_i = \alpha_i y_i$. From $\partial\Lambda/\partial b = -\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0$ we get the equality constraint $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0$. From $\partial\Lambda/\partial\xi_i = C - \alpha_i - \mu_i = 0$ together with $\mu_i \ge 0$ we get the box $0 \le \alpha_i \le C$, and the $\xi$ terms cancel out of $\Lambda$ entirely.

Substituting $w = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\phi(x_i)$: the quadratic term becomes $\tfrac12\sum_{ij}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$, the term $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle$ becomes $\sum_{ij}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$, the $b$ term vanishes by $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$, and $\tfrac12 Q - Q = -\tfrac12 Q$ leaves

$$\max_{\alpha}\ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_iy_j\,k(x_i,x_j)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0,\ \ 0\le\alpha_i\le C.$$

The Hessian is $Q = (yy^\top)\odot K$, positive semi-definite because $K$ is, so this is a convex QP in $n$ variables; the constraints are affine, so Slater's condition holds and strong duality gives zero duality gap. The learned function is $f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i k(x_i,x) + b$ — the data enter only through kernel evaluations, exactly as promised.

Theorem 7.3 (Support vectors are the active constraints)

At any primal-dual optimum of the soft-margin problem, with $r_i = y_i f(x_i)$ the functional margin: $\alpha_i = 0 \implies r_i \ge 1$ and, conversely, $r_i > 1 \implies \alpha_i = 0$ (a point strictly outside the margin is irrelevant to $f$); $0 < \alpha_i < C \implies r_i = 1$ (a free support vector, sitting exactly on the margin); $\alpha_i = C \implies r_i \le 1$ (a bounded support vector, inside the margin or misclassified). The first line is deliberately not a biconditional: $r_i = 1$ is compatible with any $\alpha_i\in[0,C]$, so a point sitting exactly on the margin may or may not be a support vector, and degenerate problems have optima with $\alpha_i=0$ at $r_i=1$.

Proof. Complementary slackness gives $\alpha_i(r_i - 1 + \xi_i) = 0$ and $\mu_i\xi_i = 0$ with $\mu_i = C-\alpha_i$. If $\alpha_i < C$ then $\mu_i > 0$, so $\xi_i = 0$; primal feasibility then reads $r_i\ge1$, and if additionally $\alpha_i>0$ the first condition forces $r_i = 1$. If $\alpha_i = 0$ then $w$ does not involve $\phi(x_i)$ and $\xi_i=0$, so $r_i\ge1$; conversely $r_i>1$ with $\xi_i = 0$ makes the bracket strictly positive, forcing $\alpha_i=0$. If $\alpha_i = C$ then $\mu_i=0$ leaves $\xi_i\ge0$ free and the first condition gives $r_i = 1-\xi_i \le 1$. $\blacksquare$

This is the sparsity that made SVMs practical, and the source of every subtlety in solvers. Because $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0$, no single $\alpha_i$ can move while staying feasible, so the smallest working set has size two. Sequential Minimal Optimization (Platt, 1998) exploits this: pick a pair $(i,j)$, solve the resulting one-dimensional problem along $\alpha_iy_i+\alpha_jy_j=\text{const}$ analytically, repeat. With $E_i=f(x_i)-y_i$ computed without the bias, Theorem 7.3 is equivalent to $\max_{i\in I_{\text{low}}}E_i \le \min_{i\in I_{\text{up}}}E_i$, over the index sets of $\alpha_i$ free to decrease and to increase the corresponding margin. Selecting the pair that maximally violates this — Keerthi's rule, LIBSVM's WSS1 — makes each step the steepest feasible descent direction among those with only two nonzero components. LIBSVM's default is the second-order rule WSS2, which keeps the same $I_{\text{up}}$ index for the pair but picks the partner maximizing the modelled objective decrease $(b_{\text{low}}-b_{\text{up}})^2/\eta_{ij}$ rather than the violation alone; it costs one extra pass over a row and typically cuts the iteration count. Verify The artifact implements WSS1 and converges in $156$ iterations on $120$ points.

Example 7.2 (A three-point SVM solved by hand)

Take $x_1=(1,1),y_1=+1$; $x_2=(-1,-1),y_2=-1$; $x_3=(2,2),y_3=+1$, linear kernel, $C=10$ (large enough to be effectively hard-margin). Guess $\alpha_3=0$ and verify afterwards. The equality constraint forces $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha$. The Gram entries are $k_{11}=k_{22}=2$, $k_{12}=-2$, so $Q_{11}=Q_{22}=2$ and $Q_{12}=y_1y_2k_{12}=(+1)(-1)(-2)=2$. The dual becomes $2\alpha - \tfrac12(2\alpha^2+2\alpha^2+2\cdot2\alpha^2) = 2\alpha - 4\alpha^2$, maximized at $\alpha=1/4$ with value $1/4$. Then $w=\tfrac14(1,1)-\tfrac14(-1,-1)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $\|w\|=1/\sqrt2$, margin $2/\|w\|=2\sqrt2\approx2.828427$ — precisely the distance between $x_1$ and $x_2$, as it must be. From $y_1(\langle w,x_1\rangle+b)=1$: $\tfrac12+\tfrac12+b=1$, so $b=0$. Checking the guess, $r_3 = 1\cdot(1+1+0) = 2 > 1$, so constraint 3 is inactive and $\alpha_3=0$ is consistent. The artifact reproduces $\alpha=(0.25,0.25,0)$, $w=(0.5,0.5)$, $b=0$ in two SMO iterations.

Common Pitfall

Recovering the bias by averaging $-E_i$ over all support vectors. Only free support vectors ($0<\alpha_i<C$) satisfy $y_if(x_i)=1$; bounded ones ($\alpha_i=C$) satisfy $y_if(x_i)\le1$, and averaging over them drags $b$ toward the majority of the misclassified points. This bug never raises an exception and never breaks the dual objective — only accuracy, by a few points, and only on noisy datasets. It is easy to underestimate how common bounded support vectors are: in the artifact's $n=120$, $C=1$ RBF problem, $46$ of the $52$ support vectors sit at the bound, so the buggy average is $88\%$ contaminated. The correct recovery uses only free support vectors, or the LIBSVM fallback $b = -\tfrac12(b_{\text{up}}+b_{\text{low}})$ when none are free. Certain

7.4 Kernel Ridge Regression

The same machinery with a squared loss produces a closed form rather than a QP, which makes it the cleanest object to reason about in Section 7.6. Minimize $\|\Phi w - y\|^2 + \lambda\|w\|^2$, where $\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ stacks the feature vectors. The normal equations give $w^\star=(\Phi^\top\Phi+\lambda I_p)^{-1}\Phi^\top y$, which is useless when $p$ is infinite. The push-through identity fixes it: since

$$\Phi^\top(\Phi\Phi^\top+\lambda I_n) \;=\; \Phi^\top\Phi\Phi^\top+\lambda\Phi^\top \;=\; (\Phi^\top\Phi+\lambda I_p)\Phi^\top,$$

left-multiplying by $(\Phi^\top\Phi+\lambda I_p)^{-1}$ and right-multiplying by $(\Phi\Phi^\top+\lambda I_n)^{-1}$ yields $(\Phi^\top\Phi+\lambda I_p)^{-1}\Phi^\top=\Phi^\top(\Phi\Phi^\top+\lambda I_n)^{-1}$. Hence $w^\star=\Phi^\top\alpha$ with $\alpha=(K+\lambda I_n)^{-1}y$ and $K=\Phi\Phi^\top$, so

$$f(x) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\, k(x_i,x), \qquad \alpha = (K+\lambda I)^{-1} y.$$

Both inverses exist for $\lambda>0$; the choice between the forms is purely computational, $O(p^3)$ against $O(n^3)$, so kernelize when $p>n$. Numerically, $\lambda$ shifts the whole spectrum of $K$ up, bounding the condition number by $(\lambda_{\max}+\lambda)/\lambda$ — which is why an unregularized interpolant on a smooth kernel is essentially unsolvable in double precision.

Example 7.3 (Kernel ridge in two points)

Scalar inputs $x_1=1$, $x_2=-1$, targets $y=(1,-1)$, linear kernel, $\lambda=1$. Then $K=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $K+I=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose inverse is $\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. So $\alpha=\tfrac13(2-1,\,1-2)=(\tfrac13,-\tfrac13)$ and $f(x)=\tfrac13 x - \tfrac13(-x)=\tfrac23 x$. The primal route: $\Phi^\top\Phi=2$, $\Phi^\top y=1\cdot1+(-1)(-1)=2$, so $w=2/(2+1)=2/3$. Identical, as the push-through identity requires.

Common Pitfall

Building the RBF Gram matrix from the expanded square $\|x-z\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|z\|^2-2\langle x,z\rangle$ and feeding the result straight to exp or sqrt. Cancellation makes the diagonal and near-duplicate pairs come out slightly negative, by roughly $\varepsilon_{\text{mach}}\|x\|^2$: about $-10^{-16}$ in float64 and $-10^{-7}$ in float32 for unit-norm inputs, and proportionally worse for larger-scale data — at $\|x\|^2\approx50$ the measured float32 minimum is $-5.3\times10^{-5}$. Kernel entries then exceed $1$ (I measure $1.0000268$ at $\gamma=0.5$), the Gram matrix loses positive semi-definiteness, and numpy.linalg.cholesky raises LinAlgError on a matrix that is mathematically PSD. The usual "fix" is a large diagonal jitter, which silently changes the model; the actual fix is one clamp, np.maximum(d2, 0.0). The float32 effect is severe enough that GP libraries keep Gram matrices in float64 regardless of model dtype. Certain

7.5 Scaling Limits of Kernel Methods

The representer theorem is a promise and a sentence. Because the solution is parameterized by the training set, every cost is tied to $n$:

StageTimeMemory
Form the Gram matrix$\Theta(n^2 d)$$8n^2$ bytes (float64)
Exact solve (Cholesky / LU)$\tfrac13 n^3$ – $\tfrac23 n^3$ flopsin place
SVM training by SMOempirically $n^2$ – $n^3$$O(n^2)$ cached, or recompute
One prediction$O(n_{\text{SV}}\, d)$$O(n_{\text{SV}}\, d)$

The memory row alone is decisive: the Gram matrix is $800$ MB at $n=10^4$, $80$ GB at $n=10^5$, and $7.3$ TiB at $n=10^6$, where the exact solve is $0.67$ EFLOP. No engineering makes a dense $O(n^2)$ object usable at web scale.

The prediction row is the underappreciated one. Steinwart's result says support-vector counts grow asymptotically linearly in $n$ on a noisy problem, with slope twice the Bayes risk. Likely The artifact shows the trend: $237, 442, 817, 1400$ support vectors at $n=250,500,1000,2000$, a factor of $5.9$ across an $8\times$ data increase. So inference cost grows with the training set; a parametric model's does not. That asymmetry, not training time, is what makes kernels unshippable at scale.

The crossover against a parametric model is a two-line calculation. Exact kernel training costs roughly $\tfrac23 n^3 + 2n^2 d$ flops; training an $N$-parameter model for $E$ epochs by SGD costs about $6NnE$ flops, using the standard forward-plus-backward accounting of Chapter 24. Setting them equal and solving the resulting quadratic in $n$ gives, for $d=100$:

Parametric modelEpochs $E$Crossover $n^\star$Gram size at $n^\star$
$N=10^5$$100$$9.3\times10^3$$0.65$ GiB
$N=10^6$$100$$3.0\times10^4$$6.6$ GiB
$N=10^8$$10$$9.5\times10^4$$67$ GiB
$N=7\times10^9$$1$$2.5\times10^5$$469$ GiB

Read the last row carefully: past a quarter-million examples, exactly solving a kernel system costs more arithmetic than one pass of a 7-billion-parameter model over the same data. Dropping the $2n^2d$ term, which is negligible once $n \gg 3d$, leaves $(2/3)n^2 = 6NE$ and the rule of thumb $n^\star\approx 3\sqrt{NE}$ — within $2\%$ of every exact root in the table, and worth memorizing. Certain It also matches the historical record: SVMs dominated at $10^3$–$10^4$ examples and had lost the frontier by $10^5$–$10^6$. Likely

The escape routes all end in the same place. Nyström subsampling picks $r\ll n$ landmarks, $K \approx K_{nr}K_{rr}^{-1}K_{rn}$, costing $O(nr^2)$. Random Fourier features (Rahimi–Recht) sample $D$ frequencies with $\langle z(x),z(y)\rangle \approx k(x,y)$ to error $O(D^{-1/2})$, costing $O(nD)$. Each replaces the $n$ data-indexed coefficients with a fixed budget of $r$ or $D$ parameters: the fix for a kernel method's scaling is to turn it back into a parametric model.

Whether the accuracy ceiling is also lower is genuinely disputed. Contested One camp points to architecture-derived kernels — CNN-GP and Myrtle kernels reach roughly $90\%$ on CIFAR-10 Verify — and calls the gap small and shrinking. The other notes that those kernels encode convolutional structure by hand, and that no kernel is close on ImageNet or language modeling, where the representation must be discovered. The position here: kernels stay competitive exactly where the invariances can be written down in advance, and lose wherever features must be learned. What would settle it is a kernel matching a compute-matched network on a large-scale task with a kernel not derived from a hand-designed architecture; none exists.

7.6 The Neural Tangent Kernel

Now the reversal. Take any differentiable $f(x;\theta)$, $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^N$, under gradient flow on $\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12\sum_i(f(x_i;\theta)-y_i)^2$. Then $\dot\theta = -\sum_i(f_i-y_i)\nabla_\theta f_i$, and by the chain rule the function evolves as

$$\frac{d}{dt} f(x;\theta_t) \;=\; \langle\nabla_\theta f(x;\theta_t),\dot\theta_t\rangle \;=\; -\sum_{i=1}^n \big(f_i - y_i\big)\,\Theta_t(x,x_i),\qquad \Theta_t(x,x')=\langle\nabla_\theta f(x;\theta_t),\nabla_\theta f(x';\theta_t)\rangle.$$
Definition 7.3 (Neural Tangent Kernel)

$\Theta_t(x,x') = \langle\nabla_\theta f(x;\theta_t),\nabla_\theta f(x';\theta_t)\rangle$ is the Neural Tangent Kernel at time $t$. It is a PSD kernel at every $t$ and every width, being a Gram matrix of Jacobian rows. The nontrivial claim is that in a specific limit it is constant in $t$, in which case the display above is a linear ODE and training is kernel regression.

Theorem 7.4 (NTK of a two-layer ReLU network)

Let $f(x;\theta)=m^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^m a_i\,\mathrm{relu}(\langle w_i,x\rangle)$ with $w_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_d)$, $a_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, both layers trained, and $\|x\|=\|x'\|=1$. Write $u=\langle x,x'\rangle$ and $\vartheta=\arccos u$ for the angle between them (not the parameter vector $\theta$). Then at initialization $\Theta_0(x,x')\to\Theta_\infty(x,x')$ in probability as $m\to\infty$, with $$\Theta_\infty(x,x') \;=\; \tfrac12\kappa_1(u) + \tfrac12\kappa_0(u)\,u \;=\; \frac{\sin\vartheta + 2(\pi-\vartheta)\cos\vartheta}{2\pi},$$ where $\kappa_0(u)=(\pi-\vartheta)/\pi$ and $\kappa_1(u)=(\sin\vartheta+(\pi-\vartheta)u)/\pi$ are the arc-cosine kernels of degree $0$ and $1$. The fluctuation is $\|\Theta_0-\Theta_\infty\|_F = O_P(m^{-1/2})$.

Proof. The two parameter blocks contribute separately. Differentiating, $\partial f/\partial a_i = m^{-1/2}\mathrm{relu}(\langle w_i,x\rangle)$ and $\partial f/\partial w_i = m^{-1/2}a_i\mathbf{1}\{\langle w_i,x\rangle>0\}\,x$. Taking the inner product of the two Jacobians and grouping,

$$\Theta_0(x,x') = \underbrace{\frac1m\sum_i \mathrm{relu}(\langle w_i,x\rangle)\,\mathrm{relu}(\langle w_i,x'\rangle)}_{\text{output layer}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac1m\sum_i a_i^2\,\mathbf{1}\{\langle w_i,x\rangle>0\}\mathbf{1}\{\langle w_i,x'\rangle>0\}\,\langle x,x'\rangle}_{\text{hidden layer}}.$$

Each sum is an average of $m$ i.i.d. terms with finite variance, so the law of large numbers gives convergence to the expectations, and the central limit theorem gives the $m^{-1/2}$ rate. For the second expectation, only the two-dimensional projection of $w$ onto $\mathrm{span}\{x,x'\}$ matters, and its direction is uniform on the circle; the event that a uniform direction has positive inner product with both $x$ and $x'$ is a wedge of angular width $\pi-\vartheta$ out of $2\pi$, so $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}] = (\pi-\vartheta)/(2\pi) = \tfrac12\kappa_0(u)$, and $\mathbb{E}[a_i^2]=1$ factors out by independence. For the first, the standard arc-cosine integral gives $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{relu}(\langle w,x\rangle)\mathrm{relu}(\langle w,x'\rangle)] = \frac{1}{2\pi}(\sin\vartheta+(\pi-\vartheta)\cos\vartheta) = \tfrac12\kappa_1(u)$. Adding, with $\langle x,x'\rangle = \cos\vartheta$, gives $\frac{1}{2\pi}[\sin\vartheta + (\pi-\vartheta)\cos\vartheta] + \frac{\pi-\vartheta}{2\pi}\cos\vartheta$, which is the stated expression. Sanity check at $\vartheta=0$: $(0+2\pi)/(2\pi)=1$, and the artifact prints a diagonal of exactly $1.000000$. $\blacksquare$

The second half of the NTK theorem — that $\Theta_t$ stays at $\Theta_0$ throughout training — needs more, and the conditions matter more than the conclusion. The $m^{-1/2}$ prefactor makes $\nabla_\theta f$ have $O(1)$ norm while each gradient coordinate is $O(m^{-1/2})$, so over a fixed-length run the parameters move a relative distance $O(m^{-1/2})$ and the Jacobian barely rotates. Making this rigorous (Jacot et al. 2018; Du et al. 2019; Arora et al. 2019) requires infinite width taken with $n$ and the horizon $T$ fixed; the NTK parameterization or an equivalent small-initialization scaling; a learning rate bounded by roughly $2/\lambda_{\max}(\Theta_\infty)$ so descent tracks flow; and, at finite width, $m$ polynomial in $n$ — early bounds needed $m \gtrsim n^6$, which describes no network anyone trains. Certain Under those conditions the dynamics reduce to kernel ridgeless regression: the Section 7.4 formula with $\lambda\to0$ and $K=\Theta_\infty$.

7.6.1 Lazy Training versus Feature Learning

Chizat, Oyallon and Bach isolated the mechanism and showed it is not about neural networks at all. Replace $f$ by $\alpha f$ and rescale the learning rate by $\alpha^{-2}$; as $\alpha\to\infty$ any differentiable model linearizes about its initialization, with relative kernel movement $\|\Theta_T-\Theta_0\|/\|\Theta_0\| = O(1/\alpha)$. Infinite width is one way to reach large effective $\alpha$, not the only one, and nothing about depth or nonlinearity is involved. The honest statement is therefore: lazy training is a scaling regime, and the NTK parameterization is the choice that puts an infinitely wide network into it. Certain

A different parameterization escapes it. Yang and Hu's maximal-update parameterization ($\mu$P) scales initialization and per-layer learning rates so features change by $\Theta(1)$ even as $m\to\infty$: infinite width with feature learning. Chapter 15 develops $\mu$P as the practical hyperparameter-transfer tool, but its theoretical role belongs here — the kernel limit is an artifact of a parameterization choice, not a consequence of width. Likely

The failures are measurable. Infinite-width kernels underperform the finite networks they come from: the convolutional NTK reaches about $77\%$ on CIFAR-10 against roughly $83\%$ for the corresponding finite CNN, and about $90\%$ for the best hand-engineered neural kernels. Verify The kernel also does not stay put — measure $\|\Theta_T-\Theta_0\|_F/\|\Theta_0\|_F$ during any realistic run at a practical learning rate and it is $O(1)$, not $O(m^{-1/2})$. Large learning rates, edge-of-stability dynamics (Chapter 4), normalization, and long training all push further out of the lazy regime. The phenomena that define modern deep learning — transferable representations, induction heads (Chapter 18), emergent interpretable features (Chapter 37) — are all statements that the feature map moved, and a kernel machine's feature map is fixed by definition.

So: infinite width plus lazy training gives a kernel machine, with the Section 7.5 costs and a frozen representation. Finite width with a learning rate large enough to move the kernel gives something with no closed form — and that is where every empirical gain of the last decade lives. Use the NTK as an instrument, not a theory: the empirical NTK at a checkpoint is the right object for influence functions and data attribution, for the near-lazy fine-tuning regime that LoRA (Chapter 26) partly occupies, and for diagnosing whether a run is learning features or merely fitting.

Artifact 7.1 — SMO from Scratch and the Empirical NTK

Four checks in one file, NumPy doing all the real work. An SMO solver with maximal-violating-pair selection solves the soft-margin dual, checked first against Example 7.2 and then against sklearn.svm.SVC on 120 RBF points — dual objectives, support-vector index sets, decision values on 400 fresh points, and Theorem 7.3's KKT conditions evaluated directly at the returned solution. The scaling section fits SMO's iteration and kernel-evaluation counts against $n$ and solves the Section 7.5 crossover exactly. The last section builds the empirical NTK as a literal Jacobian outer product $JJ^\top$, cross-checks the closed-form Jacobian against torch.autograd, and fits the convergence rate to Theorem 7.4.

"""
Artifact 7.1 -- SMO for the SVM dual, the scaling wall, and the empirical NTK.
Core is pure NumPy; sklearn and torch appear only as cross-checks.
  (1) SMO on a 3-point hand-solvable linear problem recovers alpha = (1/4, 1/4, 0);
  (2) SMO on 120 points with an RBF kernel matches sklearn.svm.SVC, and the KKT
      conditions are checked directly at the returned alpha;
  (3) SMO's iteration and kernel-evaluation counts are fitted against n, and the
      flop crossover against an N-parameter SGD model is solved exactly;
  (4) the empirical NTK of a width-m two-layer ReLU net, formed as the Jacobian
      outer product J J^T, converges to the arc-cosine limit at rate ~ m^-1/2.
Runtime ~1.5 s on CPU.
"""

import time
import numpy as np

try:
    from sklearn.svm import SVC
except ImportError:                      # cross-check only
    SVC = None
try:
    import torch
except ImportError:                      # cross-check only
    torch = None

# --- 1. Kernels --------------------------------------------------------------

def k_rbf(A, B, gamma):
    """exp(-gamma ||a-b||^2) via the expanded square; clamp to kill -1e-16 distances."""
    d2 = (A * A).sum(1)[:, None] + (B * B).sum(1)[None, :] - 2.0 * A @ B.T
    return np.exp(-gamma * np.maximum(d2, 0.0))

def k_linear(A, B):
    return A @ B.T

# --- 2. SMO for the soft-margin dual ----------------------------------------
# maximize  sum_i a_i - 1/2 sum_ij a_i a_j y_i y_j K_ij   s.t. sum_i a_i y_i = 0,
# 0 <= a_i <= C.  Working-set selection is the maximal-violating-pair rule
# (Keerthi/LIBSVM WSS1): with f_i = sum_j a_j y_j K_ij and E_i = f_i - y_i, the
# KKT system is equivalent to  max_{i in I_low} E_i  <=  min_{i in I_up} E_i.

def smo(K, y, C, tol=1e-10, max_iter=100_000):
