  • Explain the LSTM constant-error carousel and prove that along the cell-state path the gradient multiplier is exactly the forget gate: $\partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t)$.
  • Compare LSTM and GRU parameter counts — $4(d_h d_{\text{in}} + d_h^2 + d_h)$ against $3(d_h d_{\text{in}} + d_h^2 + d_h)$ — and state the empirical verdict on when the $25\%$ difference matters.
  • Quantify the parallelism deficit: $\Theta(T)$ sequential operations for recurrence against $\Theta(1)$ for attention, and convert that into a measured hardware-utilization gap.
  • Implement an LSTM cell with backpropagation through time in working code, verified against torch.nn.LSTM and instrumented to measure gradient decay.
Read alongside — Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning, for the canonical treatment of BPTT, the vanishing-gradient analysis, and echo-state initialization; its sequence-modeling material is the reference derivation for Sections 17.2–17.4. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, for the clearest gate diagrams. Chakraborty, Introduction to Large Language Models (and the NPTEL lectures), for how seq2seq with attention became the Transformer — Section 17.7 compresses that arc.

A recurrent network is a loop with a learned body: it carries a fixed-size state forward, updates it once per token, and reads outputs off the state, processing a length-$T$ sequence in $O(T)$ time and, at inference, $O(1)$ memory — a good algorithmic profile that made recurrence the default for sequences from 1990 to 2017. Two things then went wrong, and only one is the famous one. The gradient pathology of Section 17.3 is real and is largely fixed by the gating of Section 17.4; the architecture that replaced recurrence won because the update is sequential in $T$ and a GPU is a machine for doing $10^5$ things at once. Chapter 16 built spatial locality into the architecture; this chapter builds temporal locality and measures what it costs. Chapter 18 removes the loop, and Chapter 21 puts a version of it back after first making it associative — exactly the property Theorem 17.4 identifies as the missing one.

17.1 Sequence Modeling and State

A sequence model maps a variable-length prefix to a prediction, and there are three structural choices: read a fixed window (Chapter 16's convolution over time), read everything with pairwise interactions (Chapter 18's attention), or compress the prefix into a fixed-size summary and update it incrementally. The third is recurrence; its defining commitment is that the summary has bounded size.

Definition 17.1 (Recurrent map)

A recurrent model is a pair of maps $h_t = \varphi_\theta(h_{t-1}, x_t)$ and $\hat{y}_t = \psi_\theta(h_t)$, with $h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}$ the state, $h_0$ given, and $\theta$ shared across all $t$. The state is a sufficient statistic under the model: $\hat{y}_t$ depends on $x_{1:t}$ only through $h_t$.

Three consequences follow, none about gradients. Parameter count is independent of $T$, so the model applies at lengths it never saw in training. Inference is $O(1)$ per token in time and memory, which is why an RNN decoder needs no KV cache and a Transformer decoder does (Chapter 33). And the bounded state is a hard information bottleneck: whatever must survive from step $t$ to step $T$ must fit in $d_h$ real numbers. At $d_h = 1024$ in fp32 that is 4 KB for the whole history, against a Transformer's $2 \cdot 1024 \cdot 4 = 8$ KB of KV cache per token, per layer. That bottleneck is the price of the $O(1)$ inference, and Section 17.7 is the story of the field deciding, in 2014, that it was not worth paying. Certain

17.2 The Vanilla RNN and BPTT

Definition 17.2 (Elman RNN)

$h_t = \tanh(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)$ with $W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_h}$, $W_x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d_{\text{in}}}$. Write $a_t = W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b$ for the pre-activation and $D_t = \mathrm{diag}(1 - h_t \odot h_t) = \mathrm{diag}(\tanh'(a_t))$.

Training unrolls the loop into a feedforward network of depth $T$ with tied weights and applies reverse-mode autodiff (Chapter 11). That is all "backpropagation through time" means; the only structural novelty is weight tying, which turns one parameter into $T$ uses and therefore makes the parameter gradient a sum over uses.

Theorem 17.1 (BPTT gradient decomposition)

Let $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{t=1}^T \ell_t(h_t)$. Then $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_h} \;=\; \sum_{t=1}^{T}\;\sum_{k=1}^{t}\; \frac{\partial \ell_t}{\partial h_t}\,\underbrace{\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^{t} \frac{\partial h_j}{\partial h_{j-1}}\right)}_{J_{t\leftarrow k}}\,\frac{\partial^{+} h_k}{\partial W_h},$$ where $\partial^{+}$ denotes the immediate partial holding $h_{k-1}$ fixed, and for the Elman RNN $\dfrac{\partial h_j}{\partial h_{j-1}} = D_j W_h$, so $J_{t\leftarrow k} = D_t W_h D_{t-1} W_h \cdots D_{k+1} W_h$.

Proof. Unroll: $h_t$ is a function of $W_h$ both directly and through $h_{t-1}$, which is itself a function of $W_h$. The total derivative therefore satisfies the recursion $\frac{d h_t}{d W_h} = \frac{\partial^+ h_t}{\partial W_h} + \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}\frac{d h_{t-1}}{d W_h}$. Expanding the recursion down to $h_0$ (which does not depend on $W_h$) gives $\frac{d h_t}{d W_h} = \sum_{k\le t} J_{t\leftarrow k}\,\frac{\partial^+ h_k}{\partial W_h}$; contracting with $\partial\ell_t/\partial h_t$ and summing over $t$ gives the claim. Differentiating $h_j = \tanh(a_j)$ gives $\partial h_j/\partial h_{j-1} = \mathrm{diag}(\tanh'(a_j))W_h = D_jW_h$. $\blacksquare$

Reverse mode computes this in one backward sweep rather than by $O(T^2)$ path enumeration: carry $\delta_t = \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial h_t$ backwards via $\delta_{t-1} = W_h^\top D_t \delta_t + \partial\ell_{t-1}/\partial h_{t-1}$, accumulating $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W_h \mathrel{+}= (D_t\delta_t) h_{t-1}^\top$. Cost is $\Theta(T(d_h^2 + d_hd_{\text{in}}))$ FLOPs per sequence with activation memory $\Theta(Td_h)$, since every $h_t$ must be retained — the tension Chapter 11 resolved with checkpointing, and why Section 17.6 truncates.

The double sum is the whole chapter in one formula. The contribution of step $k$ to the loss at step $t$ is routed entirely through $J_{t\leftarrow k}$, a product of $t-k$ Jacobians, so long-range credit assignment is a statement about the magnitude of that product at large $t-k$.

17.3 Vanishing and Exploding Gradients

Theorem 17.2 (Growth rate of the Jacobian product)

(i) Upper bound. $\|J_{t\leftarrow k}\|_2 \le \prod_{j=k+1}^{t}\|D_j\|_2\|W_h\|_2 \le \big(\gamma\|W_h\|_2\big)^{t-k}$ where $\gamma = \sup|\varphi'|$, equal to $1$ for $\tanh$ and $\tfrac14$ for the logistic $\sigma$. Hence $\gamma\|W_h\|_2 < 1$ forces exponential vanishing.
(ii) Exact rate in the linear case. If $\varphi = \mathrm{id}$ then $J_{t\leftarrow k} = W_h^{\,t-k}$, and by Gelfand's formula $\lim_{n\to\infty}\|W_h^{\,n}\|^{1/n} = \rho(W_h)$ for any submultiplicative norm. So the asymptotic per-step growth factor is the spectral radius, not the operator norm: $\rho < 1$ vanishes, $\rho > 1$ explodes, and the two regimes are separated by a set of measure zero.

Proof. (i) is submultiplicativity of $\|\cdot\|_2$ plus $\|D_j\|_2 = \max_i \varphi'(a_{j,i}) \le \gamma$. (ii) is Gelfand's spectral radius formula. $\blacksquare$

The gap between $\rho(W_h)$ and $\|W_h\|_2$ is not a technicality. For a non-normal $W_h$ the bound in (i) can be loose by an arbitrary factor at finite $n$: transient growth followed by asymptotic decay is generic, and it is why an RNN can look stable for 20 steps and diverge at 200. The artifact measures the convergence directly — with $\rho$ set to $0.5$, $0.9$ and $1.2$ on a $32\times32$ Gaussian matrix, $\|W_h^{T}\|_2^{1/T}$ reads $0.51246$, $0.92243$, $1.22991$ at $T=16$ and $0.50077$, $0.90138$, $1.20184$ at $T=256$. Certain

Example 17.1 (Two units, done by hand)

Take $W_h = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \rho\\ \rho & 0\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are $\pm\rho$, and drop the nonlinearity. Then $W_h^2 = \rho^2 I$, so $J_{T\leftarrow 0} = W_h^{T} = \rho^{T}I$ exactly for even $T$. At $T=64$: $\rho=0.9$ gives $0.9^{64} = 1.179\times10^{-3}$, and $\rho=1.2$ gives $1.2^{64} = 1.168\times10^{5}$ — a factor of $10^8$ between two matrices whose entries differ by $0.3$. The LSTM comparison, also by hand: a single-unit cell with input gate closed and forget-gate pre-activation pinned at $4$ has $f = \sigma(4) = 0.98201$, so $\partial c_{64}/\partial c_0 = 0.98201^{64} = 0.3130$ and $\partial c_{256}/\partial c_0 = 9.60\times10^{-3}$. Over 256 steps the Elman product at $\rho=0.9$ has fallen to $1.93\times10^{-12}$; the cell has fallen by a factor of $10^{2}$.

Now the part that is usually stated wrongly. "Exploding gradients" is not the mirror image of vanishing gradients in a saturating RNN, because saturation is itself a decay mechanism: as $|h|\to1$, $D_j \to 0$ and the product collapses regardless of $\rho$. The artifact drives a $\tanh$ RNN with $\rho = 1.2$ on real inputs: $\|\partial h_T/\partial h_0\|_2$ rises to $1.894$ at $T=2$, then falls to $2.639\times10^{-27}$ at $T=256$, with $\max_t|h_t|$ reaching $0.9989$. The nonlinearity that makes the RNN expressive is the one that shuts the gradient off. Explosion in practice is local — a cliff where a small parameter change flips many units out of saturation at once — not steady $\rho^T$ growth, which is why clipping (Section 17.6) works so well on it and nothing works as well on vanishing. Likely

The received story is that RNNs failed at long-range dependencies because gradients vanish. The mechanism is real: at $\rho=0.9$ the artifact's $\tanh$ RNN reaches $2.828\times10^{-46}$ at $T=256$, so the gradient signal from 256 steps back is $46$ orders of magnitude below the signal from one step back and is annihilated by fp32 long before it reaches the optimizer. But gating largely fixes it (Section 17.4), gated RNNs still lost, and well-tuned LSTM language models stayed competitive with early Transformers on perplexity at matched parameter count. Vanishing gradients explain why vanilla RNNs failed, not why LSTMs lost. Section 17.7 gives the explanation that does. Contested

17.4 LSTM: Gates and the Cell-State Highway

The fix, due to Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) with the forget gate added by Gers, Schmidhuber and Cummins (2000): add a second state whose default dynamics are the identity, and make every write to it multiplicative and learned.

Definition 17.3 (LSTM cell)

With $z_t = W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1} + b \in \mathbb{R}^{4d_h}$ split into four blocks, $$i_t = \sigma(z_t^{(i)}),\quad f_t = \sigma(z_t^{(f)}),\quad g_t = \tanh(z_t^{(g)}),\quad o_t = \sigma(z_t^{(o)}),$$ $$c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t, \qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t).$$ The state is the pair $(h_t, c_t)$; $c_t$ is the cell and is never squashed on its own update path.

Theorem 17.3 (Constant error carousel)

Holding the gates fixed — equivalently, along the path that does not route back through $h$ — $$\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t), \qquad \frac{\partial c_T}{\partial c_k} = \mathrm{diag}\!\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^{T} f_j\right).$$ The multiplier is diagonal, elementwise, in $(0,1)$, and directly learnable through $b^{(f)}$. With $f_j \equiv 1$ the path is the exact identity for all $T$.

Proof. Differentiate $c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t$ with $f_t, i_t, g_t$ treated as constants: the second term drops and the first is elementwise multiplication by $f_t$, i.e. $\mathrm{diag}(f_t)$. Diagonal matrices commute, so the product telescopes into the elementwise product of the gates. $\blacksquare$

Three properties improve on $D_jW_h$. Diagonal: no mixing, no non-normal transient — unit $i$'s memory decays at its own rate $\prod_j f_{j,i}$ and cannot be rotated into another unit. Bounded by 1: this path cannot explode, trading a two-sided pathology for a one-sided one. Directly parameterized: raising $b^{(f)}$ raises every $f_j$, which is why initializing the forget-gate bias to $1$ or $2$ is standard. The artifact verifies the theorem to $1.084\times10^{-19}$ over 40 steps against $\prod_t f_t$.

The catch is that gates are not constant: $f_t$ depends on $h_{t-1}$, hence on $c_{t-1}$, so the true Jacobian $\partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1}$ is $\mathrm{diag}(f_t)$ plus a correction routed through the gate pre-activations. Theorem 17.3 is about one path, not the full derivative — still the right statement, because that path is the only one whose length-$T$ product is not a product of dense matrices, and empirically it dominates. The artifact's full measurement, every path included, gives $\|\partial h_T/\partial h_0\|_2 = 2.311$ at $T = 256$ against $2.828\times10^{-46}$ for the $\tanh$ RNN at $\rho=0.9$: a ratio of $8.2\times10^{45}$. Certain

Parameter count: the four gates share one $(4d_h)\times d_{\text{in}}$ input matrix, one $(4d_h)\times d_h$ recurrent matrix and $4d_h$ biases, so $N_{\text{LSTM}} = 4(d_hd_{\text{in}} + d_h^2 + d_h)$. At $d_h = d_{\text{in}} = 512$ that is $2{,}099{,}200$ per layer, of which $8d_h^2 = 2{,}097{,}152$ is matrix. Peephole connections (Gers and Schmidhuber, 2000) add $c_{t-1}$ to the gate pre-activations and $3d_h$ parameters; Greff et al.'s 5400-run ablation found removing them harmless, and they are essentially never used now.

Common Pitfall

Transplanting weights into or out of torch.nn.LSTM with the wrong gate order. Torch packs the four blocks of weight_ih_l0 (shape $(4d_h, d_{\text{in}})$) in the order $(i, f, g, o)$; TensorFlow's LSTMCell historically used $(i, g, f, o)$ and several textbook implementations use $(i, f, o, g)$. Swapping $f$ and $g$ exchanges a sigmoid gate with a $\tanh$ candidate: dimensionally legal, numerically finite, silently wrong. The artifact does exactly this swap on otherwise-identical weights and measures a relative error of $1.394$ in the hidden states — pure noise, and nothing raises. A second trap: torch keeps two bias vectors, bias_ih_l0 and bias_hh_l0, which are added together, so a single-bias implementation must write the bias into one and zeros into the other, and receives the same gradient for both. Test any transplant on forward outputs before you look at gradients.

17.5 GRU

Definition 17.4 (GRU cell)

Cho et al. (2014), written with $z_t$ as the retention weight to match torch; Cho's paper uses the complementary convention. With update gate $z_t$ and reset gate $r_t$, $$z_t = \sigma(W_zx_t + U_zh_{t-1} + b_z),\qquad r_t = \sigma(W_rx_t + U_rh_{t-1} + b_r),$$ $$\tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W x_t + U(r_t \odot h_{t-1}) + b), \qquad h_t = z_t\odot h_{t-1} + (1-z_t)\odot\tilde{h}_t.$$ There is one state, not two. The retention path multiplier is $\mathrm{diag}(z_t)$, and the input and forget gates are coupled: what is not retained is exactly what is written.

The GRU is the LSTM with the output gate deleted, the cell and hidden states merged, and $i_t$ tied to $1 - f_t$. Three gate-sized matrices instead of four gives $N_{\text{GRU}} = 3(d_hd_{\text{in}} + d_h^2 + d_h)$, exactly $75\%$ of the LSTM: $1{,}574{,}400$ against $2{,}099{,}200$ at $d_h=d_{\text{in}}=512$. The carousel argument survives verbatim with $z_t$ in place of $f_t$, but the coupling is not free: $z_{t,i}\approx1$ now means both "keep the old value" and "write nothing", so a GRU unit cannot hold a value while integrating new evidence into it.

The empirical verdict, from Chung et al. (2014) on music and speech, Greff et al.'s LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey (5400 runs, eight variants, three tasks), and Jozefowicz et al.'s (2015) search over ten thousand candidates: no consistent winner, and differences between reasonable gated variants are smaller than the effect of the learning rate. Greff's positive findings are about which components are load-bearing — the forget gate and the output activation are the two whose removal reliably hurts. Where the $25\%$ does matter is memory-bound inference: at fixed width the GRU costs $25\%$ less weight memory and bandwidth and carries half the recurrent state, since there is no $c_t$; at fixed parameter budget it buys $\sqrt{4/3}\approx15\%$ more width, not $33\%$, because parameters grow like $d_h^2$. Where it does not matter is accuracy. The one substantive claim in the LSTM's favour is that the separate output gate lets $c_t$ hold a value the network is not yet ready to expose, which shows up on explicit long-range copying; a clean test would be matched-parameter runs on a synthetic copy task with the horizon swept. Contested

One implementation note that costs people days: torch's GRU applies the reset gate after the recurrent matmul, computing $n_t = \tanh(W_nx_t + b_{in} + r_t\odot(U_nh_{t-1} + b_{hn}))$, whereas Definition 17.4 applies it before. The two are not equal; torch's is the cuDNN form because it lets $U_nh_{t-1}$ fuse with the other gates into a single GEMM. Torch names the gates $(r, z, n)$ and writes $h_t = (1-z_t)\odot n_t + z_t\odot h_{t-1}$, which is Definition 17.4 verbatim. Verify

17.6 Bidirectionality, Truncation, Gradient Clipping

Bidirectionality (Schuster and Paliwal, 1997) runs a second RNN right-to-left and concatenates: $h_t = [\overrightarrow{h}_t; \overleftarrow{h}_t]$. It doubles parameters and compute and makes $h_t$ depend on the entire sequence — correct for tagging, parsing and encoders, structurally impossible for autoregressive generation, which is why BERT-style encoders are bidirectional and GPT-style decoders are not — and it destroys streaming.

Truncated BPTT (Williams and Peng, 1990) backpropagates only $k_2$ steps and takes a gradient step every $k_1$ steps, carrying $h_t$ forward across boundaries but cutting the gradient. Memory falls from $\Theta(Td_h)$ to $\Theta(k_2d_h)$ and the estimator becomes biased: every $J_{t\leftarrow k}$ with $t-k > k_2$ is set to zero. The bias is defensible precisely when Theorem 17.2 says those terms were negligible anyway — a circular justification for a vanilla RNN, and simply false for an LSTM, where truncating at $k_2 = 35$ discards exactly the long-range signal the architecture was built to carry. Likely

Definition 17.5 (Norm clipping)

Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (2013). Given the full gradient $g$ and threshold $c$, use $\tilde{g} = g\cdot\min(1, c/\|g\|_2)$. The direction is preserved exactly; only the step length is capped.

Clipping is a trust region imposed after the fact, and it works because explosion is spiky: gradient norms sit in a narrow band with occasional $10$–$100\times$ excursions, so clipping near the running median leaves most steps untouched. Two failure modes: clipping per parameter tensor rather than globally changes the direction as well as the length and quietly reweights layers against each other; and a threshold tuned for SGD is usually far too tight for Adam (Chapter 13), whose second moment already normalizes per coordinate. Likely

17.7 seq2seq and the Attention Bottleneck That Started Everything

Sutskever, Vinyals and Le (2014) encoded a source sentence with one LSTM into its final state, decoded with a second LSTM initialized from that state, and reached $34.8$ BLEU on WMT'14 English–French with a 4-layer, 1000-unit, ~380M-parameter model trained about ten days on 8 GPUs. Verify The tell was buried in the paper: reversing the source word order improved BLEU by several points, because it shortened the distance between the first source words and the first target words. A model whose performance depends on which end of the sentence you feed first is telling you its state is the bottleneck.

Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (2015) measured it: encoder–decoder BLEU degrades sharply with source length, and the fix is to let the decoder read a learned convex combination of all encoder states, $c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij}h_j$ with $\alpha_{ij} = \mathrm{softmax}_j(\text{score}(s_{i-1}, h_j))$. That is attention, invented as a patch on a recurrent bottleneck, and Chapter 18's contribution was to notice that once you have it the recurrence is redundant.

Redundant, and expensive.

Theorem 17.4 (Sequential depth, and when it collapses)

Computing $h_T$ under Definition 17.1 requires $\Theta(T)$ sequential steps when $\varphi$ is an arbitrary nonlinearity, since $h_t$ is not defined until $h_{t-1}$ is. If instead the recurrence is linear in the state with input-dependent coefficients, $h_t = A_t h_{t-1} + b_t$, then composing two steps gives $(A,b)\circ(A',b') = (AA', Ab'+b)$, which is associative; a parallel scan therefore computes all $h_t$ in $\Theta(\log T)$ sequential steps with $\Theta(T)$ work.

Proof sketch. The first claim is the definition of the dependency chain. For the second, verify associativity by expanding both bracketings of a triple, then apply Blelloch's scan: a balanced binary tree over $T$ leaves has depth $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$, and each internal node combines two pairs at the cost of one matrix product. $\blacksquare$

Theorem 17.4 is the argument of Chapter 21 stated early. An LSTM's gate nonlinearities are precisely what breaks associativity, so it pays $T$ sequential steps; a diagonal $A_t$ makes the composition cheap as well as associative, which is what S4 and Mamba exploit. Self-attention takes the other branch: $\Theta(1)$ sequential operations and $\Theta(T^2d)$ work per layer against recurrence's $\Theta(Td^2)$, so attention is cheaper in FLOPs whenever $T < d$ and always shallower.

The hardware consequence is severe because the steps are individually tiny. Take $d_h = 1024$, batch $64$: one step's recurrent GEMM is $2 \cdot 64 \cdot 1024 \cdot 4096 \approx 5.4\times10^{8}$ FLOPs, which an H100 at ~$10^{15}$ dense bf16 FLOP/s would retire in $0.54\,\mu$s — below the $\sim3$–$5\,\mu$s cost of launching a kernel. Verify The GPU spends the step waiting. cuDNN recovers part of this by fusing the input projections for all $T$ steps into one GEMM — those are not sequential — and by fusing the elementwise gate work, but the recurrent GEMM chain is irreducible. The artifact measures the same effect on CPU, where launch overhead is smaller and the gap therefore understates the GPU case: at $T=512$, $d=256$, fp32, the sequential loop sustains $17.1$ GFLOP/s at batch 1 against $412.0$ for the time-fused GEMM, a $24\times$ utilization gap that narrows to $2.3\times$ only at batch 64 — because batch is the RNN's only parallel dimension, and using it costs memory linearly. Verify

That is the verdict. Google's GNMT needed 8 encoder and 8 decoder LSTM layers and roughly six days on 96 K80 GPUs, with explicit layer-pipelining to keep the devices busy; the original Transformer base model trained in 12 hours on 8 P100s. Verify The gap is not quality per parameter; it is that one architecture fills the machine and the other does not, compounded by a decade in which the machine got wider far faster than it got faster per lane. Chapter 21 returns with the state space model, which keeps the $O(1)$ inference of Definition 17.1 and buys back training parallelism by satisfying Theorem 17.4's associativity condition. Likely

Artifact 17.1 — LSTM with BPTT, and the decay table

A pure-NumPy LSTM with hand-written forward and BPTT passes, cross-checked against torch.nn.LSTM in float64. It then verifies Theorem 17.3, checks Gelfand's formula, tabulates $\|\partial h_T/\partial h_0\|_2$ against $T$, and times a recurrent loop against the same FLOPs issued as one GEMM.

"""
Artifact 17.1 -- An LSTM cell with full backpropagation through time, from scratch.

[1] BPTT checked against torch.nn.LSTM with the same weights transplanted in
    (torch packs the gates as [i, f, g, o]; a wrong permutation is also shown).
[2] The constant-error carousel: with the h-path cut, dc_T/dc_0 = diag(prod_t f_t).
[3] || dh_T / dh_0 ||_2 versus T -- Gelfand's rho for a linear RNN, then a tanh
    RNN and an LSTM driven by real inputs.
[4] The parallelism deficit: T sequential GEMMs vs one time-fused GEMM.

Pure NumPy for everything that matters; torch is a cross-check only.
"""
import time
import numpy as np

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))
# Gate block order is torch's: rows [0:H)=i, [H:2H)=f, [2H:3H)=g, [3H:4H)=o,
# so weights transplant without a permutation.
class LSTM:
    def __init__(self, d_in, H, forget_bias=0.0, scale=1.0, rng=None):
        rng = rng or np.random.default_rng(0)
        self.d_in, self.H = d_in, H
        s = scale / np.sqrt(H)
        self.Wx = rng.normal(0.0, s, (4 * H, d_in))   # input-to-hidden
        self.Wh = rng.normal(0.0, s, (4 * H, H))      # hidden-to-hidden
        self.bx = np.zeros(4 * H)                     # torch keeps two biases
        self.bh = np.zeros(4 * H)
        self.bx[H:2 * H] = forget_bias                # push the forget gate open

    def forward(self, X, h0, c0):
        """X: (T,B,d_in). Returns h stack (T,B,H) and a cache for BPTT."""
        T, B, H = X.shape[0], X.shape[1], self.H
        h, c = h0.copy(), c0.copy()
        Hs, cache = np.empty((T, B, H)), []
        for t in range(T):
            z = X[t] @ self.Wx.T + h @ self.Wh.T + self.bx + self.bh
            i, f = sigmoid(z[:, 0:H]), sigmoid(z[:, H:2 * H])
            g, o = np.tanh(z[:, 2 * H:3 * H]), sigmoid(z[:, 3 * H:4 * H])
            c_new = f * c + i * g                 # the additive cell update
            tc = np.tanh(c_new)
            cache.append((X[t], h, c, i, f, g, o, tc))
            h, c = o * tc, c_new
            Hs[t] = h
        return Hs, (h, c), cache

    def backward(self, cache, dHs, dh_T=None, dc_T=None, cut_h_path=False):
        """Reverse-mode BPTT.

        dHs : (T,B,H) upstream gradient injected at every step (may be zeros).
        dh_T, dc_T : extra gradient injected at the final state.
        cut_h_path : if True, do not route gate gradients back into h_{t-1}.
                     This isolates the cell-state highway (demo [2]).
        """
        T, H, B = len(cache), self.H, cache[0][1].shape[0]
        gWx, gWh = np.zeros_like(self.Wx), np.zeros_like(self.Wh)
        gb, gX = np.zeros(4 * H), np.zeros((T, B, self.d_in))
        dh = np.zeros((B, H)) if dh_T is None else dh_T.copy()
        dc = np.zeros((B, H)) if dc_T is None else dc_T.copy()
        for t in reversed(range(T)):
            x, h_prev, c_prev, i, f, g, o, tc = cache[t]
            dh = dh + dHs[t]
            do = dh * tc
            dc = dc + dh * o * (1.0 - tc * tc)      # through tanh(c_t)
            df = dc * c_prev
            di = dc * g
            dg = dc * i
            dc = dc * f                              # <-- the carousel: multiply by f
            # through the gate nonlinearities
            dz = np.concatenate([di * i * (1 - i),
                                 df * f * (1 - f),
                                 dg * (1 - g * g),
                                 do * o * (1 - o)], axis=1)
            gWx += dz.T @ x
            gWh += dz.T @ h_prev
            gb += dz.sum(axis=0)
            gX[t] = dz @ self.Wx
            dh = np.zeros((B, H)) if cut_h_path else dz @ self.Wh
        # torch carries two identical bias vectors, so each receives gb
        return dict(Wx=gWx, Wh=gWh, bx=gb, bh=gb.copy(), X=gX, h0=dh, c0=dc)

class VanillaRNN:
    """h_t = tanh(Wx x_t + Wh h_{t-1} + b), with Wh rescaled to a chosen rho."""

    def __init__(self, d_in, H, rho, rng=None):
        rng = rng or np.random.default_rng(1)
        W = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(H), (H, H))
        self.Wh = W * (rho / max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(W))))
        self.Wx = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(H), (H, d_in))
        self.H = H

    def jac_norm(self, X, h0):
        """|| d h_T / d h_0 ||_2, built exactly as prod_t diag(1-h_t^2) Wh."""
        h = h0.copy()
        J = np.eye(self.H)
        sat = 0.0
        for t in range(X.shape[0]):
            h = np.tanh(X[t] @ self.Wx.T + h @ self.Wh.T)
            J = (np.diag(1.0 - h[0] ** 2) @ self.Wh) @ J
            sat = max(sat, np.abs(h).max())
        return np.linalg.norm(J, 2), sat

def lstm_jac_norm(net, X, h0, c0):
    """|| d h_T / d h_0 ||_2 by running BPTT once per unit basis vector."""
    _, _, cache = net.forward(X, h0, c0)
    T, B, H = X.shape[0], h0.shape[0], net.H
    Z, J = np.zeros((T, B, H)), np.empty((H, H))
    for k in range(H):
        seed = np.zeros((B, H)); seed[0, k] = 1.0
        J[k] = net.backward(cache, Z, dh_T=seed)["h0"][0]  # row k of the Jacobian
    return np.linalg.norm(J, 2)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def demo_torch_check(T=12, B=4, d_in=7, H=5):
    print("[1] BPTT vs torch.nn.LSTM, weights transplanted, float64")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    net = LSTM(d_in, H, forget_bias=0.7, scale=1.0, rng=rng)
    X = rng.normal(size=(T, B, d_in))
    h0, c0 = rng.normal(size=(B, H)), rng.normal(size=(B, H))
    R = rng.normal(size=(T, B, H))                     # loss = sum(R * h)
    Hs, _, cache = net.forward(X, h0, c0)
    gn = net.backward(cache, R)
    print(f"    loss (numpy)              = {float((R * Hs).sum()):.10f}")
    if torch is None:
        print("    [skipped: torch not installed]"); return
    tl = torch.nn.LSTM(d_in, H, num_layers=1, batch_first=False, dtype=torch.float64)
    with torch.no_grad():
        tl.weight_ih_l0.copy_(torch.from_numpy(net.Wx))
        tl.weight_hh_l0.copy_(torch.from_numpy(net.Wh))
        tl.bias_ih_l0.copy_(torch.from_numpy(net.bx))
        tl.bias_hh_l0.copy_(torch.from_numpy(net.bh))
    tX = torch.tensor(X, requires_grad=True)
    th0, tc0 = (torch.tensor(v[None], requires_grad=True) for v in (h0, c0))
    out, _ = tl(tX, (th0, tc0))
    loss = (torch.tensor(R) * out).sum()
    loss.backward()
    print(f"    loss (torch)              = {loss.item():.10f}   "
          f"|dloss| = {abs(loss.item() - float((R * Hs).sum())):.3e}")
    pairs = [("h stack", Hs, out), ("dWx", gn["Wx"], tl.weight_ih_l0.grad),
             ("dWh", gn["Wh"], tl.weight_hh_l0.grad), ("dbx", gn["bx"], tl.bias_ih_l0.grad),
             ("dX", gn["X"], tX.grad), ("dh0", gn["h0"], th0.grad[0]),
             ("dc0", gn["c0"], tc0.grad[0])]
    worst = 0.0
    for name, a, b in pairs:
        b = b.detach().numpy()
        r = np.abs(a - b).max() / max(1e-12, np.abs(b).max())
        worst = max(worst, r)
        print(f"    max rel err {name:<8s}      = {r:.3e}")
    assert worst < 1e-9, worst
    # ---- the classic bug: torch's block order is (i,f,g,o), not (i,g,f,o) ----
    bad = LSTM(d_in, H, rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
    perm = np.r_[0:H, 2 * H:3 * H, H:2 * H, 3 * H:4 * H]   # swap f and g blocks
    bad.Wx, bad.Wh = net.Wx[perm], net.Wh[perm]
    bad.bx, bad.bh = net.bx[perm], net.bh[perm]
    Hb, _, _ = bad.forward(X, h0, c0)
    print(f"    same weights, gates read (i,g,f,o): rel err "
          f"{np.abs(Hb - Hs).max() / np.abs(Hs).max():.3e}  <-- silent, not a crash")
    assert np.abs(Hb - Hs).max() / np.abs(Hs).max() > 0.1

def demo_carousel(T=40, B=3, H=6):
    print("\n[2] Cell-state highway: d c_T / d c_0 with the h-path cut")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
    net = LSTM(4, H, forget_bias=1.5, scale=1.0, rng=rng)
    X = rng.normal(size=(T, B, 4))
    h0, c0 = rng.normal(size=(B, H)), rng.normal(size=(B, H))
    _, _, cache = net.forward(X, h0, c0)
    dc0 = net.backward(cache, np.zeros((T, B, H)), dc_T=np.ones((B, H)),
                       cut_h_path=True)["c0"]
    prod_f = np.ones((B, H))
    for t in range(T):
        prod_f *= cache[t][4]
    err = np.abs(dc0 - prod_f).max()
    print(f"    T = {T}, mean forget gate = {np.mean([c[4].mean() for c in cache]):.6f}")
    print(f"    prod_t f_t  in [{prod_f.min():.3e}, {prod_f.max():.3e}]")
    print(f"    max |dc0 - prod_t f_t|    = {err:.3e}")
    assert err < 1e-12, err

def demo_spectral(H=32, Ts=(16, 64, 256)):
    """Linear RNN: J = Wh^T exactly, so Gelfand's formula ||Wh^T||^(1/T) -> rho."""
    print("\n[3a] Linear RNN: the spectral radius is the growth rate (Gelfand)")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
    W = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(H), (H, H))
    print(f"    {'rho':>5} {'T':>5} {'||Wh^T||_2':>13} {'rho^T':>13} {'||Wh^T||^(1/T)':>16}")
    for rho in (0.5, 0.9, 1.2):
        Wh = W * (rho / max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(W))))
        for T in Ts:
            n = np.linalg.norm(np.linalg.matrix_power(Wh, T), 2)
            print(f"    {rho:5.1f} {T:5d} {n:13.4e} {rho ** T:13.4e} {n ** (1.0 / T):16.5f}")
        assert abs(n ** (1.0 / T) - rho) < 0.01, (rho, n ** (1.0 / T))

def demo_decay(H=32, d_in=8, Ts=(1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256)):
    print("\n[3b] || d h_T / d h_0 ||_2 versus sequence length, driven by real inputs")
    X = np.random.default_rng(3).normal(size=(max(Ts), 1, d_in))
    h0, c0 = np.zeros((1, H)), np.zeros((1, H))
    rnns = {r: VanillaRNN(d_in, H, r, rng=np.random.default_rng(4)) for r in (0.5, 0.9, 1.2)}
    lstm = LSTM(d_in, H, forget_bias=4.0, scale=0.4, rng=np.random.default_rng(5))
    print(f"    {'T':>5} | {'tanh rho=0.5':>13} {'tanh rho=0.9':>13} {'tanh rho=1.2':>13}"
          f" | {'LSTM':>11} | {'LSTM / rho=0.9':>15}")
    print("    " + "-" * 84)
    for T in Ts:
        v = {rho: r.jac_norm(X[:T], h0)[0] for rho, r in rnns.items()}
        vl = lstm_jac_norm(lstm, X[:T], h0, c0)
        print(f"    {T:5d} | {v[0.5]:13.3e} {v[0.9]:13.3e} {v[1.2]:13.3e} | "
              f"{vl:11.3e} | {vl / v[0.9]:15.3e}")
    sat = rnns[1.2].jac_norm(X, h0)[1]      # why rho > 1 does not explode here
    print(f"    tanh saturation kills even rho=1.2: max |h_t| reached {sat:.4f}, "
          f"so diag(1-h^2) shrinks the product")
    assert v[0.5] < 1e-90 and v[0.9] < 1e-40                 # decayed to nothing
    assert v[0.5] <= 0.5 ** max(Ts) and v[0.9] <= 0.9 ** max(Ts)   # |tanh'| <= 1
    assert vl > 1e-2 and vl / v[0.9] > 1e30                  # the LSTM does not

def demo_parallelism(T=512, d=256, Bs=(1, 8, 32, 64), reps=5, dt=np.float32):
    print("\n[4] Parallelism deficit: T sequential GEMMs vs one time-fused GEMM")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
    Wx = (rng.normal(size=(d, 4 * d)) / np.sqrt(d)).astype(dt)
    Wh = (rng.normal(size=(d, 4 * d)) / np.sqrt(d)).astype(dt)
    print(f"    T={T}, d={d}, fp32. Sequential depth {T} vs 1; only B is parallel.")
    print(f"    {'B':>5} {'seq ms':>9} {'seq GF/s':>10} {'fused ms':>10} "
          f"{'fused GF/s':>11} {'gap':>7}")
    for B in Bs:
        X = rng.normal(size=(T, B, d)).astype(dt)
        flops = 2.0 * T * B * d * (4 * d)
        seq, par = np.inf, np.inf
        for _ in range(reps):
            h = np.zeros((B, d), dt); t0 = time.perf_counter()
            for t in range(T):                      # the loop that cannot be unrolled
                h = np.tanh((X[t] @ Wx + h @ Wh)[:, :d])
            seq = min(seq, time.perf_counter() - t0)
        Xf = X.reshape(T * B, d)
        for _ in range(reps):
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            _ = Xf @ Wx                             # all T steps at once
            par = min(par, time.perf_counter() - t0)
        sr, pr = 2 * flops / seq / 1e9, flops / par / 1e9   # seq does 2 GEMMs/step
        print(f"    {B:5d} {seq * 1e3:9.1f} {sr:10.1f} {par * 1e3:10.2f} "
              f"{pr:11.1f} {pr / sr:6.1f}x")
        assert pr > sr, (B, sr, pr)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    demo_torch_check()
    demo_carousel()
    demo_spectral()
    demo_decay()
    demo_parallelism()
    print(f"\nall assertions passed in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")

Every gradient matches torch to at most $5.488\times10^{-16}$ relative error — float64 round-off, six orders tighter than the $10^{-9}$ threshold asserted — while the same weights read in $(i,g,f,o)$ order give a relative error of $1.394$ without raising anything. The carousel identity holds to $1.084\times10^{-19}$. The decay table is the point: at $T=256$ the $\tanh$ RNN reaches $2.828\times10^{-46}$ at $\rho=0.9$ while the LSTM sits at $2.311$, a ratio of $8.173\times10^{45}$. The timing block reports $17.1$ GFLOP/s sequential against $412.0$ fused at batch 1, closing to $180.1$ against $413.4$ at batch 64; total runtime $3.7$ s. Those four timings are the only machine-dependent numbers here and moved up to $20\%$ across repeat runs. Verify

Under Encryption

Recurrence is close to the worst case for CKKS, for the reason Theorem 17.4 names. Multiplicative depth is consumed along the dependency chain, so an LSTM over $T$ tokens costs depth $\Theta(T)$: each $f_t \odot c_{t-1}$ is a ciphertext–ciphertext multiplication shareable with no other step, and the gates are $\sigma$ and $\tanh$, needing degree-7–15 polynomial approximations — another 3–4 levels per step. At a realistic budget of 20–30 levels an encrypted LSTM bootstraps every two to four tokens, and bootstrapping dominates everything else. Attention's $\Theta(1)$ depth is what matters here, not its FLOP count. Chapter 39 takes up the approximation problem in detail. Likely

Key Takeaways
  • BPTT is reverse mode on the unrolled graph with weight tying, so the gradient is a double sum whose inner term is $J_{t\leftarrow k} = \prod_{j=k+1}^t D_jW_h$; long-range credit assignment is entirely a statement about the magnitude of that matrix product. Certain
  • The asymptotic per-step growth factor is the spectral radius $\rho(W_h)$, not $\|W_h\|_2$; measured $\|W_h^T\|_2^{1/T}$ converges to $0.50077$, $0.90138$ and $1.20184$ for $\rho = 0.5, 0.9, 1.2$ at $T=256$, and saturation of $\tanh$ turns even $\rho>1$ into decay. Certain
  • Along the LSTM cell path the gradient multiplier is exactly $\mathrm{diag}(f_t)$ — diagonal, bounded by 1, and directly settable through the forget-gate bias — which is why the measured $\|\partial h_T/\partial h_0\|_2$ at $T=256$ is $2.311$ for an LSTM and $2.828\times10^{-46}$ for a $\tanh$ RNN. Certain
  • The GRU has exactly $75\%$ of the LSTM's parameters by dropping the output gate and coupling input to forget; across large ablations neither architecture consistently wins, so the difference matters for memory and bandwidth, not accuracy. Contested
  • Recurrence costs $\Theta(T)$ sequential steps against attention's $\Theta(1)$, each step too small to fill a GPU — a measured $24\times$ utilization gap at batch 1, even on CPU — and the fix is not better gating but making the recurrence associative, which is Chapter 21. Likely
Chapter 18

Attention and the Transformer

Learning Objectives
  • Derive scaled dot-product attention and prove that the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor holds logit variance at $\Theta(1)$ under standard initialization.
  • Derive the attention backward pass, including the softmax Jacobian $J = \mathrm{diag}(p) - pp^{\top}$ and its contraction $\bar{s} = p \odot (\bar{p} - \langle \bar{p}, p\rangle)$.
  • Compute exact parameter counts and FLOPs for a transformer block, and locate the sequence length at which the $4n^2d$ attention term overtakes the feed-forward term.
  • Explain multi-head, multi-query, and grouped-query attention, and compute the KV-cache reduction each buys.
  • Implement multi-head attention and a complete pre-norm transformer block in working code, verified against a reference implementation, finite differences, and a cached-decode identity.
Read alongside — Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), for the line-by-line construction of causal multi-head attention and the KV cache, which is the closest text to this chapter's artifact. Karpathy, nanoGPT and the Zero to Hero attention lecture, for the same block written as compactly as it can be written and still be read. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, for the clearest picture of what the attention matrix is actually doing to a sequence, and for the pre-norm/post-norm comparison.

Attention is content-addressable soft retrieval: every position emits a query, every position advertises a key, the match scores become a probability distribution, and the output is the corresponding convex combination of values. That is the entire mechanism. The transformer is what you get when you make retrieval the only operation that moves information between positions, give up the recurrence of Chapter 17 along with its sequential bottleneck, and agree to pay $O(n^2)$ for the privilege. This chapter derives the mechanism (18.2), its backward pass, and the one free parameter in it — the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ temperature, which exists for exactly one reason. Then the engineering: masking and its most common bug (18.4), the full block and its parameter count (18.5), the KV-cache economics that drive multi-query and grouped-query attention (18.6), and the quadratic wall (18.7). Chapter 19 adds positional information, which the mechanism derived here conspicuously lacks; Chapter 31 makes it fast.

18.1 From seq2seq Attention to Self-Attention

Attention was invented to fix a specific defect. An encoder–decoder RNN compresses the entire source sentence into one fixed-width state $h_n$, and the decoder reads only that vector; translation quality collapses as source length grows because one vector of fixed width cannot hold a 40-word sentence. Bahdanau's fix was to let the decoder read all encoder states, weighted by a learned relevance score,

$$e_{ij} = v^{\top}\tanh(W_s s_{i-1} + W_h h_j), \qquad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp e_{ij}}{\sum_{j'} \exp e_{ij'}}, \qquad c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j .$$

Luong replaced the additive MLP score with the bilinear $e_{ij} = s_i^{\top} h_j$, which is cheaper because it is a matrix multiplication rather than an elementwise nonlinearity over $n$ pairs. Both were bolted onto a recurrence that still ran sequentially.

Self-attention is the observation that the queries need not come from a decoder at all: let a sequence attend to itself, and the recurrence has nothing left to do. The consequence is a different complexity profile, not merely a different architecture.

Layer typeCompute per layerSequential stepsMax path length
Recurrent$O(n d^2)$$O(n)$$O(n)$
Convolutional, kernel $k$$O(k n d^2)$$O(1)$$O(\log_k n)$
Self-attention$O(n^2 d)$$O(1)$$O(1)$

Two columns matter. Sequential steps is why transformers train on modern hardware and LSTMs do not: an RNN's $O(n)$ dependent steps cannot be filled with parallel work, so a GPU runs at a few percent of peak. Max path length is the gradient argument from Chapter 17 restated — any two positions are one hop apart, so the multiplicative chain that destroys long-range RNN gradients has length one. The price is the first column: attention is cheaper than recurrence only while $n < d$, and Section 18.7 makes that trade exact. Certain

18.2 Queries, Keys, Values

Definition 18.1 (Scaled dot-product attention)

Given queries $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n_q \times d_k}$, keys $K \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k \times d_k}$ and values $V \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k \times d_v}$, stored one item per row, $$\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)}_{A \,\in\, \mathbb{R}^{n_q \times n_k}} V ,$$ with the softmax taken over each row and $M$ an additive mask with entries in $\{0, -\infty\}$. Each row of $A$ is a probability vector, so each output row is a convex combination of value rows: attention cannot extrapolate outside the convex hull of $V$.

Definition 18.2 (Self-attention)

For a token matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ and weight matrices $W_q, W_k, W_v \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d}$ acting on column vectors, self-attention sets $Q = XW_q^{\top}$, $K = XW_k^{\top}$, $V = XW_v^{\top}$. Queries, keys and values are three linear views of the same sequence; nothing else in the layer depends on position, so self-attention is exactly permutation-equivariant — permuting the rows of $X$ permutes the rows of the output identically. Positional information must be injected from outside, which is Chapter 19's subject.

Backward pass. Let $\bar{Z} \equiv \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial Z$. From $O = AV$ we get $\bar{V} = A^{\top}\bar{O}$ and $\bar{A} = \bar{O}V^{\top}$ immediately. The softmax is the only interesting step.

Theorem 18.1 (Softmax Jacobian and its contraction)

For $p = \mathrm{softmax}(s)$ with $s \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$, $\;\partial p_i/\partial s_j = p_i(\delta_{ij} - p_j)$, i.e. $J = \mathrm{diag}(p) - pp^{\top}$. Consequently the vector–Jacobian product needed by backpropagation is $$\bar{s} \;=\; J^{\top}\bar{p} \;=\; p \odot \big(\bar{p} - \langle \bar{p}, p\rangle \mathbf{1}\big),$$ computable in $O(m)$ without forming $J$.

Proof. Write $p_i = e^{s_i}/Z$ with $Z = \sum_l e^{s_l}$. Then $\partial p_i/\partial s_j = (\delta_{ij}e^{s_i}Z - e^{s_i}e^{s_j})/Z^2 = p_i\delta_{ij} - p_ip_j$. $J$ is symmetric, so $\bar{s}_j = \sum_i \bar{p}_i p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j) = p_j\bar{p}_j - p_j\sum_i \bar{p}_ip_i$. $\blacksquare$

Applying Theorem 18.1 row-wise to $\bar{A}$ gives $\bar{S}$, and the rest is bilinear:

$$\bar{S} = A \odot \big(\bar{A} - \mathrm{rowsum}(\bar{A}\odot A)\mathbf{1}^{\top}\big)\big/\sqrt{d_k},\qquad \bar{Q} = \bar{S}K,\qquad \bar{K} = \bar{S}^{\top}Q,$$ $$\bar{W}_q = \bar{Q}^{\top}X,\qquad \bar{X} \;\mathrel{+}=\; \bar{Q}W_q \;+\; \bar{K}W_k \;+\; \bar{V}W_v .$$

Note that $\bar{Q}$ and $\bar{K}$ are transposes of each other's construction: the score matrix is bilinear in $Q$ and $K$, so the backward pass through it is a matched pair of matrix products. Note also what must be kept alive between forward and backward: $A$ itself, $n \times n$ per head. That $O(n^2)$ activation, not the FLOPs, is what made long context infeasible before FlashAttention recomputed $A$ tile-by-tile in the backward pass (Chapter 31). Certain

18.2.1 Why the Scaling Factor
Theorem 18.2 (Logit variance under standard initialization)

Let $q, k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ have mutually independent entries with mean $0$ and variance $1$. Then $\mathbb{E}[q^{\top}k] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(q^{\top}k) = d_k$; hence $\mathrm{Var}\big(q^{\top}k/\sqrt{d_k}\big) = 1$.

Proof. $\mathbb{E}[q^{\top}k] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}[q_i]\mathbb{E}[k_i] = 0$. For the second moment, $\mathbb{E}[(q^{\top}k)^2] = \sum_{i,j}\mathbb{E}[q_iq_jk_ik_j]$. For $i \neq j$ independence factorizes the term into $\mathbb{E}[q_i]\mathbb{E}[q_j]\mathbb{E}[k_i]\mathbb{E}[k_j] = 0$; the $i = j$ terms give $\mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\mathbb{E}[k_i^2] = 1$ each. Summing, $\mathrm{Var} = d_k$. $\blacksquare$

The hypothesis is what standard initialization delivers: if $x$ has unit-variance coordinates and $W_q$ has i.i.d. entries of variance $1/d$ (Chapter 12), then $q = W_qx$ has coordinates of variance $1$, and likewise for $k$.

Without the divisor, logit standard deviation grows as $\sqrt{d_k}$ — a factor of 8 at the near-universal $d_k = 64$ — and the largest of $n$ such logits sits on the order of $\sigma\sqrt{2\ln n}$ above the mean, so the spread of a row of logits scales with $\sigma$ too. Softmax of large-spread logits is nearly one-hot, and by Theorem 18.1 a one-hot $p$ has a Jacobian of essentially zero: if $p_m = 1-\varepsilon$, then every entry of $J$ is $O(\varepsilon)$. The layer stops passing gradient before it has learned anything about which key to select. The scale factor is a temperature, and its only job is keeping softmax out of saturation at initialization. Certain

Example 18.1 (Saturation in four dimensions)

Take $d_k = 4$, $q = (1,1,1,1)$, $k_1 = (1,1,1,1)$, $k_2 = (1,1,-1,-1)$. Then $q^{\top}k_1 = 4$ and $q^{\top}k_2 = 0$.

Unscaled. $\mathrm{softmax}(4,0) = \left(\tfrac{e^4}{e^4+1}, \tfrac{1}{e^4+1}\right) = (0.9820,\,0.0180)$, since $e^4 = 54.598$.

Scaled by $1/\sqrt{4} = 1/2$. $\mathrm{softmax}(2,0) = \left(\tfrac{e^2}{e^2+1}, \tfrac{1}{e^2+1}\right) = (0.8808,\,0.1192)$, since $e^2 = 7.389$.

The off-diagonal Jacobian entry $-p_1p_2$ is $-0.0177$ unscaled and $-0.1050$ scaled: dividing by 2 multiplied the available gradient signal by about six. At the realistic $d_k = 64$ the artifact measures the same effect on random logits — the largest of 8 attention weights is $0.9998$ unscaled and $0.5119$ scaled.

One caveat, in the setting of Chapter 15: $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ is the correct initialization-time scale, and the independence hypothesis of Theorem 18.2 fails after training, when queries and keys become correlated. The muP prescription is therefore $1/d_k$ rather than $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ for attention logits when transferring hyperparameters across widths, and it demonstrably transfers better; standard transformers nevertheless ship $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ because that is what the pretrained checkpoints were trained with. Likely

18.3 Multi-Head Attention

Definition 18.3 (Multi-head attention)

With $H$ heads and $d_h = d/H$, take $W_q^{(h)}, W_k^{(h)}, W_v^{(h)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h \times d}$ and $W_o \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$, and set $$\mathrm{MHA}(X) = \mathrm{Concat}\big(\mathrm{head}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{head}_H\big)W_o^{\top}, \qquad \mathrm{head}_h = \mathrm{Attn}\big(XW_q^{(h)\top}, XW_k^{(h)\top}, XW_v^{(h)\top}\big).$$ Splitting $W_o$ column-blockwise as $W_o = [W_o^{(1)} \cdots W_o^{(H)}]$ turns the concatenation into a sum, $\mathrm{MHA}(X) = \sum_h A_h X W_v^{(h)\top}W_o^{(h)\top}$.

The summed form is the useful one. Head $h$ contributes an additive term whose feature-space action is the single matrix $W_o^{(h)}W_v^{(h)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ of rank at most $d_h$, and whose position-space action is $A_h$, determined by $W_q^{(h)\top}W_k^{(h)}$, also of rank at most $d_h$. Only these two products are identifiable: any invertible $R$ with $W_q \to RW_q$, $W_k \to R^{-\top}W_k$ leaves the layer unchanged. Reading individual $W_q$ entries is therefore meaningless; reading the products is not. Likely

Because $d_h = d/H$, multi-head attention has exactly the parameter count of one-head attention at full width: $4d^2$ weights (plus $4d$ biases), independent of $H$. Heads buy not capacity but the ability to attend to several places at once — one head can track the syntactic subject while another tracks the previous token — which a single softmax, being one probability distribution per query, structurally cannot do. The cost is rank: at $H = 96$ and $d = 12288$, each head's OV circuit is rank $\leq 128$ out of $12288$. Certain

18.4 Masking and the Mask-Then-Softmax Ordering Bug

A decoder-only language model must not let position $i$ see position $j > i$, or the next-token objective becomes trivial. The causal mask $M_{ij} = 0$ for $j \leq i$ and $-\infty$ otherwise is added to the logits, so that $\exp(-\infty) = 0$ and the masked entries drop out of both numerator and denominator. Padding masks work identically, with an extra column pattern per sequence.

Common Pitfall

Multiplying the mask into the probabilities instead of adding it to the logits. Writing A = softmax(S) * mask rather than A = softmax(S + M) produces rows that sum to less than one, because the normalizer $Z$ still contains the future tokens' $e^{s_j}$. The output is then a shrunken, position-dependently scaled convex combination — and crucially it is still a smooth function of the parameters with a plausible-looking gradient, so the model trains, the loss goes down, and nothing crashes. It merely converges to a worse optimum, and its outputs diverge from any reference implementation. The artifact's torch cross-check catches this in one line; a training run will not.

Two companion bugs. First, hand-picking a large finite constant instead of $-\infty$ and reusing it across dtypes: $-10^9$ exceeds fp16's largest finite magnitude, $65504$, and saturates to $-\infty$ on cast, while a constant $-c$ that is too small in magnitude leaves each masked position a residual weight of order $e^{-c}$ instead of zero. Use $-\infty$, or the dtype's most negative finite value. Second, an entirely masked row — which arises for padding query positions, not for causal masking, since the diagonal is always visible — makes softmax compute $0/0$ and emit NaN that propagates through the whole batch on the backward pass. Zero those output rows explicitly.

18.5 The Full Block: Residual Stream, Feed-Forward, Norms

A transformer block is two sublayers, each wrapped in a residual connection. In the modern pre-norm arrangement,

$$h = x + \mathrm{MHA}\big(\mathrm{LN}(x)\big), \qquad y = h + W_2\,\phi\big(W_1\,\mathrm{LN}(h) + c_1\big) + c_2,$$

with $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}} \times d}$, $d_{\text{ff}} = 4d$ conventionally, and $\phi$ a GELU or a gated variant. The original post-norm form, $x \leftarrow \mathrm{LN}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$, puts a normalization on the residual path; the gradient must then pass through every LayerNorm on its way back, and training a deep post-norm stack requires a learning-rate warmup to avoid divergence in the first few hundred steps. Pre-norm leaves an unobstructed identity path from the loss to every layer's input, trains stably without that warmup (Xiong et al., 2020), and is what essentially every model since GPT-2 uses — though production runs still schedule one, for the optimizer's moment estimates rather than for the norms. Its cost is that the residual stream's variance grows roughly linearly with depth, since each block adds a roughly independent increment, so a final LayerNorm before the output head is mandatory. Certain

Parameter count, exactly, with $d_{\text{ff}} = 4d$: attention contributes $4d^2 + 4d$, the FFN $8d^2 + 5d$, and the two LayerNorms $4d$, for $12d^2 + 13d$ per block — the $12d^2$ per layer that Chapter 24's scaling laws take as given. For GPT-2 small ($d = 768$, $L = 12$, vocabulary $50257$, context $1024$): $7{,}087{,}872$ parameters per block, $85{,}054{,}464$ across 12 blocks, plus $38{,}597{,}376$ token embeddings, $786{,}432$ position embeddings and $1{,}536$ for the final LayerNorm, totalling $124{,}439{,}808$ — the familiar 124M, with the output head tied to the embedding matrix. Certain

18.6 MQA, GQA, and KV-Cache Economics

During autoregressive decoding, each new token's keys and values are appended to a cache so that previously computed ones are never recomputed. The cache holds

$$\text{bytes} \;=\; 2\,L\,n\,H_{kv}\,d_h\,b ,$$

two tensors per layer, $L$ layers, $n$ positions, $H_{kv}$ key/value heads of width $d_h$, at $b$ bytes per element. This is per sequence, and it scales with batch size, which is what makes it the binding constraint on serving throughput (Chapter 33). For $d = 4096$, $H = 32$, $L = 32$, $n = 8192$, fp16, the artifact computes $4.000$ GiB — roughly a third of the $12.5$ GiB of fp16 weights a 7B-class model of that shape carries, for a single conversation. Verify

Multi-query attention (Shazeer) keeps $H$ query heads but shares one key/value head, $H_{kv} = 1$, cutting the cache by $32\times$ to $0.125$ GiB in that configuration. Grouped-query attention interpolates: $H_{kv}$ groups, each shared by $H/H_{kv}$ query heads, so $H_{kv} = 8$ gives $1.000$ GiB at $4\times$ reduction. The reason the reduction matters more than the FLOP saving is arithmetic intensity: in the decode step each cached KV element is read once and used in a handful of multiply–adds, so the attention step is purely memory-bandwidth-bound and its wall-clock is proportional to cache bytes moved, not FLOPs (Chapter 30).

The empirical claim — that GQA at $H_{kv} = 8$ recovers essentially all of MHA's quality while MQA at $H_{kv} = 1$ measurably loses some, and that an existing MHA checkpoint can be converted by mean-pooling each group's KV projections and uptraining on a few percent of the original tokens — comes from Ainslie et al. (2023) and has been reproduced at scale by the Llama-2/3 and Mistral families. Whether the loss at $H_{kv}=1$ is intrinsic or a training-budget artifact is not settled; DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention, which caches a low-rank joint projection instead of reducing head count, reports beating MHA quality at a smaller cache than GQA, which would suggest the head-count axis was never the right one. Contested The experiment that settles it is a matched-compute sweep of $H_{kv}$ and latent rank at fixed cache bytes; published comparisons vary too many things at once.

18.7 Complexity Accounting and the Quadratic Wall

Count a multiply–add as 2 FLOPs. One block's forward pass over $n$ tokens costs

$$\underbrace{8nd^2}_{Q,K,V,O \text{ projections}} \;+\; \underbrace{4n\,d\,d_{\text{ff}}}_{\text{FFN}} \;+\; \underbrace{4n^2d}_{QK^{\top} \text{ and } AV} .$$

The quadratic term overtakes the FFN term when $4n^2d = 4nd\,d_{\text{ff}}$, i.e. at

$$n^{*} = d_{\text{ff}} = 4d \quad(\text{conventional expansion}),$$

and it overtakes all three linear terms combined at $n = 2d + d_{\text{ff}} = 6d$. This is the crossover stated in terms of model width: attention is a minor cost well below a sequence length of four times the residual width, and the single dominant term above six times it. At $n = 4d$ exactly it equals the FFN term but is still only two thirds of the linear total. For $d = 768$ that is $n^{*} = 3072$; for $d = 12288$ it is $49152$. Equivalently, the standard training-compute estimate $C \approx 6ND$ (Chapter 24), which counts only the linear terms, is short by a factor $1 + n/(6d)$ — under 3% for GPT-3's $n=2048$, $d=12288$, but a factor of $6.3$ for a 128K context at $d = 4096$. Certain

Two honest qualifications. FLOPs are not time: the two attention matmuls have far lower arithmetic intensity than the projections, and before FlashAttention the real limit was materializing the $n \times n$ matrix in HBM, not multiplying by it. And the wall is quadratic in compute, not memory, once attention is tiled — which is why 1M-token contexts exist at all despite $4n^2d$ being astronomically large.

18.8 The Residual Stream as a Communication Channel

Reading the pre-norm block as $x^{(l+1)} = x^{(l)} + (\text{increment})$ makes the residual stream the object of interest: a $d$-dimensional bus that every layer reads from and adds to, and the only channel between layers. Anything layer 20 needs from layer 3 was written into that bus and not overwritten — there is no other path. Two consequences follow. First, the bus has finite bandwidth: $d$ dimensions shared by all $L$ layers' worth of features, so features must either occupy near-orthogonal subspaces or tolerate interference, and the number of features a network represents far exceeds $d$ (Chapter 37's superposition). Second, the division of labour is clean: attention is the only operation that moves information between positions, and the FFN is the only one that transforms information within a position. Every subsequent architecture in Part IV — state space models included (Chapter 21) — keeps this factorization and replaces only the mixer. Likely

Artifact 18.1 — Multi-head attention and a pre-norm transformer block in NumPy

A complete block from scratch, with four independent verifications: the forward pass against torch.nn.MultiheadAttention with transplanted weights, the analytic backward pass against central finite differences on every parameter tensor and on the input, and token-at-a-time KV-cached decoding against full recomputation — the assertion that catches real cache bugs, since an off-by-one in the mask offset or a stale cache still produces plausible text. It closes with the FLOP and cache tables of Sections 18.6 and 18.7.

"""
Artifact 18.1 -- Multi-head attention and a pre-norm transformer block, from scratch.
Verifies: (1) logit variance is d_k unscaled and ~1 after dividing by sqrt(d_k);
(2) NumPy MHA forward == torch.nn.MultiheadAttention with transplanted weights;
(3) analytic backward (incl. softmax Jacobian) == central finite differences;
(4) incremental KV-cached decoding == full recomputation;
(5) FLOP and KV-cache tables locating where quadratic attention overtakes the FFN.
Pure NumPy core; torch is a guarded cross-check only.
"""
import numpy as np
try:
    import torch
    import torch.nn as nn
except ImportError:                      # the artifact must run without torch
    torch = None

# --------------------------------------------------------------------- primitives

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    """Max-subtracted softmax: the shift is exact (softmax is shift-invariant) and
    is the only thing keeping exp() out of overflow. See Chapter 5."""
    e = np.exp(z - np.max(z, axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / np.sum(e, axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def softmax_backward(dA, A, axis=-1):
    """VJP for p = softmax(s): ds = p * (dp - <dp, p>). This is dp contracted with
    J = diag(p) - p p^T, done without ever forming the T x T Jacobian."""
    return A * (dA - np.sum(dA * A, axis=axis, keepdims=True))

def gelu(x):
    c = np.sqrt(2.0 / np.pi)
    return 0.5 * x * (1.0 + np.tanh(c * (x + 0.044715 * x ** 3)))

def gelu_grad(x):
    c = np.sqrt(2.0 / np.pi)
    t = np.tanh(c * (x + 0.044715 * x ** 3))
    return 0.5 * (1 + t) + 0.5 * x * (1 - t * t) * c * (1 + 3 * 0.044715 * x ** 2)

def layernorm(x, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    inv = 1.0 / np.sqrt(x.var(-1, keepdims=True) + eps)
    xhat = (x - x.mean(-1, keepdims=True)) * inv
    return g * xhat + b, (xhat, inv, g)

def layernorm_backward(dy, cache):
    xhat, inv, g = cache
    d = xhat.shape[-1]
    dg = (dy * xhat).reshape(-1, d).sum(0)
    db = dy.reshape(-1, d).sum(0)
    dxhat = dy * g
    dx = inv * (dxhat - dxhat.mean(-1, keepdims=True)
                - xhat * (dxhat * xhat).mean(-1, keepdims=True))
    return dx, dg, db

# --------------------------------------------------------------------- attention

class MHA:
    """Weights act as y = W x on column vectors, so row-of-tokens code is X @ W.T."""

    def __init__(self, d, H, rng):
        self.d, self.H, self.dh = d, H, d // H
        s = d ** -0.5
        self.p = dict(Wq=rng.normal(0, s, (d, d)), Wk=rng.normal(0, s, (d, d)),
                      Wv=rng.normal(0, s, (d, d)), Wo=rng.normal(0, s, (d, d)),
                      bq=rng.normal(0, .1, d), bk=rng.normal(0, .1, d),
                      bv=rng.normal(0, .1, d), bo=rng.normal(0, .1, d))

    def _split(self, Z):                 # (T,d) -> (H,T,dh)
        return Z.reshape(Z.shape[0], self.H, self.dh).transpose(1, 0, 2)

    def _merge(self, Z):                 # (H,T,dh) -> (T,d)
        return Z.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(-1, self.d)

    def forward(self, X, causal=True, cache=None, offset=0):
        """cache=None: full forward. cache={'K':...,'V':...}: append this step's K,V
        and attend over everything stored. offset = absolute index of X[0]."""
        p = self.p
        Q = self._split(X @ p["Wq"].T + p["bq"])
        K = self._split(X @ p["Wk"].T + p["bk"])
        V = self._split(X @ p["Wv"].T + p["bv"])
        if cache is not None:
            if cache["K"] is not None:
                K = np.concatenate([cache["K"], K], axis=1)
                V = np.concatenate([cache["V"], V], axis=1)
            cache["K"], cache["V"] = K, V
        S = (Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1)) / np.sqrt(self.dh)        # (H,Tq,Tk)
        if causal:
            i = np.arange(S.shape[1])[:, None] + offset
            j = np.arange(S.shape[2])[None, :]
            # MASK THEN SOFTMAX: additive -inf on logits, never a multiply on the
            # probabilities. Zeroing after softmax leaves the denominator wrong.
            S = np.where(j <= i, S, -np.inf)
        A = softmax(S)
        Ctx = self._merge(A @ V)
        self.cache = (X, Q, K, V, A, Ctx)
        return Ctx @ p["Wo"].T + p["bo"]

    def backward(self, dO):
        X, Q, K, V, A, Ctx = self.cache
        p, g = self.p, {}
        g["Wo"], g["bo"] = dO.T @ Ctx, dO.sum(0)
        dCtx = self._split(dO @ p["Wo"])
        dA = dCtx @ V.transpose(0, 2, 1)
        dV = A.transpose(0, 2, 1) @ dCtx
        dS = softmax_backward(dA, A) / np.sqrt(self.dh)
        dQ, dK = dS @ K, dS.transpose(0, 2, 1) @ Q
        dX = np.zeros_like(X)
        for nm, dZ in (("q", self._merge(dQ)), ("k", self._merge(dK)),
                       ("v", self._merge(dV))):
            g["W" + nm], g["b" + nm] = dZ.T @ X, dZ.sum(0)
            dX = dX + dZ @ p["W" + nm]
        return dX, g

class Block:
    """Pre-norm: h = x + Attn(LN(x)); y = h + FFN(LN(h)). The residual stream is never
    normalized in place -- each sublayer reads a normalized copy of it and writes back
    an unnormalized increment."""

    def __init__(self, d, H, dff, rng):
        self.attn = MHA(d, H, rng)
        self.p = dict(g1=np.ones(d), b1=np.zeros(d), g2=np.ones(d), b2=np.zeros(d),
                      W1=rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5, (dff, d)), c1=np.zeros(dff),
                      W2=rng.normal(0, dff ** -0.5, (d, dff)), c2=np.zeros(d))

    def forward(self, X, cache=None, offset=0):
        p = self.p
        n1, c1 = layernorm(X, p["g1"], p["b1"])
        h = X + self.attn.forward(n1, cache=cache, offset=offset)
        n2, c2 = layernorm(h, p["g2"], p["b2"])
        u = n2 @ p["W1"].T + p["c1"]
        a = gelu(u)
        self.cache = (c1, c2, n2, u, a)
        return h + a @ p["W2"].T + p["c2"]

    def backward(self, dY):
        p, (c1, c2, n2, u, a) = self.p, self.cache
        g = {"W2": dY.T @ a, "c2": dY.sum(0)}
        du = (dY @ p["W2"]) * gelu_grad(u)
        g["W1"], g["c1"] = du.T @ n2, du.sum(0)
        dh, g["g2"], g["b2"] = layernorm_backward(du @ p["W1"], c2)
        dh = dh + dY                                   # residual around the FFN
        dn1, ga = self.attn.backward(dh)
        dX, g["g1"], g["b1"] = layernorm_backward(dn1, c1)
        return dX + dh, {**g, **{"attn." + k: v for k, v in ga.items()}}

    def params(self):
        return {**self.p, **{"attn." + k: v for k, v in self.attn.p.items()}}

# --------------------------------------------------------------------- checks

def check_scaling(rng, dk=64, n=200_000):
    q, k = rng.normal(size=(n, dk)), rng.normal(size=(n, dk))
    raw = (q * k).sum(1)
    print(f"  Var(q.k)          = {raw.var():8.3f}   (predicted d_k = {dk})")
    print(f"  Var(q.k/sqrt(dk)) = {(raw / np.sqrt(dk)).var():8.3f}   (predicted 1.000)")
    lo = softmax(raw[:8][None, :])[0].max()
    hi = softmax(raw[:8][None, :] / np.sqrt(dk))[0].max()
    print(f"  max prob over 8 keys: unscaled {lo:.4f}  scaled {hi:.4f}")

def check_torch(blk, X, d, H):
    if torch is None:
        print("  [skipped: torch not installed]")
        return
    m = nn.MultiheadAttention(d, H, batch_first=True, dtype=torch.float64)
    p, T = blk.attn.p, X.shape[0]
    with torch.no_grad():
        m.in_proj_weight.copy_(torch.tensor(np.concatenate([p["Wq"], p["Wk"], p["Wv"]])))
        m.in_proj_bias.copy_(torch.tensor(np.concatenate([p["bq"], p["bk"], p["bv"]])))
        m.out_proj.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(p["Wo"]))
        m.out_proj.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(p["bo"]))
        mask = torch.triu(torch.full((T, T), float("-inf"), dtype=torch.float64), 1)
        t = torch.tensor(X)[None]
        ref, _ = m(t, t, t, attn_mask=mask, need_weights=False)
    err = np.abs(blk.attn.forward(X) - ref[0].numpy()).max()
    print(f"  max|numpy - torch.nn.MultiheadAttention| = {err:.3e}")
    assert err < 1e-9, err

def check_backward(blk, X, G, rng, k=4, eps=1e-6):
    Y = blk.forward(X)
    dX, grads = blk.backward(G)
    def loss():
        return np.sum(blk.forward(X) * G)
    worst = 0.0
    targets = [(P, grads[nm]) for nm, P in blk.params().items()] + [(X, dX)]
    for P, gm in targets:
        for _ in range(k):
            ix = tuple(rng.integers(0, s) for s in P.shape)
            old = P[ix]
            P[ix] = old + eps; lp = loss()
            P[ix] = old - eps; lm = loss()
            P[ix] = old
            num = (lp - lm) / (2 * eps)
            worst = max(worst, abs(num - gm[ix]) / max(1.0, abs(num)))
    print(f"  worst relative grad error, {k} coords per tensor = {worst:.3e}")
    assert worst < 1e-6, worst
    return Y

def check_kv_cache(blk, X, Y_full):
    """The assertion that catches real cache bugs: token-at-a-time decoding must
    reproduce the full-sequence forward exactly, offset in the causal mask included."""
    cache, rows = {"K": None, "V": None}, []
    for t in range(X.shape[0]):
        rows.append(blk.forward(X[t:t + 1], cache=cache, offset=t)[0])
    err = np.abs(np.stack(rows) - Y_full).max()
    print(f"  max|cached decode - full recompute| = {err:.3e}")
    assert err < 1e-6, err

def flop_table(d=768, H=12, dff=None):
    dff = dff or 4 * d
    print(f"  d_model={d} heads={H} d_head={d//H} d_ff={dff}  (one block, fwd, 2 FLOP/MAC)")
    print(f"  {'n':>6} {'QKVO 8nd^2':>14} {'FFN 4n d dff':>15} {'attn 4n^2 d':>15} {'ratio':>7}")
    for n in (128, 512, 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096, 8192, 16384):
        qkvo, ffn, att = 8 * n * d * d, 4 * n * d * dff, 4 * n * n * d
        print(f"  {n:>6} {qkvo:>14,} {ffn:>15,} {att:>15,} {att/ffn:>7.3f}")
    print(f"  attn == FFN at n = d_ff = {dff} = {dff//d}*d_model")
    print(f"  attn == all linear terms at n = 2d + d_ff = {2*d + dff}")

def kv_cache_table(d=4096, H=32, L=32, n=8192, bytes_per=2):
    dh = d // H
    print(f"  d={d} H={H} d_head={dh} L={L} n={n}  fp16 KV cache, one sequence")
    for name, Hkv in (("MHA (H_kv=32)", 32), ("GQA (H_kv=8)", 8), ("GQA (H_kv=4)", 4),
                      ("MQA (H_kv=1)", 1)):
        b = 2 * L * n * Hkv * dh * bytes_per
        print(f"  {name:<16} {b/2**30:8.3f} GiB   reduction {H/Hkv:5.1f}x")

def main():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    d, H, dff, T = 32, 4, 64, 12
    blk = Block(d, H, dff, rng)
    X, G = rng.normal(size=(T, d)), rng.normal(size=(T, d))
    print("[1] scaling factor and logit variance")
    check_scaling(rng)
    print("[2] forward vs torch.nn.MultiheadAttention (transplanted weights)")
    check_torch(blk, X, d, H)
    print("[3] backward vs central finite differences")
    Y = check_backward(blk, X, G, rng)
    print("[4] KV-cached incremental decode vs full recompute")
    check_kv_cache(blk, X, Y)
    print("[5] FLOP accounting")
    flop_table()
    print("[6] KV-cache economics")
    kv_cache_table()
    print("all checks passed")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Running it: the empirical logit variance is $63.770$ against the predicted $d_k = 64$, and $0.996$ after scaling; the largest of 8 attention weights falls from $0.9998$ to $0.5119$, which is the saturation argument of Section 18.2.1 measured. The forward pass matches torch to $8.882\times10^{-16}$ in float64, the worst relative gradient error over four sampled coordinates per tensor is $6.474\times10^{-9}$, and cached decoding reproduces the full forward to $8.882\times10^{-16}$, which is float64 rounding and nothing else: the same operations, reordered. The FLOP table crosses over at $n = 3072 = 4d$ for $d = 768$, with the attention/FFN ratio running $0.042$ at $n=128$, $1.000$ at $n=3072$, and $5.333$ at $n=16384$.

Under Encryption

Softmax is the hardest single operation in an encrypted transformer, and it is hard three times over. It needs an exponential, which is not a polynomial and must be approximated on a bounded range; a division by a data-dependent sum, which under CKKS means an iterative inverse (Goldschmidt or Newton) costing several multiplicative levels; and a maximum subtraction for numerical stability, which is a comparison — the single most expensive primitive in homomorphic arithmetic, since comparison is a step function and needs a deep composite-polynomial approximation. The matmuls on either side, $QK^{\top}$ and $AV$, are the one thing FHE does well.

This is why every system in Chapter 40 is structurally a different answer to the same question about softmax: approximate it polynomially, hand it to a garbled circuit or a secure two-party protocol, or abandon it. Some abandon it — replacing $\mathrm{softmax}(s)$ with a normalized $\mathrm{ReLU}(s)$ or a plain quadratic, both worse in the clear but evaluable under encryption at a fraction of the depth. Note that the mask is free: adding $-\infty$ (in practice, a large negative plaintext constant) to a ciphertext logit is a plaintext addition, depth zero. Chapter 38 does the depth arithmetic for one attention block, and Chapter 39 takes up the approximation problem in detail.

Key Takeaways
  • Attention is soft dictionary lookup: $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k})V$ produces a convex combination of value rows, so it can interpolate among stored values but never extrapolate beyond them. Certain
  • The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor exists solely to keep logit variance at $\Theta(1)$ at initialization, because $\mathrm{Var}(q^{\top}k) = d_k$ and a saturated softmax has a vanishing Jacobian $\mathrm{diag}(p) - pp^{\top}$. Certain
  • Mask by adding $-\infty$ to logits, never by multiplying the probabilities: the second version leaves the softmax denominator wrong, trains anyway, and silently converges worse. Certain
  • A block costs $12d^2 + 13d$ parameters and $8nd^2 + 4nd\,d_{\text{ff}} + 4n^2d$ forward FLOPs; the quadratic term overtakes the FFN at $n = d_{\text{ff}} = 4d$ and all linear terms at $n = 6d$. Certain
  • GQA at $H_{kv} = 8$ cuts the KV cache $4\times$ (MQA, $32\times$) at little measured quality cost, but whether head-count reduction or low-rank latent caching is the right axis is unsettled and needs a matched-cache-byte comparison. Contested
Chapter 19

Positional Information and Long Context

Learning Objectives
  • Prove that rotary position embedding makes the query–key inner product a function of the position difference alone, and derive the block-rotation form from that requirement.
  • Compare sinusoidal, learned-absolute, ALiBi, rotary, and no-positional-encoding on extrapolation, and state precisely what each one generalizes.
  • Explain position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, and YaRN in terms of wavelength relative to trained context length $T_{\text{train}}$, and compute which rotary pairs are long-wavelength for a given base $b$.
  • Explain the attention-sink phenomenon and why the first key–value pair must be retained under streaming or windowed attention.
  • Implement rotary embeddings and a context-extension scheme in working code.
Read alongside — Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) for a line-by-line rotary implementation you can diff against the artifact below; Prince, Understanding Deep Learning for the clearest pictures of what a position encoding does to an attention map; and Stanford CS336, whose assignments make you write the rotary cache and then break it at long context, which is the fastest way to internalise Section 19.5.

Chapter 18 built attention and left one hole: the operator it defined is permutation-equivariant, so a transformer without extra machinery cannot tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog." This chapter fills the hole and then follows the consequences to the frontier. The through-line is a single claim: rotary embeddings won because they encode relative position as a rotation inside the dot product rather than as an additive signal on the input, and every context-extension method — position interpolation, NTK-aware base scaling, YaRN — is a different answer to one question, namely which frequency bands may be interpolated. Section 19.7 turns to the attention sink, a phenomenon that only becomes visible once you try to evict tokens from a cache; Chapter 33 uses that result when it builds a serving stack. Chapter 21 will ask whether any of this is necessary at all.

19.1 Why Attention Needs Position at All

Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ be a sequence of $T$ token representations and $P$ a $T\times T$ permutation matrix. Single-head attention computes $\mathrm{Attn}(X) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{XW_Q W_K^\top X^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) X W_V$. Substituting $PX$ gives $\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(P \frac{XW_QW_K^\top X^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} P^\top\right) P X W_V = P\,\mathrm{Attn}(X)$, because row-wise softmax commutes with a permutation that acts identically on rows and columns. The feed-forward and normalization sublayers act per position, so the whole transformer block is permutation-equivariant. The causal mask breaks the symmetry only partially: it fixes an ordering (token $t$ sees $\{1,\dots,t\}$) but supplies no metric — nothing distinguishes distance 3 from distance 300 except the number of tokens in the softmax denominator.

So position must enter somewhere. There are exactly three places: added to the input embedding (absolute encodings), added to the attention logits (relative biases), or applied as a transformation of $q$ and $k$ before their inner product (rotary). The third is the one that survived, and Section 19.4 explains why in terms of a group-theoretic uniqueness argument, not taste.

19.2 Sinusoidal and Learned Embeddings

The original transformer added a fixed sinusoidal vector to the token embedding: $\mathrm{PE}(m, 2i) = \sin\!\left(m\,\omega_i\right)$, $\mathrm{PE}(m, 2i+1) = \cos\!\left(m\,\omega_i\right)$ with $\omega_i = 10000^{-2i/d}$. Throughout this chapter $m$ and $n$ denote absolute positions and $T$ the sequence length. The design has one genuinely elegant property: $\mathrm{PE}(m+k)$ is a fixed linear function of $\mathrm{PE}(m)$, since each $(\sin, \cos)$ pair rotates by $k\omega_i$. The map is $\begin{pmatrix}\cos k\omega_i & \sin k\omega_i\\ -\sin k\omega_i & \cos k\omega_i\end{pmatrix}$ — a rotation. That is RoPE's mechanism, discovered in 2017 and then applied to the wrong object.

The wrongness is this. The attention logit is $(x_m + p_m)^\top W_Q W_K^\top (x_n + p_n)$, which expands into four terms: content–content, content–position, position–content, and position–position. Only the last depends on $(m,n)$ alone — and even it is translation-invariant only when $W_QW_K^\top$ acts as a multiple of the identity on each $(\sin,\cos)$ pair; for a general $W_QW_K^\top$ the cross-frequency products $\sin(m\omega_i)\cos(n\omega_j)$, $i\neq j$, depend on $m$ and $n$ separately. The two cross terms make the logit depend on absolute position in a way the model must learn to cancel. Empirically sinusoidal encodings extrapolate poorly — perplexity degrades sharply past the trained length even though the formula is defined for all $m$. Certain

Learned absolute embeddings (GPT-2, BERT, ViT) replace $p_m$ with a row of a trainable $T_{\max}\times d$ table. They do not extrapolate at all: position $T_{\max}$ has no row. They also spend $T_{\max} d$ parameters that carry no information for most of training — for $T_{\max}=2048$, $d=1600$ that is 3.3M parameters, which for GPT-2 XL is a rounding error but is a real waste at small scale.

19.3 Relative Position Biases and ALiBi

The obvious repair is to move position out of the input and into the logit. T5 adds a learned scalar $B_{h}[\text{bucket}(m-n)]$ per head, with logarithmically spaced buckets so that distances beyond a cap share a parameter. Buckets make the scheme technically defined at any length, but the far bucket was trained on almost no data.

ALiBi removes the parameters entirely: the logit becomes $\frac{q_m^\top k_n}{\sqrt{d_k}} - s_h\,(m-n)$ for $m \ge n$, where the per-head slope $s_h$ is a fixed geometric sequence, $s_h = 2^{-8h/H}$ for $h = 1,\dots,H$. Each head is a soft exponential recency window with a different width, since a bias linear in distance multiplies the pre-softmax exponential by $e^{-s_h(m-n)}$.

ALiBi extrapolates in the narrow sense that perplexity does not blow up past the trained length. What it generalizes is the recency prior, not long-range retrieval: the bias term is unbounded below, so a head with slope $s_h = 2^{-1}$ suppresses a token 100 positions back by $e^{-50}$. Feeding a 32k document to an ALiBi model trained at 2k gives stable perplexity and near-zero ability to retrieve from the far past, because most heads have already annihilated it. Stable perplexity at length is not long context; that distinction is the whole of Section 19.8. Certain

No-positional-encoding (NoPE) is the limiting case: give a causal decoder nothing at all.
