Summing the geometric series gives $\hat K(z) = \tilde C(I - z\bar A)^{-1}\bar B$ where $\tilde C$ absorbs the truncation correction $(I - \bar A^T)$. The resolvent $(I - z\bar A)^{-1}$ of a DPLR matrix is handled by the Woodbury identity: for rank-one $P,Q$,

$$(\Lambda - PQ^{*})^{-1} = \Lambda^{-1} + \Lambda^{-1}P\big(1 - Q^{*}\Lambda^{-1}P\big)^{-1}Q^{*}\Lambda^{-1},$$

which reduces every evaluation to four sums of the form $\sum_{n} \frac{u_n v_n}{\omega - \lambda_n}$. That is a Cauchy kernel, computable for all $T$ frequencies at once in $O((N+T)\log^2(N+T))$ by fast multipole methods, or $O(NT)$ by brute force with tiny constants. The bill: $\tilde O(N+T)$ to build the kernel, $O(T\log T)$ to apply it.

21.4 Diagonal SSMs and Gating

Then DSS and S4D showed the low-rank correction is nearly dispensable. Drop $PQ^*$, keep a complex diagonal $A = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N)$ in conjugate pairs so the kernel stays real, and initialize the poles on a line: S4D-Lin sets $\lambda_n = -\tfrac12 + i\pi n$. The kernel becomes a single matrix of powers, $K_\ell = 2\,\mathrm{Re}\sum_n C_n\bar B_n\bar\lambda_n^{\,\ell}$, computable directly — no Woodbury, no Cauchy kernel, twenty lines of code. Long Range Arena accuracy barely moves.

Since $\bar\lambda_n^\ell = e^{-\alpha_n \ell}e^{i\omega_n\ell}$, the kernel is a sum of $N$ damped sinusoids. An S4D layer is a learned bank of damped-oscillator filters, parameterized by decay rate and frequency rather than by $T$ free taps. That is why it has long memory with few parameters, and also why it is weak at anything content-addressed: the filter bank is fixed once trained, so what it attends to is a function of offset, never of content.

H3 fixed a specific failure — associative recall, the induction-head task of Chapter 18 — by pairing a shift-SSM with a diagonal SSM and a multiplicative gate. The Mamba block simplified this to: expand the residual stream by a factor of 2, apply a short causal depthwise conv1d and SiLU, run the SSM, gate elementwise against a second SiLU branch, project back. The conv1d matters more than it looks; it supplies the short-range mixing the SSM is bad at.

21.5 Mamba: Selective State Spaces

LTI is a hard ceiling. A convolution's response to a token depends only on that token's distance from the output position, so the layer cannot decide that this token is a name worth remembering and that one is a comma worth forgetting: nothing reads content before the state update is chosen. Attention's entire content is that mechanism.

Definition 21.2 (Selective SSM)

Make the discretization step and the input/output projections functions of the current token: $$\Delta_t = \mathrm{softplus}\big(s_\Delta(x_t)\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}_{>0}, \qquad B_t = W_B x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N}, \qquad C_t = W_C x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N},$$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$ (diagonal, one $N$-state system per channel) left input-independent. Discretize per step: $\bar A_t = \exp(\Delta_t \odot A)$ and, using the first-order simplification $A^{-1}(e^{\Delta A}-1)\approx\Delta$ valid for small $\Delta A$, $\bar B_t = \Delta_t B_t$. The recurrence $h_t = \bar A_t \odot h_{t-1} + \bar B_t x_t$ carries a state $h_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times N}$, read out as $y_t = h_t C_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, and is now time-varying.

Read $\Delta_t$ as a soft gate. Large $\Delta_t$ makes $\bar A_t = e^{\Delta_t A} \to 0$ and $\bar B_t$ large: reset the state and write this token in. Small $\Delta_t$ makes $\bar A_t \to 1$ and $\bar B_t \to 0$: hold the state, ignore this token. That is an LSTM's forget/input gate rediscovered through the discretization: selectivity and gating are one story.

Three things break. First, there is no longer a single kernel $K$, so the FFT convolution is gone — every position has a different filter. Second, the computation is genuinely a $T$-step recurrence. Third, the discretized tensors $\bar A_t, \bar B_t$ have shape $(B, T, d, N)$: at $B=64$, $T=4096$, $d=2048$, $N=16$ in fp32 that is $64\cdot 4096\cdot 2048\cdot 16 \cdot 4 = 3.4\times 10^{10}$ bytes, roughly 34 GB. Materializing it is not an option. Certain

Mamba's answer is a fused kernel in the FlashAttention style of Chapter 31: load $A$, $\Delta$, $B$, $C$ from HBM into SRAM, perform discretization, scan and output contraction there, write only $y$ back, and recompute the intermediates during the backward pass instead of storing them. The arithmetic is unchanged; the memory traffic drops by a factor of roughly $N$.

21.5.1 The Parallel Scan

The scan itself is the mathematically interesting part. Each step is an affine map $f_t(h) = a_t h + b_t$, and affine maps are closed under composition:

$$(f_t \circ f_s)(h) = a_t(a_s h + b_s) + b_t = (a_t a_s)h + (a_t b_s + b_t).$$

So define $\oplus$ on parameter pairs by $(a_s,b_s)\oplus(a_t,b_t) = (a_t a_s,\; a_t b_s + b_t)$, with identity $(1,0)$. Function composition is associative, hence so is $\oplus$, and $h_t$ is the $t$-th prefix of a scan under $\oplus$. This is exactly the property $\tanh$ destroys, and exactly the reason removing the nonlinearity between steps was worth the expressivity.

Blelloch's work-efficient scan realizes it in two passes over a balanced binary tree. The up-sweep computes, at each internal node, the $\oplus$-aggregate of its subtree, in $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ levels. The root is then set to the identity and the down-sweep pushes prefixes back down: a node with incoming prefix $p$ gives $p$ to its left child and $p \oplus (\text{left aggregate})$ to its right, again in $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ levels. Total work is $2T-2$ applications of $\oplus$ — linear, unlike the $O(T\log T)$ of the naive Hillis–Steele scan — at depth $2\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$. At $T=4096$ that is 12 levels each way instead of 4096 sequential steps.

Common Pitfall

Never form $\prod_{r=s+1}^{t}a_r$ by multiplying, and never exponentiate before masking. Work in log space with $g_t = \sum_{r\le t}\log a_r$, so the product is $\exp(g_t - g_s)$. Two failures follow from getting this wrong. A direct cumprod of a few thousand factors below one underflows to exactly $0.0$ in fp32 within a few hundred steps, silently truncating memory and zeroing the gradient. And in the SSD form below, computing exp(g[:,None]-g[None,:]) and then applying the causal mask overflows to inf in the upper triangle — where the exponent is large and positive — and inf multiplied by a zero mask is NaN, not zero. Mask the exponent first, exponentiate second.

21.6 Mamba-2 and Structured State-Space Duality

Mamba-2 restricts the state transition further: instead of a diagonal $A_t$, use a scalar times the identity, $\bar A_t = a_t I_N$. It is a real loss; the payoff is that the model becomes a matrix multiplication.

Theorem 21.2 (Structured state-space duality)

Let $h_t = a_t h_{t-1} + B_t x_t^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times P}$ with $h_{-1}=0$, $a_t\in\mathbb{R}$, $B_t, C_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N}$, $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{P}$, and $y_t = C_t^{\top}h_t$. Stack $B,C \in \mathbb{R}^{T\times N}$, $X,Y \in \mathbb{R}^{T\times P}$ and define $L\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T}$ by $L_{ts} = \prod_{r=s+1}^{t}a_r$ for $s\le t$ and $0$ otherwise. Then $$Y = \big(L \odot CB^{\top}\big)\,X .$$ Moreover $L$ is 1-semiseparable: every submatrix lying strictly below the diagonal has rank exactly one.

Proof. Unrolling gives $h_t = \sum_{s\le t}\big(\prod_{r=s+1}^{t}a_r\big)B_s x_s^{\top}$, so $y_t = C_t^\top h_t = \sum_{s\le t} L_{ts}\,(C_t^{\top}B_s)\,x_s$, which is row $t$ of $(L\odot CB^\top)X$. For semiseparability, write $g_t = \sum_{r\le t}\log a_r$; then for $s \le t$, $L_{ts} = e^{g_t}e^{-g_s}$, an outer product of $(e^{g_t})_t$ with $(e^{-g_s})_s$ restricted to any strictly-lower block. $\blacksquare$

Compare to causal attention, which before row normalization is $Y = \big(M \odot \exp(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})\big)V$ with $M$ the binary causal mask — masking must precede the softmax, not follow it, or the rows renormalize over positions the model cannot see. Same shape, same masked-quadratic-form skeleton. The differences are exactly two: $M$ is replaced by a decayed mask $L$, and the exponential and its row normalizer are deleted. Deleting the softmax is what makes the recurrence associative and therefore scannable; keeping a mask that is 1-semiseparable rather than binary is what gives the recurrence a finite state. Attention with a $T$-growing KV cache and an SSM with an $N\times P$ state are the two evaluation orders of the same matrix.

Three payoffs. Speed: the practical algorithm is neither form but a chunked hybrid — split the sequence into blocks of length $Q$, compute the diagonal blocks with the quadratic form (dense matmuls, which run on tensor cores at full rate) and the off-diagonal blocks through the rank-one structure, carrying one state across chunk boundaries. Mamba-2's layer is reported 2–8$\times$ faster than Mamba-1's scan at equal quality. Verify Capacity: because the expensive part is now matmul rather than a memory-bound scan, $N$ can grow from 16 to 256 at modest cost, which recovers most of what the scalar-identity restriction gave up. Systems reuse: multi-head, grouped-query sharing of $B$ and $C$, tensor parallelism and sequence parallelism all transfer unchanged from the attention stack.

21.7 Linear Attention, RWKV, RetNet, and the Unified View

Theorem 21.2 makes an entire literature collapse into one axis: what structure does the state-transition matrix have? Every model below is $S_t = G_t\,S_{t-1} + (\text{rank-1 write})$ read out by a query, differing only in $G_t$.

ModelTransition $G_t$Input-dependent?Consequence
Linear attention (2020)$I$nono forgetting; state saturates
RetNet$\gamma I$, $\gamma$ fixed per headnofixed exponential decay; still LTI
RWKV-4$e^{-w}I$, learned per channelnochannelwise decay, LTI
S4 / S4D$e^{\Delta A}$ diagonal, fixednoFFT convolution available
Mamba$\exp(\Delta_t \odot A)$ diagonalyesselective; scan only
Mamba-2 / SSD$a_t I$yesmasked matmul; large $N$
DeltaNet$I - \beta_t k_tk_t^{\top}$yesrank-1 update; state tracking
Softmax attention— (state grows with $t$)—exact recall, $O(T)$ cache

The table is a tradeoff. Richer $G_t$ means more expressive state dynamics and a more expensive scan; DeltaNet's non-diagonal $G_t$ buys genuine state tracking at the price of a much harder parallel form — but only with $\beta_t$ extended to $2$, making $I-\beta_tk_tk_t^\top$ a reflection: Grazzi et al. (2024) show $\beta_t\in[0,1]$ still fails parity, while eigenvalues reaching $-1$ compose permutations, which diagonal transitions provably cannot. Likely

21.8 Hybrids and the Recall–Efficiency Tradeoff

The central claim is contested. Contested

For. At small-to-mid scale, selective SSMs match or beat transformers on next-token perplexity trained on the same data, and the inference economics are not close: decoding is $O(1)$ memory per token against a KV cache linear in context, giving several-fold throughput at long context. NVIDIA's Nemotron-H family replaces most self-attention layers with Mamba-2 blocks and reports up to $3\times$ faster inference at matched or better accuracy against Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.1 baselines. Verify

Against. The state is $N\times P$ scalars, a number fixed at design time and independent of $T$. Jelassi et al. (2024) prove a two-layer transformer can copy strings of exponential length while any fixed-state recurrent model is information-theoretically bounded by its state size, and confirm the gap empirically on pretrained models: transformers dominate at copying and at retrieving arbitrary spans from context. Perplexity averages over a distribution in which exact recall is rare; the tasks people actually deploy — long-document question answering, in-context learning from many examples, agentic tool traces — are recall-heavy.

The decisive evidence is the deployment record. Essentially every serious production model in this family is a hybrid: Jamba interleaves attention with Mamba at roughly 1:7, Nemotron-H keeps about 8% attention, Falcon-H1 fuses the two in parallel within a layer, Zamba shares a global attention block. A hybrid is strictly more complex and more expensive than a pure SSM. That anyone builds one is the strongest available argument that the pure claim is false. My position: selective SSMs do not match transformers as a drop-in replacement, but a mostly-SSM hybrid beats both pure architectures on the quality-per-throughput frontier, and that is the real result. A handful of full-attention layers supplies the exact recall; the SSM layers supply cheap long-range mixing. What would change my mind: a pure SSM at $\ge$7B matching a same-data transformer on long-context needle retrieval and multi-hop recall, not perplexity.

The line has not stopped. Mamba-3 (Lahoti, Li, Chen, Wang, Bick, Kolter, Dao, Gu; arXiv 2603.15569, ICLR 2026; CMU, Princeton, Together AI, Cartesia) is motivated explicitly by inference cost rather than pretraining loss, and makes three changes to Mamba-2. It replaces the first-order Euler-style step of Definition 21.2 with an exponential-trapezoidal discretization, raising the local truncation error from $O(\Delta^2)$ to $O(\Delta^3)$ and implicitly convolving adjacent inputs into the state write — which lets it drop the short causal conv1d entirely. It generalizes the scalar-identity transition $a_t I$ to a complex-valued one — a rotation-scaling, shown equivalent to a real SSM with data-dependent RoPE applied to $B$ and $C$ — which restores state tracking: Mamba-3 solves parity and modular arithmetic, where Mamba-2 and other real-valued linear models are at chance. And it adds a MIMO structure that raises arithmetic intensity during decode. Reported: comparable perplexity to Mamba-2 at half the state size, +0.6 points average downstream over Gated DeltaNet at 1.5B with the MIMO variant reaching +1.8, and lower per-token decode latency. Verify Do not treat Mamba-2 as the frontier.

Artifact 21.1 — Three Equivalences: Scan, Convolution, and the SSD Duality

Pure NumPy, float64. A selective SSM computed twice (sequential recurrence, Blelloch scan); an S4D kernel applied three ways (FFT, naive Toeplitz, complex recurrence); Theorem 21.2 checked against the masked matmul, plus an SVD test of 1-semiseparability.

import time
import numpy as np

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None

RNG = np.random.default_rng(0)

# --- (A) Selective scan: h_t = abar_t (*) h_{t-1} + bbar_t ------------------
def make_selective(T, P, N, rng):
    A = -np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.5, size=(P, N)))          # A < 0: stable poles
    x = rng.normal(size=(T, P))
    # Delta = softplus(.) > 0 is the selectivity: per-token, per-channel step.
    Delta = np.log1p(np.exp(rng.normal(-0.5, 0.5, size=(T, P))))
    B = rng.normal(size=(T, N)) / np.sqrt(N)
    C = rng.normal(size=(T, N)) / np.sqrt(N)
    D = rng.normal(size=(P,))
    abar = np.exp(Delta[:, :, None] * A[None, :, :])        # (T,P,N)
    bbar = Delta[:, :, None] * B[:, None, :] * x[:, :, None]
    return abar, bbar, C, D, x

def scan_sequential(abar, bbar, C, D, x):
    """The obvious O(T) loop. Depth T: step t waits on step t-1."""
    T, P, N = abar.shape
    h = np.zeros((P, N)); y = np.empty((T, P))
    for t in range(T):
        h = abar[t] * h + bbar[t]
        y[t] = h @ C[t]
    return y + D * x

def blelloch_scan(a, b):
    """Work-efficient inclusive scan of the affine maps f_t(h) = a_t*h + b_t.
    (a_L,b_L) o (a_R,b_R) = (a_R a_L, a_R b_L + b_R), identity (1, 0).
    2T-2 total applications, ceil(log2 T) levels each way."""
    n = a.shape[0]
    m = 1 << (n - 1).bit_length()                # pad to a power of two
    tail = (m - n,) + a.shape[1:]
    A  = np.concatenate([a, np.ones(tail, a.dtype)])
    Bv = np.concatenate([b, np.zeros(tail, b.dtype)])
    a0, b0 = A.copy(), Bv.copy()
    s = 2                                        # ---- up-sweep ----
    while s <= m:
        h = s >> 1
        aL, bL = A[h - 1::s], Bv[h - 1::s]
        aR, bR = A[s - 1::s], Bv[s - 1::s]
        Bv[s - 1::s] = aR * bL + bR
        A[s - 1::s]  = aR * aL
        s <<= 1
    A[m - 1] = 1.0; Bv[m - 1] = 0.0              # root <- identity
    s = m                                        # ---- down-sweep ----
    while s >= 2:
        h = s >> 1
        ta, tb = A[h - 1::s].copy(), Bv[h - 1::s].copy()   # left aggregate
        A[h - 1::s]  = A[s - 1::s]                         # left <- prefix
        Bv[h - 1::s] = Bv[s - 1::s]
        Bv[s - 1::s] = ta * Bv[s - 1::s] + tb              # right <- prefix o left
        A[s - 1::s]  = ta * A[s - 1::s]
        s >>= 1
    return (a0 * Bv + b0)[:n]                    # exclusive -> inclusive

def scan_parallel(abar, bbar, C, D, x):
    h = blelloch_scan(abar, bbar)
    return np.einsum('tpn,tn->tp', h, C) + D * x

# --- (B) S4D: time-INVARIANT, so the whole map is one kernel ---------------
def s4d_kernel(T, N, dt):
    """S4D-Lin poles A_n = -1/2 + i*pi*n, ZOH-discretized."""
    A = -0.5 + 1j * np.pi * np.arange(N)
    Bc = np.ones(N, dtype=complex)
    Cc = (RNG.normal(size=N) + 1j * RNG.normal(size=N)) / np.sqrt(N)
    Abar = np.exp(dt * A)                        # ZOH state matrix
    Bbar = (Abar - 1.0) / A * Bc                 # ZOH input matrix
    powers = Abar[None, :] ** np.arange(T)[:, None]
    K = 2.0 * np.real(powers @ (Cc * Bbar))      # conj pairs -> real kernel
    return K, Abar, Bbar, Cc

def conv_fft(u, K):
    L = 1 << (2 * len(u) - 1).bit_length()        # zero-pad so it cannot wrap
    return np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(u, L) * np.fft.rfft(K, L), L)[:len(u)]

def conv_naive(u, K):
    T = len(u)
    idx = np.arange(T)[:, None] - np.arange(T)[None, :]
    M = np.where(idx >= 0, K[np.abs(idx)], 0.0)  # lower-triangular Toeplitz
    return M @ u

def lti_recurrence(u, Abar, Bbar, Cc):
    h = np.zeros_like(Abar); y = np.empty(len(u))
    for t, ut in enumerate(u):
        h = Abar * h + Bbar * ut
        y[t] = 2.0 * np.real(Cc @ h)
    return y

# --- (C) SSD: linear recurrence vs masked matmul ---------------------------
def make_ssd(T, P, N, rng):
    log_a = -np.exp(rng.normal(-1.0, 0.4, size=T))          # log a_t < 0
    B = rng.normal(size=(T, N)) / np.sqrt(N)
    C = rng.normal(size=(T, N)) / np.sqrt(N)
    X = rng.normal(size=(T, P))
    return log_a, B, C, X

def ssd_linear(log_a, B, C, X):
    T, N = B.shape; P = X.shape[1]
    a = np.exp(log_a); h = np.zeros((N, P)); Y = np.empty((T, P))
    for t in range(T):
        h = a[t] * h + np.outer(B[t], X[t])      # rank-1 state write
        Y[t] = C[t] @ h
    return Y

def semiseparable_mask(log_a):
    g = np.cumsum(log_a)
    E = np.tril(g[:, None] - g[None, :])         # mask first...
    return np.tril(np.exp(E))                    # ...then exponentiate

def ssd_quadratic(log_a, B, C, X):
    """Y = (L o C B^T) X. Mask the exponent BEFORE exponentiating: above the
    diagonal it is large and positive, exp() overflows to inf, and inf*0 = nan."""
    return (semiseparable_mask(log_a) * (C @ B.T)) @ X

def timed(fn, *args):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    T, P, N = 4096, 64, 16
    print(f"selective SSM: T={T} P={P} N={N}  (state = P*N = {P*N} scalars/layer)")
    abar, bbar, Cs, Ds, xs = make_selective(T, P, N, RNG)
    y_seq, t_seq = timed(scan_sequential, abar, bbar, Cs, Ds, xs)
    y_par, t_par = timed(scan_parallel,   abar, bbar, Cs, Ds, xs)
    r = np.max(np.abs(y_seq - y_par)) / np.max(np.abs(y_seq))
    print(f"  sequential recurrence   {t_seq*1e3:8.1f} ms   depth O(T)")
    print(f"  Blelloch parallel scan  {t_par*1e3:8.1f} ms   depth O(log T) "
          f"= {int(np.ceil(np.log2(T)))} levels")
    print(f"  max rel. difference     {r:.3e}")
    assert r < 1e-6, r

    Tc, Nc, dt = 4096, 64, 0.01
    K, Abar, Bbar, Cc = s4d_kernel(Tc, Nc, dt)
    u = RNG.normal(size=Tc)
    y_fft, t_fft = timed(conv_fft, u, K)
    y_nai, t_nai = timed(conv_naive, u, K)
    y_rec, t_rec = timed(lti_recurrence, u, Abar, Bbar, Cc)
    r_fft = np.max(np.abs(y_fft - y_nai)) / np.max(np.abs(y_nai))
    r_rec = np.max(np.abs(y_rec - y_nai)) / np.max(np.abs(y_nai))
    print(f"\nS4D convolution: T={Tc} N={Nc} dt={dt}")
    print(f"  FFT convolution         {t_fft*1e3:8.1f} ms   O(T log T)")
    print(f"  naive Toeplitz matmul   {t_nai*1e3:8.1f} ms   O(T^2)")
    print(f"  step-by-step recurrence {t_rec*1e3:8.1f} ms   O(T N)")
    print(f"  rel. err FFT vs naive       {r_fft:.3e}")
    print(f"  rel. err recurrence vs conv {r_rec:.3e}")
    assert r_fft < 1e-6 and r_rec < 1e-6, (r_fft, r_rec)

    Ts, Ps, Ns = 2048, 64, 64
    log_a, Bq, Cq, Xq = make_ssd(Ts, Ps, Ns, RNG)
    Y_lin,  t_lin  = timed(ssd_linear,    log_a, Bq, Cq, Xq)
    Y_quad, t_quad = timed(ssd_quadratic, log_a, Bq, Cq, Xq)
    r_ssd = np.max(np.abs(Y_lin - Y_quad)) / np.max(np.abs(Y_lin))
    print(f"\nSSD duality: T={Ts} P={Ps} N={Ns}")
    print(f"  linear recurrent form   {t_lin*1e3:8.1f} ms   O(T N P) time, O(N P) state")
    print(f"  quadratic masked matmul {t_quad*1e3:8.1f} ms   O(T^2 N) time, O(T^2) memory")
    print(f"  MAX REL DIFFERENCE      {r_ssd:.3e}   <-- the duality")
    assert r_ssd < 1e-5, r_ssd

    # Every strictly-lower submatrix of L has rank one: L[t,s] = e^{g_t} e^{-g_s}.
    Lmask = semiseparable_mask(log_a)
    sv = np.linalg.svd(Lmask[1024:1044, 1000:1020], compute_uv=False)
    print(f"  off-diagonal 20x20 block singular values: "
          f"s1={sv[0]:.3e}  s2/s1={sv[1]/sv[0]:.2e}  (rank 1)")
    assert sv[1] / sv[0] < 1e-12

    if torch is None:
        print("\n[skipped: torch not installed]")
    else:
        with torch.no_grad():
            ut, Kt = torch.from_numpy(u), torch.from_numpy(K)
            Lp = 1 << (2 * Tc - 1).bit_length()
            yt = torch.fft.irfft(torch.fft.rfft(ut, Lp) * torch.fft.rfft(Kt, Lp),
                                 Lp)[:Tc].numpy()
            Mt = torch.from_numpy(Lmask * (Cq @ Bq.T)) @ torch.from_numpy(Xq)
        print(f"\n[torch] FFT conv rel. err   "
              f"{np.max(np.abs(yt - y_nai))/np.max(np.abs(y_nai)):.3e}")
        print(f"[torch] SSD matmul rel. err "
              f"{np.max(np.abs(Mt.numpy() - Y_lin))/np.max(np.abs(Y_lin)):.3e}")
    print("\nall assertions passed")

The run completes in under 4 s. The two scan forms agree to a relative $1.845\times10^{-16}$ — machine precision, since they perform the same additions in a different order. FFT convolution matches the naive Toeplitz product to $4.320\times10^{-16}$ and the recurrence matches to $8.780\times10^{-15}$, at about $2$ ms against $800$ ms at $T=4096$. The duality assertion holds at $4.211\times10^{-14}$ ($T=2048$, $N=P=64$), and the $20\times20$ off-diagonal block of $L$ has $\sigma_2/\sigma_1 = 3.57\times10^{-17}$. One timing cuts against the story: the Blelloch scan takes roughly $700$ ms against $15$–$19$ ms for the sequential loop. NumPy on one core gives it no parallelism while charging strided, non-contiguous access: the $\log T$ depth is a latency claim that pays only on hardware with $T/2$ lanes, hence a CUDA kernel. The residuals are deterministic; the wall-clock figures are machine-dependent. Verify

Under Encryption

An SSM is a sequential recurrence, and sequential is what multiplicative depth punishes. Each step $h_t = \bar a_t h_{t-1} + \bar b_t$ is one ciphertext–ciphertext multiplication when $\bar a_t$ is itself encrypted, so a naive encrypted scan over $n$ tokens consumes depth $\Theta(n)$ — hundreds of bootstraps at any useful sequence length. The parallel-scan form is the interesting one: Blelloch's $O(\log n)$ parallel depth is also $O(\log n)$ multiplicative depth, because each level of the tree applies $\oplus$ once and $\oplus$ costs one multiplication. That turns 4096 levels into 24. Better still, $\oplus$ needs no softmax, no exponential of a ciphertext, no comparison — only multiply and add, which is exactly the polynomial fragment CKKS evaluates cheaply. The SSD form is even friendlier: it is a masked matrix multiply, and matmul is the one thing FHE does well; the mask $L$ can be computed from public or client-supplied $\Delta$ and folded in as a plaintext multiplication, which costs no depth at all. On that reasoning an SSM is a better fit for homomorphic evaluation than attention. Whether it has been done at scale is close to open: Brito's public-decay homomorphic state space models (arXiv 2605.16647, May 2026) report an encrypted SSM classifier running at depth 8 with ring dimension 32768, against depth 10 and ring 65536 for polynomial attention on the same task, roughly $5\times$ faster — but that is a fastText-feature sentiment classifier, not a language model. Verify Chapter 39 takes up the approximation problem in detail, and Chapter 42 still lists encrypted long-sequence SSM inference among the open problems rather than the solved ones.

Key Takeaways
  • A linear time-invariant recurrence is a convolution: ZOH discretization gives $\bar A = e^{\Delta A}$, $\bar B = A^{-1}(e^{\Delta A}-I)B$, and $K_\ell = C\bar A^\ell \bar B$, so training runs an FFT in $O(T\log T)$ and inference runs the recurrence in $O(N)$ per token. Certain
  • HiPPO is not a heuristic: the coefficients of the optimal Legendre projection of the input history satisfy exactly a linear ODE, and its matrix is normal-plus-rank-one, which is what makes the S4 kernel computable in $\tilde O(N+T)$ via Woodbury and a Cauchy kernel. Certain
  • Selectivity means $\Delta_t, B_t, C_t$ depend on $x_t$; this is precisely what LTI forbids and precisely what content-based recall requires. It costs the FFT and buys gating, leaving an associative scan — $2T-2$ work, $2\lceil \log_2 T\rceil$ depth — as the only parallel training algorithm. Certain
  • SSD: with $\bar A_t = a_tI$, the recurrence equals $Y = (L\odot CB^\top)X$ with $L$ 1-semiseparable — masked attention with softmax deleted and the binary mask replaced by a decay mask. The artifact asserts this to $4.2\times10^{-14}$. Certain
  • Pure SSMs do not replace transformers: they win on perplexity-per-FLOP and lose on in-context recall, and the near-universal adoption of hybrids is the field's own verdict. Mamba-3 (2026) narrows the gap with complex transitions and half the state; treat any claim about the frontier as dated. Contested
Part V

Large Language Models

A language model is a compression objective, a data pipeline, a scaling decision, and three stages of post-training. This part treats each as an engineering discipline with real numbers: what a token costs, what a scaling law predicts and where it breaks, why aligned models are trained with three different loss functions that all claim to solve the same problem, and what test-time compute actually buys. It is also where this book is most explicit about what remains contested.
Chapter 22

Mixture of Experts and Conditional Computation

Learning Objectives
  • Derive top-$k$ gating and compute the active-versus-total parameter ratio for a real production configuration such as DeepSeek-V3's 37B-of-671B.
  • Explain the load-balancing problem, derive the standard auxiliary loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha E \sum_e f_e P_e$, and explain the auxiliary-loss-free bias-adjustment alternative and precisely what it removes from the gradient.
  • Explain capacity factor, token dropping, and the difference between token-choice and expert-choice routing.
  • Compute the all-to-all communication volume of expert parallelism and explain why MoE models are bandwidth-bound during batched inference and memory-capacity-bound at serving.
  • Implement a routed mixture-of-experts layer with dispatch/combine, capacity dropping, and both load-balancing schemes in working code.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 has the closest lecture treatment of MoE architectures and routing trade-offs; the HuggingFace Ultra-Scale Playbook covers expert parallelism and all-to-all communication from the systems side; Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), for the from-scratch implementation discipline this chapter's artifact follows.

Chapter 18 built the transformer block: attention mixes information across positions, and a feed-forward network (FFN) — roughly two-thirds of the parameters — transforms each position independently. Every token pays for every FFN parameter. Mixture of experts (MoE) breaks that coupling: replace the FFN with $E$ parallel FFNs ("experts") and a learned router that sends each token to only $k \ll E$ of them. Parameter count grows with $E$; FLOPs per token grow with $k$. This decoupling is the highest-leverage efficiency idea in modern language models — nearly every frontier open-weight model released since 2024 is an MoE Likely — and, as this chapter argues, its entire difficulty lives in the routing, not the experts. The scaling consequences feed directly into Chapter 24; the distributed-systems consequences into Chapters 32 and 33; and Chapter 41 revisits the architecture under encryption, where its central trick becomes illegal.

22.1 Conditional Computation: the FLOPs/Parameters Decoupling

In a dense transformer, compute and capacity are the same knob: forward FLOPs per token are roughly $2N$ for $N$ parameters (Chapter 24 derives this), so more knowledge storage means proportionally more arithmetic on every token. Conditional computation severs the link by making the network's active subgraph a function of its input.

Definition 22.1 (Sparse MoE layer)

Given experts $\{\text{FFN}_e\}_{e=1}^{E}$, each a map $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$, a router with weights $W_g \in \mathbb{R}^{E \times d}$, and a sparsity level $k$, the layer computes for token $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$: $$ s = \mathrm{softmax}(W_g x), \qquad \mathcal{T} = \mathrm{TopK}(s, k), \qquad y = x + \sum_{e \in \mathcal{T}} g_e\, \text{FFN}_e(x), $$ where the gates $g_e = s_e / \sum_{e' \in \mathcal{T}} s_{e'}$ renormalize the selected scores. The total parameter count includes all $E$ experts; the active count per token includes only the $k$ selected plus the router and any always-on components.

The production numbers make the leverage concrete. DeepSeek-V3 Verify has 671B total parameters but activates 37B per token — 5.5%. Its configuration: 61 layers, $d_{\text{model}} = 7168$, the first 3 layers dense, and each of the remaining 58 layers carrying 256 routed experts plus 1 shared (always-on) expert, with $k=8$ routed experts active per token and per-expert hidden width 2048. It was pretrained on 14.8T tokens. Forward compute per token is that of a 37B dense model; knowledge capacity is that of a 671B one.

Example 22.1 (Parameter accounting for DeepSeek-V3)

Each expert is a SwiGLU FFN (Chapter 18) with three weight matrices, so per-expert parameters are $3 \times d \times d_{\text{ff}} = 3 \times 7168 \times 2048 = 44{,}040{,}192 \approx 44\text{M}$. Routed experts per MoE layer: $256 \times 44.04\text{M} \approx 11.27\text{B}$. Across 58 MoE layers: $58 \times 11.27\text{B} \approx 654\text{B}$ — the routed experts are the model; attention, shared experts ($58 \times 44\text{M} \approx 2.6\text{B}$), embeddings, and the 3 dense layers make up the remaining $\sim$17B of the 671B total. Active per layer: $8 \times 44.04\text{M} \approx 352\text{M}$ routed + 44M shared $\approx$ 396M, versus 11.3B resident — a 28× gap in the FFN alone. Summing active FFN, attention, and embeddings recovers $\approx$ 37B activated. Verify

The pattern generalizes across the frontier Verify (all figures from vendor reports; check model cards, these drift):

ModelTotalActiveRatioRouting
Mixtral 8×7B (2023)46.7B12.9B28%8 experts, top-2
DeepSeek-V3 (2024)671B37B5.5%256 routed top-8 + 1 shared
Llama 4 Maverick (2025)400B17B4.3%128 routed top-1 + shared
GPT-OSS-120B (2025)117B5.1B4.4%128 experts, top-4
Kimi K2 (2025)1.04T32B3.1%384 routed top-8 + 1 shared

The trend is toward more total sparsity: ratios have fallen from 28% to $\sim$3–5% in two years. Why not simply train dense 671B models? Because loss follows parameters and compute (Chapter 24), and an MoE spends its compute budget on more tokens instead of more per-token arithmetic. Empirically an MoE does not match a dense model of its total size — the exchange rate is unfavorable to sparsity — but it decisively beats the dense model of its active size at equal training compute, which is the comparison that matters when compute is the binding constraint. Likely

22.2 Top-k Routing and the Gate

The router is a single linear map producing $E$ logits per token — a few million parameters steering hundreds of billions. Two design decisions hide in Definition 22.1. First, the score nonlinearity: classic MoEs use softmax over all $E$ logits; DeepSeek-V3 uses elementwise sigmoid affinities instead, renormalizing only over the selected $k$ — this decouples experts' scores from one another, so raising one expert's affinity does not mechanically suppress the rest. Verify Second, differentiability: $\mathrm{TopK}$ is piecewise constant, so no gradient flows through the selection. Gradients reach the router solely through the gate values $g_e$ of the winners: if expert $e$'s output helped, $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial g_e$ pushes $s_e$ up, making $e$ more likely to win next time. This works — all production routers train this way — but it is a bandit-style signal: the model never observes counterfactual experts, which is the root cause of the pathologies in Section 22.3. Historically Shazeer et al. (2017) added noise to the logits to force exploration; modern systems mostly drop the noise and rely on scale. Likely

Example 22.2 (Top-2 gating by hand)

Let $E=4$, $k=2$, and router logits $z = (2.0,\ 1.0,\ 0.5,\ -1.0)$. Exponentials: $(7.389,\ 2.718,\ 1.649,\ 0.368)$, sum $12.124$, so $s = (0.6095,\ 0.2242,\ 0.1360,\ 0.0303)$. Top-2 selects experts 1 and 2. Renormalized gates: $g_1 = 0.6095/(0.6095+0.2242) = 0.7311$, $g_2 = 0.2689$. Check: renormalizing top-$k$ softmax scores equals softmax over just the winning logits, $e^{2}/(e^{2}+e^{1}) = 0.7311$. $\checkmark$ Now add a balancing bias $b = (-2, 0, 0, 0)$ to selection only: selection scores become $(0,\ 1,\ 0.5,\ -1)$, so experts 2 and 3 win, but their gates come from the raw $s$: $g_2 = 0.2242/0.3602 = 0.6225$, $g_3 = 0.3775$. The bias changed who computes, not how outputs are weighted.

22.3 Load Balancing

Left alone, routers collapse. The mechanism is a positive feedback loop: an expert that receives slightly more tokens early gets more gradient updates, improves faster, earns higher router scores, and receives still more tokens. The fixed point is a handful of overloaded experts and a graveyard of dead ones — the model degenerates toward a dense network of size $k/E \cdot N$ while paying for $N$. The failure is also a systems failure: under expert parallelism (Section 22.6) each expert lives on a device, and the step time is set by the most loaded device, so imbalance directly stalls hardware.

The standard fix, from GShard and the Switch Transformer, is an auxiliary loss. For a batch of $T$ tokens define, for each expert $e$, the dispatch fraction and the mean router probability: $$ f_e = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\mathbf{1}[\,e \in \mathcal{T}_t\,]}{k}, \qquad P_e = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} s_{t,e}, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha\, E \sum_{e=1}^{E} f_e P_e . $$ The quantity we actually care about, $f_e$, is a count — piecewise constant, gradient zero. The product form is the trick: $f_e$ is treated as a constant and the gradient flows through the differentiable $P_e$, so $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} / \partial P_e = \alpha E f_e$ pushes probability mass away from exactly the experts that are overloaded, with pressure proportional to their overload. The factor $E$ normalizes the scale: at perfect balance $f_e = P_e = 1/E$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha$ regardless of $E$.

Theorem 22.1 (The auxiliary loss is minimized at uniform routing)

Suppose the sequences $(f_e)$ and $(P_e)$ are similarly ordered — $(f_e - f_{e'})(P_e - P_{e'}) \ge 0$ for all $e, e'$ — which top-$k$ routing enforces, since dispatch counts are monotone in router scores. Then $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} \ge \alpha$, with equality iff $P$ (or $f$) is uniform.

Proof. By Chebyshev's sum inequality, for similarly ordered sequences, $\frac{1}{E}\sum_e f_e P_e \ge \left(\frac{1}{E}\sum_e f_e\right)\!\left(\frac{1}{E}\sum_e P_e\right) = \frac{1}{E^2}$, using $\sum_e f_e = \sum_e P_e = 1$. Hence $\sum_e f_e P_e \ge 1/E$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha E \sum_e f_e P_e \ge \alpha$. Chebyshev's inequality is tight iff one sequence is constant, i.e. uniform load. The similar-ordering hypothesis is what forbids the degenerate escape of making $f$ and $P$ anti-aligned instead of uniform. $\blacksquare$

The cost of this fix is the coefficient $\alpha$. The auxiliary loss's gradient flows through the router logits into $W_g$ and back into every token representation $x$ — it is an interference gradient that has nothing to do with predicting the next token. Set $\alpha$ too small and the router collapses; too large and language-modeling quality measurably degrades because the model spends capacity satisfying a bookkeeping objective. Typical values sit near $10^{-2}$, tuned by trial. Likely

22.3.1 Auxiliary-Loss-Free Balancing

The bias-adjustment alternative — introduced as "Loss-Free Balancing" by Wang et al. (2024) at DeepSeek and adopted at scale in DeepSeek-V3 Verify — removes the interference gradient entirely by moving balancing out of the loss and into a control loop. Each expert gets a scalar bias $b_e$, added to its score only for top-$k$ selection; gate values still come from the raw scores (Example 22.2). After each training step, compare each expert's load to the mean and nudge: $$ b_e \leftarrow b_e + \gamma \cdot \mathrm{sign}\!\left(\bar{c} - c_e\right), $$ where $c_e$ is expert $e$'s token count, $\bar{c}$ the mean, and $\gamma$ a small update speed ($10^{-3}$ in DeepSeek-V3 Verify). Overloaded experts have their bias walked down until they stop winning marginal tokens; underloaded ones are walked up. This is an integral controller on load, not a loss term.

What exactly is removed from the gradient: everything. The balance objective contributes zero gradient to $W_g$, zero to token representations, zero to experts — $b_e$ is a non-learned buffer updated by a rule, and because it cancels out of the gate values, the only gradients the router ever receives come from the language-modeling loss. DeepSeek-V3 reports better quality at equal balance versus auxiliary-loss training, and retains only a vestigial sequence-wise balance loss with a tiny coefficient to prevent extreme imbalance within a single sequence, which the batch-level controller cannot see. Verify In this chapter's artifact the learned biases converge, up to an additive constant and a residual of a few multiples of $\gamma$, to the negation of the skew injected into the router — the controller finds the correction.

Common Pitfall

Adding the balancing bias to the gate values rather than only to the selection scores. The code reads naturally — compute scores + bias once, take top-$k$, renormalize what you took — and it silently changes the layer's output as a function of the balancing state: the forward pass now depends on a non-learned buffer that drifts every step, gradients are taken through it, and checkpoint evaluations disagree with training behavior. DeepSeek-V3's rule: the bias steers who computes; the raw affinity decides how much it counts. A related bug: computing the router in bf16. The top-$k$ boundary is a comparison between close logits, and bf16's 7-bit mantissa makes routing decisions flip between forward and recompute passes; production systems keep router arithmetic in fp32 (Section 22.7).

22.4 Capacity, Dropping, Expert-Choice Routing

Balance losses shape averages; hardware needs guarantees. Batched execution allocates a fixed buffer per expert, the capacity $$ C = \left\lceil \mathrm{CF} \cdot \frac{kT}{E} \right\rceil, $$ where $T$ is tokens per batch and the capacity factor $\mathrm{CF} \ge 1$ is slack above the perfectly balanced share $kT/E$. Assignments beyond an expert's capacity are dropped: the token keeps flowing through the residual stream (the identity path in Definition 22.1) but loses that layer's FFN contribution — it is not removed from the batch. Dropping a few percent of assignments is tolerated in training; the artifact below shows that a badly imbalanced router at $\mathrm{CF}=1.25$ drops the majority of assignments, which is the real argument for balancing. "Dropless" systems such as MegaBlocks avoid fixed buffers entirely with block-sparse kernels over variable-size expert batches, trading kernel complexity for zero drops. Likely

Token-choice routing — everything above — lets each token pick its $k$ experts, and load balance must be coaxed. Expert-choice routing (Zhou et al., 2022) inverts the selection: each expert picks its top-$C$ tokens by score. Balance is now perfect by construction — every expert processes exactly $C$ tokens, no auxiliary loss, no dropping — and the number of experts per token becomes variable, so hard tokens can consume more compute; Zhou et al. report more than 2× faster pretraining convergence than top-1/top-2 token choice at matched compute. Verify The catch is causality: which experts serve token $t$ depends on the other tokens in the batch competing for slots. In an encoder this is fine. In autoregressive decoding it is a leak — at inference, future tokens do not exist yet and batch composition is arbitrary, so training-time routing is unreproducible. Expert choice therefore lives in encoders and non-autoregressive settings, while decoder LLMs remain token-choice. Certain

22.5 Shared and Fine-Grained Experts

Two refinements, both from DeepSeekMoE (Dai et al., 2024) and now standard Verify, address what experts learn rather than how they are chosen. Fine-grained experts: split each expert of hidden width $h$ into $m$ experts of width $h/m$ and activate $mk$ of them — identical FLOPs and identical active parameters, but the number of distinct expert combinations explodes: $\binom{16}{2} = 120$ for a 16-expert top-2 layer (DeepSeekMoE's own illustration; Mixtral's 8-expert top-2 gives only $\binom{8}{2}=28$) versus $\binom{64}{8} \approx 4.4 \times 10^{9}$ for the same budget split 4-way finer. The router composes skills combinatorially instead of choosing among monoliths; DeepSeek-V3's 256 experts of width 2048 (against $d_{\text{model}} = 7168$, an unusually thin ratio) are this idea pushed hard. Shared experts: route every token through one (or a few) always-on experts alongside the routed ones. Common structure — syntax, frequent patterns — would otherwise be redundantly copied into many routed experts; concentrating it in a shared expert frees the routed ones to specialize. The shared expert also acts as a floor: a token whose routed assignments are all dropped still gets one FFN transformation.

22.6 Expert Parallelism and All-to-All

A 671B-parameter model does not fit on a device, and MoE's natural partition is by expert: shard the $E$ experts across $P$ devices ($256/P$ experts each), replicate or shard everything else conventionally (Chapter 32). The price is that tokens must physically travel to their experts. Each MoE layer requires two all-to-all collectives: a dispatch scattering each token's hidden vector to the devices owning its $k$ experts, and a combine gathering the $k$ outputs back. Per token per layer, ignoring locality, the traffic is $$ V = 2 \cdot k \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot \text{bytes/element}. $$ For DeepSeek-V3 in bf16: $2 \times 8 \times 7168 \times 2\,\text{B} = 229\,\text{KB}$ per token per MoE layer, so $58 \times 229\,\text{KB} \approx 13.3\,\text{MB}$ per token per forward pass — and the backward pass sends the corresponding gradients back through the same collectives. Compare arithmetic: the routed FFN compute per token per layer is $2 \times 8 \times 3 \times 7168 \times 2048 \approx 0.7$ GFLOPs against 229 KB moved, and unlike a weight all-reduce this traffic scales with tokens, not parameters, crosses node boundaries where bandwidth is an order of magnitude below NVLink, and sits on the critical path of every layer. This is why MoE systems are bandwidth-bound in batched settings: the all-to-all, not the GEMM, sets the step time unless it is aggressively overlapped with compute. Production mitigations: limit each token's experts to a few nodes (DeepSeek-V3 caps routing at 4 nodes per token Verify), overlap dispatch/combine with the shared expert and attention of a second microbatch, and hand-write the collectives against the interconnect.

22.7 Training Instabilities: Router z-Loss and Expert Collapse

The router is the least stable component of an MoE. Its logits face a specific numerical failure: nothing in $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ or the LM loss bounds their scale, softmax is shift-invariant so logits can drift large together, and large logits in bf16 turn the exponentials in softmax into round-off noise — at which point routing decisions become effectively random and training diverges. ST-MoE (Zoph et al., 2022) introduced the router z-loss, $$ \mathcal{L}_{z} = \beta \cdot \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \left( \log \sum_{e=1}^{E} e^{z_{t,e}} \right)^{\!2}, \qquad \beta \approx 10^{-3}, $$ which penalizes the squared log-partition function, pulling logits toward small magnitudes without changing their ordering preferences. Verify It is a numerics regularizer, not a balance regularizer, and it coexists with either balancing scheme; keeping router arithmetic in fp32 attacks the same failure from the hardware side. The second chronic instability is expert collapse — the rich-get-richer fixed point of Section 22.3 — which is monitored, not proven away: track per-layer load CV and routing entropy, and treat a layer whose entropy falls off a cliff as an early divergence signal. Collapse is largely a solved problem at production scale under either balancing scheme, but it resurfaces whenever $\alpha$ or $\gamma$ is mistuned or the router precision drops. Likely

22.8 Serving: Memory, Batching, Offload

At serving time the decoupling shows its bill. FLOPs per token are those of the 37B active path, but every expert must be resident, because the next token may route anywhere: DeepSeek-V3 at FP8 is $\approx$671 GB of weights before KV-cache — roughly a full 8×96 GB node just to hold parameters whose per-token utilization is 5.5%. This is memory-capacity bound: the constraint is bytes of HBM, not bytes/s.

Bandwidth enters through batching. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound in general (Chapter 33): each step streams weights past the compute units, and batching amortizes one weight read across $B$ tokens. MoE breaks the amortization. With batch $B$, the expected number of distinct experts touched per layer is $E\left(1 - (1 - k/E)^B\right)$ — for DeepSeek-V3's $E=256$, $k=8$, a batch of 32 tokens already touches $\approx$163 experts — so per-expert batch size is $\approx Bk/E$, and each expert's weights are read to serve only a handful of tokens. A dense 37B model at batch 32 reads 37 GB of weights for 32 tokens; the MoE reads most of its 654 GB of expert weight for the same 32 tokens. The fix is scale: at very large batch (hundreds to thousands of tokens per step, aggregated across requests and, with expert parallelism, across many devices), every expert is saturated and per-token cost approaches the active-path ideal. This is why sparse models are served in large, latency-tiered batches by providers, and why they are painful to serve locally at batch 1. For local and cost-constrained serving, offload exploits the sparsity in the other direction: keep attention, shared experts, and router on GPU, hold routed experts in CPU RAM or NVMe, and fetch the $k$ selected experts per layer on demand — latency then tracks host-to-device bandwidth, and prediction/prefetching of the next layer's experts hides part of it. Likely

Artifact 22.1 — A Routed MoE Layer with Both Balancing Schemes

The module builds the full layer in pure NumPy: top-$k$ gating, batched dispatch into per-expert $(E, C, d)$ buffers, expert GEMMs, gated combine, and capacity dropping with token-order priority. It verifies three claims with hard assertions: (a) the dispatch–expert–combine path is numerically identical to a naive per-token loop over selected experts; (b) starting from a router skewed by a fixed logit offset, both the auxiliary loss (SGD through $P_e$ with $f_e$ held constant) and the loss-free bias controller drive the coefficient of variation of expert load down by more than 4×, printing the trajectory; (c) total and active parameter counts match the closed forms $E \cdot 2dh + dE$ and $k \cdot 2dh + dE$.

"""Artifact 22.1 -- A top-k mixture-of-experts layer from scratch.

Implements: top-k gating, batched dispatch/combine with capacity dropping,
and BOTH load-balancing schemes -- the Switch/GShard auxiliary loss and the
DeepSeek-style auxiliary-loss-free bias adjustment. Verifies:
  (a) dispatch -> expert -> combine == a dense per-token loop, to ~1e-6;
  (b) coefficient of variation (CV) of expert load falls under both schemes;
  (c) active/total parameter counts match hand-derived formulas.
Pure NumPy. Fixed seed. Runs in seconds on CPU.
"""
import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

class MoELayer:
    """E two-layer ReLU experts of width h, a linear router, top-k gating."""
    def __init__(self, d, h, E, k, rng, logit_offset=None):
        self.d, self.h, self.E, self.k = d, h, E, k
        self.W1 = rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5, (E, d, h))   # expert up-proj
        self.W2 = rng.normal(0, h ** -0.5, (E, h, d))   # expert down-proj
        self.Wg = rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5, (d, E))      # router
        # bg: a fixed router offset used to CREATE imbalance for the demo.
        self.bg = np.zeros(E) if logit_offset is None else logit_offset.copy()
        self.b  = np.zeros(E)  # aux-loss-free balancing bias (routing only)

    def route(self, X, use_bias=False):
        """Returns softmax probs, top-k expert ids (T,k), renormalized gates."""
        logits = X @ self.Wg + self.bg                 # (T, E)
        probs = softmax(logits)
        sel = logits + self.b if use_bias else logits  # bias steers SELECTION
        topk = np.argpartition(-sel, self.k - 1, axis=1)[:, :self.k]
        # order the k winners by descending selection score (deterministic)
        order = np.argsort(-np.take_along_axis(sel, topk, 1), axis=1)
        topk = np.take_along_axis(topk, order, 1)
        g = np.take_along_axis(probs, topk, 1)         # gate from RAW probs
        gates = g / g.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)       # renormalize over top-k
        return logits, probs, topk, gates

    def forward_dispatch(self, X, capacity_factor=1.25, use_bias=False):
        """Batched dispatch/combine path with capacity dropping."""
        T, (d, h, E, k) = X.shape[0], (self.d, self.h, self.E, self.k)
        _, _, topk, gates = self.route(X, use_bias)
        C = int(np.ceil(capacity_factor * T * k / E))  # per-expert capacity
        # Flatten (token, slot) assignments; priority = token order.
        tok = np.repeat(np.arange(T), k)
        exp = topk.reshape(-1)
        gat = gates.reshape(-1)
        # Position of each assignment within its expert's queue.
        pos = np.zeros(T * k, dtype=int)
        for e in range(E):
            m = exp == e
            pos[m] = np.arange(m.sum())
        keep = pos < C                                  # overflow is DROPPED
        # Scatter kept tokens into an (E, C, d) buffer, run experts batched.
        buf = np.zeros((E, C, d))
        buf[exp[keep], pos[keep]] = X[tok[keep]]
        out_buf = np.maximum(buf @ self.W1, 0.0) @ self.W2   # (E, C, d)
        # Combine: each kept assignment adds gate * expert output.
        Y = np.zeros_like(X)
        np.add.at(Y, tok[keep], gat[keep, None] * out_buf[exp[keep], pos[keep]])
        return Y, topk, gates, keep.reshape(T, k)

    def forward_dense(self, X, topk, gates, keep):
        """Reference: naive loop over each token's selected experts."""
        Y = np.zeros_like(X)
        for t in range(X.shape[0]):
            for j in range(self.k):
                if keep[t, j]:
                    e = topk[t, j]
                    hdn = np.maximum(X[t] @ self.W1[e], 0.0)
                    Y[t] += gates[t, j] * (hdn @ self.W2[e])
        return Y

def cv_of_load(topk, E):
    load = np.bincount(topk.reshape(-1), minlength=E).astype(float)
    return load.std() / load.mean(), load

def demo():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    d, h, E, k, T = 32, 64, 8, 2, 512
    # A skewed router offset makes experts 0-1 initially dominate.
    offset = np.array([3.0, 2.0, 0.5, 0.0, -0.5, -1.0, -1.5, -2.0])
    X = rng.normal(size=(T, d))

    # ---- (c) parameter accounting -------------------------------------
    m = MoELayer(d, h, E, k, rng, logit_offset=offset)
    total = m.W1.size + m.W2.size + m.Wg.size            # E*2*d*h + d*E
    active = k * 2 * d * h + d * E                       # k experts + router
    assert total == E * 2 * d * h + d * E, "total-param formula mismatch"
    print(f"[params] total={total}  active/token={active}  "
          f"ratio={active/total:.4f} (formula: (k*2dh+dE)/(E*2dh+dE))")

    # ---- (a) dispatch/combine == dense loop ---------------------------
    Y_fast, topk, gates, keep = m.forward_dispatch(X, capacity_factor=1.25)
    Y_ref = m.forward_dense(X, topk, gates, keep)
    err = np.abs(Y_fast - Y_ref).max()
    print(f"[equivalence] max |dispatch/combine - dense loop| = {err:.3e}")
    assert err < 1e-6, "dispatch path diverges from dense reference"
    dropped = (~keep).sum()
    print(f"[capacity] CF=1.25: capacity={int(np.ceil(1.25*T*k/E))}/expert, "
          f"dropped {dropped}/{T*k} assignments ({100*dropped/(T*k):.1f}%)")
    _, _, tk2, g2 = m.route(X)
    C1 = int(np.ceil(1.0 * T * k / E))
    _, _, _, keep1 = m.forward_dispatch(X, capacity_factor=1.0)
    print(f"[capacity] CF=1.00: capacity={C1}/expert, dropped "
          f"{(~keep1).sum()}/{T*k} ({100*(~keep1).sum()/(T*k):.1f}%)")

    # ---- (b) two balancing schemes, same skewed start -----------------
    # alpha here is larger than in real training (~1e-2) because the aux
    # loss is the ONLY loss in this isolated demo, so its scale is free.
    steps, alpha, lr, gamma = 300, 1.0, 2.0, 0.05
    # Scheme 1: auxiliary loss  L = alpha * E * sum_e f_e * Pbar_e,
    # SGD on router (Wg, bg) using dL/dlogits with f treated as constant.
    m1 = MoELayer(d, h, E, k, np.random.default_rng(0), logit_offset=offset)
    # Scheme 2: loss-free bias update  b_e += gamma * sign(mean - load_e).
    m2 = MoELayer(d, h, E, k, np.random.default_rng(0), logit_offset=offset)
    print(f"[balance] CV trajectories over {steps} steps "
          f"(fresh batch of {T} tokens each step):")
    print("  step |  aux-loss CV | loss-free CV")
    for s in range(steps + 1):
        Xb = np.random.default_rng(100 + s).normal(size=(T, d))
        # aux-loss scheme
        logits, probs, tk, _ = m1.route(Xb)
        cv1, load1 = cv_of_load(tk, E)
        f = load1 / load1.sum()                    # fraction routed to e
        dP = alpha * E * f / T                     # dL/dP_te (per token)
        dlog = probs * (dP - (probs * dP).sum(1, keepdims=True))
        m1.Wg -= lr * Xb.T @ dlog
        m1.bg -= lr * dlog.sum(0)
        # loss-free scheme: selection uses logits + b
        _, _, tk2, _ = m2.route(Xb, use_bias=True)
        cv2, load2 = cv_of_load(tk2, E)
        m2.b += gamma * np.sign(load2.mean() - load2)
        if s == 0:
            cv1_0, cv2_0 = cv1, cv2
        if s % 50 == 0:
            print(f"  {s:4d} |    {cv1:8.4f}  |   {cv2:8.4f}")
    assert cv1 < 0.25 * cv1_0, "aux loss failed to balance"
    assert cv2 < 0.25 * cv2_0, "loss-free bias failed to balance"
    print(f"[balance] aux-loss CV {cv1_0:.3f} -> {cv1:.3f}; "
          f"loss-free CV {cv2_0:.3f} -> {cv2:.3f}  (both < 25% of start)")
    print(f"[balance] final loss-free biases b = "
          f"{np.array2string(m2.b, precision=2)}")

    # Cross-check softmax + top-k gate against torch, if present.
    try:
        import torch
        lt = torch.from_numpy(X @ m.Wg + m.bg)
        pt = torch.softmax(lt, dim=-1).numpy()
        _, probs_np, _, _ = m.route(X)
        terr = np.abs(pt - probs_np).max()
        print(f"[torch cross-check] max softmax diff = {terr:.3e}")
        assert terr < 1e-12
    except ImportError:
        print("[skipped: torch not installed]")
    print("All assertions passed.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo()

Running it prints a maximum discrepancy of 1.332e-15 between the batched dispatch/combine path and the dense reference loop (float64 — the two paths are the same arithmetic reordered), and an active/total ratio of 0.2558 matching the closed form for the toy configuration ($E=8$, $k=2$, $d=32$, $h=64$). The skewed router makes the capacity numbers vivid: at $\mathrm{CF}=1.25$ it drops 55.7% of assignments (570 of 1024), because two experts hog the batch. Both balancing schemes then crush the imbalance: the load CV starts at 1.4736 and falls to 0.0690 (auxiliary loss) and 0.0851 (loss-free bias) within 50 steps, ending at 0.076 and 0.097 after 300. The final loss-free biases are [-2.2, -1.15, 0.2, 0.9, 1.15, 1.75, 2.4, 2.6] — up to a constant shift and a residual of a few multiples of $\gamma$, the negation of the injected skew [3, 2, 0.5, 0, -0.5, -1, -1.5, -2]: the controller recovered the correction without ever computing a gradient.

Under Encryption

Routing is data-dependent control flow, which is precisely what homomorphic encryption cannot do. The top-$k$ decision is an argmax over ciphertexts — a comparison, already expensive under CKKS (Chapter 39) — but the deeper problem is that the server must not learn the outcome: which expert a token selects is a function of the token, and expert identities in trained MoEs correlate with topic and language, so revealing the routing pattern leaks information about the plaintext. An encrypted MoE therefore cannot branch. It must evaluate every expert on every token and combine the outputs with an encrypted (approximate) one-hot gate: $y = \sum_{e=1}^{E} \hat{g}_e \odot \text{FFN}_e(x)$, paying $E/k$ times the plaintext FLOPs plus the depth of the gate approximation. For a DeepSeek-V3-shaped layer that multiplier is $256/8 = 32\times$ — the sparsity that justified the architecture is exactly the thing that cannot survive, and the 671B model must be priced as a 671B-dense model plus gate-evaluation overhead. This is the cleanest example in the book of a plaintext optimization that inverts under encryption: conditional computation is a pure win in the clear and a pure loss on ciphertext. Chapter 41 returns to this when accounting for encrypted serving cost.

Key Takeaways
  • MoE decouples parameters from FLOPs: a token activates $k$ of $E$ experts, so capacity scales with $E$ while per-token compute scales with $k$; production ratios have fallen to 3–6% active (DeepSeek-V3: 37B of 671B). Verify
  • Top-$k$ selection passes no gradient; routers learn only through the gate values of the winners, and the resulting rich-get-richer feedback makes load balancing the central training problem of the architecture. Certain
  • The auxiliary loss $\alpha E \sum_e f_e P_e$ is minimized exactly at uniform load (Chebyshev) but injects an interference gradient into every token representation; loss-free bias adjustment achieves balance through a per-expert selection bias updated by a sign rule, contributing zero gradient anywhere. Certain
  • Expert-choice routing gives perfect balance by construction but breaks causality for autoregressive decoding, which is why decoder LLMs remain token-choice with capacity-and-drop or dropless kernels. Likely
  • Expert parallelism moves $2kd$ elements per token per layer through all-to-all collectives ($\approx$13 MB/token/forward for DeepSeek-V3 in bf16), making training and batched inference interconnect-bandwidth-bound, while serving is memory-capacity-bound because all $E$ experts must stay resident for a 5% utilization. Verify
Chapter 23

Tokenization and the Language-Modeling Objective

Learning Objectives
  • Implement byte-pair-encoding training and inference, and explain why byte-level fallback and pre-tokenization regexes exist.
  • Compare BPE, WordPiece, Unigram, and byte-level tokenization on compression ratio and downstream compute cost.
  • Quantify the multilingual token tax and its consequences for both API price and effective context length.
  • Prove that perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers while bits-per-byte is, and convert between them via $\log_2 \mathrm{PPL} = \mathrm{BPB} \times (\text{bytes per token})$.
  • Implement a byte-level BPE tokenizer and a bits-per-byte evaluator in working code.
Read alongside — Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), whose opening chapters build the tokenizer-to-dataloader pipeline line by line; Karpathy, the “Let’s build the GPT tokenizer” lecture and the accompanying minbpe repository, the cleanest reference implementation of byte-level BPE; Stanford CS336, whose first assignment is training a byte-level BPE tokenizer at scale and confronting exactly the efficiency problems Section 23.3 glosses.

Everything downstream of this chapter — the scaling laws of Chapter 24, the data pipelines of Chapter 25, the evaluations of Chapter 29 — is denominated in tokens, and tokens are manufactured by a component that is trained by counting, not by gradient descent, and audited by almost nobody. This chapter first states the language-modeling objective precisely: next-token prediction is maximum-likelihood estimation under the chain rule, continuing the cross-entropy argument of Chapter 2. It then builds the tokenizer that defines the sample space: byte-pair encoding, its WordPiece and Unigram competitors, and the pathologies each inflicts on arithmetic, code, and non-Latin scripts. The centerpiece is a proof that perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers while bits-per-byte is — a fact the artifact turns into a hard assertion, and one that published comparisons still routinely violate. Section 23.8 asks whether the transformer of Chapter 18 needs a tokenizer at all.

23.1 Next-Token Prediction as Maximum Likelihood

Fix a finite vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ with $|\mathcal{V}| = V$. An autoregressive language model with parameters $\theta$ assigns probability to a token sequence $t_{1:n}$ by the chain rule, which is an identity, not an assumption:

$$p_\theta(t_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_\theta(t_i \mid t_{1:i-1}).$$

The modeling assumption is only that each conditional is computable by one network with shared parameters. Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood of a corpus of $D$ tokens,

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{D} \sum_{i=1}^{D} \log p_\theta(t_i \mid t_{<i}),$$

which by Chapter 2 is exactly the cross-entropy between the empirical next-token distribution and the model, and whose minimizer over unrestricted $p$ is the true conditional. Every position in every training sequence contributes one classification problem over $V$ classes, evaluated in parallel via teacher forcing: the conditioning context is always ground truth, never the model’s own samples. There is no separate “pretraining loss”; this single scalar objective is the entire supervision signal for the trillion-token runs of Chapter 25. Certain

Definition 23.1 (Language-modeling objective)

Given a tokenizer $\tau$ mapping byte strings to sequences over $\mathcal{V}$, and a corpus $x$, the language-modeling objective is $\min_\theta -\log p_\theta(\tau(x))$, factored autoregressively. The tokenizer is part of the objective: change $\tau$ and you change the sample space, the loss value, and the meaning of “one training step.”

That last clause is the chapter’s thesis in miniature. The model never sees text. It sees integer ids whose statistics were fixed by a counting procedure run once, before training, on a corpus that usually differs from the training corpus. Every downstream number — loss, perplexity, tokens-per-second, dollars-per-million-tokens, “context length” — inherits that choice.

23.2 Why Not Characters or Words

The two extreme tokenizations both fail on cost grounds. A word-level vocabulary is unbounded: any fixed word list meets out-of-vocabulary items immediately (morphology, typos, code identifiers, new names), and the classical <UNK> token destroys the losslessness that Section 23.7 depends on. Worse, Zipf’s law puts most of the vocabulary in a long tail seen a handful of times, so most embedding rows are undertrained — the glitch-token pathology of Section 23.6 in its most extreme form.

A byte-level vocabulary ($V = 256$) is perfectly closed but expensive. English text under a modern subword tokenizer runs around four to five bytes per token Likely, so byte sequences are roughly $4\text{–}5\times$ longer than token sequences for the same text. Per Chapter 18, the linear-cost components of a transformer scale with sequence length $n$ and attention scales with $n^2$: a $4.5\times$ longer sequence costs $4.5\times$ more FLOPs in the MLPs and up to $20\times$ in attention, while each position carries less information — and the effective context window, measured in text, shrinks by the same factor. Subword tokenization is the engineering compromise: a vocabulary of $10^4$–$10^5$ frequent fragments, with rare strings decomposing into smaller pieces, down to single bytes if necessary. Certain

One encoding detail matters throughout: UTF-8 assigns one byte to ASCII, two to most Latin-adjacent and Cyrillic characters, three to most CJK characters, and four to emoji and rarer planes. A tokenizer that operates on bytes therefore already prices scripts differently before any learning happens; the learned merges then amplify or dampen that skew depending on the training mix.

23.3 BPE: Training and Encoding

Definition 23.2 (Byte-pair encoding)

Initialize the vocabulary with the 256 single bytes. Repeat until $|\mathcal{V}| = V$: count all adjacent symbol pairs in the (pre-tokenized) corpus, pick the most frequent pair $(a,b)$, add the concatenation $ab$ as a new symbol, and replace every occurrence of $(a,b)$ with it. The ordered merge list is the tokenizer; the vocabulary is derivable from it.

23.3.1 Byte-level fallback

Because the base alphabet is all 256 byte values, every UTF-8 string — indeed every byte string — has an encoding: worst case, one token per byte. Coverage is structural, not a special case, which is why GPT-2 moved BPE from characters to bytes. The alternative, character-level BPE with an <UNK> escape (original neural-MT usage), silently loses information. A subtlety: byte-level fallback can split a multibyte character across tokens, so decoding an arbitrary token prefix can land mid-character; correct decoders buffer invalid trailing bytes rather than crash. Certain

23.3.2 Pre-tokenization regexes

Raw BPE on a corpus would happily learn merges spanning spaces (“of the”), wasting vocabulary slots on word n-grams and making segmentation hypersensitive to context. So GPT-2 first splits text with a regex into “pre-tokens” — letter runs with an attached leading space, digit runs, punctuation runs, common English contractions — and merges are learned and applied only within pre-tokens. This is why “ the” (with space) and “the” are different tokens, and it is a quiet failure mode for unsegmented scripts: Chinese has no spaces, so an entire clause becomes one pre-token and merges cross word boundaries freely. Later tokenizers tuned the regex — capping digit-run length, handling whitespace runs for code — and those regex choices are measurable in downstream behavior (Section 23.6).

23.3.3 Encoding must replay training

Inference-time encoding applies the learned merges to a new pre-token in the order they were learned, each as a left-to-right non-overlapping pass. This replays training exactly, so a word seen in training gets its training-time segmentation — assertion (b) of the artifact checks this for every unique pre-token in the corpus. Production encoders instead repeatedly apply the lowest-ranked merge present (a priority-queue formulation). The two coincide: a merge’s pair consists of symbols older than that merge, and merging only creates adjacencies involving the strictly newer merged symbol, so an earlier merge’s pair can never reappear once its pass is done. Implementations can still diverge on overlapping occurrences (aaa under the pair a,a) if one resolves them other than left to right. Certain

Example 23.1 (Two merges by hand)

Corpus pre-token counts: low×5, lower×2, lowest×2. Initial symbols are characters. Pair counts: $(l,o): 5+2+2 = 9$; $(o,w): 9$; $(w,e): 2+2 = 4$; $(e,r): 2$; $(e,s): 2$; $(s,t): 2$. Tie between $(l,o)$ and $(o,w)$ at 9; break ties deterministically (say, lexicographically), merging $(l,o) \to lo$. New counts: $(lo,w): 9$, $(w,e): 4$, rest unchanged — so merge 2 is $(lo,w) \to low$, and every occurrence of low is now one symbol. Merge 3 would be $(low,e): 4$. Note the greedy, frequency-first character: lowest will be segmented low|e|s|t or lowe|st depending on later merges, not by any morphological analysis.

Common Pitfall

An encoder that greedily matches the longest vocabulary entry (WordPiece-style inference) against a BPE merge table still round-trips perfectly — decoding is just concatenation — but produces segmentations the model never saw during training. Round-trip tests cannot catch this; the bug ships silently and shows up as a diffuse quality drop. The same drift occurs when training and serving stacks use different tokenizer implementations whose tie-breaking differs. The correct test is the artifact’s assertion (b): encode the training corpus and compare against the segmentation state at the end of BPE training, token by token.

23.4 WordPiece and Unigram

BPE’s merge criterion is raw frequency. Its two main competitors change the criterion and the inference rule:

BPEWordPieceUnigramByte/patch-level
Vocabulary constructionmerge most frequent pairmerge pair maximizing $\frac{c(ab)}{c(a)\,c(b)}$start large; prune tokens whose removal least hurts corpus likelihood (EM)none, or learned segmentation
Directionbottom-upbottom-uptop-down—
Inferencereplay merges by rankgreedy longest-match, ## continuationsViterbi max-probability segmentationidentity / entropy patching
Probabilistic?nonoyes — supports sampling segmentationsyes (model-internal)
Used byGPT family, Llama 3, QwenBERT familyT5, mT5, ALBERT (via SentencePiece)ByT5, BLT, H-Net

WordPiece’s score is a pointwise-mutual-information surrogate: it prefers pairs that co-occur more than chance, not merely often, so it resists merging frequent-but-independent pairs. Unigram (Kudo, 2018) is the most principled of the three: it posits that a word’s probability is the product of its tokens’ unigram probabilities, fits token probabilities by EM over all segmentations, and prunes to the target size. Because it is probabilistic, it supports subword regularization — sampling alternative segmentations during training as data augmentation — which BPE can only imitate via ad-hoc merge dropout. SentencePiece packages both BPE and Unigram with the whitespace-as-symbol (▁) convention; Llama 1 and 2 shipped SentencePiece BPE. In practice, measured compression differences between well-tuned BPE and Unigram at equal $V$ are small compared to the effects of vocabulary size and training-corpus composition, which is why frequency-greedy BPE, the crudest scheme, still dominates deployment. Likely

23.5 Vocabulary Size as a Scaling Variable

Vocabulary size was long frozen folklore ($\sim$32k–50k); it is now an explicit scaling variable. Production values as of this writing: Verify

Tokenizer / model family$V$Type
GPT-2 / GPT-3 (r50k)50,257byte-level BPE
Llama 1 / 232,000SentencePiece BPE
GPT-4 (cl100k)∼100kbyte-level BPE
Llama 3 family128,256tiktoken-style BPE
Qwen 2.5 / 3151,936byte-level BPE
GPT-4o and successors (o200k)∼200kbyte-level BPE
Gemma 2256,128SentencePiece

The trade is explicit. Doubling $V$ buys compression — more text per token, hence more text per context window and fewer forward passes per byte generated; Meta reported Llama 3’s 128k vocabulary as a significant efficiency gain over Llama 2’s 32k. It costs parameters and softmax compute: untied input and output embeddings cost $2Vd$ parameters, which for Llama-3-8B ($V{=}128{,}256$, $d{=}4096$) is $\approx 1.05$B — roughly 13% of the model Verify. At Gemma-2-2B’s $V{=}256{,}128$, the embedding matrix alone is $\sim$0.59B parameters, which is why small models tie input and output embeddings. Empirical scaling studies find the compute-optimal $V$ grows with model scale — larger models deserve larger vocabularies — consistent with the observed 32k → 128k–256k drift. Verify A second-order consequence for Chapter 24: “training tokens” $D$ is a tokenizer-dependent unit, so token-denominated prescriptions like tokens-per-parameter ratios do not transfer across tokenizers; bytes are the invariant denominator.

23.5.1 The multilingual token tax

A BPE vocabulary allocates merges by frequency in its training corpus. Train on an English-heavy web mix and English gets long tokens while other scripts fragment — in the worst case to the UTF-8 byte floor of 3 tokens per CJK character. Petrov et al. (2023) measured the same content across languages and found tokenized-length ratios of up to $15\times$ against English, with substantial premiums persisting even for intentionally multilingual tokenizers; API cost for equivalent content varies by an order of magnitude across languages. Verify The tax is threefold and multiplicative in the fertility ratio $k$ (tokens per unit text relative to English): price per request scales with $k$ under per-token billing; per-byte inference FLOPs scale with $k$ (each forward pass is $\approx 2N$ FLOPs per token, Chapter 24); and a fixed $n$-token context window holds $k\times$ less text, so “128k context” is an English-denominated marketing number. The artifact reproduces the mechanism in vitro: an English-dominated training mix yields 0.22 tokens per character on English text versus 1.13 tokens per character on Chinese — a $5.1\times$ per-character tax from corpus composition alone.

23.6 Tokenizer Pathologies: Digits, Whitespace, Code, Glitch Tokens

Digits. GPT-2’s frequency-greedy merges produced arbitrary digit chunks (“2024” one token, “2023” perhaps two), so the model never saw a consistent positional representation of numbers. Llama 2 split numbers into single digits; cl100k, o200k, and Llama 3 tokenize digit runs in groups of up to three. Grouping choice is causally linked to arithmetic ability: controlled studies find digit-grouping schemes change arithmetic accuracy at fixed model scale, with right-to-left three-digit grouping (aligning tokens with thousands separators) outperforming left-to-right. Likely When a model “can’t do arithmetic,” audit the tokenizer before the model.

Whitespace and code. Under GPT-3’s tokenizer, a 16-space Python indent consumed many tokens; the Codex work added dedicated tokens for whitespace runs, and successors follow. Likely Indentation-heavy code otherwise pays its own token tax, and merge tables trained on prose fragment identifiers like get_user_id unpredictably. This is one reason code-heavy models retrain tokenizers on code-heavy mixes.

Glitch tokens. The tokenizer’s training corpus and the model’s training corpus are different artifacts, so the vocabulary can contain strings that were frequent in the former and absent (often deliberately filtered) from the latter. Such tokens — the infamous  SolidGoldMagikarp, a Reddit username that entered GPT-2’s vocabulary via the counting subreddit — keep near-initialization embeddings, and feeding them produces out-of-distribution activations and bizarre behavior: evasion, insults, hallucinated definitions. Certain Land and Bartolo (EMNLP 2024) automated detection via embedding-geometry indicators and found under-trained tokens across essentially every model family they audited. Verify The lesson generalizes: the tokenizer is a supply-chain component. It is fixed before training, rarely re-audited after, and its mismatches with the training distribution become permanent, exploitable model behavior.

23.7 Perplexity, Bits-per-Byte, and Cross-Tokenizer Comparison

Definition 23.3 (Perplexity and bits-per-byte)

For a model $q$ evaluated on text tokenized into $n_T$ tokens occupying $n_B$ bytes, with total negative log-likelihood $B = -\log_2 q(t_{1:n_T})$ bits: $$\mathrm{PPL} = 2^{B / n_T}, \qquad \mathrm{BPB} = B / n_B.$$ Perplexity is the per-token branching factor; bits-per-byte is a compression rate against a physical unit of text.

Theorem 23.1 (Perplexity is tokenizer-relative; bits-per-byte is not)

Let $q$ be any probability distribution over byte strings, and let $\tau$ be a lossless tokenizer: a deterministic encoder with a decoder satisfying $\mathrm{dec}(\tau(x)) = x$ for all $x$. Define the induced token-sequence model $q_\tau(t_{1:n_T}) = q(\mathrm{dec}(t_{1:n_T}))$ on the image of $\tau$. Then for any text $x$ with $|x| = n_B$ bytes and $|\tau(x)| = n_T^{(\tau)}$ tokens: (i) the total code length $B = -\log_2 q_\tau(\tau(x)) = -\log_2 q(x)$ is independent of $\tau$, hence $\mathrm{BPB} = B/n_B$ is tokenizer-invariant; (ii) $\log_2 \mathrm{PPL}_\tau = B / n_T^{(\tau)} = \mathrm{BPB} \cdot \big(n_B / n_T^{(\tau)}\big)$ depends on $\tau$ through its compression ratio, and any two lossless tokenizers with different token counts on $x$ yield different perplexities for the same underlying model.

Proof. Determinism of the encoder makes $\tau$ injective (if $\tau(x) = \tau(x')$ then $x = \mathrm{dec}(\tau(x)) = \mathrm{dec}(\tau(x')) = x'$), so $\tau$ is a bijection onto its image and $q_\tau$ is the pushforward of $q$: a valid distribution assigning $q_\tau(\tau(x)) = q(x)$. The autoregressive factorization telescopes, $\sum_{i} -\log_2 q_\tau(t_i \mid t_{<i}) = -\log_2 q_\tau(t_{1:n_T}) = -\log_2 q(x)$, so per-token conditionals regroup the same total bits without changing them. Dividing the invariant $B$ by the invariant $n_B$ gives an invariant; dividing by the tokenizer-dependent $n_T^{(\tau)}$ does not: for $n_T^{(1)} \neq n_T^{(2)}$, $2^{B/n_T^{(1)}} \neq 2^{B/n_T^{(2)}}$ whenever $B > 0$. $\blacksquare$

The theorem yields the conversion rules. Within one model, $\log_2 \mathrm{PPL} = \mathrm{BPB} \times (\text{bytes per token})$. Between two tokenizations of the same evaluation text, perplexities renormalize by the token-count ratio: $\mathrm{PPL}_2 = \mathrm{PPL}_1^{\,n_1/n_2}$ — an exponent, which is why perplexity gaps across tokenizers can be arbitrarily large while describing identical models. The practical protocol: compare models by total held-out bits on identical byte streams, reported as BPB (or bits-per-character for a fixed Unicode normalization). Perplexity remains fine for tracking one model with one fixed tokenizer over training. Certain

Example 23.2 (Converting the artifact’s numbers)

The artifact’s byte-level trigram model spends $B$ total bits on a 24,873-byte held-out text, with $\mathrm{BPB} = 2.058529$. Tokenizer A ($V{=}300$) encodes the text in 16,248 tokens: $n_B/n_T = 24{,}873/16{,}248 = 1.5308$ bytes/token, so $\log_2 \mathrm{PPL} = 2.058529 \times 1.5308 = 3.151$ and $\mathrm{PPL} = 2^{3.151} = 8.88$.
