Tokenizer B ($V{=}800$): $24{,}873/3{,}986 = 6.240$ bytes/token, $\log_2 \mathrm{PPL} = 12.846$, $\mathrm{PPL} = 7{,}360$. Same model, same text, same bits: perplexity 8.88 versus 7,360 — an $828\times$ ratio that measures nothing but compression.

Common Pitfall

Quoting a competitor’s perplexity next to yours when the tokenizers differ — still common in papers and eval harnesses. Variants of the bug: comparing word-level WikiText-103 perplexities against subword models without renormalizing by $n_{\text{sub}}/n_{\text{word}}$; concluding a multilingual model finds language X “harder” than English from per-token perplexity, when X’s higher fertility alone predicts the gap; and leaderboards that aggregate perplexities computed under each submission’s own tokenizer. The artifact’s part (d) shows the failure can even invert rankings: of two independently trained models, the one that is genuinely better by 2× in BPB reports a 9× worse perplexity.

23.8 Tokenizer-Free Approaches

If the tokenizer is an unaudited liability, can the model learn its own segmentation? ByT5 showed raw bytes work but paid the full sequence-length cost. The current line of attack is hierarchical: spend a small model on bytes, a large model on compressed units. Meta’s Byte Latent Transformer (2024) groups bytes into dynamically sized patches segmented where next-byte entropy is high, allocating compute where the data is hard; in a FLOP-controlled study to 8B parameters and 4T training bytes it matched token-based models while improving robustness to noise and character-level manipulation, and scaled better at fixed inference cost by growing patch size alongside model size. Verify H-Net (2025) goes further: a learned, differentiable chunking module inside an end-to-end hierarchy, which compute-matched outperforms a BPE-token transformer, with the largest gains exactly where BPE heuristics are weakest — Chinese, code, and DNA (nearly $4\times$ data efficiency on DNA). Verify

Whether tokenizers disappear is genuinely contested. Contested The case for: every pathology in Section 23.6 is an artifact of frozen counting, and hierarchical byte models remove the entire class while learning segmentation jointly with the objective. The case against: BPE is embarrassingly cheap, battle-tested at $10^{25}$-FLOP scale, and the entire serving economy (billing, context limits, KV caches, speculative decoding of Chapter 33) is denominated in its tokens; byte-level architectures add engineering complexity that has, as of this writing, kept them out of frontier production models. Our position: the token tax and glitch-token liabilities are structural, not fixable by bigger vocabularies, so hierarchical dynamic chunking wins eventually; the evidence that would settle it is a frontier-scale deployment reporting equal-quality serving economics. Until then, everything in Parts V–VI assumes BPE.

Artifact 23.1 — Byte-Level BPE and a Bits-per-Byte Evaluator

The artifact builds byte-level BPE end to end — pre-tokenization regex, merge training, training-order replay encoding, byte fallback — and then makes the chapter’s thesis executable. It trains two tokenizers ($V{=}300$ and $V{=}800$) on a synthetic English-dominated corpus with a rare CJK tail, asserts (a) exact round-trip on ASCII, code, CJK, and scripts never seen in training; (b) that encoding reproduces every training-time segmentation exactly; and (c) that one fixed byte-level trigram distribution, read through both tokenizers, yields bits-per-byte identical to within $10^{-9}$ while perplexities differ enormously. Part (d) trains two independent token-bigram models and shows perplexity misranking them; part (e) measures the token tax directly.

"""
Artifact 23.1 -- Byte-level BPE and a bits-per-byte evaluator, from scratch.

Trains byte-level BPE tokenizers (base vocab = the 256 raw bytes, so ANY
UTF-8 input is encodable -- byte fallback is structural, not a special case),
verifies that the encoder exactly reproduces training-time segmentation, and
demonstrates the chapter's thesis with hard assertions: perplexity is NOT
comparable across tokenizers; bits-per-byte IS. Pure stdlib + numpy.
"""
import math, re, time
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np

# --- Pre-tokenization: a simplified GPT-2-style regex. It partitions the ---
# --- text completely (word runs, punctuation runs, whitespace runs), so ----
# --- no byte is ever dropped. Real tokenizers use \p{L} classes (regex lib).
PRETOK = re.compile(r" ?\w+| ?[^\w\s]+|\s+", re.UNICODE)

def pretokenize(text):
    """Split text into pre-tokens, each returned as raw UTF-8 bytes."""
    return [m.group().encode("utf-8") for m in PRETOK.finditer(text)]

def merge_seq(seq, pair, new_id):
    """One left-to-right, non-overlapping pass replacing `pair` by `new_id`.
    The SAME routine is used in training and inference -- that identity is
    what makes assertion (b) hold exactly."""
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(seq):
        if i + 1 < len(seq) and seq[i] == pair[0] and seq[i + 1] == pair[1]:
            out.append(new_id); i += 2
        else:
            out.append(seq[i]); i += 1
    return out

class ByteBPE:
    def __init__(self):
        self.vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)}  # byte fallback base
        self.merges = []                                  # [((a,b), new_id)]
        self._cache = {}

    def train(self, text, vocab_size):
        """Greedy BPE: repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair.
        Returns the final training-time segmentation of every unique word."""
        words = Counter(pretokenize(text))          # word bytes -> frequency
        segs = {w: list(w) for w in words}          # current id sequences
        while len(self.vocab) < vocab_size:
            pairs = Counter()
            for w, cnt in words.items():
                s = segs[w]
                for a, b in zip(s, s[1:]):
                    pairs[(a, b)] += cnt
            if not pairs:
                break
            # deterministic tie-break: highest count, then smallest pair ids
            best = min(pairs.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[0]
            new_id = len(self.vocab)
            self.vocab[new_id] = self.vocab[best[0]] + self.vocab[best[1]]
            self.merges.append((best, new_id))
            for w in segs:                          # apply merge everywhere
                segs[w] = merge_seq(segs[w], best, new_id)
        return segs

    def encode_word(self, wb):
        """Apply the learned merges IN TRAINING ORDER. This replays training
        exactly, so encoding a training word reproduces its training seg."""
        if wb in self._cache:
            return self._cache[wb]
        s = list(wb)
        for pair, nid in self.merges:
            if len(s) < 2:
                break
            if any(s[i] == pair[0] and s[i+1] == pair[1] for i in range(len(s)-1)):
                s = merge_seq(s, pair, nid)
        self._cache[wb] = s
        return s

    def encode(self, text):
        return [t for w in pretokenize(text) for t in self.encode_word(w)]

    def decode(self, ids):
        return b"".join(self.vocab[i] for i in ids).decode("utf-8")

class ByteTrigramLM:
    """Interpolated byte trigram LM. Defines ONE distribution over byte
    strings; both tokenizers below inherit their token probabilities from it
    (a token's probability = product of its bytes' probabilities), so total
    bits MUST agree while per-token perplexity does not."""
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.n = len(data)
        self.uni = Counter(data)
        self.bi = Counter(zip(data, data[1:]))
        self.tri = Counter(zip(data, data[1:], data[2:]))

    def logp2(self, a, b, c):  # log2 p(c | a, b)
        p1 = (self.uni[c] + 1) / (self.n + 256)          # add-1 smoothed
        p2 = self.bi[(b, c)] / self.uni[b] if self.uni[b] else 0.0
        p3 = self.tri[(a, b, c)] / self.bi[(a, b)] if self.bi[(a, b)] else 0.0
        return math.log2(0.6 * p3 + 0.25 * p2 + 0.15 * p1)

    def byte_bits(self, text_bytes):
        pad = b"\x00\x00" + text_bytes
        return [-self.logp2(pad[i], pad[i+1], pad[i+2]) for i in range(len(text_bytes))]

class TokenBigramLM:
    """Independently trained token-level bigram LM (the empirical check)."""
    def __init__(self, tokens, V):
        prev = [-1] + tokens[:-1]
        self.V, self.N = V, len(tokens)
        self.uni, self.bi, self.ctx = Counter(tokens), Counter(zip(prev, tokens)), Counter(prev)

    def bits(self, tokens):
        total, prev = 0.0, -1
        for t in tokens:
            p2 = self.bi[(prev, t)] / self.ctx[prev] if self.ctx[prev] else 0.0
            p = 0.90 * p2 + 0.09 * self.uni[t] / self.N + 0.01 / self.V
            total += -math.log2(p); prev = t
        return total

WORDS = ("the model token byte pair encoding merge vocabulary corpus text language "
         "compression ratio perplexity bits per entropy likelihood objective next "
         "prediction training inference sequence context window frequency adjacent "
         "greedy subword unit segmentation boundary whitespace digit code python "
         "function return loop count print assert vector matrix gradient loss "
         "optimizer batch layer attention scale data sample probability estimate "
         "measure evaluate compare across different sizes cost price effective "
         "length script latin multibyte unicode fallback rare frequent common "
         "stream buffer parse split join encode decode exact round trip").split()
ZH = list("语言模型把文本切分成子词单元分词器决定世界每个汉字通常需要三字节压缩率因而异")
CODE = "def f(x):\n    return x + 1  # 42\n"

def build_corpus(rng):
    """Random sentences over a fixed word pool: English-dominated with a rare
    CJK long tail and occasional code, mimicking web-corpus composition."""
    def sentence():
        ws = [WORDS[i] for i in rng.integers(0, len(WORDS), rng.integers(4, 11))]
        r = rng.random()
        if r < 0.06:   # rare CJK run: the multilingual long tail
            ws.append("".join(ZH[i] for i in rng.integers(0, len(ZH), 4)))
        elif r < 0.10: # occasional code
            ws.append(CODE)
        return " ".join(ws) + ". "
    train = "".join(sentence() for _ in range(2500))
    test = "".join(sentence() for _ in range(450))
    en_sample = ("the model must encode text and estimate the next token "
                 "probability across a common vocabulary of frequent subword units. ") * 4
    zh_sample = "语言模型把文本切分成子词单元。分词器决定模型的世界。每个汉字通常需要三字节。" * 4
    unseen = "이 문장은 학습 데이터에 없다 وهذه جملة غير مرئية 🦑"  # scripts NEVER trained on
    return train, test, en_sample, zh_sample, unseen

if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.time()
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    train_text, test_text, en_sample, zh_sample, unseen = build_corpus(rng)
    print(f"corpus: train={len(train_text.encode())} bytes, test={len(test_text.encode())} bytes")
    assert b"".join(pretokenize(test_text)) == test_text.encode()  # regex partitions fully

    tokA, tokB = ByteBPE(), ByteBPE()
    segsA = tokA.train(train_text, 300)
    segsB = tokB.train(train_text, 800)

    # (a) HARD ASSERTION: exact round-trip on ASCII + code + CJK + unseen scripts.
    for s in (train_text[:5000], test_text, zh_sample, unseen):
        for tok in (tokA, tokB):
            assert tok.decode(tok.encode(s)) == s
    print("[a] round-trip exact on ASCII/code/UTF-8 incl. never-seen scripts: OK")

    # (b) HARD ASSERTION: encoder reproduces training-time segmentation.
    checked = 0
    for tok, segs in ((tokA, segsA), (tokB, segsB)):
        for w, seg in segs.items():
            assert tok.encode_word(w) == seg; checked += 1
    print(f"[b] encoder == training segmentation on {checked} unique pre-tokens: OK")

    # (c) HARD ASSERTION (thesis): one byte-level distribution, two tokenizers.
    lm = ByteTrigramLM(train_text.encode())
    bb = lm.byte_bits(test_text.encode())
    n_bytes, total_bits = len(bb), sum(bb)
    stats = {}
    for name, tok in (("V=300", tokA), ("V=800", tokB)):
        ids = tok.encode(test_text)
        bits, pos = 0.0, 0                      # regroup byte bits per token
        for t in ids:
            L = len(tok.vocab[t]); bits += sum(bb[pos:pos+L]); pos += L
        assert pos == n_bytes                   # tokens tile the byte stream
        stats[name] = (len(ids), 2 ** (bits/len(ids)), bits/n_bytes)
        print(f"[c] {name}: {len(ids):5d} tokens  PPL={stats[name][1]:8.3f}  BPB={stats[name][2]:.6f}")
    (nA, pplA, bpbA), (nB, pplB, bpbB) = stats["V=300"], stats["V=800"]
    assert abs(bpbA - bpbB) < 1e-9 and abs(bpbA - total_bits/n_bytes) < 1e-6
    assert pplB / pplA > 1.3
    print(f"[c] THESIS: |BPB diff|={abs(bpbA-bpbB):.2e} (<1e-9), PPL ratio={pplB/pplA:.2f}x")

    # (d) Worse: perplexity MISRANKS independently trained models. A bigram LM
    # over V=800 tokens sees ~4x more bytes of context per conditioning step
    # than one over V=300 tokens, so it is the genuinely better model -- and
    # BPB says so. Per-token perplexity says the opposite.
    for name, tok in (("V=300", tokA), ("V=800", tokB)):
        tr, te = tok.encode(train_text), tok.encode(test_text)
        bits = TokenBigramLM(tr, len(tok.vocab)).bits(te)
        stats[name] = (2 ** (bits/len(te)), bits/n_bytes)
        print(f"[d] {name}: PPL={stats[name][0]:8.3f}  BPB={stats[name][1]:.4f}")
    (pplA, bpbA), (pplB, bpbB) = stats["V=300"], stats["V=800"]
    assert pplB > 1.5 * pplA   # PPL claims the V=800 model is far worse...
    assert bpbB < bpbA         # ...BPB shows it is in fact the better model.
    print(f"[d] PPL misranks: V=800 looks {pplB/pplA:.1f}x worse by PPL, "
          f"yet is {bpbA/bpbB:.2f}x better by BPB")

    # (e) The token tax: tokens per byte, English vs Chinese, same tokenizer.
    for name, s in (("English", en_sample), ("Chinese", zh_sample)):
        ids, nb = tokB.encode(s), len(s.encode())
        print(f"[e] V=800 {name}: {len(ids)/nb:.3f} tokens/byte "
              f"({nb/len(ids):.2f} bytes/token, {len(ids)/len(s):.2f} tokens/char)")

    try:  # cross-check our entropy arithmetic against scipy
        from scipy.stats import entropy
        cnt = np.bincount(np.frombuffer(train_text.encode(), np.uint8), minlength=256)
        ours = -sum(c/cnt.sum() * math.log2(c/cnt.sum()) for c in cnt if c)
        ref = entropy(cnt, base=2)
        assert abs(ours - ref) < 1e-10
        print(f"[x] byte unigram entropy {ours:.4f} bits matches scipy (|diff|={abs(ours-ref):.1e})")
    except ImportError:
        print("[x] [skipped: scipy not installed]")

    longest = sorted(tokB.vocab.values(), key=len)[-3:]
    print(f"longest V=800 tokens: {[t.decode('utf-8', 'replace') for t in longest]}")
    print(f"all assertions passed in {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")

Running it: the round-trip and segmentation-replay assertions pass over 488 unique pre-tokens; the shared trigram model gives BPB $= 2.058529$ under both tokenizers (measured difference $1.87 \times 10^{-14}$) while perplexities are 8.884 versus 7,359.6 — a measured $828\times$ ratio from tokenization alone. The independent bigram models print PPL 8.46 / BPB 2.012 at $V{=}300$ against PPL 79.7 / BPB 1.012 at $V{=}800$: perplexity calls the second model 9.4× worse when it is 1.99× better. The token-tax measurement prints 0.219 tokens/byte for English against 0.377 for Chinese (0.22 vs. 1.13 tokens per character), the scipy entropy cross-check agrees to $3.6 \times 10^{-15}$ bits, and the full run completes in 1.1 s (5.4 s on a cold interpreter start).

Under Encryption

Tokenization itself never runs on ciphertext: private-inference systems tokenize on the client, in plaintext, and encrypt the resulting embeddings. What the tokenizer does set is $V$, and $V$ scales the one genuinely expensive step of encrypted decoding. The LM head’s matrix product is cheap under CKKS, but emitting a token requires an argmax over $V$ logits, and comparison is non-polynomial: a tournament argmax needs $V-1$ approximate comparisons at depth $\log_2 V$ ($\approx 17$ rounds for a 128k vocabulary), each a polynomial iteration consuming multiplicative depth from a budget refilled only by expensive bootstrapping. Large vocabularies, a free win in plaintext serving, are a direct cost multiplier under encryption. Chapter 39 takes up the approximation problem in detail.

Key Takeaways
  • Next-token prediction is maximum-likelihood estimation via the chain rule; the tokenizer fixes the sample space before the first gradient step and is itself trained only by counting. Certain
  • Byte-level BPE can never fail on unseen input, but a correct encoder must reproduce training-time segmentation — round-trip success alone does not certify a tokenizer. Certain
  • Production vocabularies grew from 32k–50k to 128k–256k (Llama 3: 128,256; Qwen: 151,936; Gemma 2: 256,128; o200k: ∼200k), trading $2Vd$ embedding parameters for compression and effective context. Verify
  • Tokenizer fertility differences reach 15× across languages, multiplying price, per-byte FLOPs, and effective context loss for non-Latin scripts. Verify
  • Perplexity is exponential in the tokenizer’s compression ratio and can even invert model rankings; only bits-per-byte (total bits over an invariant denominator) is comparable across tokenizers. Certain
Chapter 24

Scaling Laws

Learning Objectives
  • Derive the $C \approx 6ND$ training-FLOP estimate and the $2N$ per-token inference estimate from first principles, and state when each breaks down.
  • State the Kaplan and Chinchilla parametric forms, and derive the compute-optimal allocation $N^* \propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}$, $D^* \propto C^{\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)}$ from the Chinchilla loss surface.
  • Explain precisely why Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. disagreed about optimal model size, and which was right about what.
  • Formulate the inference-aware optimum of Sardana and Frankle and show why counting served tokens makes the optimal model strictly smaller and the optimal dataset strictly larger than Chinchilla prescribes.
  • Implement a Chinchilla-form scaling-law fit — Huber loss on log-loss, multi-start L-BFGS-B, analytic allocation check — in working code.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 (Language Modeling from Scratch) devotes a full unit to scaling laws and is the closest course treatment of this chapter, including the Chinchilla fitting mechanics. Chakraborty, Introduction to Large Language Models, covers the Kaplan-to-Chinchilla arc from the NLP side and is useful for the historical framing.

Chapter 23 fixed the objective: next-token cross-entropy over a tokenized corpus. This chapter asks the question that objective makes quantitative: given a compute budget $C$, how should you split it between parameters $N$ and tokens $D$? Scaling laws are the only instrument in deep learning that reliably predicts the performance of a model before it is trained, and they decide budgets measured in tens of millions of dollars. But the field's most-quoted answer — Chinchilla's twenty tokens per parameter — is now violated by nearly every deployed model, on purpose, and correctly so: Chinchilla optimized training compute alone, and nobody deploys under that objective. We derive the FLOP accounting, both classic laws and their reconciliation, the 2024 replication that corrected Chinchilla's own numbers, and the inference-aware optimum that explains modern over-training. Chapter 25 uses these results to design pretraining runs; Chapters 28 and 33 revisit the compute ledger at test time.

24.1 Power Laws and Why They Appear

Definition 24.1 (Neural scaling law)

A neural scaling law is an empirical relation of the form $\mathcal{L}(x) = E + c\,x^{-\alpha}$, where $x$ is a resource (parameters $N$, tokens $D$, or compute $C$), $\alpha > 0$ is the scaling exponent, and $E \ge 0$ is the irreducible loss — the entropy of the data that no model can remove. Subtracting $E$, the law is a straight line in log-log coordinates: $\log(\mathcal{L} - E) = \log c - \alpha \log x$.

The empirical fact comes first: language-model loss follows such power laws across at least seven orders of magnitude of compute, with deviations from the fit smaller than the run-to-run noise Certain. This is not a generic property of curve fitting — exponentials, logarithms, and saturating rationals all fit badly — and it is the entire reason small-scale experiments transfer: you fit the law on runs costing $10^{-4}$ of the target budget and extrapolate.

Why power laws? Two theoretical accounts cover most observed regimes. Sharma and Kaplan (2020) argue that when a network regresses a function on a data manifold of intrinsic dimension $d$, approximation error scales as $N^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha \approx 4/d$: the exponent measures the effective dimension of the data, which is why it is stable across architectures but shifts across datasets Likely. Bahri, Dyer, Kaplan, Lee, and Sharma (PNAS 2024) separate a resolution-limited regime — the model or dataset is too small to resolve the target function, giving dataset- and architecture-dependent exponents — from a variance-limited regime where the exponent is a universal $1/2$ or $1$ in the fluctuation statistics Likely. The practical consequence of both accounts is the same: exponents are properties of the data distribution more than of the model, so they survive architecture tweaks and die under data changes. Section 24.8 returns to when they die.

One fitting caution before the laws themselves: because of $E$, ordinary least squares on $\log \mathcal{L}$ against $\log x$ is biased — the curve flattens as it approaches $E$, and a straight-line fit through the flattening region underestimates $\alpha$. Every serious fit estimates $E$ jointly with the exponent, which is exactly what the Chinchilla parametric form does.

24.2 Kaplan et al. (2020)

24.2.1 The Compute Ledger: $C \approx 6ND$ and $2N$ per Token

Training cost is dominated by matrix multiplications, and each weight in a matmul participates in one multiply-accumulate per token: the forward pass costs $2N$ FLOPs per token (one multiply, one add, per parameter). The backward pass runs two matmuls for every forward one — gradients with respect to activations, and gradients with respect to weights (Chapter 11) — costing $4N$. Hence

$$C \;\approx\; \underbrace{2ND}_{\text{forward}} + \underbrace{4ND}_{\text{backward}} \;=\; 6ND.$$

What this ignores: attention-score computation, which per layer and token costs about $2 T d_{\text{model}}$ forward FLOPs for $QK^\top$ and the same for $AV$ — halved to $\approx 2Td_{\text{model}}$ total by causal masking, since a token attends to $T/2$ positions on average. Against the parameter term $2N \approx 24 L d_{\text{model}}^2$ per token, the attention term is then a fraction $\sim T/(12\,d_{\text{model}})$: negligible for $T \ll 12\,d_{\text{model}}$, dominant for very long contexts (Chapter 19) Certain. Inference is forward-only with a KV cache (Chapter 33), so generating one token costs $\approx 2N$ FLOPs plus the attention term. These two constants, $6N$ per training token and $2N$ per served token, are the entire arithmetic of this chapter.

Example 24.1 (The ledger for a 7B model)

Train $N = 7\times10^9$ on $D = 2\times10^{12}$ tokens: $C = 6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} = 8.4\times10^{22}$ FLOPs. Now serve it for $10^{12}$ generated tokens: $2 \times 7\times10^9 \times 10^{12} = 1.4\times10^{22}$ FLOPs. Six such serving campaigns equal the entire training run — and popular models serve far more than $6\times10^{12}$ tokens over their lifetime. Inference is not a rounding error in the lifetime budget; Section 24.5 makes this the objective.

24.2.2 The Kaplan Laws

Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020) fit single-variable power laws on transformer language models, with $N$ counted as non-embedding parameters: $\mathcal{L}(N) = (N_c/N)^{\alpha_N}$ with $\alpha_N \approx 0.076$; $\mathcal{L}(D) = (D_c/D)^{\alpha_D}$ with $\alpha_D \approx 0.095$ for early-stopped training; and along the compute-efficient frontier $\mathcal{L}(C_{\min}) = (C_c/C_{\min})^{\alpha_C^{\min}}$ with $\alpha_C^{\min} \approx 0.050$ Certain. They also fit a joint form, $\mathcal{L}(N,D) = \big[(N_c/N)^{\alpha_N/\alpha_D} + D_c/D\big]^{\alpha_D}$, an ancestor of the Chinchilla surface. Their headline allocation: optimal model size grows as $N^* \propto C^{0.73}$, with tokens absorbing only $D \propto C^{0.27}$ — "big models, briefly trained." Tokens per parameter should fall as $C^{-0.46}$ under this rule. GPT-3 was its direct product: $175$B parameters on $300$B tokens, about $1.7$ tokens per parameter Certain.

24.3 Chinchilla (2022)

Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022) reran the question with over 400 training runs from 70M to 16B parameters and three estimation strategies: (1) for fixed $N$, sweep training duration and take the loss envelope; (2) isoFLOP profiles — for fixed $C$, sweep $N$ with $D = C/6N$ and locate the parabola minimum in $\log N$; (3) fit a parametric surface to all runs. Writing $N^* \propto C^{a}$, the three approaches gave $a = 0.50$, $0.49$, and $0.46$ — against Kaplan's $0.73$ Certain. The parametric form is the one you should carry:

$$\mathcal{L}(N, D) \;=\; E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}},$$

with published fit $E = 1.69$, $A = 406.4$, $B = 410.7$, $\alpha = 0.34$, $\beta = 0.28$ Certain. The three terms are irreducible entropy, finite-capacity error, and finite-data error. The fit minimized a Huber loss ($\delta = 10^{-3}$) between predicted and observed $\log \mathcal{L}$, using a log-sum-exp parameterization and a grid of L-BFGS-B restarts — details that matter in Section 24.4.

Theorem 24.1 (Compute-optimal allocation)

Minimizing $\mathcal{L}(N,D) = E + AN^{-\alpha} + BD^{-\beta}$ subject to $6ND = C$ yields

$$N^*(C) = G\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{a}, \quad D^*(C) = G^{-1}\left(\frac{C}{6}\right)^{b}, \quad a = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},\; b = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\; G = \left(\frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}}.$$

Proof. Substitute $D = C/(6N)$: $\mathcal{L}(N) = E + AN^{-\alpha} + B(C/6)^{-\beta}N^{\beta}$. Setting $\mathcal{L}'(N) = -\alpha A N^{-\alpha-1} + \beta B (C/6)^{-\beta} N^{\beta-1} = 0$ gives $N^{\alpha+\beta} = \frac{\alpha A}{\beta B}(C/6)^{\beta}$, i.e. $N^* = G(C/6)^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}$; $D^* = (C/6)/N^*$ follows, and $\mathcal{L}''(N^*) > 0$ since both terms of $\mathcal{L}''$ are positive there. $\blacksquare$

The corollary that reorganized the field: with $\alpha \approx \beta$, $a \approx b \approx 0.5$ — parameters and tokens should scale equally, each as $\sqrt{C}$, and the ratio $D^*/N^* = G^{-2}(C/6)^{(\alpha-\beta)/(\alpha+\beta)}$ is nearly constant. Empirically, approaches 1 and 2 put that constant near 20 tokens per parameter Certain. DeepMind's demonstration was brutal: at Gopher's budget of $5.76\times10^{23}$ FLOPs, they trained Chinchilla — 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens instead of Gopher's 280B on 300B — and it won essentially every evaluation at identical training cost, with a 4× cheaper forward pass forever after Certain.

24.4 The Chinchilla Replication and Its Corrections

24.4.1 The 2024 Refit

Besiroglu, Erdil, Barnett, and You (Epoch AI, 2024) reconstructed the run data from the Chinchilla paper's figures and attempted to replicate Approach 3 — the parametric fit. Three findings Certain: the published parameters fit the reconstructed data poorly; the implied scaling policy is inconsistent with Approaches 1 and 2 and with the 20-tokens-per-parameter ratio used to train Chinchilla itself; and the paper's confidence intervals are implausibly narrow — tight enough to require on the order of 600,000 runs, where fewer than 500 existed. You can verify the inconsistency by hand from Theorem 24.1: the published $\alpha = 0.34$, $\beta = 0.28$ give $a = 0.28/0.62 \approx 0.452$, and Artifact 24.1 computes the implied optimum at the Gopher budget as $N^* = 3.2\times10^{10}$ with $D^*/N^* \approx 93$ tokens per parameter — not 20, and not the 70B that was actually trained.

The diagnosed cause is an optimization bug, not a conceptual one: the objective averaged Huber losses over runs instead of summing, shrinking the objective's scale so that L-BFGS-B's termination tolerances triggered before convergence — in the original fit and in every bootstrap replicate, which is what manufactured the narrow intervals. Epoch's corrected fit is $E = 1.82$, $A = 482.0$, $B = 2085.4$, $\alpha = 0.348$, $\beta = 0.366$, giving $a = \beta/(\alpha+\beta) \approx 0.51$ Verify (check against arXiv:2404.10102). The correction is reassuring, not damning: the refit agrees with Approaches 1 and 2 and with the ratio Chinchilla actually used. The headline — scale $N$ and $D$ together, roughly 20:1 — survived its own paper's broken fit.

Common Pitfall

Averaging a robust loss instead of summing it, then trusting default optimizer tolerances. With 300+ points and Huber $\delta = 10^{-3}$, the mean objective and its gradients sit orders of magnitude below the sum's, and L-BFGS-B's default stopping tests — the projected-gradient threshold pgtol and an ftol comparison that becomes absolute-scale for objectives below 1 — declare victory far from the optimum. This single line produced published parameters inconsistent with the paper's own training run, and bootstrap intervals ~30× too tight. Defenses: sum, not average; multi-start from a coarse grid and demand the starts agree; and sanity-check the fitted optimum against a policy you know is good.

24.4.2 Why Kaplan and Chinchilla Disagreed

$0.73$ versus $0.50$ is not noise, and the resolution is now well understood from two independent studies. Pearce and Song (2024) attribute most of the gap to Kaplan counting non-embedding parameters and fitting at small scale, where embeddings are a large fraction of the model: measured in total parameters, small models look relatively better, tilting the fitted exponent toward "grow $N$ faster" Likely. Porian et al. (NeurIPS 2024) reproduced Kaplan's law and then transformed it into Chinchilla's by fixing three things: the last layer's computational cost (again an accounting effect largest at small scale), a warmup schedule too long for small models, and failure to re-tune optimizer hyperparameters with scale; notably, careful cosine decay — Hoffmann et al.'s own hypothesis for the discrepancy — turned out not to be essential Likely. The verdict: Chinchilla was right about the allocation; Kaplan was right about the deeper claims — power-law form, smooth predictability, exponents as data properties — and wrong at small scale for reasons that are bookkeeping, not physics. The meta-lesson is the one to keep: a scaling law is a fit to a specific training procedure, and it extrapolates only while the procedure does.

24.5 Inference-Aware and Over-Training Regimes

Chinchilla's objective is training compute alone. But Example 24.1 showed lifetime inference is comparable to training, and Theorem 24.1's optimum is a flat one: near $N^*$, first-order deviations cost only second-order loss. So consider the deployment objective of Sardana and Frankle (MosaicML, ICML 2024): reach a quality target $\ell$ while minimizing lifetime compute, with $D_{\text{inf}}$ tokens to be served:

$$\min_{N, D} \;\; 6ND + 2ND_{\text{inf}} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathcal{L}(N, D) = \ell.$$

The constraint pins $D$ as a function of $N$: $D(N) = \big(B / (\ell - E - AN^{-\alpha})\big)^{1/\beta}$, defined for $N > (A/(\ell - E))^{1/\alpha}$, a hard floor below which no amount of data reaches $\ell$. The Chinchilla-optimal $N$ is precisely the minimizer of the first term $6ND(N)$ — minimal training cost for the target — and the added term $2ND_{\text{inf}}$ is strictly increasing in $N$. The optimum therefore moves strictly left: smaller $N$, and, since $D(N)$ is decreasing in $N$ along the constraint, strictly larger $D$ Certain. The model gets smaller and trains longer, paying extra training FLOPs once to save $2\,\Delta N$ FLOPs on every served token forever. Sardana and Frankle validated the regime empirically with 47 trained models, finding loss still improving at token-to-parameter ratios up to 10,000, and estimate that at realistic demand (order $10^9$ requests) the optimal configuration deviates substantially from Chinchilla Certain. Their later revision weights FLOPs by real hardware cost and utilization, which differ between training and inference and shift the optimum further Verify.

Practice ran ahead of the theory. Llama 2 (2023) trained 7B on 2T tokens ($\approx 285$ tokens/parameter, 14× Chinchilla); Llama 3 (2024) trained 8B on over 15T tokens — roughly 1,900 tokens per parameter, two orders of magnitude past the 20:1 rule Verify. Gadre et al. (ICLR 2025) showed this regime is itself law-governed: across 104 models with token multipliers up to $M = 640$ (where $M = 20$ is roughly Chinchilla-optimal), over-trained runs sit on predictable power laws; they forecast the loss of a 1.4B model trained on 900B tokens to within 0.7% relative error using 300× less compute than the run itself Certain. Over-training is not off the map; it is a charted region Chinchilla's objective simply never asked about.

Contested Is Chinchilla-optimal the right training target at all? One side: the fit and Theorem 24.1 are sound, and for a fixed training budget with no deployment — ablations, scaling-study points, research baselines — 20:1 remains the correct prescription. The other side: as deployment guidance the rule is simply wrong, because the objective omits the dominant cost term; every serious deployed model since 2023 is over-trained by 10–100×, and correctly so. Our position: treat "Chinchilla-optimal" as a statement about training-compute efficiency only, and size deployed models with the inference-aware objective; the burden of proof now falls on anyone training a flagship model at 20:1. What would change this: evidence that loss stops obeying the fitted surface at extreme $D/N$ (Gadre et al. and Sardana & Frankle both looked and found the opposite up to their tested ranges), or a deployment profile where $D_{\text{inf}} \ll D$ — in which case the two objectives coincide.

24.6 Data-Constrained Scaling

The inference-aware optimum demands enormous $D$, and the web is finite — so what happens when you must repeat data? Muennighoff et al. (NeurIPS 2023) trained up to 9B-parameter models on up to 900B tokens with controlled repetition and fit a modified law in which repeated tokens contribute a decaying effective data count: with $U$ unique tokens read for $R$ epochs, effective data is $D' = U + U R^{*}\!\left(1 - e^{-(R-1)/R^{*}}\right)$, an exponential discount with fitted decay constant around $R^{*} \approx 15$ repetitions Verify (check the fitted constants against arXiv:2305.16264). The operational findings: up to about 4 epochs, repeated data is nearly indistinguishable from fresh data at fixed compute; returns then decay, and by tens of epochs additional repetition contributes essentially nothing — the value of extra compute on repeated data "decays to zero" Certain. They also find that at fixed compute under data constraint, the optimum shifts toward more epochs and fewer parameters than naive Chinchilla scaling. For the "data wall" debate this is the load-bearing result: multiplying every over-training prescription by a usable factor of ~4, but not more. Chapter 25 takes up the complementary levers — data quality, curricula, and synthetic data.

24.7 Scaling Laws for MoE and for Downstream Tasks

Mixture-of-experts models (Chapter 22) break the single-$N$ abstraction: total parameters and per-token FLOPs become independent axes. Clark et al. (DeepMind, 2022) fit unified laws over model size and expert count and collapsed all routed models onto one curve via an effective parameter count; their fits suggested routing's benefit shrinks as the base model grows Certain — but their runs held training tokens roughly fixed, a Kaplan-style protocol flaw. Krajewski et al. (2024) refit with token budgets scaled properly and an extra axis, expert granularity, and reached the opposite operating conclusion: compute-for-compute, MoE beats dense at essentially every budget, with the gap widening as budgets grow, and the convention of sizing experts to mirror the dense FFN is suboptimal at almost any budget Likely. The same lesson as Section 24.4.2, one architecture over: the exponents were less wrong than the protocol.

Downstream capability is the harder target because the loss-to-task mapping need not be smooth. Wei et al. (2022) catalogued emergent abilities — tasks flat at small scale, then abruptly above chance. Schaeffer et al. (NeurIPS 2023) countered that most catalogued emergence is manufactured by discontinuous metrics: exact-match accuracy on a $k$-token answer thresholds a smoothly improving per-token likelihood, and under continuous metrics the same models improve smoothly Likely. The pragmatic middle: aggregate downstream performance tracks pretraining loss well enough to fit — Gadre et al. predict average top-1 error across 46 tasks from loss to within about one percentage point — while individual tasks remain genuinely hard to forecast, which is a serious problem for safety cases and product planning alike Likely. Chapter 29 confronts the measurement side of this.

24.8 Where Scaling Laws Break

A scaling law is an interpolation of a fixed procedure, dressed as a prediction. It breaks in identifiable ways. Protocol drift: change the parameter accounting, warmup, or tokens-per-run protocol and the fitted exponents change — Kaplan-versus-Chinchilla and Clark-versus-Krajewski are both this failure, published Certain. Data drift: exponents are data properties (Section 24.1), so a new mixture or heavy filtering moves the constants; fits do not transfer across corpora unmeasured. Non-monotone tasks: the Inverse Scaling Prize (McKenzie et al., 2023) documented tasks that get worse with scale, several of which later turn U-shaped at still-larger scale (Wei et al.) — smooth power laws cannot represent either, and Caballero et al.'s "broken neural scaling laws" (ICLR 2023) fit such transitions only by adding explicit break points Likely. Numerics: precision is a hidden axis — Kumar et al. (2024) fit scaling laws in which low-precision training acts like a reduction in effective parameter count, coupling Chapter 5's concerns directly into the allocation problem Likely. And the objective itself keeps moving: test-time compute (Chapter 28) adds a third spending axis that trades against both $N$ and $D$, and the exchange rate is an open research front. The durable core is smaller than the headlines but real: within a fixed procedure and data distribution, loss versus compute is predictable to remarkable precision — and nothing else about a model is guaranteed to be.

Artifact 24.1 — Chinchilla Fit, Compute-Optimal Allocation, and the Inference-Aware Correction

The artifact plants the published Chinchilla parameters as ground truth, generates 324 noisy synthetic runs on a $(N, D)$ grid (1% log-normal noise, 5% gross outliers), and recovers all five parameters by minimizing a summed Huber loss ($\delta = 10^{-3}$) on log-loss with a log-sum-exp parameterization and 243 L-BFGS-B restarts — the corrected version of Hoffmann et al.'s Approach 3. It then verifies Theorem 24.1 by brute force, checks the fit reproduces the analytic allocation, and re-solves under the Sardana-Frankle objective with 5T lifetime served tokens.

"""Artifact 24.1 -- Chinchilla parametric fit, compute-optimal allocation,
and the inference-aware correction.

Plan: (1) plant the published Chinchilla ground truth
L(N,D) = E + A/N^alpha + B/D^beta  with (E,A,B,alpha,beta) =
(1.69, 406.4, 410.7, 0.34, 0.28); (2) generate noisy synthetic loss
observations on a grid of (N, D), including 5% heavy-tailed outliers;
(3) recover the five parameters by minimizing a SUMMED Huber loss on
log-loss with an LSE parameterization, exactly as Hoffmann et al. (2022)
Approach 3 did -- and as the Besiroglu et al. (2024) replication showed
must be summed, not averaged, to avoid premature L-BFGS termination;
(4) derive the compute-optimal (N*, D*) analytically, cross-check by
brute force, and check the fit reproduces it; (5) re-solve under the
Sardana-Frankle inference-aware objective  6*N*D_tr + 2*N*D_inf  at a
fixed loss target and show N shrinks while D grows. Pure NumPy + scipy.
"""
import time
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize, minimize_scalar
from scipy.special import logsumexp

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# ----- ground truth: Hoffmann et al. (2022), Table "Approach 3" (rounded) ---
TRUE = dict(E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7, alpha=0.34, beta=0.28)


def surface(N, D, p):
    """Chinchilla parametric loss surface L(N, D)."""
    return p["E"] + p["A"] * N ** -p["alpha"] + p["B"] * D ** -p["beta"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- synthetic
def make_data(n_side=18):
    """Grid of (N, D) runs, 1e7..1e11 params x 1e9..3e12 tokens, with
    multiplicative log-normal noise (sigma = 1%) plus 5% gross outliers
    (extra sigma = 8%) -- the case Huber loss exists to survive."""
    N, D = np.meshgrid(np.logspace(7, 11, n_side), np.logspace(9, 12.5, n_side))
    N, D = N.ravel(), D.ravel()
    eps = rng.normal(0.0, 0.01, N.size)
    out = rng.random(N.size) < 0.05
    eps[out] += rng.normal(0.0, 0.08, out.sum())
    return N, D, surface(N, D, TRUE) * np.exp(eps)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the fit
def huber_sum(r, delta=1e-3):
    """SUMMED Huber loss. Averaging instead of summing shrinks the objective
    scale ~300x and made L-BFGS-B stop early in the original paper's fit
    (Besiroglu et al. 2024) -- so we sum."""
    a = np.abs(r)
    return np.sum(np.where(a <= delta, 0.5 * r * r, delta * (a - 0.5 * delta)))


def objective(x, logN, logD, logL):
    a, b, e, al, be = x  # A = exp(a), B = exp(b), E = exp(e)
    pred = logsumexp(np.stack([a - al * logN, b - be * logD,
                               np.full_like(logN, e)]), axis=0)
    return huber_sum(pred - logL)


def fit(N, D, L):
    """L-BFGS-B from a grid of inits (Hoffmann et al. style); keep the best."""
    logN, logD, logL = np.log(N), np.log(D), np.log(L)
    best = None
    for a0 in (0.0, 5.0, 10.0):
        for b0 in (0.0, 5.0, 10.0):
            for e0 in (-1.0, 0.0, 1.0):
                for al0 in (0.1, 0.3, 0.7):
                    for be0 in (0.1, 0.3, 0.7):
                        r = minimize(objective, x0=(a0, b0, e0, al0, be0),
                                     args=(logN, logD, logL), method="L-BFGS-B")
                        if best is None or r.fun < best.fun:
                            best = r
    a, b, e, al, be = best.x
    return dict(E=np.exp(e), A=np.exp(a), B=np.exp(b), alpha=al, beta=be)


# ------------------------------------------- compute-optimal allocation
def compute_optimal(p, C):
    """argmin_{6ND=C} L(N,D):  N* = G (C/6)^a with a = beta/(alpha+beta),
    G = (alpha A / (beta B))^{1/(alpha+beta)};  D* = (C/6)/N*."""
    al, be = p["alpha"], p["beta"]
    a = be / (al + be)
    G = (al * p["A"] / (be * p["B"])) ** (1.0 / (al + be))
    Nopt = G * (C / 6.0) ** a
    return Nopt, (C / 6.0) / Nopt


# --------------------------------------- inference-aware optimum (Sardana)
def inference_aware(p, ell, D_inf):
    """min_N  6 N D_tr(N) + 2 N D_inf   s.t.  L(N, D_tr) = ell, where
    D_tr(N) = (B / (ell - E - A N^-alpha))^{1/beta}. 1-D bounded search."""
    E, A, B, al, be = (p[k] for k in ("E", "A", "B", "alpha", "beta"))
    N_min = (A / (ell - E)) ** (1.0 / al)          # below this, ell unreachable

    def D_tr(N):
        return (B / (ell - E - A * N ** -al)) ** (1.0 / be)

    def total(logN):
        N = 10.0 ** logN
        return 6.0 * N * D_tr(N) + 2.0 * N * D_inf

    res = minimize_scalar(total, bounds=(np.log10(N_min) + 1e-3, 13.0),
                          method="bounded",
                          options={"xatol": 1e-10})
    N = 10.0 ** res.x
    return N, D_tr(N), res.fun


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.time()
    N, D, L = make_data()
    print(f"synthetic runs: {N.size} (N in [1e7,1e11], D in [1e9,3e12])")

    # ---- 1. recover the planted parameters ------------------------------
    f = fit(N, D, L)
    print("\nparam    truth      fitted")
    for k in ("E", "A", "B", "alpha", "beta"):
        print(f"{k:5s} {TRUE[k]:9.4f} {f[k]:11.4f}")
    assert abs(f["alpha"] - TRUE["alpha"]) < 0.02, "alpha not recovered"
    assert abs(f["beta"] - TRUE["beta"]) < 0.02, "beta not recovered"
    assert abs(f["E"] - TRUE["E"]) / TRUE["E"] < 0.02, "E not recovered"
    assert abs(np.log(f["A"] / TRUE["A"])) < 0.25, "A not recovered"
    assert abs(np.log(f["B"] / TRUE["B"])) < 0.25, "B not recovered"

    # ---- 2. compute-optimal allocation, analytic vs brute force ---------
    C0 = 5.76e23                                   # the Gopher/Chinchilla budget
    a_true = TRUE["beta"] / (TRUE["alpha"] + TRUE["beta"])
    a_fit = f["beta"] / (f["alpha"] + f["beta"])
    Nc_t, Dc_t = compute_optimal(TRUE, C0)
    Nc_f, Dc_f = compute_optimal(f, C0)
    # brute force on the planted surface: scan N at fixed C, D = C/(6N)
    Ng = np.logspace(8, 12, 400_001)
    Nbf = Ng[np.argmin(surface(Ng, C0 / (6.0 * Ng), TRUE))]
    print(f"\nexponent a = beta/(alpha+beta): true {a_true:.4f}  fitted {a_fit:.4f}")
    print(f"N* at C={C0:.2e}: analytic {Nc_t:.3e}  brute-force {Nbf:.3e}  "
          f"fitted-law {Nc_f:.3e}")
    print(f"tokens/param at C0: true {Dc_t/Nc_t:.1f}  fitted {Dc_f/Nc_f:.1f}")
    assert abs(np.log(Nbf / Nc_t)) < 1e-3, "closed form disagrees w/ brute force"
    assert abs(a_fit - a_true) < 0.02, "allocation exponent not recovered"
    assert abs(np.log((Dc_f / Nc_f) / (Dc_t / Nc_t))) < 0.10, \
        "fitted tokens/param ratio off by >10%"

    # ---- 3. inference-aware re-solve (Sardana & Frankle objective) ------
    ell = surface(Nc_f, Dc_f, f)                   # fix the quality target
    D_inf = 5e12                                   # 5T served tokens over life
    Ni, Di, tot_i = inference_aware(f, ell, D_inf)
    tot_c = 6.0 * Nc_f * Dc_f + 2.0 * Nc_f * D_inf
    print(f"\nloss target {ell:.4f}, lifetime inference demand {D_inf:.1e} tokens")
    print("              Chinchilla-optimal   inference-aware")
    print(f"N            {Nc_f:15.3e} {Ni:17.3e}")
    print(f"D_train      {Dc_f:15.3e} {Di:17.3e}")
    print(f"tokens/param {Dc_f/Nc_f:15.1f} {Di/Ni:17.1f}")
    print(f"train FLOPs  {6*Nc_f*Dc_f:15.3e} {6*Ni*Di:17.3e}")
    print(f"infer FLOPs  {2*Nc_f*D_inf:15.3e} {2*Ni*D_inf:17.3e}")
    print(f"total FLOPs  {tot_c:15.3e} {tot_i:17.3e}"
          f"   (saves {100*(1-tot_i/tot_c):.1f}%)")
    assert Ni < Nc_f, "inference-aware N must be strictly smaller"
    assert Di > Dc_f, "inference-aware D must be strictly larger"
    assert tot_i < tot_c, "re-solved optimum must lower total FLOPs"
    # same quality, by construction: verify numerically
    assert abs(surface(Ni, Di, f) - ell) < 1e-9

    print(f"\nall assertions passed  ({time.time()-t0:.1f}s)")

Running it (21.6 s on CPU): from 324 noisy runs the fit recovers $\alpha = 0.3350$, $\beta = 0.2741$, $E = 1.6696$ against planted $(0.34, 0.28, 1.69)$, and the allocation exponent $a$ comes out $0.4500$ against the analytic $0.4516$; the brute-force minimum over 400,001 candidates matches the closed-form $N^* = 3.219\times10^{10}$ to the printed precision. Note the printed tokens-per-parameter ratio at the Gopher budget under the published Approach 3 parameters: 92.6 — the internal inconsistency of Section 24.4, reproduced from the paper's own numbers. The inference-aware re-solve at 5T served tokens moves the optimum from $N = 3.12\times10^{10},\ D = 3.07\times10^{12}$ (98.4 tokens/param) to $N = 2.02\times10^{10},\ D = 5.08\times10^{12}$ (251.5 tokens/param) at identical loss 1.9225, cutting lifetime FLOPs by 8.0%. All assertions pass.

Key Takeaways
  • Training costs $C \approx 6ND$ FLOPs (2 forward + 4 backward per parameter per token) and inference costs $\approx 2N$ per generated token; attention adds a term of relative size $\sim T/(12\,d_{\text{model}})$. Certain
  • Minimizing $E + AN^{-\alpha} + BD^{-\beta}$ under $6ND = C$ gives $N^* \propto C^{\beta/(\alpha+\beta)}$; with $\alpha \approx \beta$ this means scaling $N$ and $D$ equally, about 20 tokens per parameter at the training-compute optimum. Certain
  • Kaplan's $N^* \propto C^{0.73}$ came from protocol artifacts — non-embedding parameter counting at small scale, last-layer cost, warmup, and untuned optimizers — not from different physics; the power-law form itself was right. Likely
  • The 2024 replication showed Chinchilla's published Approach 3 fit was internally inconsistent (an averaged Huber loss stopped L-BFGS-B early and produced ~600,000-run confidence intervals from <500 runs); the corrected fit re-agrees with the 20:1 policy. Certain
  • As deployment guidance, 20:1 is obsolete: counting served tokens makes the optimal model strictly smaller and the optimal dataset strictly larger, and flagship models are correctly over-trained by 10–100× — though Chinchilla-optimal remains right for train-once research budgets. Contested
Chapter 25

The Pretraining Pipeline: Data, Curricula, Mid-Training

Learning Objectives
  • Implement MinHash locality-sensitive hashing for near-duplicate detection, and state its false-positive and false-negative rates as explicit functions of the band count $b$ and rows-per-band $r$.
  • Compare heuristic filtering, classifier-based filtering, and perplexity filtering, citing the measured downstream effect of each in controlled experiments.
  • Explain data mixing and domain reweighting, and why code and mathematics data improve reasoning on tasks outside those domains.
  • Explain mid-training and annealing phases, and why the final few percent of training tokens carries disproportionate influence on benchmark performance.
  • Implement a deduplication and decontamination pipeline in working code, verified against brute-force Jaccard similarity and planted benchmark leaks.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 (Language Modeling from Scratch): its data lectures and the filtering/deduplication assignment are the closest thing to a lab course on this chapter. Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), for the mechanics of turning raw text into training batches, including packing.

Chapter 24 treated the dataset size $D$ as a scalar in a scaling law, as if tokens were interchangeable. They are not, and since roughly 2023 the evidence says the data pipeline — not the architecture — is where most model-quality variance at fixed compute now comes from: identical Transformers trained on differently-filtered versions of the same crawl differ by more on downstream benchmarks than most architectural interventions in Part IV buy you. This chapter walks the pipeline in execution order: acquisition (25.1), extraction and heuristic filtering (25.2), deduplication (25.3, with the MinHash mathematics done properly), model-based quality filtering (25.4), mixture weights (25.5), synthetic data and the collapse debate (25.6), decontamination (25.7) — without which Chapter 29's measurements are fiction — mid-training and annealing (25.8), and sequence packing (25.9). Chapter 26 picks up where pretraining hands off.

25.1 Where Tokens Come From

Almost every open pretraining corpus is, by token count, mostly Common Crawl: a nonprofit web crawl publishing snapshots since 2008, each recent snapshot containing on the order of billions of pages of raw WARC (HTML plus HTTP metadata). The pipeline's job is to turn petabytes of markup into trillions of clean tokens. The reference open corpora as of this writing Verify: FineWeb (Hugging Face, 2024) — 15T tokens distilled from 96 Common Crawl snapshots; FineWeb-Edu — a 1.3T-token classifier-filtered subset; DCLM (DataComp-LM) — a 240T-token raw pool and the 3.8T-token filtered DCLM-Baseline; Nemotron-CC (NVIDIA) — 6.3T tokens (4.4T deduplicated real + 1.9T synthetic) combining classifier ensembles with synthetic rephrasing; plus curated non-web sources — code (the Stack v2), academic text, books, forums — that fill the remaining ten-or-so percent of typical mixtures.

The chapter's central irony is documented in the disclosure gap. DCLM demonstrated that holding architecture and training recipe fixed and varying only the dataset moves a 7B model to 64% five-shot MMLU at 2.6T tokens — 6.6 points above the previous best open-data model while using 40% less compute Verify. Meanwhile frontier technical reports describe architecture in detail and data in a paragraph: Llama 3's data section names no sources; GPT-4's names nothing at all. The parts that matter most are the parts disclosed least, which is precisely why the open replications above are scientifically important: they are the only controlled experiments we have Likely.

25.2 Extraction, Language ID, Heuristic Filters

Common Crawl ships pre-extracted plain text (WET files), and the first empirical surprise of the modern pipeline is that you should not use it. Both FineWeb and DCLM found that re-extracting text from raw HTML with a boilerplate-aware extractor (trafilatura and resiliparse respectively) beats WET-trained models by a clear downstream margin — extraction quality was worth more than several filtering refinements combined, because WET text is saturated with menus, cookie banners, and navigation chrome that no later filter fully removes Likely. Language identification follows, typically a fastText classifier over character n-grams; FineWeb keeps documents scoring $\geq 0.65$ for English Verify.

Then come heuristic filters: hand-written rules of the C4 and Gopher lineage. C4 (2019) dropped lines without terminal punctuation, pages containing lorem ipsum or JavaScript, and anything matching a bad-words list — the last infamously deleting large amounts of legitimate medical and legal text. Gopher's rules (2021) are the durable set: document length between 50 and 100{,}000 words, mean word length in $[3, 10]$, symbol-to-word ratio below 0.1, bullet-point line fraction below 90%, and a minimum stopword count — the stopword rule alone removing enormous quantities of keyword-stuffed SEO spam. These rules are cheap, transparent, and embarrassingly effective; every serious pipeline still runs a variant of them before anything learned touches the data Certain.

25.3 Exact and Near Deduplication

The web is massively self-plagiarizing: mirrors, boilerplate, syndication, quotation. Duplicated training text wastes compute on gradient steps the model has already taken, and worse, it drives verbatim memorization: Lee et al. (2021) showed that deduplication reduces the rate at which models emit memorized training sequences by an order of magnitude while slightly improving perplexity Likely. Exact deduplication is easy — hash each document (or, in the suffix-array variant, remove every repeated substring of 50+ tokens). The hard problem is near-duplicates: the same article with a different footer. Comparing all $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs of $n \approx 10^{10}$ documents is out of the question; the standard solution is MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing, which finds high-similarity pairs in $O(n)$ expected work.

Definition 25.1 (Jaccard similarity)

For finite sets $A, B$ (in practice: the sets of word $n$-gram "shingles" of two documents), the Jaccard similarity is $J(A,B) = |A \cap B| \,/\, |A \cup B| \in [0,1]$. Two documents are near-duplicates at level $s$ if $J \geq s$; production pipelines use 5-word shingles and $s \approx 0.7$–$0.8$.

25.3.1 MinHash and LSH

MinHash compresses a set into a short signature whose entries collide with probability exactly equal to the Jaccard similarity.

Theorem 25.1 (MinHash collision probability)

Let $\pi$ be a uniformly random permutation of the shingle universe $\mathcal{U}$, and define $h_\pi(A) = \min_{x \in A} \pi(x)$. Then for any $A, B \subseteq \mathcal{U}$, $\Pr[\,h_\pi(A) = h_\pi(B)\,] = J(A,B)$.

Proof. The element of $A \cup B$ achieving $\min_{x \in A \cup B}\pi(x)$ is uniform over $A \cup B$, since $\pi$ is a uniform permutation. The two minima agree iff that argmin lies in $A \cap B$: if it does, it is the minimum of both sets; if it lies in $A \setminus B$, then $h_\pi(A) < h_\pi(B)$, and symmetrically. Hence the collision probability is $|A \cap B|/|A \cup B|$. $\blacksquare$

A signature of $k$ independent MinHashes therefore gives an unbiased Jaccard estimator with variance $s(1-s)/k$ — but pairwise signature comparison is still $O(n^2)$. Banding fixes this: split the $k = br$ signature rows into $b$ bands of $r$ rows, hash each band to a bucket, and declare any two documents sharing any bucket a candidate pair. Only candidates are ever compared.

Theorem 25.2 (The LSH S-curve)

With $b$ bands of $r$ independent MinHash rows, a pair with Jaccard similarity $s$ becomes a candidate with probability $$P(s) = 1 - \left(1 - s^{r}\right)^{b},$$ an S-shaped curve whose transition is centered at $s^{*} = (1/b)^{1/r}$, where $P(s^{*}) = 1 - (1 - 1/b)^{b} \to 1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632$ for large $b$.

Proof. By Theorem 25.1 each row agrees independently with probability $s$, so a fixed band of $r$ rows agrees entirely with probability $s^r$, no band agrees with probability $(1-s^r)^b$, and the complement gives $P(s)$. At $s = s^*$, $s^r = 1/b$ by construction. $\blacksquare$

The design trade-off is now explicit. The false-negative rate for a true duplicate at similarity $s > s^*$ is $(1-s^r)^b$, decaying geometrically in $b$; the false-positive rate for a dissimilar pair at $s < s^*$ is $1-(1-s^r)^b \approx b\,s^r$, growing linearly in $b$ but decaying geometrically in $r$. Raising $r$ sharpens the curve and suppresses false positives; raising $b$ lowers the threshold and rescues borderline duplicates. False positives are cheap (candidates are verified with exact Jaccard); false negatives are silent and permanent — which is why production settings put $s^*$ slightly below the similarity they actually care about Certain. FineWeb uses 5-word shingles with $k = 112$ hashes in $b=14$ bands of $r=8$ rows, targeting $\sim$75% similarity Verify.

Example 25.1 (FineWeb's banding, by hand)

Take $b = 14$, $r = 8$. Threshold: $s^* = (1/14)^{1/8} = e^{-\ln(14)/8} = e^{-2.6391/8} = e^{-0.3299} = 0.719$. Detection probability at $s = 0.8$: $s^r = 0.8^8 = 0.1678$, so $P = 1 - (0.8322)^{14} = 1 - e^{14\ln 0.8322} = 1 - e^{-2.571} = 1 - 0.0765 = 0.924$. At $s = 0.6$: $0.6^8 = 0.0168$, $P = 1 - (0.9832)^{14} = 1 - 0.789 = 0.211$. At $s^*$ itself: $P = 1 - (13/14)^{14} = 1 - 0.354 = 0.646$. So an 80%-similar pair is caught 92% of the time, a 60%-similar pair only 21% — a 0.2 change in similarity swings detection by 0.71. Artifact 25.1 measures this curve empirically and matches the analytic form to within 0.04 at every sampled similarity.

One counterintuitive empirical result deserves its own sentence: FineWeb found that deduplicating each Common Crawl snapshot independently produced better models than deduplicating globally across all 96 snapshots, even though global deduplication removes far more text — it deleted up to $\sim$90% of the oldest snapshots, and what it preferentially deleted was legitimately re-published quality content, while what survived skewed toward junk that appears only once Verify. Deduplication is not monotonically good; it is a filter whose selection bias must be measured like any other.

Common Pitfall

Computing shingle or band-bucket hashes with Python's built-in hash(). Since Python 3.3, string hashing is salted with a per-process random seed (PYTHONHASHSEED), so two worker processes in your sharded dedup job compute different signatures for identical documents. Every cross-shard duplicate silently survives, the pipeline reports success, and you discover the bug months later as verbatim memorization in the trained model. Use an explicit seeded hash family (as in Artifact 25.1) or a keyed hash like xxHash with a fixed seed. The same salt bug breaks n-gram decontamination (Section 25.7) in the same silent way.

25.4 Quality Classifiers and Model-Based Filtering

Three families of "is this document worth training on" filters compete. Heuristics (Section 25.2) are recall-oriented trash removal. Perplexity filtering (CCNet lineage) scores documents with a small language model — classically a KenLM 5-gram trained on Wikipedia — and keeps the low-perplexity fraction. It is cheap but circular: it keeps text that resembles the reference corpus, so it systematically discards unfamiliar-but-valuable text (dialogue, tables, code-adjacent prose) while retaining fluent spam. Classifier filtering trains a discriminative model on labeled positives and scores every document. The controlled comparison is DCLM's: on their CORE metric, a fastText bigram classifier trained on OpenHermes-2.5 instruction data plus r/ExplainLikeImFive answers, keeping the top 10% of documents, beat perplexity filtering and LLM-based quality prompting by wide margins, and that single choice accounts for most of DCLM-Baseline's advantage over prior open corpora Verify. FineWeb-Edu took the other modern route: annotate ~500k documents with Llama-3-70B-Instruct on a 0–5 educational-value scale, distill into a small embedding-based regressor, keep scores $\geq 3$ — yielding large gains on MMLU and ARC at the 1.3T-token scale Verify.

The caveat that keeps this from being a solved problem: aggressive filtering trades diversity for quality. A top-10% filter leaves fewer unique tokens, and Chapter 24's data-constrained scaling results say repeated tokens depreciate. At long token horizons (15T+), ensembles that recover more unique tokens — Nemotron-CC's combination of multiple classifiers plus synthetic rephrasing of borderline documents — outperform any single aggressive filter Likely. Filtering strength is a hyperparameter of the token budget, not a constant.

25.5 Data Mixtures and Domain Weights

Given filtered domains (web, code, academic, books, multilingual…), what fraction of $D$ should each contribute? For years the answer was folklore ratios tuned by hand. Three lines of work made it quantitative. DoReMi (2023) trains a small proxy model with group-DRO over domains: upweight whichever domain currently shows the largest excess loss relative to a reference model, producing weights without any downstream-task signal; weights found with a 280M proxy transferred to an 8B model and reached baseline downstream accuracy 2.6× faster on The Pile Verify. RegMix (2024) instead trains many tiny models on random mixture vectors, fits a regression from mixture to downstream score, and optimizes the fitted surrogate — matching or beating DoReMi at ~10% of its search cost Verify. Data mixing laws (Ye et al., 2024) go further and fit an explicit functional form for loss as a function of mixture proportions, nested inside ordinary scaling laws so mixtures can be optimized from small-scale runs. The shared lesson: mixture weights are a measurable, optimizable object with real headroom — typically worth a constant-factor compute saving — but the optimum shifts with scale and token budget, so proxy-to-target transfer is the fragile step Likely.

The most consequential single mixture decision is how much code and mathematics to include, because the effect is not confined to code and mathematics. Aryabumi et al. (ICLR 2025), in controlled ablations at 470M–2.8B parameters, found that adding code to pretraining improved natural-language reasoning by up to 8.2% relative over text-only training (and world knowledge by up to 4.2%), with the best variants initializing from a code-heavy model before a text-dominant phase Verify. The standard explanation — plausible and partially tested, not proven — is that code is a dense corpus of explicit multi-step procedure: long-range structural dependencies, exact variable binding, and compositional syntax that natural prose states only implicitly, giving the model gradient signal for exactly the state-tracking abilities that reasoning benchmarks measure Likely. Whatever the mechanism, every modern frontier mixture is code-heavy out of proportion to any interest in code generation per se, and mathematics plays the same role for symbolic manipulation.

25.6 Synthetic Data and Model Collapse

Model-generated text is now both a contaminant (LLM output is a growing share of the crawled web) and a deliberate ingredient (rephrased web text, synthetic textbooks, generated exercises). "Model collapse" names the fear that training on model output degrades models recursively — and the literature, read carefully, supports a much narrower claim than the headlines did. Shumailov et al. (Nature, 2024) demonstrated collapse under full replacement: generation $t{+}1$ trains only on generation $t$'s outputs, real data discarded. Under that protocol the distribution's tails vanish first and test error grows across generations — the result is real and reproducible Certain. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) changed one experimental variable: accumulate — keep all previous data, real and synthetic, and add each generation's output to the pool. Under accumulation, test error stays bounded across generations, in both their linear-model theory (where replacement gives error growing linearly in generations, accumulation a finite limit) and language-model experiments Verify.

Contested The remaining live question is whether web-scale reality behaves like accumulation or like something worse: accumulation-with-decay, where synthetic text increasingly crowds real text out of fixed crawl-and-filter budgets. Position taken here: the collapse-is-coming reading is overstated — real data is never deleted from the web or from lab archives, curation pipelines select on quality rather than provenance, and the strongest small models of 2024–25 (the Phi series; Nemotron-CC, whose classifier-plus-rephrasing high-quality subset beat DCLM by 5.6 MMLU points in matched 1T-token runs Verify) were built by adding curated synthetic data to real data, which is the accumulation regime. What would settle it: multi-generation experiments at scale with realistic contamination fractions and quality-filtered (not provenance-filtered) recrawls. Until then, the operative engineering rule is unambiguous: never let synthetic data replace the real-data stream; dilution, not generation count, is the variable that matters.

25.7 Decontamination and Benchmark Leakage

If a benchmark's test items are in $D$, Chapter 29's numbers measure retrieval, not capability. Decontamination is the removal (or at least flagging) of training documents overlapping evaluation sets, and the workhorse is n-gram overlap: GPT-3 used 13-gram matching; Llama 2 used token-level 8-gram matching with a document flagged when a large fraction of its tokens sit inside matched n-grams Verify. Overlap checkers are cheap, exact for verbatim leaks — Artifact 25.1's checker recovers 100% of planted verbatim leaks by construction — and trivially defeated by paraphrase. Yang et al. (2023) made the failure quantitative: a 13B model fine-tuned on rephrased test sets reached 85.9% on MMLU — GPT-4-level — while passing standard n-gram decontamination undetected Verify. Semantic decontamination (embedding similarity, LLM judges) closes part of the gap at much higher cost and with genuine false-positive problems: a GSM8K-style word problem and a legitimate textbook exercise can be semantically identical without either being a leak.

Two structural points. First, decontamination must run against every benchmark you will ever report, which is why it belongs late in the pipeline where the benchmark list is known, and why new benchmarks are contaminated by default the day they are published from web text. Second, the incentive gradient is bad: contamination inflates exactly the numbers a release is judged on, detection from the outside is statistical at best, and labs' decontamination protocols are — consistent with this chapter's thesis — among their least-disclosed components Likely.

25.8 Mid-Training, Annealing, and Long-Context Phases

Pretraining is no longer one homogeneous pass over $D$. The modern schedule has phases: a long main phase on the broad mixture, then a mid-training phase of order $10^{10}$–$10^{11}$ tokens where the mixture pivots toward high-quality, domain-dense data (curated math, code, instruction-formatted text, synthetic exercises) while the learning rate anneals toward zero, and typically a long-context extension phase (Chapter 19) in which the context window is grown in stages near the end. Concrete published recipes: Llama 3 linearly annealed the learning rate to zero over its final tokens while upsampling very-high-quality sources; OLMo 2 mid-trained on a curated 50B-token mixture ("Dolmino"), ran the anneal three times with different data orderings, and averaged the resulting checkpoints; MiniCPM's warmup-stable-decay schedule injects the high-quality data precisely in the decay phase, where its loss drops fastest Verify.

Why should the final few percent of tokens matter disproportionately? Two mechanisms, one optimization-theoretic and one empirical. First, data seen at a low learning rate near the end of training is written into weights that are barely perturbed afterwards: earlier gradients are progressively overwritten by billions of subsequent steps (catastrophic interference), while final-phase gradients persist essentially unmodified into the released checkpoint. The anneal-to-zero endpoint also means the final weights are close to an average over the last phase's trajectory, further favoring recent data Likely. Second, the effect is directly measured: Llama 3 used "annealing runs" — resume a checkpoint, anneal to zero on a candidate dataset, measure — as a cheap probe of data value, and found that annealing on GSM8K-style training data improved the 8B model's GSM8K validation score by 24.0% while the same intervention was negligible at 405B Verify. That last clause is worth dwelling on: mid-training leverage shrinks with scale, and small-model results on curriculum tricks routinely fail to transfer upward. The boundary between "late pretraining" and "early post-training" is now genuinely blurred — instruction-formatted data appears before pretraining officially ends, which is why Chapter 26 should be read as continuous with this section rather than as a separate regime.

25.9 Sequence Packing

The training batch is a dense $(B, T)$ tensor, but documents have variable length, so documents are concatenated — usually separated by an end-of-text token — and sliced into fixed windows. Two defects follow. First, naive concatenation truncates documents at arbitrary window boundaries, training the model to predict from amputated context; best-fit packing (Ding et al., 2024) instead bin-packs documents into sequences to minimize truncation, measurably improving downstream performance and reducing closed-domain hallucination, at no token-count cost Verify. Second, within a packed window, attention by default flows across document boundaries, letting the model attend from one document into an unrelated neighbor. Cross-document attention masking — block-diagonal masks per document, cheap under FlashAttention's variable-length interface (Chapter 31) — removes this, and is standard in current recipes, though measured ablations show the harm from cross-document attention is modest at scale and some long-context recipes deliberately re-enable it to teach multi-document integration Likely. Packing is the unglamorous end of the pipeline, but it is where "the dataset" finally becomes "the gradient": the loss is averaged over whatever tokens actually fill the windows, so packing policy silently reweights long versus short documents — one more place where an undisclosed engineering choice moves the measured model.

Artifact 25.1 — MinHash LSH and a Decontamination Checker, Verified Against Brute Force

The artifact builds the chapter's two core tools from scratch in NumPy and verifies both with hard assertions. Experiment 1 is the real content: it constructs 600 pairs of shingle sets at each of 19 controlled Jaccard levels, runs FineWeb's exact configuration ($b=14$, $r=8$, 112 multiply-add hash functions mod $2^{64}$), and checks the measured candidate-detection frequency against Theorem 25.2's curve $1-(1-s^r)^b$ pointwise. Experiment 2 plants 100 mutated near-duplicates (word-replacement rates 0–15%) among 500 base documents (600 total), computes ground truth by brute-force Jaccard over all 179{,}700 pairs, and asserts recall and precision of LSH candidate generation at the $s^*=(1/b)^{1/r}$ threshold. Experiment 3 splices 25 benchmark items verbatim into training documents and asserts the 8-gram rolling-hash decontamination checker recovers all 25 with zero false positives.

"""Artifact 25.1 -- MinHash LSH near-duplicate detection + n-gram decontamination.

Pure NumPy. Three experiments, each self-verifying with hard assertions:
  (1) The measured LSH detection-probability curve matches the analytic
      S-curve  P(candidate) = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b  to a stated tolerance.
  (2) On a synthetic corpus with PLANTED near-duplicates, LSH candidate
      generation achieves stated recall/precision at the theoretical
      threshold s* = (1/b)^(1/r), judged against brute-force Jaccard.
  (3) An 8-gram decontamination checker recovers 100% of planted
      benchmark leaks with zero false positives.
"""
import time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
U64 = np.uint64

# ---------------- MinHash configuration (FineWeb's: 14 bands x 8 rows) ----
B_BANDS, R_ROWS = 14, 8
K_HASH = B_BANDS * R_ROWS                       # 112 hash functions
S_STAR = (1.0 / B_BANDS) ** (1.0 / R_ROWS)      # ~0.719 similarity threshold

# One multiply-add hash per signature row: h_i(x) = a_i*x + c_i  (mod 2^64).
# a_i is forced odd so the map is a bijection on Z_{2^64}. Wraparound IS the
# modulus -- NumPy uint64 arithmetic wraps silently, which is exactly what
# we want. Never use Python's built-in hash() here: it is salted per process.
HASH_A = (rng.integers(1, 2**62, K_HASH, dtype=U64) << U64(1)) | U64(1)
HASH_C = rng.integers(0, 2**63, K_HASH, dtype=U64)


def minhash_batch(shingle_mat):
    """(n_docs, m) uint64 shingle IDs -> (n_docs, K_HASH) signatures.
    Row i of a signature is min over the doc's shingles of h_i(shingle)."""
    hv = shingle_mat[:, None, :] * HASH_A[None, :, None] + HASH_C[None, :, None]
    return hv.min(axis=2)


def band_fold(sigs):
    """Fold each band of R_ROWS rows into a single uint64 bucket key.
    (n, K_HASH) -> (n, B_BANDS). Two docs collide in band j iff all R_ROWS
    signature entries of that band agree (up to 2^-64 fold collisions)."""
    bands = sigs.reshape(sigs.shape[0], B_BANDS, R_ROWS)
    key = np.zeros((sigs.shape[0], B_BANDS), dtype=U64)
    for j in range(R_ROWS):                      # polynomial fold of the band
        key = key * U64(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) + bands[:, :, j]
    return key


def analytic_curve(s):
    """P(>=1 band collision) for a pair with per-row match probability s."""
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - s ** R_ROWS) ** B_BANDS


# ================ Experiment 1: the S-curve is the content ================
def detection_curve(m=80, trials=600):
    """Pairs of m-element sets with controlled Jaccard: c shared random IDs,
    m-c private each => J = c/(2m-c). Measure band-collision frequency."""
    rows = []
    for s in np.linspace(0.05, 0.95, 19):
        c = int(round(2 * m * s / (1 + s)))     # shared count achieving ~s
        s_true = c / (2 * m - c)                # exact Jaccard actually built
        shared = rng.integers(0, 2**63, (trials, c), dtype=U64)
        A = np.concatenate([shared, rng.integers(0, 2**63, (trials, m - c), dtype=U64)], 1)
        Bm = np.concatenate([shared, rng.integers(0, 2**63, (trials, m - c), dtype=U64)], 1)
        ka, kb = band_fold(minhash_batch(A)), band_fold(minhash_batch(Bm))
        emp = (ka == kb).any(axis=1).mean()     # any band agrees -> candidate
        rows.append((s_true, emp, analytic_curve(s_true)))
    return np.array(rows)


# ============ Experiment 2: planted near-duplicates in a corpus ===========
VOCAB, DOC_LEN, N_BASE, N_PLANT = 2000, 160, 500, 100

def make_corpus():
    """500 random word-ID docs + 100 mutated copies (replacement rate 0..15%).
    A rate-rho copy keeps ~(1-rho)^3 of 3-word shingles => J ~ u/(2-u)."""
    docs = [rng.integers(0, VOCAB, DOC_LEN) for _ in range(N_BASE)]
    pairs = []
    for k in range(N_PLANT):
        rate = 0.15 * k / (N_PLANT - 1)
        d = docs[k].copy()
        mask = rng.random(DOC_LEN) < rate
        d[mask] = rng.integers(0, VOCAB, int(mask.sum()))
        docs.append(d)
        pairs.append((k, N_BASE + k))
    return docs, pairs


def shingle_sets(docs, n=3):
    """Pack each 3-word shingle into one uint64: x0*V^2 + x1*V + x2."""
    out = []
    for d in docs:
        d = d.astype(U64)
        sh = d[:-2] * U64(VOCAB) ** U64(2) + d[1:-1] * U64(VOCAB) + d[2:]
        out.append(np.unique(sh))
    return out


def jaccard(a, b):
    return len(np.intersect1d(a, b)) / len(np.union1d(a, b))


def lsh_candidates(shingles):
    """Bucket docs by (band, key); every same-bucket pair is a candidate."""
    m_min = min(len(s) for s in shingles)       # pad-free: truncate to m_min
    mat = np.stack([s[:m_min] for s in shingles])
    keys = band_fold(minhash_batch(mat))
    buckets, cands = {}, set()
    for i in range(keys.shape[0]):
        for bnd in range(B_BANDS):
            k = (bnd, int(keys[i, bnd]))
            for j in buckets.setdefault(k, []):
                cands.add((j, i))
            buckets[k].append(i)
    return cands


# ============ Experiment 3: n-gram decontamination checker ================
def ngram_hashes(seq, n=8):
    """Rolling polynomial hash of every n-gram, mod 2^64."""
    h = np.zeros(len(seq) - n + 1, dtype=U64)
    for j in range(n):
        h = h * U64(1099511628211) + seq[j:len(seq) - n + 1 + j].astype(U64)
    return h


def decontaminate(docs, benchmark, n=8):
    """Flag any doc sharing >=1 n-gram with any benchmark item."""
    bench = set()
    for item in benchmark:
        bench.update(ngram_hashes(item, n).tolist())
    flagged = {}
    for i, d in enumerate(docs):
        hits = sum(h in bench for h in ngram_hashes(d, n).tolist())
        if hits:
            flagged[i] = hits
    return flagged


if __name__ == "__main__":
    t0 = time.time()
    # ---- (1) S-curve --------------------------------------------------
    curve = detection_curve()
    dev = np.abs(curve[:, 1] - curve[:, 2]).max()
    print(f"[curve] b={B_BANDS} r={R_ROWS}  s* = (1/b)^(1/r) = {S_STAR:.4f}")
    print("[curve]   s_true   empirical   analytic 1-(1-s^r)^b")
    for s, e, a in curve[[4, 8, 12, 13, 14, 16]]:
        print(f"[curve]   {s:.3f}     {e:.3f}       {a:.3f}")
    print(f"[curve] max |empirical - analytic| over 19 points = {dev:.4f}")
    assert dev < 0.07, "S-curve deviates beyond tolerance"
    near = curve[np.argmin(np.abs(curve[:, 0] - S_STAR))]
    print(f"[curve] at s={near[0]:.3f} (nearest s*): measured {near[1]:.3f}, "
          f"1-(1-1/b)^b = {1-(1-1/B_BANDS)**B_BANDS:.3f}")

    # ---- (2) planted near-duplicates ---------------------------------
    docs, planted = make_corpus()
    sh = shingle_sets(docs)
    # brute-force ground truth over all 600*599/2 pairs
    J = {}
    for i in range(len(sh)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(sh)):
            J[(i, j)] = jaccard(sh[i], sh[j])
    cands = lsh_candidates(sh)
