    pos = {p for p, v in J.items() if v >= S_STAR}          # true positives set
    hi = {p for p, v in J.items() if v >= 0.80}
    rec_star = len(cands & pos) / len(pos)
    rec_hi = len(cands & hi) / len(hi)
    prec_05 = sum(J[p] >= 0.50 for p in cands) / len(cands)
    verified = {p for p in cands if J[p] >= S_STAR}          # verification pass
    print(f"[dedup] docs={len(docs)}  pairs={len(J)}  planted={len(planted)}  "
          f"pairs with J>=s*: {len(pos)}")
    print(f"[dedup] LSH candidates: {len(cands)}   "
          f"background (J<0.3) among them: {sum(J[p] < 0.3 for p in cands)}")
    print(f"[dedup] recall @ J>=s*: {rec_star:.3f}   recall @ J>=0.80: {rec_hi:.3f}")
    print(f"[dedup] candidate precision w.r.t. J>=0.50: {prec_05:.3f}   "
          f"after exact-Jaccard verification w.r.t. s*: "
          f"{len(verified & pos)/max(len(verified),1):.3f}")
    assert rec_star >= 0.75 and rec_hi >= 0.90, "LSH recall below threshold"
    assert prec_05 >= 0.90, "LSH candidate precision below threshold"
    assert verified <= pos and len(verified) == len(cands & pos)

    # ---- (3) decontamination -----------------------------------------
    bench = [rng.integers(0, VOCAB, 30) for _ in range(40)]
    corpus = [d.copy() for d in docs]
    leak_ids = rng.choice(len(corpus), 25, replace=False)
    for i in leak_ids:                       # splice item verbatim into doc
        item = bench[int(rng.integers(0, 40))]
        off = int(rng.integers(0, DOC_LEN - 30))
        corpus[i][off:off + 30] = item
    flagged = decontaminate(corpus, bench)
    tp = set(flagged) & set(leak_ids.tolist())
    fp = set(flagged) - set(leak_ids.tolist())
    print(f"[decon] planted leaks: {len(leak_ids)}  flagged: {len(flagged)}  "
          f"recovered: {len(tp)}  false positives: {len(fp)}")
    print(f"[decon] matching 8-grams per leaked doc: "
          f"min={min(flagged.values())} max={max(flagged.values())}")
    assert len(tp) == len(leak_ids) and not fp, "decontamination missed a leak"

    print(f"[done] all assertions passed in {time.time() - t0:.1f}s")

Running it prints the measured curve against the analytic one — at true similarity 0.649 it measures detection 0.358 versus analytic 0.363; at 0.860, 0.995 versus 0.993 — with maximum absolute deviation 0.0396 over all 19 similarity levels, inside the 0.07 tolerance (600 Bernoulli trials per level put the 3$\sigma$ sampling band at $\approx 0.06$). On the planted corpus, LSH emits 51 candidate pairs out of 179,700 possible; recall is 0.972 on the 36 pairs with $J \geq s^*$ and 1.000 on pairs with $J \geq 0.80$ (Example 25.1 predicts per-pair detection 0.924 there, and misses concentrate just above threshold where $P(s^*)=0.646$); every candidate has $J \geq 0.50$, and after the exact-Jaccard verification pass precision at $s^*$ is exactly 1.000. The decontamination checker flags 25 of 25 planted leaks (23 matching 8-grams each) with zero false positives. Total wall-clock: 12.4 s, dominated by the deliberately brute-force ground-truth pass.

Key Takeaways
  • At fixed compute and architecture, the data pipeline is the dominant lever: DCLM's dataset-only intervention moved a 7B model +6.6 MMLU points over the prior open state of the art with 40% less compute. Verify
  • MinHash rows collide with probability exactly $J(A,B)$; banding $k=br$ rows gives candidate probability $1-(1-s^r)^b$ with threshold $s^*=(1/b)^{1/r}$, false negatives decaying geometrically in $b$ and false positives in $r$. Certain
  • Classifier-based filtering beats heuristic and perplexity filtering in controlled comparisons, but aggressive filtering trades unique tokens for quality, so its optimal strength depends on the token budget $D$. Likely
  • Model collapse is demonstrated when synthetic data replaces real data across generations; accumulating synthetic alongside real data bounds test error in both theory and experiment, and dilution of real data — not synthetic fraction per se — is the variable to control. Likely
  • The final few percent of pretraining tokens, delivered during the learning-rate anneal, has disproportionate influence on benchmarks — which makes mid-training both the cheapest place to add capability and the easiest place to hide contamination. Likely
Chapter 26

Supervised Fine-Tuning and Parameter-Efficient Adaptation

Learning Objectives
  • Explain instruction tuning, chat templating, and loss masking, and identify the regime — long prompts, short responses, small datasets — in which masking the prompt tokens is the wrong choice.
  • Derive the LoRA reparameterization $W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$, prove it is exactly as expressive as full fine-tuning when $r = \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})$, and compute the optimizer-state saving $2 d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}$ vs. $2r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})$ floats.
  • Explain NF4 quantization, double quantization, and paged optimizers, and quantify NF4's round-trip error against uniform int4 on Gaussian weights.
  • Compare LoRA, DoRA, rank-stabilized LoRA, and full fine-tuning on quality versus memory, and state precisely where LoRA measurably loses.
  • Implement a LoRA linear layer and a normal-float 4-bit quantizer in working code, with merge, gradient, and full-rank-equivalence checks.
Read alongside — Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), whose instruction-fine-tuning chapters implement templating and loss masking line by line; Stanford CS336 for the post-training lectures that place SFT between pretraining and RLHF; Chakraborty, Introduction to Large Language Models, for the NLP-side view of instruction tuning.

Chapter 25 ended with a base model: a next-token predictor that completes text but does not converse, follow instructions, or stop talking. This chapter covers the first post-training stage, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and the parameter-efficient machinery that makes it cheap. The central claims are two. First, SFT mostly teaches format and elicits capabilities the base model already has; it rarely creates new ones. Second, LoRA works because the fine-tuning update genuinely is low-rank in the directions that matter for such format-teaching tasks — and the documented cases where LoRA loses to full fine-tuning are exactly the cases (continued pretraining on large new corpora) where that assumption fails. We build LoRA and an NF4 quantizer from scratch, then close with a decision rubric for fine-tuning versus prompting versus retrieval. Chapter 27 takes the next step, preference optimization; Chapter 34 treats quantization for inference in full generality.

26.1 What SFT Changes

Mechanically, SFT is nothing new: it is the same next-token cross-entropy of Chapter 23, on a curated dataset of (prompt, response) pairs, initialized from the pretrained weights instead of from scratch. The learning rate is small (typically $10^{-5}$–$10^{-6}$ for full fine-tuning of billion-parameter models, versus $10^{-3}$–$10^{-4}$ at pretraining time), the token budget is minuscule — millions to low billions of tokens against the trillions of pretraining — and the epochs are few, usually one to three. Likely

What can a procedure that moves the weights so little accomplish? The evidence says: it changes the distribution over behaviors, not the underlying competence. The LIMA experiment fine-tuned a 65B base model on just 1,000 carefully curated examples and produced a usable assistant, which its authors read as support for a superficial alignment hypothesis: almost all capability is acquired in pretraining, and SFT selects the sub-distribution of formats and personas to surface. Likely The hypothesis in its strong form is contested — SFT on domain data demonstrably adds narrow skills, and continued training on new corpora adds knowledge — but the weak form is now the working consensus: if the base model cannot do the task under any prompt, SFT on a few thousand examples will not make it able to. Contested The evidence that would settle it: capability probes on base vs. SFT checkpoints at matched sampling effort, i.e. pass@$k$ at large $k$ (Chapter 28 examines the analogous question for RL).

This framing has an immediate practical corollary: SFT failures are usually data failures, not optimization failures. Which brings us to the data.

26.2 Data for SFT: Quality over Quantity

SFT datasets are small enough that individual examples matter. A thousand excellent demonstrations beat a hundred thousand mediocre ones, because the model imitates everything in the response distribution: reasoning style, hedging habits, formatting tics, and errors alike. Three properties dominate: correctness (the model will reproduce your mistakes at scale), diversity (narrow data collapses the output distribution; the model learns "always respond in this one register"), and response quality in the stylistic sense — the responses are the target distribution. Modern pipelines therefore spend their budget on filtering and rewriting rather than collection: LLM-graded quality scores, deduplication (Chapter 25's near-duplicate machinery reapplies here), and distillation, in which a stronger model writes the responses. Distillation works precisely because of Section 26.1: the student is not learning the capability from the teacher, it is learning the teacher's surface policy for deploying capabilities it already shares through common pretraining data. Likely

26.3 Chat Templates, Special Tokens, Loss Masking

A conversation is not a string until a chat template makes it one: a deterministic serialization that wraps each turn in role markers, e.g. special tokens delimiting a system turn, user turns, and assistant turns, with a designated end-of-turn token whose emission is how the model "decides" to stop. Two consequences are worth stating plainly. First, the template is part of the model. A checkpoint fine-tuned with one template and served with another is silently degraded — the model is conditioning on token sequences it never saw. Second, any special tokens introduced at SFT time start as randomly initialized embedding rows; they are trained only by the SFT gradient, which is one reason templates reuse pretraining-era special tokens where possible. Certain

Definition 26.1 (SFT objective with loss masking)

Given a templated token sequence $x_{1:T}$ and a mask $m_t \in \{0,1\}$ marking response tokens, SFT minimizes $$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{\sum_t m_t} \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} m_{t+1} \log p_\theta(x_{t+1} \mid x_{1:t}),$$ i.e. cross-entropy over the masked positions only. Prompt masking sets $m_t = 0$ on system, user, and template tokens so the model is never trained to predict its own inputs; the labels are the inputs shifted by one, and masked positions are conventionally marked with an ignore index (e.g. $-100$) rather than deleted, so the prompt still conditions the prediction.

Masking the prompt is the standard default, and it is usually right: without it, gradient signal is spent teaching the model to imitate users, and with long prompts the response signal is diluted by an order of magnitude. But it is not always right. Shi et al. (NeurIPS 2024, "Instruction Tuning with Loss over Instructions") show that unmasking the prompt improves downstream quality precisely when (i) prompts are long relative to responses and (ii) the dataset is small — the regime where short responses are easily memorized, and prompt-token loss acts as a regularizer against overfitting the responses. On LIMA-scale data the gains are large; on large datasets with long responses the effect washes out or reverses. Likely The rule of thumb: mask by default; consider unmasking when your dataset looks like a thousand long-prompt, short-answer pairs.

Common Pitfall

Masking the assistant's end-of-turn token. A masking implementation that marks "everything that is not response text" as ignored will often catch the end-of-turn special token, since it is template syntax, not content. The model then never receives gradient toward emitting it, and the fine-tuned model cannot stop: generations run to the token limit, rambling past the answer. The fix is one line — the end-of-turn token terminating each assistant span belongs inside the mask — but the symptom (endless generations) is routinely misdiagnosed as a sampling problem. The dual bug, computing loss over padding tokens because the collator pads labels with the pad id instead of the ignore index, biases the model toward emitting padding and corrupts the loss scale.

26.4 LoRA

Full fine-tuning of an $N$-parameter model with Adam (Chapter 13) stores, per parameter: the weight, the gradient, and two optimizer moments. In mixed precision that is roughly 16 bytes per parameter before activations — about 112 GB for a 7B model, out of reach of any single commodity GPU. Certain Low-Rank Adaptation (Hu et al., 2021) attacks the dominant terms — gradients and optimizer states — by freezing the pretrained weights and training only a low-rank correction.

Definition 26.2 (LoRA)

For a frozen linear layer $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$, LoRA reparameterizes the layer as $$h = Wx + \frac{\alpha}{r}\, B A\, x, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}},$$ with rank $r \ll \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})$ and scale hyperparameter $\alpha$. $A$ is initialized with small Gaussian entries and $B = 0$, so the model at initialization computes exactly the base model. Only $A$ and $B$ receive gradients: by the chain rule, if $G = \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W'$ is the gradient a full update would apply to the effective weights $W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$, then $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial B = \frac{\alpha}{r} G A^\top$ and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A = \frac{\alpha}{r} B^\top G$ — both computable without ever materializing the $d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}$ matrix $G$ as an optimizer state. After training, the update merges: $W' = W + \frac{\alpha}{r} BA$, and inference cost is identical to the base model.

Theorem 26.1 (Full-rank equivalence)

Let $r = \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})$. Then the set of functions realizable by the LoRA-adapted layer equals the set realizable by full fine-tuning: for every $\Delta W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}$ there exist $B, A$ with $\frac{\alpha}{r}BA = \Delta W$, and conversely every $\frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ is a valid full update.

Proof. The converse is immediate. For the forward direction, any $\Delta W$ has $\operatorname{rank}(\Delta W) \le \min(d_{\text{out}}, d_{\text{in}}) = r$. Take the SVD $\Delta W = U \Sigma V^\top$ with $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}$, and set $B = \frac{r}{\alpha} U \Sigma^{1/2}$, $A = \Sigma^{1/2} V^\top$. Then $\frac{\alpha}{r} BA = U\Sigma V^\top = \Delta W$. $\blacksquare$

Two caveats keep this theorem honest. Expressive equivalence is not trajectory equivalence: LoRA optimizes over a factored parameterization with different gradient geometry, so intermediate iterates differ from full fine-tuning even at full rank. On a convex problem both reach the same global optimum — Artifact 26.1 verifies this to relative error $7 \times 10^{-16}$ — but on non-convex losses the endpoints can differ. And at $r$ near full rank the memory advantage inverts: LoRA's optimizer state is $2r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})$ floats against full fine-tuning's $2\,d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}$, so LoRA saves memory only when $r < \frac{d_{\text{in}} d_{\text{out}}}{d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}}$ — $r < d/2$ for a square $d \times d$ layer. In the artifact's deliberately tiny full-rank run, LoRA's 288 state floats exceed full fine-tuning's 160. At practical ranks the saving is enormous. Certain

Example 26.1 (Optimizer memory for one attention projection)

Take a $4096 \times 4096$ projection ($d_{\text{in}} = d_{\text{out}} = 4096$) and $r = 16$. Full fine-tuning: $4096^2 = 16{,}777{,}216$ weights; Adam's two fp32 moments cost $2 \times 16{,}777{,}216 \times 4 \text{ B} = 134.2$ MB, plus a $67$ MB fp32 gradient. LoRA: $2 \times 16 \times 4096 = 131{,}072$ trainable parameters — $0.78\%$ of the layer — with moments $2 \times 131{,}072 \times 4 \text{ B} = 1.05$ MB. The state ratio is $\frac{2 d^2}{4 r d} = \frac{d}{2r} = \frac{4096}{32} = 128\times$, exactly what Artifact 26.1 counts. Summed over every linear layer of a Llama-architecture 7B model, LoRA at $r=16$ trains about 80 million parameters instead of seven billion, and the adapter checkpoint is $\sim$160 MB at bf16 instead of 14 GB.

26.4.1 Rank, Alpha, and Which Modules to Target

The original paper adapted only the attention query and value projections; that default has not survived. The strongest current evidence — Biderman et al.'s controlled comparison ("LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less," 2024) and Thinking Machines' 2025 "LoRA Without Regret" study — agrees that LoRA should be applied to all linear layers, and that the MLP (and MoE) matrices matter more than attention; attention-only adaptation underperforms even at matched trainable-parameter count. Likely On rank: for instruction-tuning-scale data, modest ranks ($r$ of 8–64) suffice, and the "LoRA Without Regret" experiments find rank-1 adapters can match full fine-tuning for RL fine-tuning, where the information content of the reward signal is tiny. The same study reports LoRA's optimal learning rate is consistently about $10\times$ the full fine-tuning optimum, and that parity holds when batch sizes are not extreme and the adapter's capacity exceeds the information content of the dataset. Verify — these are one lab's sweeps on particular model families; check against your own validation loss before adopting the constants. The $\alpha$ convention is a source of silent bugs: the effective update is scaled by $\alpha/r$, so changing $r$ at fixed $\alpha$ changes the effective step size. A common heuristic sets $\alpha = 2r$; Section 26.6's rsLoRA replaces the convention outright.

26.5 QLoRA: NF4, Double Quantization, Paging

LoRA removes optimizer state for the frozen weights, but the weights themselves still occupy 14 GB at bf16 for a 7B model. QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) stores them in 4 bits instead, dequantizing on the fly for each matmul while gradients flow through to bf16 LoRA adapters. Its three components are worth understanding separately.

Definition 26.3 (NF4, 4-bit NormalFloat)

NF4 is a 16-level codebook data type built from the quantiles of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$: with tail offset $\delta = \frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{32} + \frac{1}{30})$, take 9 evenly spaced $p$ in $[\tfrac12, 1-\delta]$ and drop $p = \tfrac12$, giving 8 positive levels $\Phi^{-1}(p)$; take 8 evenly spaced $p$ in $[\delta, \tfrac12]$ and drop $p = \tfrac12$, giving 7 negative levels; add an exact zero (dropping $p=\tfrac12$ twice is what keeps the level count at $8+7+1=16$ without a duplicated zero), and normalize the result to $[-1, 1]$. Weights are quantized blockwise: each block of 64 values is scaled by its absolute maximum into $[-1,1]$, then each value is snapped to the nearest codebook level and stored as a 4-bit index alongside the block's scale.

The design encodes two decisions. The asymmetric split (8 positive, 7 negative levels) exists to make zero an exact level — symmetric quantile grids straddle zero, and pruned or zero weights would round to noise. And quantile spacing matches the codebook to the source distribution: pretrained weight tensors are approximately zero-centered Gaussians, so equal-probability bins put resolution where the mass is, unlike uniform int4, which spends a quarter of its levels beyond $2\sigma$ of a typical block's scale (mean absmax of 64 Gaussians $\approx 2.6\sigma$), where under 5% of the mass lives. The QLoRA paper calls NF4 "information-theoretically optimal"; strictly, quantile quantization equalizes bin occupancy, which is not the same as minimizing expected squared error (a Lloyd–Max quantizer does that), so read the claim as optimal-within-quantile-codes. Likely The practical win is real but moderate at the codebook level: on $2^{16}$ Gaussian weights with block size 64, Artifact 26.1 measures round-trip RMSE 0.0919 for NF4 against 0.1012 for a uniform 16-level grid — a $1.10\times$ error reduction that the QLoRA ablations show compounding into consistently better downstream perplexity than int4/fp4. Certain (measured, for the RMSE)

Double quantization attacks the metadata: one fp32 scale per 64 weights adds $32/64 = 0.5$ bits per parameter. QLoRA quantizes the scales themselves to 8 bits in second-level blocks of 256 (with one fp32 scale for those), cutting the overhead to $8/64 + 32/(64 \cdot 256) \approx 0.127$ bits — a saving of about $0.37$ bits per parameter, roughly 3 GB on a 65B model. Certain Paged optimizers handle the remaining failure mode, transient memory spikes (notably during gradient checkpointing with long sequences), by allocating optimizer state in NVIDIA unified memory so pages evict to CPU RAM under pressure instead of raising out-of-memory — a correctness feature, not a speedup. Together these fit 65B-parameter fine-tuning on a single 48 GB GPU while matching 16-bit LoRA performance on the paper's benchmarks. Verify against the QLoRA paper's Table 4 lineage if you need the exact parity claims; they are benchmark-specific.

One interaction deserves care: merging a LoRA adapter into an NF4 base is lossy in a way merging into bf16 is not, because $\text{quant}(W) + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ must be re-quantized to serve at 4 bits, and $\text{quant}(\text{dequant}(\text{quant}(W)) + \Delta) \ne \text{quant}(W + \Delta)$ in general. Serving quantized therefore usually keeps the adapter unmerged, at the cost of the extra low-rank matmul per layer.

26.6 DoRA, rsLoRA, and the Variants Worth Knowing

Of the many LoRA descendants, two have mechanisms worth internalizing. rsLoRA (Kalajdzievski, 2023) is a one-line fix to the scale convention: replace $\alpha/r$ with $\alpha/\sqrt{r}$. The argument is a signal-propagation one in the style of Chapter 12: with entries of $A$ at scale $1/\sqrt{d_{\text{in}}}$ and $B$ learned, the product $BAx$ aggregates $r$ terms whose magnitude grows like $\sqrt{r}$, so dividing by $r$ makes the update — and its gradients — shrink as $1/\sqrt{r}$, and high-rank adapters undertrain: the paper demonstrates stable learning up to $r = 2048$ under $\alpha/\sqrt{r}$ where $\alpha/r$ stalls. At the small ranks most people use, the two conventions differ only by a constant absorbable into the learning rate; the fix matters when you raise the rank because Section 26.7 says you should. Likely

DoRA (Liu et al., ICML 2024) decomposes each pretrained weight matrix into a magnitude vector and a direction, $W = m \odot \frac{V}{\|V\|_c}$ with $\|\cdot\|_c$ the column-wise norm, trains $m$ directly, and applies LoRA only to the directional part $V$. The motivation is an empirical observation: full fine-tuning tends to make directional adjustments with small magnitude changes (and the two anticorrelate), while vanilla LoRA couples them — it cannot rotate a column without rescaling it proportionally. Decoupling recovers a learning pattern closer to full fine-tuning, and DoRA outperforms LoRA across the paper's commonsense-reasoning and multimodal benchmarks, with the margin largest at low rank; after training, everything merges, so inference cost is unchanged, though training is somewhat slower due to the normalization. Likely

MethodTrainable params (per $d\times d$ layer)Quality (SFT-scale data)Where it loses
Full fine-tuning$d^2$Ceiling; best on large-corpus continued pretrainingMemory ($\sim$16 B/param); forgets the most (Sec. 26.7)
LoRA$2rd$Matches full FT when all layers targeted, capacity sufficesLarge-data CPT; gap grows with dataset size

26.7 Catastrophic Forgetting and Model Merging

The honest accounting of LoRA versus full fine-tuning is due to Biderman et al. (2024), and its title is the summary: LoRA learns less and forgets less. On instruction-tuning data, LoRA at sufficient rank ($r = 256$ in their sweeps) approaches full fine-tuning's target-domain performance. On continued pretraining over billions of tokens of code or mathematics, LoRA loses clearly, and the gap widens with data — consistent with their spectral analysis showing full fine-tuning's weight perturbations have effective rank 10–100$\times$ higher than typical LoRA configurations. The low-rank hypothesis is a property of the task, not of fine-tuning in general: format-teaching updates are low-rank; knowledge-injection updates are not. Likely Reconciling this with "LoRA Without Regret" is straightforward: that study's parity claims are scoped to SFT- and RL-scale datasets, where the adapter's capacity in bits exceeds the information the data can transmit — the two papers agree once you condition on the regime, and neither supports LoRA parity for large-corpus domain adaptation. Likely

The flip side is that LoRA is a strong regularizer toward the base model: Biderman et al. find it preserves out-of-domain performance and generation diversity better than full fine-tuning even when the latter is regularized with weight decay or dropout. Geometrically this is unsurprising — the update is confined to a $2rd$-dimensional subspace, and $\|\Delta W\|_F$ stays small — but it makes rank a knob on a learning–forgetting frontier rather than a pure capacity parameter. When forgetting still bites, the crudest remedies are the most used: mix replayed pretraining data into the SFT stream, or interpolate weights after the fact. Because adapters are just weight deltas, they compose linearly — averaging or task-arithmetic-style addition of adapters trained on different tasks often works surprisingly well, and the failure mode (interference between deltas that share subspaces) is an active research area rather than a solved one. Contested — merging results are benchmark-sensitive; systematic evaluations disagree on when addition beats retraining, and a head-to-head on your task is the only reliable evidence.

26.8 When to Fine-Tune versus Prompt versus Retrieve

The chapter's thesis compresses to a decision rubric. Prompt first: if a capability can be elicited with instructions and a handful of in-context examples, that is strictly cheaper than any training, and by Section 26.1 the ceiling is similar for capabilities the base model has. Retrieve for knowledge: facts that change, long-tail entities, and private corpora belong in context via retrieval, not in weights — SFT-scale gradient updates are a poor and unauditable way to store facts, and Biderman et al.'s CPT results show how expensive real knowledge injection is. Fine-tune for behavior: reliable format compliance, tone, tool-call syntax, a fixed output schema, latency (shorter prompts than few-shot), and distillation of a larger model's policy into a smaller one. When you do fine-tune: LoRA on all linear layers at moderate rank is the right default for behavior-shaping; full fine-tuning (or high-rank LoRA with rsLoRA scaling) is reserved for the large-data regime where low-rank measurably loses; QLoRA is the same decision under a tighter memory budget. Likely

Artifact 26.1 — LoRA and a NormalFloat Quantizer from Scratch

The artifact implements LoRA as a wrapper over a frozen linear layer and asserts the chapter's four load-bearing claims: (a) bit-identity with the base layer at initialization ($B=0$); (b) merged weights $W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ reproduce the two-path forward below $10^{-12}$; (c) at full rank $r = \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})$, LoRA trained with Adam reaches the same loss as full fine-tuning on a convex regression (Theorem 26.1 in optimization form); (d) counted Adam state equals $2r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})$ versus $2d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}$. It then rebuilds the NF4 codebook from the QLoRA quantile recipe, checks it against the published bitsandbytes constants, and races it against uniform int4 on blockwise round-trip error. Gradients are cross-checked against torch autograd when available.

"""Artifact 26.1 -- LoRA from scratch + a normal-float 4-bit quantizer.

Verifies four claims about LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) and one about NF4
(Dettmers et al., QLoRA, 2023), all in pure NumPy (scipy only for the
Gaussian quantile function; torch only as an optional gradient cross-check):

  (a) at init (B = 0) the wrapped layer is BIT-identical to the base layer;
  (b) merging W + (alpha/r) B A reproduces the two-path output to ~1e-12;
  (c) at full rank r = min(d_in, d_out), LoRA reaches the same loss as full
      fine-tuning on a convex regression problem (same global optimum);
  (d) Adam state memory scales as 4*r*d (two moments for A and B) versus
      2*d_in*d_out for full fine-tuning -- verified by counting floats.

The NF4 codebook is rebuilt from the QLoRA recipe (quantiles of N(0,1) with
offset 0.5*(1/32 + 1/30)) and checked against the bitsandbytes constants,
then compared with uniform int4 on blockwise-absmax round-trip error.
"""
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# LoRA wrapper around a frozen linear layer  y = W x + b
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class LoRALinear:
    def __init__(self, W, b, r, alpha, rng):
        self.W, self.b = W, b            # frozen base weights
        self.r, self.s = r, alpha / r    # LoRA scale s = alpha / r
        d_out, d_in = W.shape
        # Kaiming-style A, zero B: the update s*B@A starts exactly at 0.
        self.A = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(d_in), (r, d_in))
        self.B = np.zeros((d_out, r))

    def forward(self, x):                # two-path: base + low-rank update
        return (x @ self.W.T + self.b) + self.s * (x @ self.A.T) @ self.B.T

    def merged(self):                    # fold the update into the base
        return self.W + self.s * (self.B @ self.A)

    def grads(self, x, dY):              # dY = dL/d(output), shape (m, d_out)
        dW = dY.T @ x                    # what full FT would use
        return self.s * (dW @ self.A.T), self.s * (self.B.T @ dW)  # dB, dA


class Adam:
    """Minimal Adam; keeps two moment arrays per parameter (state counting)."""
    def __init__(self, shapes, lr=0.02, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
        self.m = [np.zeros(s) for s in shapes]
        self.v = [np.zeros(s) for s in shapes]
        self.lr, self.b1, self.b2, self.eps, self.t = lr, b1, b2, eps, 0

    def state_floats(self):
        return sum(a.size for a in self.m) + sum(a.size for a in self.v)

    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        for p, g, m, v in zip(params, grads, self.m, self.v):
            m[:] = self.b1 * m + (1 - self.b1) * g
            v[:] = self.b2 * v + (1 - self.b2) * g * g
            mh = m / (1 - self.b1 ** self.t)
            vh = v / (1 - self.b2 ** self.t)
            p -= self.lr * mh / (np.sqrt(vh) + self.eps)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# NF4: 16 levels at the quantiles of N(0,1), with an exact zero
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def nf4_codebook():
    """QLoRA appendix recipe: asymmetric quantile grid so that 0 is a level.
    8 positive levels, 7 negative levels, plus exact 0 -> 16 = 2^4 levels."""
    offset = 0.5 * (1 / 32 + 1 / 30)                    # tail probability
    pos = norm.ppf(np.linspace(1 - offset, 0.5, 9)[:-1])  # 8 positive quantiles
    neg = norm.ppf(np.linspace(offset, 0.5, 8)[:-1])       # 7 negative quantiles
    q = np.sort(np.concatenate([neg, [0.0], pos]))
    return q / np.abs(q).max()                          # normalize to [-1, 1]


def quantize_blockwise(w, code, block=64):
    """Absmax blockwise quantization: per-block scale, nearest codebook level."""
    wb = w.reshape(-1, block)
    scale = np.abs(wb).max(axis=1, keepdims=True)       # one fp32 per block
    idx = np.abs(wb[:, :, None] / scale[:, :, None] - code).argmin(axis=2)
    return (code[idx] * scale).reshape(-1)              # dequantized round trip


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    d_in, d_out, m = 10, 8, 200
    W0 = rng.normal(0, 0.3, (d_out, d_in)); b0 = rng.normal(0, 0.1, d_out)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (m, d_in))

    # --- (a) bit-identity at initialization --------------------------------
    lora = LoRALinear(W0, b0, r=4, alpha=8, rng=rng)
    base_out, lora_out = X @ W0.T + b0, lora.forward(X)
    assert base_out.tobytes() == lora_out.tobytes(), "init not bit-identical"
    print("(a) B=0 output bit-identical to base layer: PASS")

    # --- (b) merged == unmerged -------------------------------------------
    lora.B = rng.normal(0, 0.5, lora.B.shape)           # make the update nonzero
    err = np.abs(X @ lora.merged().T + b0 - lora.forward(X)).max()
    assert err < 1e-12, err
    print(f"(b) merge residual |merged - two-path|_max = {err:.2e}  (< 1e-12)")

    # --- (c) full-rank LoRA reaches the full fine-tuning loss --------------
    Wstar = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (d_out, d_in))           # target weights
    Y = X @ Wstar.T + b0 + rng.normal(0, 0.01, (m, d_out))
    loss = lambda P: 0.5 * np.mean((X @ P.T + b0 - Y) ** 2)

    Wf = W0.copy()                                      # full fine-tuning
    opt_f = Adam([Wf.shape])
    for t in range(8000):
        opt_f.lr = 0.02 if t < 4000 else 0.002          # decay to kill Adam noise
        dY = (X @ Wf.T + b0 - Y) / (m * d_out)
        opt_f.step([Wf], [dY.T @ X])

    r_full = min(d_in, d_out)                           # r = 8 = full rank
    lr8 = LoRALinear(W0, b0, r=r_full, alpha=r_full, rng=rng)  # s = 1
    opt_l = Adam([lr8.B.shape, lr8.A.shape])
    for t in range(8000):
        opt_l.lr = 0.02 if t < 4000 else 0.002
        dY = (lr8.forward(X) - Y) / (m * d_out)
        dB, dA = lr8.grads(X, dY)
        opt_l.step([lr8.B, lr8.A], [dB, dA])

    Lf, Ll = loss(Wf), loss(lr8.merged())
    rel = abs(Ll - Lf) / Lf
    assert rel < 1e-3, (Lf, Ll)
    print(f"(c) full FT loss {Lf:.8f} vs full-rank LoRA loss {Ll:.8f}"
          f"  (rel diff {rel:.2e} < 1e-3)")

    # --- (d) optimizer-state memory: 4rd vs 2*d_in*d_out -------------------
    nf, nl = opt_f.state_floats(), opt_l.state_floats()
    assert nf == 2 * d_in * d_out and nl == 2 * r_full * (d_in + d_out)
    d, r = 4096, 16                                     # a realistic layer
    print(f"(d) Adam state floats: full={nf} (=2*d_in*d_out), "
          f"LoRA={nl} (=2r(d_in+d_out))")
    print(f"    at d={d}, r={r}: full={2*d*d:,} vs LoRA={4*r*d:,} floats "
          f"-> {2*d*d/(4*r*d):.0f}x smaller")

    # --- optional torch cross-check of the LoRA gradients ------------------
    try:
        import torch
        tX = torch.tensor(X); tA = torch.tensor(lr8.A, requires_grad=True)
        tB = torch.tensor(lr8.B, requires_grad=True)
        out = tX @ torch.tensor(W0).T + torch.tensor(b0) \
            + lr8.s * (tX @ tA.T) @ tB.T
        (0.5 * ((out - torch.tensor(Y)) ** 2).mean()).backward()
        dY = (lr8.forward(X) - Y) / (m * d_out)
        dB, dA = lr8.grads(X, dY)
        ga = np.abs(tA.grad.numpy() - dA).max()
        gb = np.abs(tB.grad.numpy() - dB).max()
        assert max(ga, gb) < 1e-10
        print(f"    torch autograd cross-check: max grad diff {max(ga, gb):.2e}")
    except ImportError:
        print("    [skipped: torch not installed]")

    # --- NF4 vs uniform int4 round-trip error ------------------------------
    code = nf4_codebook()
    # spot-check against the bitsandbytes NF4 constants
    ref = {1: -0.6961928009986877, 7: 0.0, 14: 0.7229568362236023}
    for i, v in ref.items():
        assert abs(code[i] - v) < 1e-6, (i, code[i], v)
    print("NF4 codebook matches bitsandbytes constants to <1e-6: PASS")

    w = rng.normal(0, 1, 1 << 16)                       # 65,536 Gaussian weights
    int4 = np.linspace(-1, 1, 16)                       # uniform 16-level grid
    rms = lambda cb: np.sqrt(np.mean((quantize_blockwise(w, cb) - w) ** 2))
    e_nf4, e_int4 = rms(code), rms(int4)
    print(f"round-trip RMSE on N(0,1) weights (block=64): "
          f"NF4={e_nf4:.5f}  int4={e_int4:.5f}  "
          f"(int4/NF4 = {e_int4/e_nf4:.2f}x)")
    assert e_nf4 < e_int4, "NF4 should beat uniform int4 on Gaussian weights"
    # memory arithmetic incl. double quantization of the per-block scales
    print(f"bits/param: fp32 scale 4+32/64 = {4+32/64:.3f}; "
          f"double-quantized 4+8/64+32/(64*256) = {4+8/64+32/(64*256):.3f}")

Running it (about 4 seconds on CPU) prints all four assertions passing with measured residuals: the merge residual is $1.78 \times 10^{-15}$; full fine-tuning and full-rank LoRA converge to loss $4.698 \times 10^{-5}$ with relative difference $7.21 \times 10^{-16}$ — the same global optimum to machine precision; the counted Adam state is 160 floats for full fine-tuning versus 288 for full-rank LoRA on the toy layer (the inversion discussed in Section 26.4), and the projected saving at $d=4096$, $r=16$ is $128\times$ (33,554,432 vs. 262,144 floats). The torch autograd cross-check agrees with the hand-derived gradients to $1.35 \times 10^{-19}$. The rebuilt NF4 codebook matches the bitsandbytes constants below $10^{-6}$, and on 65,536 Gaussian weights the round-trip RMSE is 0.09189 for NF4 against 0.10115 for uniform int4 — a $1.10\times$ error reduction at identical storage cost — while double quantization cuts metadata from 0.500 to 0.127 bits per parameter.

Under Encryption

LoRA is unusually well suited to encrypted inference, for a reason that has nothing to do with training cost. Under CKKS-style homomorphic encryption, the dominant expense of a linear layer is not the multiplications but the rotations needed to align ciphertext slots for the matrix–vector product, and rotation count scales with the matrix dimensions (for a $d \times d$ diagonal-method matvec, $O(d)$ rotations, or $O(\sqrt{d})$ with baby-step–giant-step). A rank-$r$ update factors one $d \times d$ multiply into two thin multiplies — $A x$ then $B(Ax)$ — costing $O(rd)$ work with correspondingly fewer ciphertexts and rotations. The price is one extra multiplicative level: the two thin matrices apply in sequence, and each plaintext–ciphertext multiplication consumes depth from the fixed budget that bootstrapping must otherwise refresh. Merging the update into the base weights in the clear removes that extra level but restores the full $d \times d$ rotation cost, so serving an adapter under encryption is a genuine depth-versus-throughput trade rather than a free win — and the right answer flips depending on how close the circuit is to its next bootstrap. Chapters 40 and 41 return to this trade in full private-inference systems.

Key Takeaways
  • SFT is next-token cross-entropy on curated (prompt, response) pairs; it primarily selects formats and behaviors the base model already supports, which is why a thousand excellent examples can outperform a hundred thousand mediocre ones. Likely
  • Mask prompt tokens by default, but keep the assistant's end-of-turn token in the loss; with long prompts, short responses, and small datasets, unmasking the prompt is a measurable regularizer. Likely
  • LoRA's update $\frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ is exactly as expressive as full fine-tuning at $r = \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})$ (SVD factorization), and cuts Adam state from $2d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}$ to $2r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})$ floats — $128\times$ for $d = 4096$, $r = 16$, verified by counting. Certain
  • NF4 places its 16 levels at Gaussian quantiles with an exact zero; on Gaussian weights it beats uniform int4's round-trip RMSE (measured 0.0919 vs. 0.1012), and double quantization trims per-parameter metadata from 0.5 to 0.127 bits. Certain
  • LoRA learns less and forgets less: it matches full fine-tuning on SFT- and RL-scale data when applied to all linear layers with a $\sim$10$\times$ learning rate, but loses — increasingly with data — on large-corpus continued pretraining, where the true update is high-rank. Verify
Chapter 27

Preference Optimization: RLHF, DPO, GRPO

Learning Objectives
  • Derive the Bradley–Terry reward model and the KL-regularized reinforcement-learning objective, and derive the closed-form optimal policy $\pi^*(y|x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)$.
  • Derive DPO by inverting that closed form for the reward, and state exactly which assumptions make DPO equivalent to RLHF and which fail in practice.
  • Explain the clipped policy-gradient objective and the value function, derive the group-relative advantage that eliminates the critic, and quantify the memory saved.
  • Compare KTO, ORPO, SimPO, and IPO on the data each requires and the pathology each addresses.
  • Implement the DPO and GRPO losses in working code, gradient-checked and verified against the closed-form RLHF optimum.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 covers RLHF and GRPO with the same from-scratch discipline as this chapter; Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), has a line-by-line DPO implementation in its supplementary material; Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics, is the reference for the policy-gradient machinery underneath Section 27.4.

Chapter 26 ended with a model that imitates demonstrations. This chapter makes it prefer: given that response A is better than response B, push probability toward A without collapsing onto it. The central object is one KL-regularized objective with a closed-form solution, and every method here is a different route to that solution. RLHF (Section 27.4) climbs toward it with policy gradients against a learned reward. DPO (Section 27.5) inverts the closed form and regresses on it directly — the derivation proves it targets the same optimum, and the artifact verifies that numerically. GRPO (Section 27.7) keeps the RL route but deletes the critic. The differences that matter in practice — on-policy data, KL estimation, reward-model generalization — live outside the loss functions, which is the thesis this chapter defends. Chapter 28 builds reasoning models on top of exactly this machinery; Chapter 29 measures what it did.

27.1 Why Likelihood Is Not Enough

Supervised fine-tuning maximizes $\log \pi_\theta(y|x)$ on responses someone wrote. That objective has no mechanism for expressing this response is worse than that one. Every gradient step says "more of this"; nothing ever says "less of that." Three consequences follow. First, quality ceilings: the model can at best match its demonstration distribution, and demonstrators are expensive precisely where quality matters (long proofs, careful refusals, working code). Ranking two responses is far cheaper than writing the better one — this asymmetry between verification and generation is the economic engine of the whole field. Second, SFT is mass-covering: cross-entropy (Chapter 2) forces $\pi_\theta$ to put mass everywhere the data does, including on the demonstrators' mistakes. Third, there is no notion of degree — a barely-acceptable answer and a superb one contribute identical loss if both appear as targets. Preference optimization fixes all three by learning from comparisons, and the entire chapter is the study of one question: comparisons between what, sampled from where?

27.2 Reward Modeling and Bradley–Terry

Definition 27.1 (Bradley–Terry preference model)

Given a latent reward function $r(x,y)$, the probability that response $y_w$ is preferred to $y_l$ for prompt $x$ is $$P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) \;=\; \frac{e^{r(x,y_w)}}{e^{r(x,y_w)} + e^{r(x,y_l)}} \;=\; \sigma\!\big(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)\big),$$ where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid. Preferences depend only on reward differences, so $r$ is identifiable only up to an additive prompt-dependent constant $c(x)$.

A reward model $r_\phi$ is trained by maximum likelihood on human comparisons: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{RM}} = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\log \sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w) - r_\phi(x,y_l))$. In practice $r_\phi$ is the SFT model with its unembedding replaced by a scalar head reading the final token's hidden state, so the reward model is as large as the policy. This is logistic regression (Chapter 6) on the feature "difference of two forward passes," and it inherits logistic regression's failure mode: on comparisons the annotators always agree on, the loss is minimized only as the score gap $\to \infty$. The identifiability gap matters later: any per-prompt shift $r + c(x)$ yields identical preferences and, as Theorem 27.1 shows, an identical optimal policy — DPO exploits exactly this freedom. The Bradley–Terry form itself is an assumption: it forces preferences to be transitive and consistent across annotators, which human data is not; annotator agreement on typical chat comparisons is far from unanimous, so the achievable RM accuracy is bounded well below 100% Likely.

27.3 The KL-Regularized Objective and Its Closed-Form Solution

Definition 27.2 (KL-regularized alignment objective)

Given reward $r$, reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (the SFT model), and temperature $\beta > 0$, $$\max_{\pi}\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\, y\sim\pi(\cdot|x)}\big[r(x,y)\big] \;-\; \beta\, \mathbb{E}_{x}\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot|x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x)\big).$$ The KL term is not decoration: $r$ is only trustworthy near the distribution it was trained on, and the penalty prices distance from that region.

Theorem 27.1 (Closed-form optimal policy)

The objective of Definition 27.2 is maximized by $$\pi^*(y|x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\, \exp\!\big(r(x,y)/\beta\big), \qquad Z(x) = \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\, e^{r(x,y)/\beta}.$$

Proof. Fix $x$ and write the per-prompt objective as $\sum_y \pi(y) r(y) - \beta \sum_y \pi(y) \log\frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y)}$. Because $\log \pi^*(y) = \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y) + r(y)/\beta - \log Z(x)$, dividing the objective by $\beta$ gives exactly $-\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi^*) + \log Z(x)$, and $\log Z(x)$ does not depend on $\pi$. KL divergence is non-negative and zero iff its arguments coincide, so the unique maximizer is $\pi = \pi^*$. $\blacksquare$

Three facts to hold onto. The optimum reweights $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ multiplicatively — it can never resurrect a response with $\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)=0$. As $\beta \to \infty$ it collapses to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$; as $\beta \to 0$ it concentrates on the argmax of $r$ within $\pi_{\text{ref}}$'s support. And $Z(x)$ sums over all possible responses, so for sequences the closed form is unnormalizable in practice — which is why RLHF exists as an algorithm at all.

Example 27.1 (Closed form by hand)

Three actions, $\pi_{\text{ref}} = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$, $r = (1, 0, -1)$, $\beta = 1$. Unnormalized weights: $0.5\,e^{1} = 1.3591$, $\;0.3\,e^{0} = 0.3$, $\;0.2\,e^{-1} = 0.0736$. Then $Z = 1.7327$ and $\pi^* = (0.7844,\, 0.1731,\, 0.0425)$. The best action gains mass ($0.5 \to 0.784$), the worst keeps a floor ($0.2 \to 0.042$) because the KL anchor forbids abandoning it entirely. With $\beta = 0.5$ the same arithmetic ($0.5\,e^{2} = 3.6945$, $0.3$, $0.2\,e^{-2} = 0.0271$, $Z = 4.0216$) gives $\pi^* = (0.9187,\, 0.0746,\, 0.0067)$: smaller $\beta$, sharper reweighting.

27.4 PPO for Language Models

Since $\pi^*$ cannot be normalized over sequences, RLHF ascends toward it. Generation is a token-level MDP: state = prompt plus tokens so far, action = next token, reward = $r_\phi(x,y)$ at the end minus a per-token KL penalty $\beta \log\frac{\pi_\theta(y_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_t|s_t)}$ folded into the reward, following InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022). The vanilla policy gradient $\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[R] = \mathbb{E}[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_t|s_t)\, A_t]$ needs an advantage estimate $A_t$, and its variance is unusable without a baseline. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) supplies both pieces. A learned value function $V_\psi(s_t)$ — the critic, a second full-size network — predicts expected return from each prefix and feeds generalized advantage estimation. And the clipped surrogate makes multiple gradient steps on one batch of samples safe: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{PPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_t\Big[\min\big(\rho_t A_t,\; \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t,\, 1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon)\, A_t\big)\Big], \qquad \rho_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(y_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y_t|s_t)}.$$ The importance ratio $\rho_t$ corrects for the policy having moved since sampling; the clip (typically $\epsilon = 0.2$) zeroes the gradient once a token's probability has moved a factor $1{\pm}\epsilon$ in the advantage's direction, preventing any single batch from dragging the policy far off-distribution. The cost is an engineering monster: four models live in memory — policy, reference, reward model, critic — two of them training, plus a generation loop inside the training loop. This machine is what DPO and GRPO each partially dismantle.

27.5 DPO: the Derivation, and What It Silently Assumes

DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) begins by solving Theorem 27.1 backwards for the reward: $$r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)} + \beta \log Z(x).$$ Substituting into Bradley–Terry, the intractable $\beta\log Z(x)$ terms cancel in the difference — this is the identifiability freedom of Definition 27.1 doing real work — giving $$P(y_w \succ y_l \mid x) = \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right).$$ Now replace $\pi^*$ by the trainable $\pi_\theta$ and fit by maximum likelihood on the preference data: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_w,y_l)}\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}\right).$$ No reward model, no sampling, no critic: a classification loss over log-probabilities you can compute with two forward passes per example. The quantity $\hat r_\theta(x,y) = \beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}$ is the implicit reward; DPO is logistic regression on implicit-reward differences.

Theorem 27.2 (Population equivalence of DPO and RLHF)

Suppose (i) preferences are generated by Bradley–Terry with true reward $r$; (ii) the comparison distribution covers a connected graph over the support of $\pi_{\text{ref}}$; (iii) $\pi_\theta$ can represent $\pi^*$; and (iv) $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}$ is minimized globally, with the same $\beta$ as the RLHF objective. Then the DPO minimizer equals the RLHF optimum $\pi^*$ of Theorem 27.1.

Proof sketch. The population loss is a proper scoring rule in the margin: for each pair, expected loss $-p\log\sigma(m) - (1-p)\log\sigma(-m)$ is uniquely minimized at $m = \log\frac{p}{1-p} = r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)$. So at the optimum, implicit-reward differences match true-reward differences on every covered pair; connectivity extends this to $\hat r_\theta = r + c(x)$ globally; and a policy whose implicit reward is $r$ up to a per-prompt constant is exactly $\pi^*$ by Theorem 27.1. $\blacksquare$

Every hypothesis of Theorem 27.2 fails in deployment, and the failures are the whole story. Coverage fails first: the preference dataset is a fixed offline sample, typically of responses from some earlier policy, and it pins down the implicit reward only where it has data. Off that support, DPO says nothing — and its optimization pressure actively moves mass to unconstrained regions, since raising $\pi_\theta(y_w)/\pi_\theta(y_l)$ can be achieved by shrinking both while some unseen response absorbs the mass. RLHF is different in kind here: the reward model generalizes (well or badly) to fresh on-policy samples, so the policy is graded exactly where it currently puts mass. Bradley–Terry fails: real labels are noisy, intransitive, and near-deterministic on easy pairs; with empirical hard labels the finite-sample DPO optimum pushes margins toward infinity, the same pathology as separable logistic regression (Chapter 6). Global optimization fails: a few epochs of AdamW on a fixed dataset is not the population minimizer. Artifact 27.1 makes the first two failures numerical: DPO on the population loss, with exact Bradley–Terry labels over every pair, recovers $\pi^*$ to total-variation distance $6\times 10^{-7}$, while fitting sampled comparisons leaves TV distance $0.017$ at 30,000 pairs and $0.23$ at 30 — five orders of magnitude off the population optimum, from data alone, with the loss function held fixed.

Common Pitfall

DPO's loss depends only on the margin between chosen and rejected log-probabilities, and in practice it routinely decreases $\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)$ — the model becomes less likely to produce the preferred response, just faster at deprobabilizing the rejected one. A run whose loss curve looks healthy can be destroying the policy's ability to say anything in-distribution. Always log $\log\pi_\theta(y_w|x)$ and $\log\pi_\theta(y_l|x)$ separately; if both dive, you are watching probability mass leak to sequences no annotator ever saw. This is the sequence-level shadow of the coverage failure above, and it is why recipes cap DPO at 1–2 epochs with small learning rates.

27.6 The Variants: IPO, KTO, ORPO, SimPO

Each successor targets one specific DPO pathology; the table is the fastest way to see the design space. IPO (Azar et al., 2023) is the theoretically sharpest: it shows DPO's log-sigmoid loss is unbounded under deterministic preferences and replaces it with a squared loss regressing the log-ratio margin $\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} - \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}$ onto the fixed target $\tfrac{1}{2\beta}$, so the optimum exists even when annotators never disagree. KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) discards pairing entirely — it needs only per-response thumbs-up/down, which production systems collect for free at orders-of-magnitude larger volume than paired comparisons. ORPO (Hong et al., 2024) folds preference into SFT via an odds-ratio penalty, dropping both the reference model and the separate alignment stage. SimPO (Meng et al., 2024) drops the reference too and length-normalizes the implicit reward, attacking the length bias of Section 27.8 directly in the loss.

MethodData requiredReference modelPathology addressed
DPOpaired preferencesyesRLHF's cost and instability
IPOpaired preferencesyesunbounded margins under deterministic labels
KTOunpaired good/bad labelsyespaired data is scarce and expensive
ORPOpaired preferencesno (single stage with SFT)two-stage pipeline, reference memory
SimPOpaired preferencesnolength bias; reference memory

None of these escape Theorem 27.2's coverage assumption — they are all offline losses on a fixed dataset, and all inherit DPO's silence off-support Certain.

27.7 GRPO and Critic-Free RL

GRPO — Group Relative Policy Optimization, introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024) and made famous by DeepSeek-R1 (2025) — keeps PPO's on-policy sampling and clipped surrogate but deletes the critic. The observation: PPO's value function exists only to reduce variance by estimating "how good is a typical completion from here," but for LLM tasks you can measure that by sampling. Draw $G$ responses $y_1,\dots,y_G$ per prompt (DeepSeekMath samples 64 per question), score each with reward $r_i$, and define the group-relative advantage $$A_i = \frac{r_i - \mathrm{mean}(r_1,\dots,r_G)}{\mathrm{std}(r_1,\dots,r_G) + \varepsilon},$$ shared across all tokens of response $i$. The group mean plays the value function's role as baseline — and unlike a learned critic it is unbiased for the on-policy expected reward and free of its own optimization dynamics. By construction the advantages sum to zero within each group (the artifact verifies this to $10^{-16}$): each prompt's update is purely redistributive, reinforcing the above-average responses at the expense of the below-average ones. The surrogate is PPO's, applied with these advantages, plus an explicit KL-to-reference term estimated with the low-variance $k_3$ estimator $\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}}{\pi_\theta} - \log\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}}{\pi_\theta} - 1$ rather than folded into the reward.

The memory saving is exactly the critic's training state. For a 7B-parameter critic trained in mixed precision with Adam (Chapter 13's accounting: 2-byte weights and gradients, 12 bytes of FP32 master weights and moments), that is roughly $7{\times}10^9 \times 16 \text{ B} \approx 112$ GB of state deleted, plus the critic's forward/backward compute — the difference between RLHF fitting on a node or not. The price is sampling: $G$ completions per prompt instead of one, which shifts cost from memory to inference-time compute, a favorable trade on modern serving stacks (Chapter 33).

The 2025 follow-ups are a case study in how much pathology hides in "minor" normalization choices Verify — this literature is moving; attributions checked against the arXiv versions of each paper as of mid-2026. DAPO (ByteDance Seed, 2025) diagnoses four failure modes of naive GRPO at scale and patches each: decoupled clip ranges ($\epsilon_{\text{high}} > \epsilon_{\text{low}}$, "clip-higher") to stop entropy collapse; dynamic sampling that discards groups where every response is right or every response is wrong, since those yield $A_i = 0$ and starve the batch of gradient; token-level rather than per-response loss averaging for long chains of thought; and reward shaping for truncated responses. Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) shows two of GRPO's own normalizations are biased estimators: dividing each response's loss by its length underpenalizes long wrong answers (so failures grow longer during training), and dividing advantages by the group std upweights near-deterministic prompts; removing both gives an unbiased gradient and markedly shorter incorrect responses. GSPO (Qwen team, 2025) replaces token-level importance ratios with a single sequence-level, length-normalized ratio $\big(\pi_\theta(y|x)/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y|x)\big)^{1/|y|}$ and clips whole sequences; the motivation is Mixture-of-Experts training (Chapter 22), where routing shifts between the sampling policy and the updated policy — the Qwen team reports on the order of 10% of activated experts changing per update in Qwen3-30B-A3B Verify — make per-token ratios noise; GSPO stabilized Qwen3's RL without the routing-replay workaround GRPO needed.

Contested Do the differences between DPO, PPO, and GRPO survive equal tuning budgets? Theorem 27.2 says the objectives coincide in the ideal limit, so any persistent gap must come from the assumptions that break. The best-known head-to-head (Xu et al., 2024, "Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment?") finds PPO ahead, with DPO degrading sharply on out-of-distribution prompts; Ivison et al. (2024) find preference-data quality moves results more than the choice of algorithm. Both camps' comparisons are vulnerable to the same critique: PPO/GRPO have many more knobs, and most academic studies tune one side far harder than the other — several published "DPO wins" results used PPO baselines without the batch-size and advantage-normalization fixes practitioners consider mandatory, and vice versa. Position: for offline alignment on fixed human-preference data, the algorithm gap is second-order next to data quality, and DPO-family methods are the right default. For tasks with a generalizing reward signal — above all verifiable rewards (Section 27.9) — on-policy methods win and the gap is real, because they collect gradient exactly where the policy currently is, which no offline method can. What would change this position: a tuning-matched study at frontier scale where each method is configured by its strongest proponents; none exists as of this writing.

27.8 Reward Hacking, Length Bias, Over-Optimization

The reward model is a proxy, and optimizing a proxy hard enough makes it stop tracking the target (Goodhart's law, made quantitative). Gao, Schulman, and Hilton (2023) trained a large "gold" reward model, used smaller RMs as proxies, and measured both while RL optimized the proxy: proxy reward rises monotonically, gold reward rises, peaks, and then falls, with the peak arriving sooner for smaller proxies and the curves well-fit by simple functional forms in $d = \sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})}$. Over-optimization is thus measurable and predictable: KL distance from the reference is the resource being spent, and the KL coefficient $\beta$, early stopping, and RM ensembles are all ways of budgeting it. DPO is not exempt — its implicit reward over-optimizes on finite data in exactly the way Artifact 27.1's coverage sweep shows.

The most consequential concrete hack is length. Human raters — and LLM judges — systematically prefer longer, more confident-sounding answers, so reward models inherit a length bias, so policies inflate. Every family reinvents a fix: explicit length penalties in the reward; SimPO's length-normalized implicit reward; Dr. GRPO's removal of the length normalization that let wrong answers grow; length-controlled evaluation (Chapter 29) to stop the metric rewarding the hack. When a policy's mean response length climbs during preference optimization, treat it as a reward-hacking alarm first and an improvement second.

27.9 RLAIF and Verifiable Rewards

Two developments attack the reward's provenance rather than the optimizer. RLAIF replaces human annotators with an LLM judge: Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) had a model critique and rank responses against written principles, and Lee et al. (2023) found AI preference labels can match human labels' downstream effect on standard chat tasks at a small fraction of the cost Likely. The judge inherits and amplifies its own biases — length and sycophancy above all — so RLAIF raises the stakes of Section 27.8 rather than settling it.

Verifiable rewards (RLVR) dissolve the problem where they apply: when the reward is a program — unit tests pass, the boxed answer equals the reference, the proof checks — there is no reward model to hack and no generalization gap, only the true objective. Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024) named the recipe; DeepSeek-R1 showed rule-based correctness-plus-format rewards under GRPO suffice to elicit long-chain reasoning from a base model. This is where the chapter's thesis lands hardest: with the reward exact, the remaining differences between methods are purely the data-and-optimization differences — and offline methods have no way to exploit an exact verifier on their own fresh mistakes, which is why the reasoning-model era (Chapter 28) runs on on-policy RL, not DPO.

Artifact 27.1 — DPO Against the Closed Form

A 6-armed bandit with known reward, known $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, and $\beta = 0.3$, so the RLHF optimum $\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}} e^{r/\beta}$ is computable exactly. The module implements DPO, IPO, SimPO, the GRPO group-relative advantage, and the clipped GRPO surrogate from scratch in NumPy with analytic gradients, checks every gradient against central finite differences, then runs the chapter's thesis as an experiment: minimize the population DPO loss over all 15 action pairs with exact Bradley–Terry labels and compare to $\pi^*$; then refit on progressively smaller sampled preference sets and print the divergence.

"""Artifact 27.1 -- DPO/IPO/SimPO losses, the GRPO advantage, and the bandit
where DPO's equivalence to RLHF can be checked against a closed form.

Setup: a K-armed bandit with known reward r(a) and reference policy pi_ref.
The KL-regularized RLHF optimum is available in closed form:
    pi*(a) = pi_ref(a) * exp(r(a)/beta) / Z.
We (1) gradient-check every loss against central finite differences,
(2) show that minimizing the *population* DPO loss over ALL preference pairs
recovers pi* to numerical precision, (3) show that with finite sampled
preference data the DPO solution measurably diverges from pi*, and
(4) verify GRPO group-relative advantages are zero-mean within each group.
Pure NumPy core; torch appears only as an autograd cross-check.
"""
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# ----------------------------- utilities ------------------------------------
def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max()
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

def softplus(x):                       # log(1+e^x), stable
    return np.maximum(x, 0.0) + np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(x)))

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))

# ------------------------- losses (analytic grads) --------------------------
# Policy is pi_theta = softmax(theta) over K actions. For pairwise losses the
# log-partition cancels in log pi(w) - log pi(l), so Delta uses raw logits.
def dpo_loss_grad(theta, ref_logp, w, l, wt, beta):
    """L = sum_i wt_i * -log sigmoid(beta*Delta_i);  Delta = (th_w-th_l)-(ref_w-ref_l)."""
    d = (theta[w] - theta[l]) - (ref_logp[w] - ref_logp[l])
    z = beta * d
    loss = float(np.sum(wt * softplus(-z)))
    coef = -beta * wt * sigmoid(-z)            # dL/dtheta_w per pair
    g = np.zeros_like(theta)
    np.add.at(g, w, coef); np.add.at(g, l, -coef)
    return loss, g

def ipo_loss_grad(theta, ref_logp, w, l, wt, beta):
    """IPO (Azar et al.): L = sum wt_i (Delta_i - 1/(2 beta))^2."""
    d = (theta[w] - theta[l]) - (ref_logp[w] - ref_logp[l])
    e = d - 1.0 / (2.0 * beta)
    loss = float(np.sum(wt * e * e))
    coef = 2.0 * wt * e
    g = np.zeros_like(theta)
    np.add.at(g, w, coef); np.add.at(g, l, -coef)
    return loss, g

def simpo_loss_grad(theta, w, l, wt, beta, gamma):
    """SimPO (Meng et al.): reference-free, length-normalized margin.
    Bandit 'responses' have length 1, so L = sum wt_i -log sigmoid(beta*(th_w-th_l)-gamma)."""
    z = beta * (theta[w] - theta[l]) - gamma
    loss = float(np.sum(wt * softplus(-z)))
    coef = -beta * wt * sigmoid(-z)
    g = np.zeros_like(theta)
    np.add.at(g, w, coef); np.add.at(g, l, -coef)
    return loss, g

def grpo_advantages(rewards):
    """Group-relative advantage: standardize rewards within each group (row)."""
    mu = rewards.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sd = rewards.std(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return (rewards - mu) / (sd + 1e-8)

def grpo_loss_grad(theta, actions, old_pi, adv, eps=0.2):
    """Clipped surrogate, single-token episodes: L = -mean_i min(rho_i A_i, clip(rho_i)A_i),
    rho_i = pi_theta(a_i)/pi_old(a_i). Analytic grad uses d pi_a/d theta = pi_a (e_a - pi)."""
    pi = softmax(theta)
    rho = pi[actions] / old_pi[actions]
    unc, cl = rho * adv, np.clip(rho, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * adv
    loss = float(-np.mean(np.minimum(unc, cl)))
    g = np.zeros_like(theta)
    for i, a in enumerate(actions):                 # only unclipped terms carry gradient
        if unc[i] <= cl[i]:
            drho = rho[i] * ((np.arange(len(theta)) == a) - pi)
            g += -adv[i] * drho / len(actions)
    return loss, g

def fd_check(f, theta, h=1e-5):
    """Max abs error between analytic grad and central finite differences."""
    _, g = f(theta)
    num = np.zeros_like(theta)
    for k in range(len(theta)):
        tp, tm = theta.copy(), theta.copy()
        tp[k] += h; tm[k] -= h
        num[k] = (f(tp)[0] - f(tm)[0]) / (2 * h)
    return np.abs(g - num).max()

# ------------------------------- experiment ---------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    K, beta = 6, 0.3
    r = np.array([1.0, 0.5, 0.0, -0.5, -1.0, 0.25])          # known reward
    ref_logits = rng.normal(0, 1, K)
    pi_ref = softmax(ref_logits)
    ref_logp = np.log(pi_ref)
    pi_star = softmax(ref_logp + r / beta)                    # closed-form RLHF optimum

    # 1) gradient checks at a generic point
    th0 = rng.normal(0, 1, K)
    ii, jj = np.triu_indices(K, 1)                            # all 15 unordered pairs
    p_win = sigmoid(r[ii] - r[jj])                            # Bradley-Terry soft labels
    w_all = np.concatenate([ii, jj]); l_all = np.concatenate([jj, ii])
    wt_all = np.concatenate([p_win, 1 - p_win]) / len(ii)
    print(f"[grad] DPO   max|analytic-FD| = {fd_check(lambda t: dpo_loss_grad(t, ref_logp, w_all, l_all, wt_all, beta), th0):.2e}")
    print(f"[grad] IPO   max|analytic-FD| = {fd_check(lambda t: ipo_loss_grad(t, ref_logp, w_all, l_all, wt_all, beta), th0):.2e}")
    print(f"[grad] SimPO max|analytic-FD| = {fd_check(lambda t: simpo_loss_grad(t, w_all, l_all, wt_all, 2.0, 0.5), th0):.2e}")
    G, n_g = 8, 16
    rew = rng.normal(0, 1, (n_g, G))
    adv = grpo_advantages(rew)
    print(f"[GRPO] max |group mean of advantages| = {np.abs(adv.mean(axis=1)).max():.2e}")
    assert np.abs(adv.mean(axis=1)).max() < 1e-9, "GRPO advantages must be zero-mean per group"
    acts = rng.integers(0, K, 32)
    old_pi = softmax(rng.normal(0, 1, K))
    adv1 = grpo_advantages(rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 16))).ravel()
    err = fd_check(lambda t: grpo_loss_grad(t, acts, old_pi, adv1), th0)
    print(f"[grad] GRPO clipped surrogate max|analytic-FD| = {err:.2e}")
    for e in [err]:
        assert e < 1e-6
    assert fd_check(lambda t: dpo_loss_grad(t, ref_logp, w_all, l_all, wt_all, beta), th0) < 1e-6

    try:
        import torch
        tt = torch.tensor(th0, requires_grad=True)
        d = (tt[w_all] - tt[l_all]) - torch.tensor(ref_logp[w_all] - ref_logp[l_all])
        Lt = (torch.tensor(wt_all) * torch.nn.functional.softplus(-beta * d)).sum()
        Lt.backward()
        print(f"[torch] DPO grad max diff vs autograd = {np.abs(tt.grad.numpy() - dpo_loss_grad(th0, ref_logp, w_all, l_all, wt_all, beta)[1]).max():.2e}")
    except ImportError:
        print("[skipped: torch not installed]")

    # 2) full preference coverage: population DPO loss over all pairs w/ exact
    #    Bradley-Terry labels. Its minimizer must be the closed-form pi*.
    res = minimize(lambda t: dpo_loss_grad(t, ref_logp, w_all, l_all, wt_all, beta),
                   np.zeros(K), jac=True, method="L-BFGS-B",
                   options={"maxiter": 2000, "gtol": 1e-14})
    pi_hat = softmax(res.x)
    tv_full = 0.5 * np.abs(pi_hat - pi_star).sum()
    print(f"\npi*      = {np.array2string(pi_star, precision=4)}")
    print(f"pi_DPO   = {np.array2string(pi_hat, precision=4)}  (full coverage)")
    print(f"[full coverage] TV(pi_DPO, pi*) = {tv_full:.2e}")
    assert tv_full < 1e-4, "DPO under full coverage must recover the RLHF optimum"

    # 3) finite coverage: sample N comparisons (uniform pair, BT winner), fit
    #    the empirical DPO loss, measure divergence from pi*.
    print("\n  N pairs   TV(pi_DPO, pi*)")
    tvs = {}
    for N in [30000, 3000, 300, 30]:
        pk = rng.integers(0, len(ii), N)                      # which unordered pair
        first_wins = rng.random(N) < p_win[pk]
        w = np.where(first_wins, ii[pk], jj[pk])
        l = np.where(first_wins, jj[pk], ii[pk])
        res = minimize(lambda t: dpo_loss_grad(t, ref_logp, w, l, np.full(N, 1.0 / N), beta),
                       np.zeros(K), jac=True, method="L-BFGS-B", options={"maxiter": 500})
        tvs[N] = 0.5 * np.abs(softmax(res.x) - pi_star).sum()
        print(f"  {N:7d}   {tvs[N]:.4f}")
    assert tvs[30] > 10 * tvs[30000], "divergence must grow as coverage shrinks"
    assert tvs[30000] < 0.05
    print("\nAll assertions passed: DPO = RLHF optimum under full coverage; "
          "measurably not otherwise.")

Running it prints gradient errors of at most $3.5\times 10^{-11}$ against central finite differences for all four losses, a torch-autograd cross-check agreeing to $6.9\times 10^{-18}$, and GRPO group-advantage means at $1.25\times 10^{-16}$. The headline is the coverage contrast: with full pair coverage and exact Bradley–Terry labels the DPO fit matches $\pi^* = (0.7594, 0.1108, 0.0453, 0.0050, 0.0005, 0.0789)$ to $\mathrm{TV} = 5.81\times 10^{-7}$; with sampled data the divergence climbs from $0.0166$ at 30,000 pairs to $0.0371$ at 3,000, $0.1593$ at 300, and $0.2268$ at 30. Same loss, same optimizer — only the data changed. That is Theorem 27.2 and its failure in four printed lines.

Key Takeaways
  • The KL-regularized objective has the closed-form optimum $\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\, e^{r/\beta}$, and DPO is an exact reparametrization of it: under Bradley–Terry preferences with full coverage, the population DPO minimizer is the RLHF optimum. Certain
  • The practical gaps between RLHF, DPO, and GRPO come from what the losses don't capture — on-policy sampling, finite offline coverage, and reward-model generalization — not from the objectives, which coincide in the ideal limit. Likely
  • GRPO replaces the learned critic with the within-group reward mean; the advantages are zero-mean per group by construction, and the deletion saves the critic's entire training state — roughly 16 bytes per critic parameter under mixed-precision Adam. Certain
  • GRPO's normalizations carry real biases — length normalization grows wrong answers, std division distorts prompt weighting, token-level ratios destabilize MoE — and DAPO, Dr. GRPO, and GSPO are the 2025 corrections; check current recipes before adopting any of them verbatim. Verify
  • Whether PPO/GRPO beat DPO under equal tuning budgets is unresolved — most head-to-heads under-tune one side; data quality dominates for offline alignment, while on-policy RL wins decisively wherever rewards are verifiable. Contested
Chapter 28

Reasoning Models and Test-Time Compute

Learning Objectives
  • Explain chain-of-thought as conditional computation, and state the expressivity argument for why generating intermediate tokens strictly increases what a fixed-depth transformer can compute.
  • Distinguish parallel test-time scaling (sample $k$ chains, select one) from sequential scaling (one longer chain), and state the regimes where each dominates.
  • Explain reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) as used in current reasoning models, including what the cold-start-free DeepSeek-R1-Zero result does and does not show.
  • Distinguish pass@1 from pass@$k$ rigorously, and explain why RLVR frequently raises the former while lowering the latter at large $k$.
  • Implement best-of-$n$, majority voting, and verifier-guided selection in working code, and verify the analytic pass@$k$ law against an unbiased empirical estimator.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 covers inference-time scaling and RL post-training closest to this chapter's level; Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), for the mechanics of sampling and generation loops that every method here is built on.

Chapter 24 established that pretraining loss scales with parameters $N$ and data $D$; Chapter 27 built GRPO, the policy-gradient method this chapter's training recipes run on. Here we ask what a third axis buys: compute spent at inference. The central claim is deflationary and worth stating up front. Test-time compute converts serial thinking into accuracy on tasks with checkable answers, and the celebrated pass@$k$ curves measure coverage — the probability that at least one of $k$ samples is correct — not capability. Conflating coverage with capability is currently the most common analytical error in this literature, and it flows in both directions: it inflates claims for parallel sampling and inverts the interpretation of RLVR training curves. Section 28.9's cost accounting feeds directly into serving (Chapter 33); the evaluation pathologies resurface in Chapter 29.

28.1 Chain-of-Thought and Intermediate Computation

A transformer with $L$ layers performs a fixed amount of computation per emitted token: one forward pass, roughly $2N$ FLOPs (Chapter 24). If the answer to "what is $437 \times 892$?" must be emitted as the very next token, every intermediate quantity must be computed inside one pass of depth $L$, in parallel, with no working memory beyond the residual stream. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting — eliciting intermediate steps before the answer, introduced by Wei et al. (2022) — changes the computational model, not just the prompt: each generated token is an additional full forward pass whose output is written into the context and re-read by attention at every subsequent step.

Definition 28.1 (Chain-of-thought as conditional computation)

Let $f_\theta$ be an autoregressive model and $x$ a prompt. A chain-of-thought decode emits tokens $z_1, \dots, z_t$ with $z_i \sim f_\theta(\cdot \mid x, z_{<i})$ before the answer $y \sim f_\theta(\cdot \mid x, z_{\le t})$. The compute spent on input $x$ is $(t+|y|)\cdot 2N$ FLOPs plus attention terms — data-dependent, because $t$ is chosen at decode time. The context acts as an external, re-readable tape: token $z_i$ is a function of all of $z_{<i}$, giving a serial dependency chain of length $t$ that no fixed-depth parallel circuit provides.

This is conditional computation in the same sense as mixture-of-experts (Chapter 22), but along the opposite axis: MoE varies which parameters fire per token at fixed depth; CoT varies how many serial steps a given input receives at fixed parameters. Reasoning models — o1, DeepSeek-R1, and their successors — are models trained so that this serial budget is spent productively rather than on decorative prose.

28.2 The Expressivity Argument for Thinking Tokens

The claim that intermediate tokens increase what a transformer can compute is a theorem, not an intuition.

Theorem 28.1 (Expressive power of CoT; Merrill & Sabharwal 2023–24, Li et al. 2024)

A log-precision, fixed-depth transformer decoder that must answer immediately (zero intermediate tokens) decides only languages in the circuit class $\mathsf{TC}^0$ — constant-depth threshold circuits, which under standard conjectures cannot solve even $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete problems such as evaluating Boolean formulas, nor graph connectivity, nor linear algebra of the kind Chapter 1 treats as primitive. With $t(n)$ intermediate tokens on inputs of length $n$, the same architecture can simulate $t(n)$ steps of a Turing machine; with polynomially many tokens it decides exactly the class $\mathsf{P}$. Certain

Proof sketch. Upper bound (no CoT): each attention head and MLP in a log-precision forward pass is computable by a constant-depth threshold circuit; composing $L$ layers keeps constant depth, so the whole pass sits in $\mathsf{TC}^0$. Lower bound (with CoT): encode the Turing machine's configuration changes into the token stream itself. Each emitted token records the machine's current state, the symbol written, and the head move. To execute step $i{+}1$, the decoder must recover the current tape cell's latest contents: a position-aware attention head selects, among prior tokens that wrote to the current head position, the most recent one — an argmax over positions that hard attention implements exactly and soft attention implements at log precision. Generation thus becomes a recurrence: the context window is the tape, autoregression is the clock. $\blacksquare$

Two caveats keep this honest. First, expressivity is not learnability: the theorem says a parameter setting exists, not that gradient descent finds it, and empirical chains are noisy natural language rather than TM transcripts. Second, Pfau et al. (2024, "Let's Think Dot by Dot") showed transformers can sometimes exploit meaning-free filler tokens ("......") to solve tasks unaided decoding fails on — extra parallel width, since filler creates no serial dependency — but filler provably cannot buy the serial power of Theorem 28.1, and in practice fails on exactly the tasks needing it. Likely The practical reading: the value of a thinking token is the conditional computation it enables, and the ladder from $\mathsf{TC}^0$ toward $\mathsf{P}$ is climbed by chain length, which is why Section 28.4's sequential scaling is not interchangeable with Section 28.3's parallel scaling.
