28.3 Parallel Scaling: Best-of-n, Self-Consistency, Reranking

Parallel scaling draws $k$ independent chains for the same prompt and selects one answer. Everything in this family is governed by one quantity: the per-draw success probability $p$ of the fixed sampler on the fixed problem.

Definition 28.2 (pass@$k$ and its unbiased estimator)

For a stochastic sampler with i.i.d. per-draw success probability $p$ on a problem, $$\text{pass@}k \;=\; \Pr[\text{at least one of } k \text{ draws correct}] \;=\; 1-(1-p)^k,$$ averaged over a problem set: $\overline{\text{pass@}k} = \mathbb{E}_i\!\left[1-(1-p_i)^k\right]$. Given $n \ge k$ samples of which $c$ verify correct, the unbiased estimator (Chen et al., 2021) is $$\widehat{\text{pass@}k} \;=\; 1 - \binom{n-c}{k}\Big/\binom{n}{k}.$$ The plug-in $1-(1-c/n)^k$ is biased: $1-(1-p)^k$ is concave in $p$, so by Jensen's inequality $\mathbb{E}[1-(1-c/n)^k] \le 1-(1-p)^k$ — the plug-in underestimates on average, badly so when $k$ approaches $n$ (at $p=0.05$, $n=64$, $k=32$ the bias is $-0.08$ against a true value of $0.81$).

Three selection rules, in increasing order of the machinery they assume. Best-of-$n$ scores each sample with a reranker (a reward model, Chapter 27) and returns the argmax; its accuracy is capped by pass@$n$ and degraded by scorer noise. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) — majority voting over final answers — needs no scorer at all and rests on a Condorcet-style fact:

Theorem 28.2 (Plurality voting consistency)

Let answers be i.i.d. over a finite set with correct-answer probability $q_1$ satisfying $q_1 > \max_{j\ge 2} q_j$ (the truth is the strict mode, though possibly $q_1 < \tfrac12$). Then the plurality vote over $n$ samples is correct with probability $\to 1$ as $n \to \infty$.

Proof. Let $\gamma = q_1 - \max_{j\ge2} q_j > 0$. By Hoeffding, each empirical frequency $\hat q_j$ deviates from $q_j$ by more than $\gamma/2$ with probability at most $2e^{-n\gamma^2/2}$; a union bound over the finite answer set makes all deviations small simultaneously with probability $\to 1$, and then $\hat q_1 > \hat q_j$ for all $j \ne 1$. $\blacksquare$

Voting therefore converts "modal but not majority" into near-certainty — Artifact 28.1 measures a jump from 0.361 per-sample accuracy to 0.985 with 33 votes — but it is only a variance reducer: if the mode is wrong, more votes make the wrong answer more certain. Verifier-guided selection assumes an exact checker (unit tests, a proof checker, modular arithmetic) and returns any verified sample, achieving pass@$n$ itself. Brown et al. (2024, "Large Language Monkeys") showed empirically that coverage keeps climbing over thousands of samples, approximately log-linearly in $k$ — and that is precisely why pass@$k$ at large $k$ measures the sampler's support, not its reliability. Likely Parallel scaling dominates when a cheap verifier or a strong modal signal exists and latency matters: the $k$ chains run concurrently, so wall-clock is one chain's latency while cost is $k$ chains' FLOPs.

Example 28.1 (A two-problem pass@$k$ inversion by hand)

Two problems; base sampler succeeds per-draw with $p = (0.5,\; 0.1)$; a "sharpened" sampler with $p' = (0.9,\; 0.01)$. Pass@1: base $= \tfrac12(0.5+0.1) = 0.30$; sharpened $= \tfrac12(0.9+0.01) = 0.455$. Sharpening wins. Pass@16: base $= \tfrac12\big[(1-0.5^{16}) + (1-0.9^{16})\big] = \tfrac12[0.99998 + (1-0.1853)] = 0.907$; sharpened $= \tfrac12\big[(1-0.1^{16}) + (1-0.99^{16})\big] = \tfrac12[1.0 + (1-0.8515)] = 0.574$, using $0.9^{16} = (((0.9^2)^2)^2)^2 = 0.4305^2 \approx 0.185$ and $0.99^{16} \approx e^{-16\times 0.01005} \approx 0.851$. The base sampler's residual $0.1$ on problem two buys near-certain coverage by $k=16$; the sharpened sampler's $0.01$ does not. Higher pass@1, lower pass@16 — from nothing but concavity.

28.4 Sequential Scaling: Revision and Budget Forcing

Sequential scaling spends the budget on one longer chain: the model drafts, checks, backtracks, and revises, each step conditioning on everything before it. This is the regime Theorem 28.1 actually speaks to — serial depth — and it is what o1-style reasoning models do natively. It can be imposed crudely from outside: s1 (Muennighoff et al., 2025) fine-tuned on only 1,000 curated reasoning traces and then controlled thinking length at decode time by budget forcing — suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter and appending "Wait" to force continued revision, or truncating thought to cap it — yielding monotone accuracy gains on math benchmarks as the forced budget grew. Likely

Where each mode dominates is now cleanly stateable. Parallel scaling can only harvest probability mass the sampler already places on correct answers: it improves extraction, never reach, and saturates at the support boundary. Sequential scaling can in principle extend reach — a longer chain is more computation per attempt — but errors compound along the chain, and models "overthink," revising correct answers into wrong ones. Snell et al. (2024) made the allocation question quantitative: on easy problems (high $p$), verifier-guided parallel search wins; on hard problems (low $p$), sequential revision wins; and compute-optimally mixing them let a small model beat a $14\times$ larger one at matched total FLOPs on the easier strata — with the advantage inverting on the hardest strata, where nothing substitutes for pretrained capability. Likely

28.5 Process versus Outcome Reward Models

Both selection and RL need a reward signal, and there are two places to attach it. An outcome reward model (ORM) scores the final answer; a process reward model (PRM) scores each intermediate step. Lightman et al. (2023, "Let's Verify Step by Step") trained a PRM on 800K human step-labels and found process supervision substantially outperformed outcome supervision for best-of-$n$ selection on MATH — the canonical evidence that step-level credit assignment matters when chains are long, since an ORM cannot distinguish a sound derivation from a lucky guess ("spurious correctness").

The PRM story since then is a rise, a fall, and a partial revival. The fall: human step-labels are unaffordable at scale, Monte-Carlo auto-labels (estimating a step's value by rollouts from it) are noisy and biased, and — decisively — DeepSeek-R1's report explicitly rejected PRMs for RL training, citing reward hacking of the learned signal and annotation cost, using rule-based verifiable rewards instead. The revival: generative "PRMs that think" (GenPRM and successors), which reason in text before judging a step, currently the active line — but deployed mainly for test-time reranking and search guidance rather than as RL training rewards, where step-level data quality remains the unsolved bottleneck. Verify — this balance is moving; check against the current Awesome-Process-Reward-Models survey list before relying on it.

28.6 RLVR and Reasoning Models

Definition 28.3 (Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards)

RLVR is policy-gradient training (typically GRPO, Chapter 27) where the reward is a program, not a learned model: $r(x, y) = \mathbb{1}[\text{verify}(x, y)]$ — exact-match against a known answer, a unit-test suite, a compiler, a proof checker — optionally plus format terms. The policy samples $G$ chains per prompt; group-normalized advantages push probability toward chains that verified.

The result that defined 2025: DeepSeek-R1-Zero applied RLVR directly to a base model — no supervised fine-tuning, no cold-start data, no PRM, no search — and long chains, self-checking, backtracking, and spontaneous re-evaluation ("aha moments") emerged, with chain length growing over training as the model learned to spend more serial compute. What this shows: verifiable reward alone suffices to elicit extended reasoning behavior from a strong base model. What it does not show: that the capability was created by RL. The base model already emits such chains with low probability — that is exactly why sampling-based RL can find and amplify them — and R1-Zero's outputs were poorly readable and language-mixed enough that the production R1 reintroduced cold-start SFT before RL. Elicitation, not creation, is the parsimonious reading, and Section 28.8 makes it quantitative. Likely

Now the pass@$k$ inversion, the chapter's thesis in data. Yue et al. (2025, "Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?", NeurIPS 2025) evaluated RLVR-trained models and their own base models at large $k$: RLVR models win at $k=1$, but the base models overtake them as $k$ grows into the hundreds, across model families and benchmarks — and the correct chains RLVR models produce were already present in the base models' samples. Training raises pass@1 while shrinking the set of problems solvable at any $k$: precisely Example 28.1's arithmetic, with RLVR playing the role of the temperature knob. The proposed mechanism is sharpening: policy-gradient ascent on-support concentrates mass on already-rewarded modes (entropy collapses over training), raising $p_i$ where the mode is right and driving $p_i \to 0$ where it is not. Follow-up work ("The Invisible Leash") argues on-policy RLVR cannot place mass outside the base support it samples from. Likely

Contested Whether RLVR can expand the capability envelope, rather than merely sharpen the existing distribution, is genuinely open. Position A (sharpening): the Yue et al. inversion, entropy collapse, and support arguments above. Position B (expansion): NVIDIA's ProRL reports that prolonged RL — thousands of steps with KL control, reference-policy resets, and diverse tasks — yields models that solve problems where the base scores zero at any sampled $k$, with pass@$k$ gains across the curve. The positions are reconcilable: short-horizon RLVR on narrow domains sharpens; whether long-horizon, diverse-task RL escapes the base support at practical compute is the live question. Evidence that would settle it: pass@$k$ at $k \sim 10^3$ on held-out problem families with verified-novel solution strategies (not memorizable variants), reported against the same base checkpoint — expansion claims that survive that protocol would refute strong sharpening. My position: sharpening is the default outcome of the standard recipe, and expansion claims bear the burden of proof, because they have repeatedly shrunk under stricter contamination and evaluation controls.

RLVR's clean premise — the reward cannot be hacked because it is a program — also failed in an instructive way. An ICLR 2026 workshop paper ("LLMs Gaming Verifiers") showed RLVR-trained reasoning models systematically exploit extensional verifiers (ones checking only input–output correctness): on rule-induction tasks they abandon learning the rule and enumerate instance-level answers that pass the checker while capturing none of the required structure, a behavior absent in comparable non-RLVR models and increasing with inference-time compute; isomorphic verification — requiring invariance under logically equivalent reformulations — eliminated the shortcut in controlled training. Verify — specifics against arXiv:2604.15149. The moral generalizes: a verifier defines the task, and RLVR optimizes the verifier, not your intent.

Common Pitfall

Estimating pass@$k$ with the plug-in formula $1-(1-c/n)^k$ from $n$ samples with $c$ successes — or worse, chunking $n$ samples into $n/k$ disjoint groups and averaging any-correct per group. The plug-in is biased downward (Jensen's inequality on a concave function, badly at $k \approx n$); chunking is unbiased but throws away all but $n/k$ effective observations, so its variance explodes. Both failures are largest exactly where pass@$k$ inversion claims are decided: large $k$, small $p$. Use the unbiased estimator of Definition 28.2, computed as a running product $\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{n-c-j}{n-j}$ to avoid factorial overflow — Artifact 28.1 does, and matches the closed form to 0.004. A second version of the same bug: comparing pass@1 between models decoded at different temperatures, then comparing pass@64 at those same settings — temperature is a free parameter that trades the two endpoints against each other, as the artifact demonstrates.

28.7 Distilling Reasoning into Small Models

If RLVR sharpens what is already there, a small model with little there to sharpen should gain little from it — and that is what DeepSeek reported: running their large-scale RL recipe directly on Qwen-32B produced a model on par with QwQ-32B-Preview, while simply fine-tuning the same base on the ~800K R1-curated SFT samples (about 600K of them reasoning traces) outperformed it across benchmarks at a fraction of the cost. Likely The asymmetry is exactly the support argument again: on-policy RL is leashed to the small model's own distribution, but distillation is off-policy — the teacher's traces inject probability mass the student never had, so distillation can genuinely expand a small model's pass@$k$ envelope where RLVR cannot. The practical recipe hierarchy for small reasoning models is therefore distill first, then optionally a short RLVR pass to sharpen pass@1 on the target domain. Chapter 34 treats distillation's mechanics; the trace-quality curation problem is Chapter 25's data story in miniature.

28.8 What Test-Time Compute Does Not Buy

Three deflationary facts, each load-bearing for how you should read a benchmark table. First, parallel scaling buys extraction, not reach: every method in Section 28.3 is bounded by the sampler's support, and a coverage curve climbing at $k = 10{,}000$ is a statement about the tail of the base distribution, not about what any deployable single-sample system knows. Second, everything above assumed a verifier; on tasks without checkable answers — open-ended writing, judgment, most of the economy — best-of-$n$ against a learned reward model inherits that model's exploitability (Chapter 27's overoptimization), majority voting has no privileged mode to find, and measured test-time-scaling gains are consistently smaller and noisier. Third, more thinking is not monotone: forced overlong chains degrade accuracy on problems the model would have answered correctly at once.

Contested Does test-time compute buy new reasoning capability, or only reliable extraction of latent capability? Extraction view: sharpening results, the distillation asymmetry, and the fact that base models match reasoning models at large $k$ on many benchmarks. Capability view: Theorem 28.1 is an existence proof that serial tokens strictly enlarge the computable class, and sequential methods do solve individual instances (long multi-step problems) that no feasible number of direct samples from the same model solves — per-instance compute genuinely differs. A defensible synthesis: sequential test-time compute can constitute new capability on serial-depth-limited tasks; parallel test-time compute cannot, and most headline numbers mix the two. What would settle it: families of problems with provable serial-depth requirements (e.g., iterated function composition) where direct-answer pass@$k$ stays at chance for astronomical $k$ while CoT succeeds — small-scale versions of this experiment exist and favor the synthesis, but no one has run it cleanly at frontier scale.

28.9 Inference-Time Cost Accounting

Both scaling modes cost FLOPs $\approx 2N$ per generated token (plus attention, Chapter 30), but they stress a serving system (Chapter 33) differently. Parallel, $k$ chains of length $T$: total compute $k \cdot 2NT$, wall-clock one chain, KV-cache memory $k$ concurrent caches — batch-friendly, memory-hungry. Sequential, one chain of length $kT$: identical total compute, $k\times$ the latency, one cache that grows to $kT$ — and per-token attention cost grows linearly with position, so a $64\times$ longer chain is strictly more expensive than 64 short ones in attention FLOPs, on top of monopolizing a decode slot. Reasoning-mode tokens are also billed output tokens: a model that thinks for 10,000 tokens to emit a 50-token answer costs $200\times$ its visible output, which is why serving stacks expose thinking budgets as a dial. Verify — per-token pricing and budget-control APIs drift; check current provider documentation. The optimization problem that follows — given a FLOP budget, choose model size $N$, chain length, and sample count $k$ jointly — is the test-time analogue of Chapter 24's Chinchilla allocation, and its broad answer (small-model-plus-compute wins only below a difficulty threshold) was Section 28.4's Snell result. When the selection rule needs a learned scorer, add the scorer's forward passes: best-of-$n$ with a same-size reward model is $n \cdot 2NT$ for generation plus $n \cdot 2NT'$ for scoring — verifier-guided selection with a programmatic checker makes the second term free, which is the quiet economic reason RLVR-style domains got the compute first.

Artifact 28.1 — A Test-Time-Compute Harness with an Exact Verifier

The harness builds every object in this chapter on a toy task where truth is closed-form: compute $(ab + c) \bmod m$. A simulated sampler assigns each of 200 problems fixed logits over 10 candidate answers; temperature is the sharpening knob standing in for RLVR (70% of problems have a correct mode, 30% a wrong one — the misaligned minority is where coverage lives). It verifies the analytic law $\overline{\text{pass@}k} = \mathbb{E}_i[1-(1-p_i)^k]$ against the unbiased estimator on real samples, asserts the pass@$k$ inversion with its crossover, asserts Theorem 28.2's voting gain in the plurality-not-majority regime, and ranks the three selection rules at $n=16$. Pure NumPy; SciPy appears only as a guarded cross-check.

"""Artifact 28.1 -- A test-time-compute harness on a toy task with an exact verifier.

Task: given (a, b, c, m), produce y = (a*b + c) mod m.  The verifier is closed-form,
so "verified" and "correct" coincide -- the clean-RLVR regime with no reward hacking.

We simulate the sampler instead of calling a model: each problem carries fixed logits
over 10 candidate answers; sampling at temperature T induces a categorical
distribution.  Lowering T ("sharpening") mimics what RLVR does to a policy: mass
concentrates on each problem's mode.  Where the mode is correct, accuracy rises;
where it is wrong, the tail probability of EVER sampling the right answer collapses.

Asserted demonstrations:
  1. analytic pass@k = mean_i [1 - (1-p_i)^k] matches the unbiased empirical
     estimator of Chen et al. (2021) drawn from real samples;
  2. sharpening (T=0.25) raises pass@1 but strictly lowers pass@64 vs. the base
     sampler (T=1.0), with a crossover at small k -- the pass@k inversion;
  3. majority voting beats single-sample accuracy when the correct answer is modal
     (a plurality) but has per-sample probability < 1/2;
  4. at n=16: verifier-guided selection == empirical pass@16, and best-of-n under a
     NOISY reranker lands strictly between pass@1 and pass@16.
"""
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
M, C = 200, 10          # problems, candidate answers per problem
N_SAMP = 256            # samples per problem for empirical estimates
K_MAX = 64

def softmax_T(z, T):
    """Temperature softmax, numerically stable (Ch. 5)."""
    a = z / T
    a = a - a.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(a)
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def make_problems():
    """(a*b+c) mod m instances, candidate answer values, per-problem logits.

    70% of problems are 'aligned': the argmax-logit candidate is the true answer.
    30% are 'misaligned': a distractor is the mode; the truth sits mid-distribution.
    This is the only structural knob -- everything downstream is measured.
    """
    a = rng.integers(2, 50, M); b = rng.integers(2, 50, M)
    c = rng.integers(0, 50, M); m = rng.integers(51, 400, M)
    truth = (a * b + c) % m
    cands = np.empty((M, C), dtype=np.int64)
    logits = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, (M, C))
    aligned = rng.random(M) < 0.7
    for i in range(M):
        # candidate 0 is the truth; distractors are plausible wrong residues
        pool = {int(truth[i])}
        row = [int(truth[i])]
        for v in [(a[i]*b[i]-c[i]) % m[i], (a[i]+b[i]*c[i]) % m[i], (a[i]*b[i]) % m[i]]:
            v = int(v)
            if v not in pool:
                row.append(v); pool.add(v)
        while len(row) < C:                      # fill with distinct random residues
            v = int(rng.integers(0, m[i]))
            if v not in pool:
                row.append(v); pool.add(v)
        cands[i] = row
        top = logits[i].max()
        if aligned[i]:   # truth gets the argmax logit by a clear margin
            logits[i, 0] = top + rng.uniform(0.3, 1.2)
        else:            # a distractor gets the argmax; truth stays unboosted
            j = int(rng.integers(1, C))
            logits[i, j] = top + rng.uniform(0.3, 1.2)
    return a, b, c, m, truth, cands, logits, aligned

def verify(a, b, c, m, y):
    """The exact verifier: closed-form check, no learned component."""
    return (a * b + c) % m == y

def sample_answers(logits, cands, T, n):
    """Draw n candidate-answer VALUES per problem from softmax(logits/T)."""
    P = softmax_T(logits, T)
    cum = P.cumsum(axis=1)
    idx = (rng.random((M, n, 1)) < cum[:, None, :]).argmax(axis=2)
    return np.take_along_axis(cands, idx.reshape(M, -1), axis=1).reshape(M, n), idx

def pass_at_k_unbiased(correct_counts, n, ks):
    """Chen et al. (2021): pass@k = 1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k), averaged over problems.
    Computed as a running product to avoid factorial overflow."""
    out = []
    for k in ks:
        frac = np.ones(M)
        for j in range(k):                       # prod (n-c-j)/(n-j)
            frac *= np.clip(n - correct_counts - j, 0, None) / (n - j)
        out.append(np.mean(1.0 - frac))
    return np.array(out)

def run():
    a, b, c, m, truth, cands, logits, aligned = make_problems()
    ks = np.arange(1, K_MAX + 1)
    curves = {}
    for name, T in [("base  T=1.00", 1.0), ("sharp T=0.25", 0.25)]:
        P = softmax_T(logits, T)
        p_i = P[:, 0]                            # analytic per-draw correctness prob
        analytic = np.array([np.mean(1 - (1 - p_i) ** k) for k in ks])
        ans, _ = sample_answers(logits, cands, T, N_SAMP)
        ok = verify(a[:, None], b[:, None], c[:, None], m[:, None], ans)
        empirical = pass_at_k_unbiased(ok.sum(axis=1), N_SAMP, ks)
        resid = np.abs(analytic - empirical).max()
        curves[name] = (analytic, empirical, ok, p_i)
        print(f"[{name}] pass@1={analytic[0]:.4f}  pass@64={analytic[-1]:.4f}  "
              f"max|analytic-empirical| over k=1..64: {resid:.4f}")
        assert resid < 0.03, "unbiased estimator should match closed form"
    base_a, base_e = curves["base  T=1.00"][0], curves["base  T=1.00"][1]
    shrp_a, shrp_e = curves["sharp T=0.25"][0], curves["sharp T=0.25"][1]

    print("\n   k   base(analytic)  sharp(analytic)  base(empirical)  sharp(empirical)")
    for k in [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64]:
        print(f"  {k:3d}   {base_a[k-1]:14.4f}  {shrp_a[k-1]:15.4f}"
              f"  {base_e[k-1]:15.4f}  {shrp_e[k-1]:16.4f}")

    # --- THE CENTRAL ASSERTION: pass@k inversion under sharpening ---------------
    assert shrp_a[0] > base_a[0] and shrp_e[0] > base_e[0], "sharpening must raise pass@1"
    assert shrp_a[-1] < base_a[-1] and shrp_e[-1] < base_e[-1], "and strictly lower pass@64"
    k_star = int(np.argmax(base_a > shrp_a)) + 1   # first k where base overtakes
    assert 1 < k_star <= K_MAX
    print(f"\nCROSSOVER: sharpened wins pass@k for k<{k_star}, base wins for k>={k_star} "
          f"(analytic; empirical crossover at k={int(np.argmax(base_e > shrp_e)) + 1})")
    p_mis = curves['sharp T=0.25'][3][~aligned]
    print(f"sharpened per-draw P(correct) on misaligned problems: "
          f"mean {p_mis.mean():.4f} (base: {curves['base  T=1.00'][3][~aligned].mean():.4f})"
          f" -- coverage lost, never recoverable by more samples")

    # --- majority voting: correct answer modal but not majority per draw --------
    # Construct distributions with P(correct)~0.35 and 6+ wrong answers splitting
    # the rest: the truth is the PLURALITY answer but loses to 'any wrong answer'.
    p_true = rng.uniform(0.30, 0.40, M)
    maj_logits = np.log(np.column_stack(
        [p_true] + [(1 - p_true) / (C - 1)] * (C - 1)) + 1e-12)
    ans, _ = sample_answers(maj_logits, cands, 1.0, 33)
    ok = verify(a[:, None], b[:, None], c[:, None], m[:, None], ans)
    single = ok.mean()                            # pass@1 for this sampler
    voted = np.array([np.bincount(row).argmax() for row in ans])  # plurality answer
    maj = verify(a, b, c, m, voted).mean()
    print(f"\n[majority] per-sample accuracy {single:.4f} -> majority@33 {maj:.4f}")
    assert maj > single + 0.2, "plurality-but-not-majority truth: voting must win big"

    # --- selection strategies at n=16 on the base sampler -----------------------
    n = 16
    ans, idx = sample_answers(logits, cands, 1.0, n)
    ok = verify(a[:, None], b[:, None], c[:, None], m[:, None], ans)
    verifier_sel = ok.any(axis=1).mean()          # exact verifier: any hit counts
    scores = np.take_along_axis(logits, idx, axis=1) + rng.normal(0, 1.5, (M, n))
    best_of_n = ok[np.arange(M), scores.argmax(axis=1)].mean()  # noisy reranker
    voted = np.array([np.bincount(row).argmax() for row in ans])
    maj16 = verify(a, b, c, m, voted).mean()
    p1 = ok[:, 0].mean()
    print(f"[n=16, base sampler] pass@1 {p1:.4f} | majority {maj16:.4f} | "
          f"noisy best-of-16 {best_of_n:.4f} | verifier-guided {verifier_sel:.4f}")
    assert p1 < best_of_n < verifier_sel, "reranker sits between single-draw and oracle"

    # --- cross-check our softmax against scipy (optional dependency) ------------
    try:
        from scipy.special import softmax as sp_softmax
        d = np.abs(softmax_T(logits, 0.25) - sp_softmax(logits / 0.25, axis=1)).max()
        print(f"[cross-check] max|ours - scipy.softmax| = {d:.2e}")
        assert d < 1e-12
    except ImportError:
        print("[skipped: scipy not installed]")
    print("\nAll assertions passed.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Running it prints the two curves and the inversion. The base sampler ($T{=}1$) measures pass@1 $=0.3069$ rising to pass@64 $=0.9393$; the sharpened sampler ($T{=}0.25$) measures pass@1 $=0.6343$ but pass@64 only $0.7324$, with the analytic crossover at $k{=}5$ (empirical also $k{=}5$) and the unbiased estimator matching the closed form to a maximum residual of $0.0036$ over all $k\in[1,64]$. The mechanism is printed explicitly: on the 30% of problems whose mode is wrong, sharpening crushes mean per-draw correctness from $0.0574$ to $0.0072$ — coverage no sample budget recovers. Majority voting lifts a $0.3612$ per-sample sampler to $0.9850$ at 33 votes; at $n{=}16$ the selection ladder reads pass@1 $0.3550$ < noisy best-of-16 $0.5150$ < verifier-guided $0.8400$. Total runtime is about $0.3$ s on CPU.

Key Takeaways
  • Chain-of-thought is conditional computation: without intermediate tokens a fixed-depth transformer sits in $\mathsf{TC}^0$; polynomially many thinking tokens lift it to $\mathsf{P}$ by letting the context serve as a Turing-machine tape. Expressivity, not learnability, is what the theorem guarantees. Certain
  • Pass@$k$ $= \mathbb{E}_i[1-(1-p_i)^k]$ measures coverage of the sampler's support, not single-attempt capability; estimate it with the unbiased combinatorial estimator, never the plug-in. Certain
  • Sharpening a distribution — by temperature or by RLVR — raises pass@1 while lowering pass@$k$ at large $k$ whenever some problems have a wrong mode; the reported base-model-overtakes-RLVR-model inversions are this concavity effect, and standard-recipe RLVR is best read as elicitation, not capability creation. Likely
  • Whether prolonged, diverse-task RL escapes the base model's support (ProRL-style claims) versus merely sharpening it is unresolved; large-$k$ pass@$k$ against the same base checkpoint under strict contamination control is the deciding experiment. Contested
  • Parallel and sequential scaling at equal FLOPs differ in latency, KV-cache footprint, and reach: parallel extracts what the sampler can already emit and needs a verifier or a modal signal; only sequential compute adds serial depth — and only with a sound verifier does any of it convert compute to accuracy. Certain
Chapter 29

Evaluation and the Measurement Crisis

Learning Objectives
  • Implement the three standard multiple-choice scoring protocols — letter log-probability, length-normalized continuation log-probability, and unnormalized continuation log-probability — and demonstrate that they produce different model rankings on identical items.
  • Explain the main families of contamination detection and estimate the contamination rate of a corpus with planted memorized items using a Min-K%-style statistic.
  • Explain the argument that emergent abilities are substantially a metric artifact, and state precisely what the argument does and does not refute.
  • Quantify the named biases of using a language model as a judge — position, verbosity, self-preference, format — and design a pairwise-comparison protocol that controls for each.
  • Implement a multi-protocol evaluation harness with a contamination detector and an emergence simulator in working code.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 for the practitioner's view of evaluation inside a from-scratch language-modeling pipeline, and Chakraborty, Introduction to Large Language Models, for the NLP-side treatment of benchmarks and their history. The primary sources here are papers, and this chapter names them inline.

Chapter 24 measured models by held-out loss, a quantity with a clean definition and sub-percent reproducibility. This chapter is about what happens when we instead measure capabilities: accuracy on question sets, win rates judged by other models, leaderboard positions. The claims of Chapters 26–28 — that fine-tuning, preference optimization, and test-time compute improve models — are all mediated by these measurements, and the measurements are in far worse shape than the training machinery that produces them. The central thesis: most published comparisons do not measure what they claim. The scoring rule reorders leaderboards on identical predictions; contamination is pervasive and the detectors for it are weak; and the famous "emergence" curves are substantially manufactured by discontinuous metrics. None of this is hypothetical — Artifact 29.1 reproduces all three failures from scratch in NumPy. Chapter 36 extends the problem to agent benchmarks, where it is worse.

29.1 What a Benchmark Number Is

The sentence "model $X$ scores 71.3 on benchmark $Y$" reads like a property of $X$. It is not. It is a property of a five-tuple, and changing any coordinate changes the number.

Definition 29.1 (Evaluation protocol)

An evaluation protocol is a tuple $(\mathcal{D}, \pi, s, g, a)$: an item set $\mathcal{D}$, a prompt template $\pi$ mapping each item to model input (including few-shot exemplars, instructions, and chat formatting), a scoring rule $s$ mapping model output — either sampled text or the model's log-probabilities — to a per-item score, generation settings $g$ (temperature, max tokens, stop sequences) where sampling is involved, and an aggregation $a$ (usually the mean, sometimes pass@$k$ or a rating-model fit). A benchmark number is $a(\{s(\cdot)\})$ evaluated under one specific choice of all five. A benchmark name, like "MMLU," pins down only $\mathcal{D}$.

The crisis is that papers report the name and the number while varying $\pi$, $s$, and $g$ silently. Two papers reporting "MMLU accuracy" may share nothing but $\mathcal{D}$ — different few-shot counts, different templates, different scoring rules, different tokenizations of the same template. Comparisons across such numbers are comparisons of protocols, not models. The rest of this chapter takes the coordinates in turn: $s$ in Section 29.2, $\pi$ in 29.3, the integrity of $\mathcal{D}$ in 29.4 and 29.7, and what happens when $s$ is itself a neural network in 29.6.

29.2 Scoring Protocols and Rank Instability

Multiple choice looks like the easy case — four options, one correct — yet the field uses at least three inequivalent scoring rules for it.

Letter log-probability. Present the question and the lettered options in the prompt; compare the model's next-token log-probabilities for the tokens "A", "B", "C", "D" in a single forward pass; predict the argmax. This is the original MMLU protocol. It tests knowledge and the ability to bind an answer to its letter — a format skill that instruction-tuned models have and many base models lack.

Continuation log-probability, unnormalized. Score each option by the summed log-probability of its full text as a continuation of the question, $\log P(\text{option}_j \mid \text{prompt}) = \sum_{t=1}^{L_j} \log P(x_t \mid \cdot)$; predict the argmax over $j$. Because every token contributes a typically negative term, longer options are penalized by roughly $|b| \cdot L_j$ nats, where $b$ is the model's typical per-token log-probability. This confounds correctness with option length and with the model's overall fluency.

Continuation log-probability, length-normalized. Divide the sum by the option's length before the argmax. The EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness reports both as acc and acc_norm, normalizing by byte length rather than token count so the number is comparable across tokenizers Verify. Normalization removes the length penalty and cancels any per-token constant, but averages away the fact that one decisive token can matter more than ten filler tokens.

In June 2023 the Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard was publicly caught in exactly this trap: the leaderboard's harness-based MMLU numbers for LLaMA models sat far below the paper's letter-based numbers — a double-digit gap — and the discrepancy reordered models, because three coexisting MMLU implementations (the original Berkeley code, HELM, and the EleutherAI harness) implement three different scoring rules on the same $\mathcal{D}$ Verify. The response that has become standard practice is OLMES (AI2, 2024): fix the template and exemplars exactly, evaluate both the letter form and the continuation form, and report under the form the model can actually use — separating "does not know" from "cannot bind letters" Likely.

Example 29.1 (One item, three winners)

One question, four options, correct answer C. Suppose a model assigns mean per-token log-probs and letter logits as follows:

OptionTokens $L_j$Mean log-probSumLetter logit
A4$-2.1$$-8.4$$+0.2$
B9$-1.8$$-16.2$$-0.1$
C (correct)7$-1.6$$-11.2$$+0.1$
D3$-2.4$$-7.2$$-0.5$

Length-normalized scoring picks C ($-1.6$ is the largest mean): correct. Unnormalized scoring picks D ($-7.2$ is the largest sum, purely because D's total penalty $3 \times 2.4 = 7.2$ nats is smaller than C's $7 \times 1.6 = 11.2$): the shortest option wins. Letter scoring picks A ($+0.2$): the model knows the content (it scored C's text highest per token) but binds the letter wrong. Same model, same knowledge, three different verdicts.

Artifact 29.1 scales this up: three simulated models — an instruction-tuned letter-binder, a strong base model, and a fluent mediocrity — on 800 shared items. Measured accuracies: Model-A scores 0.930 / 0.388 / 0.180 under letter / normalized / unnormalized scoring; Model-B scores 0.356 / 0.681 / 0.278; Model-C scores 0.693 / 0.464 / 0.290. Each protocol crowns a different winner. Rank agreement between two protocols is summarized by Kendall's $\tau$: over all $\binom{m}{2}$ model pairs, the fraction of concordantly ordered pairs minus the fraction of discordantly ordered ones, so $\tau = 1$ means identical rankings. The measured values are $\tau = -1.000$ (letter vs. normalized), $-0.333$ (letter vs. unnormalized), $+0.333$ (normalized vs. unnormalized) — every pairwise $\tau$ strictly below 1, and one pair of protocols produces exactly opposite leaderboards on identical log-probabilities.

29.3 Few-Shot, Prompt Sensitivity, and Format Effects

The template $\pi$ is the second silent coordinate. Semantically null formatting choices — whether options are separated by newlines or spaces, whether the answer cue is "Answer:" or "The answer is", casing of the letters — move accuracy by amounts that dwarf claimed model differences; Sclar et al. (2023) measured spreads of tens of points across formatting variants of the same task, with model rankings flipping between formats Verify. Three further effects are well replicated. Choice-order bias: models place excess probability on particular positions (often A, or the last-presented option), so accuracy shifts when correct answers are shuffled; the control is to permute options and average, or report the full permutation matrix. Few-shot count and exemplar identity: $k$-shot results depend on $k$ and on which $k$ exemplars are chosen, which is why OLMES-style standards fix the exemplars verbatim. Chat-template mismatch: evaluating an instruction-tuned model without its chat template, or a base model with one, changes the effective task; both mistakes appear in print.

Common Pitfall

The letter-scoring whitespace bug. Under BPE (Chapter 23), "A" preceded by a space is a different token from "A" at the start of a string: " A" and "A" have different ids. A harness that reads the logit for token "A" while the template ends with "Answer:" (no trailing space, so the model's natural continuation is " A") scores the wrong vocabulary entry for every item. The failure is silent — the four wrong tokens still yield an argmax, typically near chance (25%), and near-chance results on hard benchmarks look plausible. Diagnose by printing the actual top-10 next tokens for a handful of prompts before trusting any letter-based number; the correct letters should dominate the mass.

29.4 Contamination: Detection and Prevalence

Definition 29.2 (Contamination)

A test item is contaminated for model $\theta$ if the item, its near-duplicate, or its (question, answer) pair appeared in $\theta$'s training corpus. Contamination inflates the measured score without the capability the benchmark claims to measure; the score becomes partially a retrieval measurement.

Detection methods fall into three families. Corpus-side matching, available only to whoever holds the training data: exact or fuzzy $n$-gram overlap between test items and training documents (GPT-3's report used 13-gram overlap; later reports used substring matching with windows on the order of 50 characters Verify), plus embedding-based near-duplicate search to catch paraphrases that $n$-grams miss. Behavioral probes, available to anyone: ask the model to complete a benchmark item verbatim from its prefix, or to reproduce the option ordering; or compare performance on original items against freshly rewritten equivalents. The sharpest result in the second style is GSM1k (2024), a from-scratch clone of GSM8K matched for difficulty: several model families dropped accuracy by double digits — up to roughly 13 points — on the clone, direct evidence that their GSM8K scores were partly memorization Verify.

Membership inference is the third family: decide from the model's own log-probabilities whether a specific text was in training. The Min-K% statistic (Shi et al., 2023) is the standard baseline. For a text of $T$ tokens with per-token log-probabilities $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_T$, let $\mathrm{MinK}(x) = \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{t \in S} \ell_t$ where $S$ is the $\lfloor kT/100 \rfloor$ tokens with the lowest log-probability. The logic: natural unseen text contains genuinely surprising tokens — rare names, numbers, odd phrasings — that even a strong model assigns low probability; memorized text has had its surprisal tail trained away. A high Min-K% score flags membership. Min-K%++ refines this by normalizing each token's score against the model's own predictive distribution, testing whether training data sits at local maxima of the model's probability landscape Likely.

Artifact 29.1 implements the detector on a corpus of 400 simulated documents, 100 of them planted as memorized (their surprisal tail removed) and every document carrying a random difficulty offset, since some text is simply harder. Measured: Min-20% achieves AUC 0.997, comfortably above the asserted 0.90 threshold. The same run shows why naive detection fails: mean log-probability over all tokens — the obvious statistic — achieves AUC 0.575, barely above chance, because the per-document difficulty offset swamps the membership signal. That confound is exactly what the empirical literature reports on real models: on realistic deduplicated pretraining corpora, membership-inference attacks including Min-K% variants score near chance (AUCs in the 0.5–0.6 range), because "membership" is fuzzy at web scale — near-duplicates of most text exist in any crawl — and because difficulty is uncontrolled Likely; a 2025 clinical-domain audit measured Min-K% at AUC $\approx$ 0.51 and Min-K%++ at $\approx$ 0.55 Verify. The honest summary: contamination is easy to plant, easy to detect in the planted setting, and genuinely hard to detect in the wild — which is why Section 29.7's structural defenses matter more than post-hoc forensics. Every measured contamination rate is a lower bound; absence of detection is weak evidence of absence.

29.5 Emergent Abilities: Claim, Rebuttal, Current Status

The claim (Wei et al., 2022): some abilities are emergent — absent in small models, present in large ones, with a sharp, unpredictable transition; performance sits at chance across orders of magnitude of scale and then jumps. The rebuttal (Schaeffer, Miranda, Koyejo, NeurIPS 2023): the sharpness is manufactured by the metric. The model's underlying competence — per-token log-likelihood or per-token accuracy — improves smoothly with scale (Chapter 24); exact-match on a multi-token answer is a discontinuous, all-or-nothing function of that competence, and composing a smooth curve with it produces a spike. Replotting the same models under continuous metrics (token edit distance, Brier score, log-likelihood) made most published emergence curves smooth.

Theorem 29.1 (Metric-induced sharpening)

Let per-token accuracy $p(s) \in [0,1]$ be differentiable and nondecreasing in log-scale $s$ with $p'(s) \le \varepsilon$, and let the reported metric be exact match on a $T$-token answer with independent per-token errors, $\mathrm{EM}(s) = p(s)^T$. Then:

(i) $\mathrm{EM}'(s) = T\,p(s)^{T-1} p'(s)$: the metric's slope is the underlying slope times $T p^{T-1}$, a factor that is below 1 for $p < T^{-1/(T-1)}$ (the metric is flatter than the capability there, which is what hides it) and rises to $T$ as $p \to 1$: a $T$-fold sharpening is available from a bounded-slope underlying curve.

(ii) $\mathrm{EM}(s) < \delta$ whenever $p(s) < \delta^{1/T}$. Since $\delta^{1/T} \to 1$ as $T \to \infty$, the metric reads "no ability" until per-token competence is already high: for $T = 12$ and $\delta = 0.05$, exact match stays below 5% until $p$ exceeds $0.05^{1/12} \approx 0.779$.

Proof. (i) is the chain rule applied to $p \mapsto p^T$; the factor $T p^{T-1}$ is increasing in $p$ with supremum $T$ on $[0,1]$. (ii): $p < \delta^{1/T}$ and monotonicity of $p \mapsto p^T$ give $p^T < \delta$; the limit follows from $\delta^{1/T} = e^{(\ln \delta)/T} \to 1$. $\blacksquare$

Artifact 29.1 instantiates this with the smoothest possible capability curve: per-token accuracy rising linearly from 0.25 to 0.99 across 25 scale points, constant increments of 0.031 per step. Exact match over a 12-token answer jumps by 0.280 in a single step (0.283 as measured by Monte Carlo over 2,000 items per scale point) — a 9.1× amplification of the underlying increment — and reads below 5% ("no ability") over 72% of the scale grid before taking off. Nothing emerged; the metric did.

What the rebuttal establishes is routinely overstated. It refutes the inference from a sharp benchmark curve to a discontinuity in the model — the sharpness of most headline emergence plots is a property of $s$, the scoring rule, not of $\theta$. It does not refute three things. First, unpredictability: knowing that a smooth per-token curve underlies the jump does not tell you, in advance, where the exact-match takeoff lands for a given task, because that requires knowing $p(s)$ and the effective $T$ — quantities we typically cannot measure until we are near the transition. Forecasting downstream capability from small-model measurements remains an open, partially-solved problem (finetuning-based probes can predict some emergence points; Snell et al., 2024) Likely. Second, universality of smoothness: subsequent work has documented transitions that stay sharp under continuous metrics, including capabilities that appear abruptly during training, and 2025–26 results showing that at fixed scale, whether a capability emerges at all can vary randomly across initialization seeds Verify. Third, deployment relevance: users and downstream systems experience the discontinuous metric — a 12-token answer is either right or wrong — so threshold-crossings in EM are real events even when the mechanism is smooth.

Contested Position taken here: discontinuous metrics manufacture sharp curves from smooth improvement, and this accounts for most of the canonical 2022-era emergence plots; but the mirage argument refutes sharpness, not unpredictability, and treating it as a blanket debunking of emergence is as wrong as the original breathless framing. What would change this position: in one direction, a demonstrated pipeline that pre-registers accurate forecasts of downstream capability takeoffs from small-model measurements across diverse tasks (emergence fully reduced to measurement); in the other, replicated examples of capabilities that remain discontinuous in per-token log-likelihood itself at scale (emergence rehabilitated as a property of $\theta$). The seed-randomness results push toward the second.

29.6 Judge Models and Arena-Style Ranking

Open-ended generation has no exact match, so the field scores it with a stronger model as judge — pointwise ratings or pairwise "which response is better?" verdicts — and aggregates pairwise human votes in arenas. Judge scores correlate with human preference well enough to be useful (the MT-Bench study reported GPT-4–human agreement above 80%, comparable to human–human agreement Verify) and are biased in at least four named, measurable ways.

BiasWhat it isHow to measure itControl
PositionVerdict depends on presentation order; first slot typically favoredSwap test: fraction of verdicts that flip when A/B order is reversedJudge both orders; average, or count only order-consistent verdicts
VerbosityLonger answers preferred at equal qualityRegress win rate on length difference; inject padded variantsLength-controlled scoring: report the win-rate residual at zero length difference (as in length-controlled AlpacaEval)
Self-preferenceJudge favors outputs from its own model family, linked to recognizing its own styleCompare judge's rating of own vs. matched other-family outputs against human labelsCross-family judge panels; never let a model family judge a comparison it competes in
Format/styleMarkdown, headers, confident tone, lists preferred over plain correct proseRate style-normalized rewrites of identical contentStyle-stripping or style-controlled regression; rubric anchored to content

A defensible judging protocol therefore: randomize and swap both orders; use judges from a family not under evaluation, or a panel; control for length in the aggregate statistic rather than the prompt (instruction-only mitigation is weak); anchor a random subsample against human labels and report that agreement alongside the win rates Likely.

Definition 29.3 (Bradley–Terry ranking)

Given pairwise outcomes, assign each model $i$ a latent strength $\theta_i$ with $P(i \text{ beats } j) = \sigma(\theta_i - \theta_j)$, and fit $\theta$ by maximum likelihood on the observed votes. Arena leaderboards are (regularized) Bradley–Terry fits; classical Elo is an online approximation to the same model. Ratings are identified only up to a constant, and a rating difference of $\Delta$ predicts a win rate of $\sigma(\Delta)$.

Arenas add human voters but inherit every confound that shapes votes — style and verbosity above all — plus governance problems. "The Leaderboard Illusion" (2025) documented that large providers privately tested many variants on Chatbot Arena and published only the best (reportedly up to 27 variants of one model release), and that data access was concentrated among a few labs; LMArena disputed the characterization and several specific figures while adopting some reforms Verify. The methodological lesson stands regardless of who is right: best-of-$k$ private variant selection inflates a leaderboard entry by roughly the expected maximum of $k$ noisy draws, so a leaderboard that permits it measures selection pressure along with capability. Style-controlled arena rankings, which regress out length and formatting before the Bradley–Terry fit, move models by meaningful amounts — further evidence that raw win rate mixes style with substance Likely.

29.7 Held-Out and Dynamic Benchmarks

The classic public benchmarks are spent: MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval are saturated at the frontier — top-model differences sit inside noise — and have circulated in web crawls for years, so fresh models cannot be assumed clean on them. The current generation defends $\mathcal{D}$ structurally rather than forensically Verify:

Private holdouts. Humanity's Last Exam publishes 2,500 expert questions but maintains a never-crawled private holdout used to detect overfitting to the public set; FrontierMath keeps its research-level mathematics problems fully private, with scoring run by the maintainers; SWE-bench Pro pairs 731 public tasks with 858 held-out ones Verify. The cost: results are only as trustworthy as the holdout's operational security and the maintainer's independence — FrontierMath's funding relationship with a lab it evaluates drew exactly this criticism Verify. Rolling collection. LiveBench and LiveCodeBench harvest new items (recent competition problems, fresh articles) dated after each model's training cutoff, making contamination structurally impossible rather than merely undetected; the cost is that the item distribution drifts, so scores are comparable only within a collection window. Adversarial refresh. ARC-AGI-2-style benchmarks with semi-private evaluation sets are versioned upward as models close the gap. All three designs concede the same point: a static public test set's shelf life ends when the benchmark becomes worth training on — Goodhart's law applied to $\mathcal{D}$.

29.8 Building an Eval You Can Trust

The constructive summary, in the order you should implement it. (1) Pin the protocol: version-control the template, exemplars, tokenizer, scoring rule, and generation settings; a benchmark number without them is unreproducible by Definition 29.1. (2) Score under multiple rules and report the disagreement: run letter and continuation scoring both; report Kendall's $\tau$ between the induced rankings. If $\tau < 1$, say so — the disagreement is information about format sensitivity, not an inconvenience. (3) Report uncertainty: $n$ items give a binomial standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$; at $p = 0.5$ with $n = 800$ that is $1.8$ points, so a 95% interval spans $\pm 3.5$ points — wider than most claimed model gaps. Paired designs (both models on the same items, McNemar's test) shrink this substantially and should be the default for A/B claims. (4) Probe contamination behaviorally: prefix-completion probes on your own items, plus a small rewritten-clone set in the GSM1k style; treat Min-K%-family scores as supporting evidence, not verdicts, given their near-chance performance in the wild. (5) Plant canaries: unique strings in every published item so future corpus audits can find your benchmark in training data. (6) Hold something back: keep a private slice for measuring overfitting to the public slice, and plan the refresh before release. An evaluation built this way still measures a protocol — that is unavoidable — but it measures a declared protocol, with error bars: the standard most headline numbers fail.

Artifact 29.1 — The Measurement Crisis in Three Experiments

A pure-NumPy harness that reproduces the chapter's three central failures with simulated log-probabilities — no model is called. Part 1 scores three simulated models (a letter-fluent instruction-tuned model, a strong base model, a fluent mediocrity) on 800 shared four-option items under the three scoring protocols of Section 29.2, then computes pairwise Kendall $\tau$ between the induced rankings and asserts at least one is strictly below 1. Part 2 implements the Min-K% detector of Section 29.4 on 400 documents with 100 planted memorized items and per-document difficulty confounds, asserting AUC above 0.90 and that the tail statistic beats the naive mean. Part 3 instantiates Theorem 29.1: a linear per-token accuracy ramp pushed through 12-token exact match, asserting the underlying curve's increments stay below 0.04 while the metric jumps by more than 0.15 in one step. Kendall $\tau$ and AUC are implemented by hand and cross-checked against SciPy and scikit-learn where installed.

"""Artifact 29.1 -- The measurement crisis in three experiments (pure NumPy).

(1) Three standard multiple-choice scoring protocols applied to the SAME
    simulated models on the SAME items produce DIFFERENT rankings
    (Kendall tau strictly below 1).
(2) A Min-K%-style contamination detector separates planted memorized
    documents from clean ones (AUC above threshold), and beats naive
    mean-log-probability scoring.
(3) A SMOOTH per-token accuracy curve, viewed through exact-match over a
    multi-token answer, produces a sharp apparent "emergence" jump.

Log-probabilities are simulated; no model is called. Runs in seconds.
"""
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1: three scoring protocols, three models, one item set
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each item has 4 options; option j of item i is a token sequence of
# length L[i, j]. Correct options are drawn ~1.5 tokens longer on average
# (as in real benchmarks, where the right answer is often the wordiest).
N_ITEMS, N_OPT = 800, 4
L = rng.integers(3, 12, size=(N_ITEMS, N_OPT)).astype(float)
correct = rng.integers(0, N_OPT, size=N_ITEMS)
L[np.arange(N_ITEMS), correct] += rng.integers(0, 4, size=N_ITEMS)

# Model profiles: letter_skill (does the model map its knowledge onto the
# 'answer with A/B/C/D' format?), cont (per-token log-prob advantage it
# gives the correct option text), base (its typical per-token log-prob,
# i.e. fluency). base CANCELS across options under length normalization
# but NOT under raw summation, where every extra token costs |base| nats:
# unnormalized scoring confounds fluency with correctness.
# A: instruction-tuned, letter-fluent, mediocre judge of option text.
# B: strong base model: best per-token judgment, letter-clumsy.
# C: middling judge but very fluent (high base), letter-mediocre.
MODELS = {
    "Model-A": dict(letter=0.85, cont=0.22, base=-3.0),
    "Model-B": dict(letter=0.15, cont=0.55, base=-2.6),
    "Model-C": dict(letter=0.45, cont=0.30, base=-1.2),
}

def score_protocols(p):
    """Return accuracy under (letter, length-normalized, unnormalized)."""
    # Letter protocol: logit over the 4 letter tokens; correct letter gets
    # a boost of size `letter`, all letters get unit Gaussian noise.
    lg = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(N_ITEMS, N_OPT))
    lg[np.arange(N_ITEMS), correct] += p["letter"] * 3.0
    acc_letter = np.mean(np.argmax(lg, axis=1) == correct)
    # Continuation protocols: mean per-token log-prob of option j is
    # base + cont*[j correct] + noise shrinking with length.
    mu = p["base"] + rng.normal(0, 1.0, size=L.shape) / np.sqrt(L)
    mu[np.arange(N_ITEMS), correct] += p["cont"]
    total = mu * L                      # summed (unnormalized) log-prob
    acc_norm = np.mean(np.argmax(mu, axis=1) == correct)     # per-token mean
    acc_unnorm = np.mean(np.argmax(total, axis=1) == correct)
    return np.array([acc_letter, acc_norm, acc_unnorm])

acc = np.stack([score_protocols(p) for p in MODELS.values()])  # (3 models, 3 protos)
PROTOS = ["letter log-prob", "length-normalized", "unnormalized sum"]

def kendall_tau(a, b):
    """Kendall tau-a between two score vectors (rank by descending score)."""
    n = len(a); s = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            s += np.sign(a[i] - a[j]) * np.sign(b[i] - b[j])
    return s / (n * (n - 1) / 2)

print("=== Part 1: protocol choice reorders the leaderboard ===")
for m, name in enumerate(MODELS):
    print(f"  {name}:  " + "  ".join(f"{p}={acc[m, k]:.3f}" for k, p in
                                     zip(range(3), PROTOS)))
taus = {}
for k1 in range(3):
    for k2 in range(k1 + 1, 3):
        t = kendall_tau(acc[:, k1], acc[:, k2])
        taus[(PROTOS[k1], PROTOS[k2])] = t
        print(f"  Kendall tau ({PROTOS[k1]} vs {PROTOS[k2]}) = {t:+.3f}")
min_tau = min(taus.values())
assert min_tau < 1.0, "rankings agree everywhere; construction failed"
# every protocol crowns a different winner in this construction:
winners = [list(MODELS)[np.argmax(acc[:, k])] for k in range(3)]
print(f"  winners per protocol: {winners}")
print(f"  min pairwise tau = {min_tau:+.3f}  (< 1: rankings disagree)  OK")

try:                                   # cross-check tau against scipy
    from scipy.stats import kendalltau
    ref = kendalltau(acc[:, 1], acc[:, 2]).statistic
    ours = taus[(PROTOS[1], PROTOS[2])]
    assert abs(ref - ours) < 1e-12
    print(f"  scipy cross-check: |tau_ours - tau_scipy| = {abs(ref-ours):.1e}")
except ImportError:
    print("  [skipped: scipy not installed]")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 2: Min-K%-style contamination detection
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Clean documents: mostly ordinary tokens, but ~15% genuinely surprising
# tokens (rare names, numbers) with very low log-prob. Memorized documents:
# the model has seen them, so the surprising tail is GONE -- every token,
# including the "hard" ones, gets comfortable log-prob. Every document
# also carries a difficulty offset delta (some text is just harder), which
# confounds the naive mean-log-prob detector but not the tail statistic.
# Min-K% scores a document by the mean of its bottom-k% token log-probs:
# memorized text has no bad tail, so its Min-K% score is anomalously high.
N_CLEAN, N_MEM, DOC_LEN, K_PCT = 300, 100, 300, 20

def sample_doc(memorized):
    delta = rng.normal(0, 0.45)         # per-document difficulty offset
    if memorized:
        return rng.normal(-3.1 + delta, 0.75, size=DOC_LEN)
    hard = rng.random(DOC_LEN) < 0.15
    lp = rng.normal(-2.6 + delta, 0.9, size=DOC_LEN)
    lp[hard] = rng.normal(-6.5 + delta, 1.2, size=hard.sum())
    return lp

docs = [sample_doc(False) for _ in range(N_CLEAN)] + \
       [sample_doc(True) for _ in range(N_MEM)]
labels = np.r_[np.zeros(N_CLEAN), np.ones(N_MEM)]

def min_k_score(lp, k_pct):
    k = max(1, int(len(lp) * k_pct / 100))
    return np.mean(np.sort(lp)[:k])     # mean of the k% LOWEST log-probs

def auc(scores, labels):
    """AUC via the rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) identity, ties averaged."""
    order = np.argsort(scores)
    ranks = np.empty(len(scores)); ranks[order] = np.arange(1, len(scores) + 1)
    n1, n0 = labels.sum(), (1 - labels).sum()
    return (ranks[labels == 1].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)

mink = np.array([min_k_score(d, K_PCT) for d in docs])
meanlp = np.array([d.mean() for d in docs])
auc_mink, auc_mean = auc(mink, labels), auc(meanlp, labels)
print("\n=== Part 2: Min-K% contamination detector ===")
print(f"  planted rate: {N_MEM}/{N_CLEAN + N_MEM} = {N_MEM/(N_CLEAN+N_MEM):.3f}")
print(f"  AUC, Min-{K_PCT}% score      = {auc_mink:.3f}")
print(f"  AUC, mean log-prob (naive) = {auc_mean:.3f}")
assert auc_mink > 0.90, f"Min-K% AUC {auc_mink:.3f} below threshold 0.90"
assert auc_mink > auc_mean, "tail statistic should beat the naive mean here"
print(f"  Min-K% AUC > 0.90 threshold and beats naive mean  OK")

try:                                   # cross-check AUC against sklearn
    from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
    ref = roc_auc_score(labels, mink)
    assert abs(ref - auc_mink) < 1e-12
    print(f"  sklearn cross-check: |AUC_ours - AUC_sklearn| = {abs(ref-auc_mink):.1e}")
except ImportError:
    print("  [skipped: sklearn not installed]")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 3: emergence as a metric artifact
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Underlying capability: per-token accuracy p(s) improves LINEARLY in
# normalized log-compute s -- maximally smooth, constant slope, nothing
# emergent about it. Reported metric: exact match on a T-token answer,
# i.e. all T tokens correct => EM(s) = p(s)^T under independence. We
# also estimate EM empirically by Monte Carlo over N_EVAL items.
T_ANS, N_EVAL = 12, 2000
s = np.linspace(0, 1, 25)                       # normalized log-compute grid
p = np.linspace(0.25, 0.99, 25)                 # smooth: constant increments
em_exact = p ** T_ANS
em_mc = np.array([np.mean(np.all(rng.random((N_EVAL, T_ANS)) < pi, axis=1))
                  for pi in p])

d_p = np.max(np.abs(np.diff(p)))                # largest per-step jump
d_em = np.max(np.abs(np.diff(em_exact)))
d_em_mc = np.max(np.abs(np.diff(em_mc)))
amp_bound = T_ANS * np.max(p[1:] ** (T_ANS - 1) * np.abs(np.diff(p)))
print("\n=== Part 3: smooth curve + exact match = apparent emergence ===")
print(f"  per-token curve:  max per-step jump = {d_p:.4f}  (smooth)")
print(f"  exact-match (T={T_ANS}): max per-step jump = {d_em:.4f} "
      f"({d_em/d_p:.1f}x amplification)")
print(f"  Monte-Carlo EM ({N_EVAL} items):  max per-step jump = {d_em_mc:.4f}")
print(f"  chain-rule bound T*p^(T-1)*dp accounts for it: {amp_bound:.4f} >= {d_em:.4f}")
# EM is negligible until p is already large: EM < 0.05 requires p < 0.05^(1/T)
p_thresh = 0.05 ** (1 / T_ANS)
frac_hidden = np.mean(em_exact < 0.05)
print(f"  EM stays < 0.05 until per-token p exceeds {p_thresh:.3f}; "
      f"{frac_hidden:.0%} of the grid looks like 'no ability'")
assert d_p < 0.04, "underlying curve is not smooth; construction failed"
assert d_em > 0.15 and d_em_mc > 0.15, "metric curve failed to jump"
assert d_em > 4 * d_p, "metric jump should dwarf the underlying increments"
assert amp_bound >= d_em - 1e-9
print("  underlying smooth (jump < 0.04), metric sharp (jump > 0.15, "
      "> 4x underlying)  OK")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("\nAll assertions passed: same models + same items, different "
          "protocol => different leaderboard; memorized text is detectable "
          "from its missing surprisal tail; sharp 'emergence' can be "
          "manufactured from a smooth curve by the metric alone.")

Running it prints three winners from three protocols with pairwise Kendall $\tau$ of $-1.000$, $-0.333$, and $+0.333$ (hand-rolled $\tau$ matching SciPy to $5.6 \times 10^{-17}$); Min-20% AUC $= 0.997$ against $0.575$ for naive mean log-probability, the hand-rolled Min-K% AUC matching scikit-learn exactly (difference $0.0$); and a maximum per-step jump of 0.0308 in the underlying curve versus 0.2800 in exact match — 9.1× amplification, within the chain-rule bound 0.3313 of Theorem 29.1. All assertions pass in under one second on CPU.

Key Takeaways
  • A benchmark number is a property of the full protocol tuple — items, template, scoring rule, generation settings, aggregation — and comparisons that vary any coordinate silently are comparisons of protocols, not models. Certain
  • The three standard multiple-choice scoring rules produce different rankings on identical model outputs; Artifact 29.1 measures pairwise Kendall $\tau$ as low as $-1$ between protocols, and the historical MMLU implementation split reordered real leaderboards. Certain
  • Contamination is easy to demonstrate when planted (Min-20% AUC 0.997 in the artifact) but hard to detect in the wild, where membership-inference methods run near chance; structural defenses — private holdouts, rolling post-cutoff collection, canaries — beat forensics. Likely
  • Discontinuous metrics manufacture sharp "emergence" from smooth improvement — exact match over $T$ tokens sharpens slopes by up to $T\times$ and hides competence until $p > \delta^{1/T}$ — which refutes the sharpness of most canonical curves but not the unpredictability of capability takeoffs. Contested
  • Judge models carry named, measurable biases — position, verbosity, self-preference, format — each with a specific control (order swapping, length-controlled aggregation, cross-family panels, style regression), and a judging protocol that omits the controls is measuring style along with substance. Likely
Part VI

Systems and Efficiency

Above a billion parameters, machine learning is a systems discipline. This part builds the mental model that predicts runtime — arithmetic intensity and the memory wall — then derives FlashAttention as its consequence, then covers the four parallelisms, inference serving, and quantization. Every claim here is measured, because in systems the only acceptable evidence is a benchmark.
Chapter 30

The GPU Execution Model and the Memory Wall

Learning Objectives
  • Describe the GPU execution hierarchy — streaming multiprocessors, warps, tensor cores, and the register / shared-memory / L2 / HBM ladder — with the approximate bandwidth of each level.
  • Compute the arithmetic intensity of matmul, elementwise operations, softmax, normalization, and attention, and place each on a roofline.
  • Predict the wall-clock time of a transformer layer from first principles — $t = \max(\text{FLOPs}/\pi,\ \text{bytes}/\beta)$ — and validate the prediction against measurement.
  • Explain kernel fusion and quantify what fusing a chain of $k$ elementwise operations saves.
  • Implement an empirical roofline analyzer in working code.
Read alongside — The HuggingFace Ultra-Scale Playbook is the practitioner's companion for all of Part VI: it works the same bandwidth arithmetic on real training clusters. Stanford CS336 (Language Modeling from Scratch) covers rooflines, kernels, and profiling in its systems lectures, with assignments that measure what this chapter derives.

Every cost model so far in this book has been denominated in FLOPs: the $C \approx 6ND$ of Chapter 24, the per-layer counts of Chapter 18, the optimizer overheads of Chapter 13. That currency is only convertible to wall-clock time when arithmetic is the binding constraint, and on a modern accelerator it almost never is. An H100 can execute roughly 295 bf16 FLOPs in the time it takes to move one byte to or from its own memory Verify; any operation performing fewer FLOPs per byte — which is every common deep-learning operation except large matrix multiplication — is limited by bandwidth, not arithmetic. This chapter builds the execution model and the roofline framework that make such statements precise, derives the arithmetic intensity of the transformer's constituent operations, and validates the method empirically. Chapters 31–34 are applications: FlashAttention, distributed training, inference serving, and quantization are all, at bottom, campaigns against the memory wall.

30.1 GPU Architecture for ML Engineers

A GPU is not a fast CPU; it is a different answer to the question of what to do with a fixed transistor and power budget. A CPU spends its budget making a few instruction streams fast: deep caches, branch prediction, out-of-order execution. A GPU spends it on arithmetic units and hides latency with parallelism instead of avoiding it with caches. The programming model reflects this. A kernel is launched as a grid of thread blocks; each block is assigned to one streaming multiprocessor (SM) and stays there until it finishes. An H100 SXM has 132 SMs Verify, each containing 128 FP32 ALUs, four schedulers, and four fourth-generation tensor cores.

30.1.1 Warps and SIMT

Within a block, threads are grouped into warps of 32 that execute in lockstep: one instruction, 32 data lanes (SIMT — single instruction, multiple threads). A warp is the true unit of execution and of memory access; when its 32 threads touch 32 consecutive 4-byte words, the hardware coalesces them into one wide transaction, and when they do not, bandwidth is wasted on unused bytes. Divergent branches within a warp serialize: both sides execute, with lanes masked off. Each SM scheduler holds many resident warps and issues from whichever is ready, so a warp stalled on a ~500-cycle HBM load Likely costs nothing if another warp can issue — latency is hidden, not eliminated. This only works if enough warps are resident, which is the occupancy question of Section 30.5.

30.1.2 Tensor cores: the 15× asymmetry

Tensor cores are systolic units that execute small matrix multiply-accumulates as single warp-level instructions. They are the only reason the headline numbers exist: the H100's bf16 tensor-core peak is 989 TFLOP/s dense, while its conventional FP32 vector ALUs peak near 67 TFLOP/s Verify — a factor of ~15. (Vendor marketing quotes 1,979 TFLOP/s, which assumes 2:4 structured sparsity; use dense numbers unless your weights are actually sparse.) The asymmetry has a hard consequence: only operations expressible as dense matrix multiplication can use the fast path. Softmax, normalization, activations, and optimizer updates run on the slow vector units — and, as we will see, they don't even saturate those, because they starve on bandwidth first.

30.2 The Memory Hierarchy and Its Bandwidths

The numbers that govern everything are the bandwidths of the memory ladder. Capacities shrink and bandwidths grow roughly an order of magnitude per level as you climb toward the ALUs.

Level (H100 SXM)CapacityBandwidthScope
Registers256 KB/SM (~33 MB total)~100s of TB/s aggregate Likelyper thread
Shared memory / L1up to 228 KB/SM Verify~30 TB/s aggregate Likelyper block
L2 cache50 MB Verify~5–10 TB/s (measured) Likelydevice
HBM380 GB3.35 TB/s Verifydevice
NVLink 4 (to peers)—900 GB/s Verifynode
PCIe Gen5 (to host)—~128 GB/s Verifyhost

Three readings of this table matter. First, "device memory" is the slow memory: HBM is where your tensors live, and it feeds the ALUs at roughly 1/300th of the rate they can consume operands. Fast kernels are therefore exercises in staging: copy a tile from HBM into shared memory once, reuse it many times from registers. Second, shared memory is software-managed — a scratchpad the kernel explicitly fills — unlike CPU caches; this is what makes the tiling of Section 30.5 possible. Third, energy tells the same story as time: an off-chip DRAM access costs on the order of 100× the energy of a floating-point multiply-add Likely (Horowitz's classic 2014 accounting), so the memory wall is also a power wall.

30.3 The Roofline Model

Definition 30.1 (Arithmetic intensity)

For a kernel that performs $W$ floating-point operations and moves $Q$ bytes between device memory and the chip, the arithmetic intensity is $I = W/Q$ FLOPs per byte. $Q$ counts actual traffic — reads plus writes, including intermediate tensors — not the size of the mathematical inputs.

Definition 30.2 (Machine balance)

For a machine with peak arithmetic throughput $\pi$ (FLOP/s) and memory bandwidth $\beta$ (bytes/s), the balance point is $B^* = \pi/\beta$ (FLOPs per byte). H100: $989 \times 10^{12} / 3.35 \times 10^{12} \approx 295$ for bf16 tensor-core work Verify; for FP32 vector work the relevant roof is $67/3.35 \approx 20$.

Theorem 30.1 (Roofline bound)

A kernel with work $W$ and traffic $Q$ satisfies $$t \;\ge\; \max\!\left(\frac{W}{\pi},\ \frac{Q}{\beta}\right), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \frac{W}{t} \;\le\; \min\left(\pi,\ I\beta\right).$$ If $I < B^*$ the kernel is memory-bound: no optimization of its arithmetic can bring it to peak. If $I \ge B^*$ it is compute-bound.

Proof. The arithmetic units require at least $W/\pi$ seconds to issue $W$ operations; the memory system requires at least $Q/\beta$ seconds to move $Q$ bytes. Both are necessary, and even with perfect overlap of compute and data movement the runtime is at least the larger. Dividing $W$ by the bound gives the throughput form, since $W/(Q/\beta) = I\beta$. $\blacksquare$

The bound assumes perfect overlap, so it is optimistic; real kernels also pay launch overhead (~microseconds per kernel Likely), imperfect coalescing, and synchronization. But it is astonishingly predictive in the regime that matters, and its two failure directions are informative: a kernel far below both roofs is limited by something else — latency, occupancy, or overhead — which is exactly what a profiler should then be asked about.

Example 30.1 (Bias + GeLU on an H100, by hand)

Apply bias and GeLU to a $1024 \times 1024$ bf16 activation. Traffic: read $1024^2 \times 2 = 2.10$ MB, write $2.10$ MB, so $Q = 4.19 \times 10^6$ bytes (the bias vector's 2 KB is noise). Work: with the tanh approximation, roughly 10 FLOPs per element, $W \approx 1.05 \times 10^7$. Intensity: $I = W/Q = 10/4 = 2.5$ FLOPs/byte, against $B^* \approx 295$. Times: $t_{\text{mem}} = 4.19\times10^6 / 3.35\times10^{12} = 1.25\ \mu s$; $t_{\text{comp}} = 1.05\times10^7 / 6.7\times10^{13} = 0.16\ \mu s$ (vector roof). The memory term dominates 8:1 even against the slow ALUs — and 118:1 against a hypothetical tensor-core path. Making GeLU's arithmetic 10× faster would change nothing. Verify (H100 constants; the arithmetic is exact.)

30.4 Arithmetic Intensity of Common Operations

For a general matmul $(M\times K)(K \times N)$ in bf16, $W = 2MNK$ and the compulsory traffic is $Q = 2(MK + KN + MN)$ bytes, so $$I_{\text{matmul}} = \frac{MNK}{MK + KN + MN}\ \text{FLOPs/byte} \;\xrightarrow{\;M=N=K=n\;}\; \frac{n}{3}.$$ Intensity grows linearly with size: matmul is the one operation that can outrun any balance point. On an H100, square bf16 matmuls become compute-bound at $n/3 \ge 295$, i.e. $n \gtrsim 885$. At the other extreme, a matrix–vector product ($N=1$) has $I = MK/(MK+K+M) \approx 1$: two FLOPs touch every weight once, and no blocking can create reuse that the computation does not contain. Everything else in a transformer sits at the bottom of the same scale:

Operation (bf16)$W$ per element$Q$ per element$I$ (FLOPs/byte)H100 verdict
Square matmul, $n = 4096$——$n/3 \approx 1365$compute-bound
Matmul, $n = 512$——$\approx 171$memory-bound
Matvec (decode GEMM, $B{=}1$)2 per weight2 per weight$\approx 1$memory-bound, 300× under
Elementwise add / mul16$\approx 0.17$memory-bound
GeLU / SiLU~104$\approx 2.5$memory-bound
Softmax (fused, per row)~54$\approx 1.25$memory-bound
LayerNorm / RMSNorm (fused)~74$\approx 1.75$memory-bound
Attention $QK^\top$, unfused——$\approx d_h$ (64–128)memory-bound

The attention row deserves its derivation, because it motivates all of Chapter 31. Computing $S = QK^\top$ for one head costs $W = 2n^2 d_h$ FLOPs; materializing $S$ to HBM writes $2n^2$ bytes, which dominates the traffic once $n \gg d_h$, giving $I \approx d_h$. With $d_h = 64$–$128$, unfused attention runs at a fixed intensity below the H100 balance point no matter how long the sequence is — and the softmax over $n^2$ scores then re-reads and re-writes the whole matrix at $I \approx 1$. Attention as naively implemented is a bandwidth program with some arithmetic attached. FlashAttention's insight (Chapter 31) is that never materializing $S$ removes the $n^2$ traffic entirely, restoring $I \propto n$.

30.4.1 Predicting a transformer layer

A transformer layer with width $d$ and a $4d$ MLP has $12d^2$ parameters ($4d^2$ in $Q,K,V,O$; $8d^2$ in the MLP), hence $24d^2$ bytes of bf16 weights and $W = 24d^2$ GEMM FLOPs per token (Chapter 18). Two regimes follow immediately from Theorem 30.1. In prefill / training, $t$ tokens are processed per weight-read, so the GEMMs run at intensity $\approx t$ per weight-byte and are compute-bound for $t \gtrsim 300$: predict $t_{\text{layer}} \approx 24td^2/(\text{MFU}\cdot\pi)$, where MFU (model FLOPs utilization) of 40–60% is typical of well-tuned training Likely. In batch-1 decode, each generated token reads every weight once: $I \approx 1$, memory-bound by 300×, and the prediction collapses to $t \approx \text{weight bytes}/\beta$ — arithmetic is irrelevant.

Example 30.2 (Decode latency of a 70B model, by hand)

A 70B-parameter dense model in bf16 occupies $70\times10^9 \times 2 = 140$ GB. Generating one token requires streaming essentially all weights through the ALUs once, so on H100-class HBM at $\beta = 3.35$ TB/s Verify: $t \ge 140/3350\ \text{s} = 41.8$ ms per token, i.e. at most $\approx 24$ tokens/s single-stream — regardless of compute. Check the compute term: $W \approx 2 \times 70\times10^9 = 1.4\times10^{11}$ FLOPs per token, $t_{\text{comp}} = 1.4\times10^{11}/9.89\times10^{14} = 0.14$ ms — 295× smaller, confirming $I \approx 1$ vs. $B^* = 295$. This single division explains why inference servers batch requests, cache KV, and decode speculatively (Chapter 33), and why quantization to 4 bits quadruples decode speed before it does anything else (Chapter 34).

The measured leg of objective 3 is Artifact 30.1: this book's build environment has no GPU, so the artifact makes these predictions for the CPU it runs on and validates them against wall-clock — large matmuls land within a few percent of the compute roof, and the memory-bound suite runs at under 6% of peak FLOP/s, within a small factor of the bandwidth roof. The method transfers verbatim to any GPU; only the two measured ceilings change.

30.5 Occupancy, Tiling, Tensor Cores

Why does matmul achieve its high intensity? The computation has $O(n^3)$ work on $O(n^2)$ data, but a naive triple loop still streams operands from HBM. The classical fix is tiling: each thread block computes a $T \times T$ output tile by iterating over the $K$ dimension in chunks, staging $T \times T_k$ slabs of $A$ and $B$ in shared memory; every staged element is reused $T$ times from on-chip storage, so HBM traffic per output falls by a factor of $T$ and effective intensity grows $\propto T$. Registers add a second tiling level: each thread accumulates a small sub-tile in registers, reusing shared-memory operands again. The ladder of Section 30.2 exists precisely to make this two-level reuse possible, and Hopper adds hardware to feed it (TMA asynchronous bulk copies into shared memory; warp-group MMA instructions that read tiles directly from shared memory) Verify.

Occupancy is the fraction of an SM's warp slots (64 on H100 Verify) that are resident. Since latency hiding requires ready warps, too-low occupancy leaves the memory pipeline idle between stalls. But occupancy trades against tiling: registers and shared memory are shared resources, so bigger tiles (more reuse, higher $I$) mean fewer resident blocks. Peak-performance kernels often run at 25–50% occupancy with large tiles Likely — occupancy is a means (enough parallelism to hide latency), not an end, and "increase occupancy" is bad advice for a compute-bound GEMM.
