Tensor cores add a final constraint: they consume operands in fixed small-matrix shapes, so problem dimensions that are not multiples of the tile granularity waste lanes on padding — one reason vocabulary sizes and hidden widths are chosen divisible by 64 or 128 (Chapter 23).

30.6 Kernel Fusion and Compilers

Consider a chain of $k$ elementwise operations applied to a tensor of $n$ elements — say scale, add-bias, activation, dropout-mask. Executed as $k$ separate kernels, each reads and writes $n$ elements: $Q_{\text{unfused}} = 2kn \cdot s$ bytes for element size $s$. Fused into one kernel, each element is read once, transformed $k$ times in registers, and written once: $Q_{\text{fused}} = 2ns$. The FLOPs are identical; the traffic falls by $k$; and since every such chain sits far below $B^*$, Theorem 30.1 predicts a speedup approaching $k\times$. Fusion is not an optimization of arithmetic at all — it is a refusal to launder intermediate values through HBM. The same logic yields fused softmax and normalization (one read, one write, per-row statistics kept on-chip, giving the "fused" intensities in the table above), GEMM epilogue fusion (bias and activation applied to the output tile while it is still in registers, making the elementwise work free), and, at the far end, FlashAttention, which fuses two matmuls and a softmax into one kernel (Chapter 31).

Doing this by hand for every operator chain is why compilers took over. torch.compile traces the graph and emits fused Triton kernels for elementwise-and-reduction regions; XLA does the equivalent for JAX. What compilers still cannot generally do is invent FlashAttention-grade algorithmic restructurings — fusing across a matmul requires changing the order of reductions and re-deriving numerical stability, which is Chapter 31's subject. Artifact 30.1 demonstrates fusion's limit case honestly: on its CPU, blockwise "fusion" of a 4-op chain yields only 1.28× because NumPy's per-element instruction overhead becomes the new roof — whereas torch.softmax, internally fused and threaded, beats the unfused NumPy softmax by 3.0× on identical data. Fusion buys exactly the distance between the traffic roof and the next constraint.

30.7 Profiling: What to Measure and What Lies

Three instruments, in order of increasing honesty: nvidia-smi, wall-clock timing, and a kernel profiler (Nsight Compute, torch.profiler). The first lies the most: its "GPU utilization" reports the fraction of time any kernel was resident, so a memory-bound kernel using 0.3% of peak FLOP/s shows 100% utilization. The number that tracks the roofline is MFU — achieved model FLOP/s divided by $\pi$ — which you compute yourself from token throughput and the analytic FLOP count (Chapter 24's $6ND$). Similarly, compare achieved bandwidth against the measured ceiling, not the spec sheet: a copy microbenchmark typically reaches only 85–93% of quoted HBM bandwidth Likely, and that measured number is the fair denominator — Artifact 30.1's first act is to measure both ceilings rather than trust any datasheet.

Common Pitfall

Timing GPU code without synchronization. Kernel launches are asynchronous: t0 = time.time(); y = model(x); t1 = time.time() measures the time to enqueue work, often microseconds for a computation taking milliseconds — a 1000× error that has produced many published "speedups." Call torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading both timestamps, or use CUDA events. Two further lies to control: the first call pays compilation, autotuning, and memory-pool growth (always warm up, then report a robust statistic — the artifact uses best-of-$k$, since interference on a shared machine is one-sided), and sustained runs downclock under power and thermal limits, so a 30-second benchmark can report 10–15% slower steady-state than a 100 ms burst Likely.

30.8 The Hardware Landscape

Numbers as of August 2026, from vendor datasheets; every figure below drifts with hardware generations and should be re-verified before use Verify. Dense (non-sparse) throughputs throughout.

Acceleratorbf16 denseMemoryBandwidth$B^*$ (FLOPs/byte)
NVIDIA H100 SXM989 TFLOP/s80 GB HBM33.35 TB/s295

Two structural observations survive any refresh of this table. First, the balance point sits between roughly 150 and 300 bf16 FLOPs/byte across vendors and generations — the H200 is literally an H100 with a better memory system, and it was a successful product precisely because decode is memory-bound. Second, compute has historically grown faster than bandwidth (the "memory wall" named by Wulf and McKee in 1995 Certain), and lower-precision formats sharpen it further: FP8 and FP4 double and quadruple $\pi$ while $\beta$ stands still, pushing $B^*$ past 1000 on Blackwell's FP4 path Verify. Every technique in the next four chapters — fused attention, overlap of communication with compute, batched and speculative decoding, weight quantization — is a response to the same inequality.

Artifact 30.1 — An Empirical Roofline Analyzer

This environment has no GPU, so the artifact builds a genuine roofline for the CPU it runs on rather than pantomiming one: it measures the machine's two ceilings (streaming bandwidth via copies whose 512 MiB read-plus-write working set exceeds the 260 MiB L3; peak FLOP/s as the best large-sgemm rate observed anywhere in the run, so a contended probe window cannot depress the ceiling), computes the arithmetic intensity of seven operations from their FLOP and byte counts, classifies each against the measured balance point, predicts runtimes via Theorem 30.1, and asserts that the classifications and compute-bound predictions hold. It then demonstrates fusion by cache-blocking a four-op elementwise chain. The identical procedure applies to any GPU — replace the two ceiling measurements and rerun.

"""Artifact 30.1 -- An empirical roofline analyzer for the machine it runs on.

No GPU exists in this environment, so we build the roofline for the CPU,
honestly: measure the two ceilings (streaming memory bandwidth via large
array copies; peak FLOP/s as the best large-sgemm rate observed anywhere
in the run), compute each operation's arithmetic intensity
AI = FLOPs / bytes moved, classify it as compute- or memory-bound against
the measured machine balance point B* = peak/BW, and predict its runtime
as  t = max(FLOPs/peak, bytes/BW).  The identical procedure applies
verbatim to any GPU -- only the two ceiling measurements change.
Pure NumPy core; torch appears only as a cross-check.
"""
import time
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def tmin(f, reps=3, budget=0.35, cap=600):
    """Best-of-many wall clock. Warm up twice first (page faults, BLAS
    thread-pool spin-up, caches), then sample until we have both `reps`
    samples and `budget` seconds of measurement, capped at `cap` calls.
    Min, not mean: noise on a shared VM is one-sided -- interference only
    ever makes you slower -- and it arrives in bursts of ~100 ms, so many
    short samples give the min a chance to catch a quiet window."""
    f(); f()
    ts, spent = [], 0.0
    while (len(ts) < reps or spent < budget) and len(ts) < cap:
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); f(); ts.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
        spent += ts[-1]
    return min(ts)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- ceilings
def measure_bandwidth():
    """STREAM-style copy, 256 MiB arrays: the 512 MiB read+write working
    set exceeds the L3 (260 MiB reported by lscpu on this VM), so the
    copy streams from DRAM -- the measured rate is DRAM-class, an order
    of magnitude under cache rates. Convention: count bytes read + bytes
    written, so a copy moves 2x the array size."""
    x = rng.random(2**26, dtype=np.float32); y = np.empty_like(x)
    t = tmin(lambda: np.copyto(y, x), reps=7)
    return 2 * x.nbytes / t                      # bytes/s

def measure_peak_flops():
    """Provisional peak: large-sgemm rate. n=3072 amortizes overheads;
    2n^3 = 58 GFLOP per call. Refined below: the honest ceiling is the
    best sgemm rate seen anywhere in the run, because on a shared VM this
    dedicated probe can itself land in a contended window."""
    n = 3072
    a = rng.standard_normal((n, n), dtype=np.float32); b = a.copy()
    t = tmin(lambda: a @ b)
    return 2 * n**3 / t                          # FLOP/s

BW   = measure_bandwidth()
PEAK = measure_peak_flops()                      # provisional; see below

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- op suite
# Each op: (name, callable-on-prealloc-buffers, flops, bytes moved by the
# implementation as written).  exp counted as 1 FLOP (roofline convention;
# its true cost shows up as memory-bound ops running above prediction).
R, C = 8192, 8192                                 # X,T,OUT: 3 x 256 MiB, past L3
X  = rng.random((R, C), dtype=np.float32)   # uniform: cheap to generate
T  = np.empty_like(X); OUT = np.empty_like(X)
n1 = 2**26                                        # 256 MiB per fp32 array
xa = rng.random(n1, dtype=np.float32)
za = rng.random(n1, dtype=np.float32); ya = np.empty_like(xa)
G  = {n: rng.standard_normal((n, n), dtype=np.float32) for n in (512, 1024, 2048)}
GB = {n: G[n].copy() for n in G}
nv = 16384                                        # 1 GiB matrix: DRAM-resident
Av = rng.random((nv, nv), dtype=np.float32)
xv = rng.random(nv, dtype=np.float32)

def softmax_rows():        # 5 unfused kernels, 7 full passes over R*C floats
    m = X.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)             # read X
    np.subtract(X, m, out=T)                     # read X, write T
    np.exp(T, out=T)                             # read T, write T
    s = T.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)             # read T
    np.divide(T, s, out=OUT)                     # read T, write OUT

def layernorm_rows():      # 5 unfused kernels, 8 full passes
    mu = X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)           # read X
    np.subtract(X, mu, out=T)                    # read X, write T (T = x-mu)
    np.multiply(T, T, out=OUT)                   # read T, write OUT (scratch)
    v = OUT.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)          # read OUT
    np.multiply(T, 1.0/np.sqrt(v + 1e-5), out=OUT)  # read T, write OUT

ops = []                   # (name, fn, flops, bytes)
for n in (512, 1024, 2048):
    ops.append((f"matmul {n}^3", (lambda n=n: G[n] @ GB[n]), 2*n**3, 12*n**2))
ops.append((f"matvec {nv}^2", (lambda: Av @ xv), 2*nv**2, 4*(nv**2 + 2*nv)))
ops.append(("triad y=2x+z", (lambda: np.add(np.multiply(xa, 2.0, out=ya), za, out=ya)),
            2*n1, 12*n1))
ops.append((f"softmax {R}x{C}", softmax_rows, 5*R*C, 7*4*R*C))
ops.append((f"layernorm {R}x{C}", layernorm_rows, 7*R*C, 8*4*R*C))

# Measure everything FIRST, then classify: the final compute ceiling is
# the best sgemm rate observed in the whole run (probe or suite).
raw  = [(name, flops, byts, tmin(fn)) for name, fn, flops, byts in ops]
PEAK = max(PEAK, max(f/m for name, f, _, m in raw if name.startswith("matmul")))
BSTAR = PEAK / BW                                # machine balance, FLOPs/byte
print(f"memory bandwidth (copy, r+w) : {BW/1e9:8.1f} GB/s")
print(f"peak compute (best sgemm)    : {PEAK/1e9:8.1f} GFLOP/s")
print(f"MACHINE BALANCE POINT B*     : {BSTAR:8.1f} FLOPs/byte")

print(f"\n{'op':<20}{'AI':>7}{'bound':>9}{'pred ms':>9}{'meas ms':>9}"
      f"{'meas/pred':>10}{'%peak':>7}")
results = []
for name, flops, byts, meas in raw:
    ai    = flops / byts
    bound = "compute" if ai >= BSTAR else "memory"
    pred  = max(flops / PEAK, byts / BW)          # the roofline prediction
    frac  = flops / meas / PEAK                   # fraction of peak achieved
    results.append((name, ai, bound, pred, meas, frac))
    print(f"{name:<20}{ai:>7.2f}{bound:>9}{pred*1e3:>9.2f}{meas*1e3:>9.2f}"
          f"{meas/pred:>10.2f}{100*frac:>6.1f}%")

# ------------------------------------------------------------- assertions
for name, ai, bound, pred, meas, frac in results:
    if bound == "memory":
        # A memory-bound op must be nowhere near the compute ceiling...
        assert frac < 0.35, f"{name}: 'memory-bound' but hit {frac:.0%} of peak"
        # ...and land within [1/6x, 4x] of the bandwidth prediction (above
        # 1x means unmodeled cost: exp, reduction overhead; below 1x means
        # a multithreaded BLAS kernel beat our single-thread copy ceiling,
        # as sgemv does here -- a read-only stream on all four cores runs
        # several times faster than one core's read+write copy).
        assert 1/6 <= meas/pred <= 4.0, f"{name}: ratio {meas/pred:.2f}"
    else:
        # A compute-bound op must run near the ceiling: within factor 2.
        assert frac >= 0.35, f"{name}: 'compute-bound' at {frac:.0%} of peak"
        assert meas/pred <= 2.0, f"{name}: ratio {meas/pred:.2f}"
print("\nall classification + prediction assertions passed")

# ---------------------------------------------------- fusion, demonstrated
# Chain of 4 elementwise ops on 256 MiB: y = relu(2x+1) * 3.
# Unfused: 4 kernels, each a full read+write pass over DRAM-resident data.
# 'Fused': one loop over 256 KiB cache-resident blocks -- exactly what a
# fused GPU kernel (or torch.compile) does with registers/shared memory.
def unfused():
    np.multiply(xa, 2.0, out=ya); np.add(ya, 1.0, out=ya)
    np.maximum(ya, 0.0, out=ya);  np.multiply(ya, 3.0, out=ya)
def fused(blk=2**16):
    scratch = np.empty(blk, dtype=np.float32)
    for i in range(0, n1, blk):
        s = scratch[: n1 - i] if n1 - i < blk else scratch
        np.multiply(xa[i:i+blk], 2.0, out=s); np.add(s, 1.0, out=s)
        np.maximum(s, 0.0, out=s);            np.multiply(s, 3.0, out=ya[i:i+blk])
tu, tf = tmin(unfused, budget=0.7), tmin(fused, budget=0.7)
print(f"\nfusion: unfused {tu*1e3:6.1f} ms ({8*4*n1/tu/1e9:.1f} GB/s of traffic)"
      f" | fused {tf*1e3:6.1f} ms | speedup {tu/tf:.2f}x")
assert tf < tu, "fusion must win: same FLOPs, 4x less DRAM traffic"

# ------------------------------------------------------ torch cross-check
try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None
if torch is not None:
    xt = torch.from_numpy(X)
    t = tmin(lambda: torch.softmax(xt, dim=1))
    print(f"torch.softmax (internally fused/threaded): {t*1e3:.1f} ms vs "
          f"numpy unfused {results[-2][4]*1e3:.1f} ms")
else:
    print("[skipped: torch not installed]")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"\nsummary: every op with AI below B*={BSTAR:.0f} FLOPs/byte was "
          "memory-bound in measurement; only matmul was compute-bound.")

On this book's 4-core build VM the run measures $\beta = 21.0$ GB/s, $\pi = 480.4$ GFLOP/s, and prints MACHINE BALANCE POINT B* : 22.9 FLOPs/byte. The $2048^3$ matmul ($I = 341$) is predicted at 35.76 ms and measured at 35.94 ms — a ratio of 1.00 at 99.5% of peak (the $1024^3$ case, measured independently of the ceiling, hits 98.7%) — while every op with $I < B^*$ achieved under 5.3% of peak FLOP/s, exactly as classified: matvec measured 20.96 ms against a 51.24 ms single-thread prediction (multithreaded BLAS beat the one-thread copy ceiling, ratio 0.41), and softmax ran 2.62× over its bandwidth prediction (the unmodeled cost of exp and reduction overhead). The fusion demo saves traffic for a 1.28× speedup before NumPy's per-element overhead becomes the binding roof, while the fused, threaded torch.softmax cross-check runs in 77.9 ms against unfused NumPy's 235.1 ms. All assertions pass in about 22 s.

Key Takeaways
  • Runtime obeys $t \ge \max(W/\pi, Q/\beta)$: an operation whose arithmetic intensity $I = W/Q$ is below the machine balance $B^* = \pi/\beta$ is memory-bound, and no arithmetic optimization can save it. Certain
  • On current accelerators $B^*$ is roughly 150–300 bf16 FLOPs/byte (H100: $\approx$295), and every common deep-learning operation except sufficiently large matmul sits far below it — elementwise, softmax, and normalization near $I \approx 1$, unfused attention at $I \approx d_h$. Verify
  • Matmul intensity grows with size ($n/3$ for square bf16), which is why tiling through shared memory and registers — and the tensor cores it feeds — can reach peak; batch-1 decode is a matvec at $I \approx 1$ and is bounded by weight bytes over bandwidth (~42 ms/token for 70B bf16 on H100-class HBM). Verify
  • Fusing a $k$-op elementwise chain cuts HBM traffic by $k\times$ at identical FLOPs; fusion, epilogues, and FlashAttention are all the same idea — keep intermediates on-chip. Certain
  • Profile against measured ceilings, not spec sheets or "GPU utilization": compute MFU from analytic FLOPs, synchronize before timing, warm up, and expect ~85–93% of quoted bandwidth to be attainable. Likely
Chapter 31

FlashAttention and Writing Fast Kernels

Learning Objectives
  • Derive online (streaming) softmax and prove it equals batch softmax exactly, up to floating-point rounding.
  • Derive the tiled FlashAttention forward pass, count its HBM accesses as $\Theta(n^2 d^2 / M)$, and explain why activation memory drops from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$.
  • Explain the backward-pass recomputation strategy and quantify the extra FLOPs it accepts (about 17% of total training matmul FLOPs for attention) in exchange for never storing the score matrix.
  • State what FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-3 each changed — work partitioning; Hopper asynchrony and FP8 — with attributed numbers.
  • Implement tiled online-softmax attention in working code, with explicit memory and I/O accounting.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 (Language Modeling from Scratch): the kernel-writing assignments are the closest thing to doing this chapter by hand, including a Triton FlashAttention exercise. The HuggingFace Ultra-Scale Playbook situates fused attention kernels inside the full training-systems stack. The primary sources are short and readable: Dao et al. (2022), Dao (2023), and Shah et al. (2024).

Chapter 30 established the memory wall: modern accelerators execute matmul FLOPs one to two orders of magnitude faster than they can move bytes to and from HBM, so any operation whose arithmetic intensity falls below the machine's ridge point is billed by traffic, not by arithmetic. This chapter applies that lens to the single most-optimized operation in deep learning. FlashAttention computes exactly the attention of Chapter 18 — same FLOPs, same output, no approximation — yet runs several times faster, because it reorganizes the computation so the $n \times n$ score matrix never touches HBM. It is the cleanest existence proof of this book's systems thesis: the binding constraint is movement, not arithmetic. We derive the enabling identity (online softmax), the tiled forward pass and its I/O complexity, the backward pass's recompute-instead-of-store bargain, then survey FlashAttention-2 and -3 and the wider kernel ecosystem. Chapter 33 reuses these ideas for inference; Chapter 32 scales them across devices.

31.1 Attention Cost Is Memory, Not FLOPs

Fix one attention head with sequence length $n$ and head dimension $d_k$ (typically 64–128, with $n$ in the thousands). The forward pass of standard attention is

$$S = \frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, \qquad P = \mathrm{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S), \qquad O = PV \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k}.$$

The two matmuls cost $2n^2 d_k$ FLOPs each, $4n^2 d_k$ total; softmax adds $O(n^2)$ exponentials. The FLOP count is what it is — the algorithm is exact and its arithmetic is fixed (and Dao et al. proved that the traffic, separately, cannot be beaten asymptotically either; Section 31.3). What a naive implementation adds on top is exactly that traffic: it writes $S$ to HBM ($n^2$ entries), reads it back to compute the row max and sum, writes $P$, then reads $P$ again for the final matmul. Every elementwise pass over an $n^2$ buffer — masking, softmax, dropout — has arithmetic intensity of roughly one FLOP per byte, hopelessly below the ridge point of $\sim$160 FLOPs/byte for an A100's BF16 tensor cores against its $\sim$2 TB/s of HBM bandwidth Verify.

Concretely, at $n=4096$, $d_k=128$ in FP16: $Q, K, V, O$ together occupy $4nd_k \cdot 2\,\text{B} = 4$ MB, while $S$ and $P$ each occupy $n^2 \cdot 2\,\text{B} = 33.5$ MB. The quadratic buffers are $16\times$ larger than all the actual inputs and outputs combined, and the naive schedule streams them through HBM four times. Multiply by heads and layers and the score matrices also dominate activation memory: 32 heads of stored $P$ at these sizes is 1.07 GB per layer, which is why pre-FlashAttention training runs hit out-of-memory on sequence length long before they hit it on model size. Certain

FlashAttention (Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra, Ré, NeurIPS 2022) restructures the computation so that tiles of $S$ live only in on-chip SRAM (Chapter 30: ~100–200 KB per SM, ~19 TB/s aggregate on A100 Verify) and are discarded after use. The paper reports up to 7.6$\times$ speedup on GPT-2's attention computation, 3$\times$ end-to-end GPT-2 speedup over the HuggingFace implementation of the day, and a 15% improvement over the MLPerf 1.1 BERT-large training record Verify — all with zero FLOPs saved and outputs identical up to floating-point rounding (the tiled summation order differs, so bits do not match; the artifact measures the discrepancy at $\sim 10^{-15}$). Two problems must be solved to make tiling work: softmax normalizes across an entire row of $S$, which we only see one tile at a time (Section 31.2), and the backward pass ordinarily needs the full $P$ (Section 31.4).

31.2 Online Softmax

Numerically safe softmax subtracts the row max before exponentiating: $\mathrm{softmax}(x)_i = e^{x_i - m}/\sum_j e^{x_j - m}$ with $m = \max_j x_j$. That is a three-pass algorithm — max, sum, divide — and each pass wants the whole row. Milakov and Gimelshein (2018) showed the max and sum passes fuse into one streaming pass with a rescaling trick; FlashAttention's contribution was to extend the same rescaling to the output accumulator so that even the third pass streams.

Definition 31.1 (Online softmax state)

For a row $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ processed in blocks $x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \ldots$, maintain a running max $m$ and running normalizer $\ell$, initialized $m_0 = -\infty$, $\ell_0 = 0$. On block $t$:

$$m_t = \max\!\big(m_{t-1},\, \max_i x^{(t)}_i\big), \qquad \ell_t = \ell_{t-1}\, e^{\,m_{t-1} - m_t} + \sum_i e^{\,x^{(t)}_i - m_t}.$$

The factor $e^{\,m_{t-1}-m_t} \le 1$ rescales the stale normalizer, which was accumulated relative to the old max, into the new max's frame.

Theorem 31.1 (Exactness of online softmax)

After processing all blocks covering $x$, $m_T = \max_j x_j$ and $\ell_T = \sum_j e^{x_j - m_T}$, so $e^{x_i - m_T}/\ell_T$ is exactly the numerically safe softmax. Moreover the two-state merge $m = \max(m_a, m_b)$, $\ell = \ell_a e^{m_a - m} + \ell_b e^{m_b - m}$ is associative and commutative, so any partition of the row into blocks, merged in any order or grouping, yields the same result in exact arithmetic.

Proof. Induction on $t$ with invariant $\ell_t = \sum_{j \in \text{seen}(t)} e^{x_j - m_t}$. Base: $\ell_0 = 0$ over the empty set. Step: assume the invariant at $t-1$. Then $$\ell_{t-1} e^{m_{t-1}-m_t} = \Big(\sum_{j \in \text{seen}(t-1)} e^{x_j - m_{t-1}}\Big) e^{m_{t-1}-m_t} = \sum_{j \in \text{seen}(t-1)} e^{x_j - m_t},$$ because $e^{x_j - m_{t-1}} e^{m_{t-1} - m_t} = e^{x_j - m_t}$ exactly as real numbers. Adding the new block's terms $\sum_i e^{x^{(t)}_i - m_t}$ extends the sum over $\text{seen}(t)$, and $m_t$ is the max over $\text{seen}(t)$ by construction. At $t = T$, $\text{seen}(T)$ is the whole row. The same computation shows that merging any two states, each summarizing its block set as $(\max,\ \sum_j e^{x_j - \max})$, yields the state summarizing the union — the merge is symmetric in its arguments and grouping-independent, giving commutativity and associativity. Since each $m_t$ equals the max over elements seen so far, no exponent argument is ever positive, so no intermediate overflows — the streaming version inherits the safety of the batch version. $\blacksquare$

In floating point the two computations differ only by rounding; the artifact measures a worst-case discrepancy of $4.4\times10^{-16}$ across chunk sizes from 1 to 1000 on rows with logits spanning $\pm 15$. The associativity is what everything downstream leans on: it is why tiles can arrive in any order (FlashAttention-2's parallelism), from any device (Ring Attention), and why the same merge rule gives split-KV inference decoding for free (Chapter 33). Certain

Example 31.1 (Online softmax by hand)

Row $x = (1, 3, 2, 5)$ in two chunks $(1,3)$ and $(2,5)$. Chunk 1: $m_1 = 3$, $\ell_1 = e^{1-3} + e^{3-3} = 0.1353 + 1 = 1.1353$. Chunk 2: $m_2 = \max(3,5) = 5$; rescale factor $e^{3-5} = 0.1353$; $\ell_2 = 1.1353 \times 0.1353 + (e^{2-5} + e^{0}) = 0.1536 + 1.0498 = 1.2034$. Batch check: $e^{-4}+e^{-2}+e^{-3}+e^{0} = 0.0183+0.1353+0.0498+1 = 1.2034$. Identical. Final probability for the last element: $1/1.2034 = 0.831$.

31.3 Tiling and the Forward Pass

Partition $Q$ into row blocks $Q_1,\ldots,Q_{T_r}$ of $B_r$ rows and $K, V$ into row blocks $K_1,\ldots,K_{T_c}$, $V_j$ of $B_c$ rows, with block sizes chosen so a working set of one $Q_i$, one $K_j$, one $V_j$, and one $B_r \times B_c$ score tile fits in SRAM. Extend the online-softmax state to vectors $m_i, \ell_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r}$ (one scalar per query row) and add an unnormalized output accumulator $\tilde{O}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{B_r \times d_k}$. For each query block $i$, loop over key blocks $j$:

$$S_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}} Q_i K_j^\top, \quad m^{\text{new}} = \max(m_i, \mathrm{rowmax}\, S_{ij}), \quad \tilde{P}_{ij} = e^{\,S_{ij} - m^{\text{new}}},$$ $$\alpha = e^{\,m_i - m^{\text{new}}}, \qquad \ell_i \leftarrow \alpha \odot \ell_i + \mathrm{rowsum}\, \tilde{P}_{ij}, \qquad \tilde{O}_i \leftarrow \mathrm{diag}(\alpha)\, \tilde{O}_i + \tilde{P}_{ij} V_j,$$

and after the last key block, $O_i = \mathrm{diag}(\ell_i)^{-1} \tilde{O}_i$. The output rescaling is Theorem 31.1 applied to the numerator: $\tilde{O}_i$ accumulates $\sum_j e^{S_{ij} - m}V_j$-style terms, all relative to the current max, and each max update multiplies the stale accumulator by the same $\alpha$ that fixes $\ell_i$. Division by the normalizer is deferred to a single step at the end — the whole softmax has been smeared across the tile loop without ever holding a full row of $P$. Causal masking composes trivially: skip tiles entirely above the diagonal, mask the tiles it crosses.

Memory: what survives the loop is $O$ ($n d_k$ floats) and one logsumexp scalar per row (Section 31.4) — $O(n)$ in sequence length, versus $O(n^2)$ for stored $S$ and $P$. The inner-loop working set is $O(B_r B_c + (B_r + B_c) d_k)$, independent of $n$: the artifact verifies that doubling $n$ from 257 to 514 leaves the measured peak at exactly 24,832 elements while naive storage quadruples. Certain

Theorem 31.2 (HBM access count; Dao et al. 2022)

With SRAM of size $M$ floats and $d_k \le M$, the tiled forward pass makes $\Theta(n^2 d_k^2 / M)$ HBM accesses, versus $\Theta(n d_k + n^2)$ for the standard implementation. Moreover no exact attention algorithm can do asymptotically better over all $M \in [d_k, n d_k]$.

Proof sketch. Each query block $Q_i$ is loaded once and held while all of $K$ and $V$ stream past: that inner sweep costs $\Theta(n d_k)$ reads, repeated $T_r = \lceil n/B_r \rceil$ times, for $\Theta(T_r\, n d_k)$ total. The SRAM budget forces $B_r = \Theta(M/d_k)$ (the $Q_i$ tile and score tile must fit), so $T_r = \Theta(n d_k / M)$ and the total is $\Theta(n^2 d_k^2 / M)$. On real hardware $M > d_k^2$ (an A100 SM's 192 KB of SRAM holds $M \approx 49{,}000$ FP32 floats against $d_k^2 = 4096$–$16{,}384$), so this beats the standard $\Theta(n^2)$ term by the factor $M/d_k^2$, roughly $3\times$–$12\times$ per SM at these sizes (the aggregate across 108 SMs is what the measured speedups reflect). The lower bound is a counting argument in the style of Hong–Kung red–blue pebbling: any algorithm computing all $n^2$ score interactions with $M$ fast memory must re-stream inputs $\Omega(n^2 d_k^2/M)$ times in the worst case. $\blacksquare$

The artifact's accounting table makes the constant concrete: counted K/V reads equal $\lceil n/B_r\rceil \cdot n \cdot 2d_k$ exactly, falling from $559{,}232$ elements at $B_r = 16$ (17 full passes over $K,V$) to $32{,}896$ at $B_r = n$ (one pass) — traffic inversely proportional to the tile size that SRAM affords. That $1/M$ dependence is the whole economic content of FlashAttention. Rabe and Staats (2021) had independently shown self-attention needs only $O(\log n)$ extra memory in principle — $O(\sqrt{n})$ in their practical implementation — via the same lazy-normalization idea; FlashAttention's advance was recognizing and engineering the I/O claim, not just the memory claim. Likely

31.4 The Backward Pass and Recomputation

The backward pass needs $P$ (for $dV = P^\top dO$) and $S$ (for the softmax Jacobian). Storing them would reintroduce the $O(n^2)$ buffers, so FlashAttention stores neither; it saves only the per-row logsumexp $L_i = m_i + \log \ell_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and recomputes score tiles on the fly: $P_{ij} = \exp(S_{ij} - L_i)$, exactly the forward value with no renewed max-tracking, because $L_i$ already encodes the finished normalization. Note the pitfall the $L$ encoding avoids: storing $m$ and $\ell$ separately and recombining via $e^{-m}/\ell$ risks overflow; the log-domain sum is safe.

The FLOP bill is explicit. Forward: 2 matmuls ($QK^\top$, $PV$), $4n^2d_k$ FLOPs. Backward with stored $P$: 4 matmuls ($dV = P^\top dO$, $dP = dO\, V^\top$, $dQ = dS\, K$, $dK = dS^\top Q$), $8n^2 d_k$. Backward with recomputation adds one matmul, re-forming $S = QK^\top$ tile-by-tile: $10 n^2 d_k$. Training-step attention matmul FLOPs rise from $12 n^2 d_k$ to $14 n^2 d_k$ — a 16.7% arithmetic surcharge, deliberately paid because those FLOPs run at tensor-core speed while the avoided $n^2$ HBM round-trips run at bandwidth speed. Recomputation is cheaper than remembering. Certain This is gradient checkpointing's logic (Chapter 32) applied inside a single operator, and it compounds: the memory freed by not storing $P$ is what makes 32K–128K-token training contexts feasible at all.

One further identity keeps the backward streaming. The softmax Jacobian term $dS_{ij} = P_{ij} \odot (dP_{ij} - D_i)$ needs the row sums $D_i = \mathrm{rowsum}(dP_i \odot P_i)$, which naively couple all tiles of a row. But $D_i = \mathrm{rowsum}(dO_i \odot O_i)$ — provable in one line from $O = PV$ and the softmax Jacobian — so $D$ is precomputed from tensors already in HBM, $O(n d_k)$ traffic, and the backward tile loop stays single-pass. The backward's HBM complexity matches the forward's $\Theta(n^2 d_k^2/M)$.

31.5 FlashAttention-2: Work Partitioning

FlashAttention-1 got the algorithm right and the GPU mapping wrong enough to leave 2$\times$ on the table. Dao (2023; ICLR 2024) reports the original reaching only 25–40% of theoretical peak FLOPs/s, and attributes the gap to suboptimal partitioning of work between thread blocks and between warps Verify. FlashAttention-2 made three changes, all scheduling, none algorithmic:

Fewer non-matmul FLOPs. Tensor cores execute matmul FLOPs roughly 16$\times$ faster than the CUDA cores execute everything else (A100: 312 TFLOPs/s FP16 matmul vs. 19.5 TFLOPs/s FP32 scalar Verify), so a non-matmul FLOP is ~16$\times$ more expensive. FA-2 defers the $\mathrm{diag}(\ell)^{-1}$ rescaling to once per query block rather than once per tile iteration, and keeps only $L_i$ rather than $m_i, \ell_i$ separately.

Parallelism over sequence length. FA-1 parallelized over batch $\times$ heads only; one thread block per head. At long context the batch shrinks to keep memory bounded, so batch $\times$ heads falls below the ~108 SMs of an A100 and the GPU idles. FA-2 additionally parallelizes over query blocks — correctness is free because query rows are independent — restoring occupancy exactly in the long-sequence regime that FlashAttention exists to serve.

Warp-level partitioning. Within a thread block, FA-1 split $K$ across warps ("split-K"), forcing warps to write partial results to shared memory and synchronize to reduce them. FA-2 splits $Q$ across warps instead: each warp owns whole output rows, needs no inter-warp reduction for the accumulator, and shared-memory traffic drops.

Attributed results: ~2$\times$ speedup over FlashAttention-1, reaching 50–73% of theoretical peak FLOPs/s on A100 in the forward pass, and end-to-end GPT-style training at up to 225 TFLOPs/s per A100 — 72% model FLOPs utilization (Dao 2023) Verify. The lesson generalizes: after the I/O algorithm is right, the next factor of two lives in occupancy and intra-block communication.

31.6 FlashAttention-3: Asynchrony and FP8

Hopper (H100) changed the hardware contract: the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) issues bulk HBM→SRAM copies asynchronously, and warpgroup matmul instructions (WGMMA) run asynchronously too, so a kernel written in the synchronous FA-2 style leaves both engines waiting on each other. Shah, Bikshandi, Zhang, Thakkar, Ramani, and Dao (NeurIPS 2024) rebuilt the kernel around three techniques. First, warp specialization: producer warpgroups do nothing but issue TMA loads of upcoming $K_j, V_j$ tiles while consumer warpgroups compute on current ones, a hardware-level pipeline hiding memory latency behind arithmetic. Second, pingpong scheduling: the softmax of one tile (slow exponentials on the multi-function units) is interleaved with the WGMMA matmuls of another tile, so the non-matmul work that FA-2 minimized is instead hidden. Third, FP8 with error control: block quantization (one scale per tile rather than per tensor) plus incoherent processing — multiplying $Q$ and $K$ by a random orthogonal (Hadamard-based) matrix, which leaves $QK^\top$ mathematically unchanged but spreads outlier magnitudes across dimensions before quantization (the same trick Chapter 34 uses for weight quantization).

Attributed results, from the NeurIPS camera-ready (the initial July 2024 release reported slightly lower figures): 1.5–2.0$\times$ faster than FlashAttention-2, with BF16 reaching up to 840 TFLOPs/s — 85% utilization of H100's theoretical peak, versus roughly 35% for FA-2 on the same part; with FP8, up to 1.3 PFLOPs/s; and FP8 numerical error 2.6$\times$ lower than a baseline per-tensor-quantized FP8 attention (Shah et al. 2024) Verify. Read the trajectory as a statement about hardware, not cleverness exhaustion: FA-1 fixed the I/O algorithm, FA-2 fixed the parallel decomposition, FA-3 fixed the pipeline — each layer of the Chapter 30 execution model claimed in turn, and each rewrite forced by a new architecture. Kernels are not written once. Likely

31.7 PagedAttention, FlexAttention, Ring Attention

Three descendants show the ideas' reach. PagedAttention (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023; the vLLM engine) targets inference, where the quadratic problem is not activations but the KV cache (Chapter 33): serving systems that pre-allocated contiguous per-request KV buffers wasted 60–80% of cache memory to fragmentation and over-reservation. PagedAttention stores KV in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks behind a page table, exactly like virtual memory — possible because the tiled attention loop never needed contiguity, only block-at-a-time access. The paper reports waste under 4% and 2–4$\times$ serving throughput over then-state-of-the-art systems Verify.

FlexAttention (PyTorch 2.5+) attacks the variant explosion: causal, sliding-window, ALiBi, PrefixLM, and document masking each traditionally needed a hand-written fused kernel or fell back to the slow path. FlexAttention lets the user supply a Python score_mod function and block-sparse mask; torch.compile fuses it into the tiled loop, generating forward and backward kernels the PyTorch team reports at roughly 90% of hand-tuned FlashAttention-2 performance Verify. It is the compiler bet: encode the FlashAttention schedule once, let codegen handle the algebra.

Ring Attention (Liu, Zaharia, Abbeel, 2023) is Theorem 31.1 stretched across machines: shard the sequence over devices, and pass $K,V$ blocks around a ring while each device updates its queries' running $(m, \ell, \tilde{O})$ state against each arriving block, overlapping the communication with the blockwise compute. Because online softmax is order-independent, the result is exact, and maximum context length scales linearly with device count — the mechanism behind million-token contexts. Chapter 32 covers its placement in the parallelism taxonomy.

31.8 What Writing a Kernel Actually Involves

Demystifying the artifact’s real-GPU counterpart: a production FlashAttention kernel is the same ~40 lines of algorithm embedded in ~10$\times$ that of scheduling. The working sequence, in the order practitioners actually iterate: (1) derive the tiling from the SRAM budget — pick $B_r, B_c$ so $Q_i, K_j, V_j$, the score tile, and the accumulator fit in shared memory and registers, with headroom for double-buffering; (2) make every HBM access coalesced and every shared-memory layout bank-conflict-free (swizzling); (3) balance occupancy against register pressure — the accumulator $\tilde{O}_i$ lives in registers, and spilling it to local memory silently reintroduces the traffic the algorithm exists to avoid; (4) overlap: async copies (cp.async, TMA on Hopper) prefetching tile $j{+}1$ during tile $j$; (5) autotune tile sizes, warp counts, and pipeline stages per (GPU, $d_k$, dtype) triple, because the optimum moves. Triton occupies the productive middle ground — you write the tile program, the compiler handles layouts and pipelining — and a Triton FlashAttention lands within a few tens of percent of CUTLASS-based CUDA on most shapes, at a tenth of the code Likely. Validate the way the artifact does: exactness against a reference at FP32/FP64 first, adversarial shapes (ragged tails, $n$ not divisible by tiles, huge logits) second, a roofline measurement (Chapter 30) third — achieved bytes and FLOPs against the machine ceilings, never wall-clock alone.

Common Pitfall

Forgetting to rescale the output accumulator when the running max updates. The buggy inner loop updates $\ell_i \leftarrow \alpha \ell_i + \mathrm{rowsum}\,\tilde P_{ij}$ correctly but writes $\tilde{O}_i \leftarrow \tilde{O}_i + \tilde{P}_{ij}V_j$, dropping the $\mathrm{diag}(\alpha)$ factor. This passes small unit tests whenever the first tile happens to contain the row max (then $\alpha = 1$ forever after) — e.g. tests with i.i.d. small-magnitude logits and one tile, or causal tests where early positions dominate — and then produces subtly wrong attention on real data where later keys score highest. The symptom is outputs biased toward early-sequence values, which looks like a modeling problem, not a kernel bug. Test specifically with the row max forced into the last tile; the artifact's $\pm 15$-range logits across many chunk splits exist for exactly this reason.

Artifact 31.1 — Tiled Online-Softmax Attention with I/O Accounting

The full forward pass of Sections 31.2–31.3 in pure NumPy, instrumented rather than timed: since no CPU run can demonstrate GPU speedups, the artifact instead verifies the four claims the speedups rest on. It checks (a) exactness of the tiled pass against naive attention across seven tile shapes, including ragged edges ($n = 257$ against tiles of 16, 53, 100, 128); (b) exactness of streaming softmax against batch softmax across chunk sizes; (c) that peak intermediate allocation is $O(n)$, by counting live array elements inside the tile loop and comparing against the $2n^2$ elements the naive version materializes; and (d) that counted K/V block reads equal $\lceil n/B_r \rceil \cdot n \cdot 2d_k$ exactly, reproducing the $1/M$ tile-size dependence of Theorem 31.2 as a measured table. A torch SDPA cross-check runs if available.

"""Artifact 31.1 -- Tiled online-softmax attention (FlashAttention forward) in NumPy.

Verifies four claims from the chapter:
  (a) tiled output == naive attention to ~1e-6, across tile sizes incl. ragged edges;
  (b) running-rescale online softmax == batch softmax to ~1e-12 on a chunked row;
  (c) peak intermediate memory is O(N), not O(N^2)  (explicit allocation accounting);
  (d) HBM-equivalent reads of K/V blocks scale as N^2 * d / Br  (inverse in tile size),
      matching the paper's O(N^2 d^2 / M) analysis with Br ~ M/d.
No GPU is used or simulated for timing; "HBM reads" here means counted array elements
that a real kernel would have to fetch from off-chip memory. Everything else is exact.
"""
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- reference path
def naive_attention(Q, K, V):
    """Standard attention: materializes the full N x N score matrix.

    Returns (output, peak_intermediate_elements). The peak intermediate is the
    N x N score matrix plus its N x N softmax -- what a framework without a fused
    kernel actually allocates (scores and probs coexist during softmax)."""
    N, d = Q.shape
    S = (Q @ K.T) / np.sqrt(d)                    # N x N   <- the quadratic buffer
    m = S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)              # stabilize
    P = np.exp(S - m)
    P /= P.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)             # N x N softmax
    return P @ V, 2 * N * N                        # S and P both live: 2*N^2 elements


def batch_softmax(x):
    e = np.exp(x - x.max())
    return e / e.sum()


# ---------------------------------------------------- (b) online softmax, one row
def online_softmax(x, chunk):
    """Streaming softmax over a 1-D array seen in chunks of size `chunk`.

    Maintains running max m and running normalizer l; every time a new chunk
    raises the max, the old normalizer is rescaled by exp(m_old - m_new).
    Algebraically identical to batch softmax (Theorem 31.1)."""
    m, l = -np.inf, 0.0
    for j in range(0, len(x), chunk):
        xj = x[j:j + chunk]
        m_new = max(m, xj.max())
        l = l * np.exp(m - m_new) + np.exp(xj - m_new).sum()
        m = m_new
    # second pass just to emit probabilities (attention never needs this pass:
    # it folds the division into the running output accumulator instead)
    return np.exp(x - m) / l


# ------------------------------------------------- (a,c,d) tiled forward pass
def flash_forward(Q, K, V, Br, Bc):
    """FlashAttention forward pass: tile Q into Br-row blocks, K/V into Bc-row
    blocks; never materialize more than a Br x Bc score tile.

    Returns (O, logsumexp L, stats) where stats counts
      kv_read_elems : elements of K and V blocks loaded across the whole loop
                      (the HBM traffic a real kernel pays), and
      peak_elems    : max intermediate elements alive inside the tile loops
                      (excludes inputs Q,K,V and the returned O,L)."""
    N, d = Q.shape
    scale = 1.0 / np.sqrt(d)
    O = np.zeros((N, d))
    L = np.zeros(N)                                # logsumexp per row, kept for backward
    kv_read_elems = 0
    peak_elems = 0
    for i in range(0, N, Br):                      # outer loop over query blocks
        Qi = Q[i:i + Br]                           # Br x d (ragged at the edge)
        bi = Qi.shape[0]
        mi = np.full(bi, -np.inf)                  # running row max
        li = np.zeros(bi)                          # running normalizer
        Oi = np.zeros((bi, d))                     # unnormalized output accumulator
        for j in range(0, N, Bc):                  # inner loop over key/value blocks
            Kj, Vj = K[j:j + Bc], V[j:j + Bc]      # each "loaded from HBM"
            bj = Kj.shape[0]
            kv_read_elems += 2 * bj * d            # count the load: K block + V block
            Sij = (Qi @ Kj.T) * scale              # bi x bj score TILE -- the only
            m_new = np.maximum(mi, Sij.max(axis=1))  # quadratic-shaped object, tiny
            Pij = np.exp(Sij - m_new[:, None])     # bi x bj
            alpha = np.exp(mi - m_new)             # rescale factor for stale state
            li = li * alpha + Pij.sum(axis=1)
            Oi = Oi * alpha[:, None] + Pij @ Vj    # rescale old accumulator, add new
            mi = m_new
            # everything alive right now inside the loops, in elements:
            live = (bi * d          # Qi
                    + 2 * bj * d    # Kj, Vj
                    + 2 * bi * bj   # Sij, Pij
                    + 3 * bi        # mi, li, alpha (m_new aliases into mi next)
                    + bi            # m_new
                    + bi * d)       # Oi
            peak_elems = max(peak_elems, live)
        O[i:i + Br] = Oi / li[:, None]             # single deferred division per row
        L[i:i + Br] = mi + np.log(li)              # logsumexp: all backward needs
    return O, L, {"kv_read_elems": kv_read_elems, "peak_elems": peak_elems}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------- checks
if __name__ == "__main__":
    N, d = 257, 64                                 # deliberately not a tile multiple
    Q = rng.standard_normal((N, d))
    K = rng.standard_normal((N, d))
    V = rng.standard_normal((N, d))
    O_ref, naive_peak = naive_attention(Q, K, V)

    # (b) online softmax == batch softmax to ~1e-12, chunked ragged
    x = rng.standard_normal(1000) * 5              # spread ~ +-15: overflow-prone naively
    worst_b = 0.0
    for chunk in (1, 7, 100, 333, 1000):
        err = np.abs(online_softmax(x, chunk) - batch_softmax(x)).max()
        worst_b = max(worst_b, err)
        assert err < 1e-12, (chunk, err)
    print(f"(b) online softmax vs batch, worst over chunk sizes {{1,7,100,333,1000}}: "
          f"max|diff| = {worst_b:.2e}  (< 1e-12)")

    # (a) tiled forward == naive across tile shapes, incl. ragged edges
    print("\n(a) tiled forward vs naive (N=257, d=64):")
    worst = 0.0
    for (Br, Bc) in [(16, 16), (32, 64), (64, 32), (64, 53), (128, 128), (257, 257), (100, 17)]:
        O, L, st = flash_forward(Q, K, V, Br, Bc)
        err = np.abs(O - O_ref).max()
        worst = max(worst, err)
        assert err < 1e-6, (Br, Bc, err)
        print(f"    Br={Br:>3} Bc={Bc:>3}  max|diff| = {err:.2e}")
    print(f"    worst over all tilings: {worst:.2e}  (< 1e-6)")

    # (c) peak intermediate memory: O(N) vs the naive O(N^2)
    _, _, st = flash_forward(Q, K, V, 64, 64)
    print(f"\n(c) peak intermediates, Br=Bc=64: tiled {st['peak_elems']:,} elements "
          f"vs naive {naive_peak:,} elements "
          f"(ratio {naive_peak / st['peak_elems']:.1f}x); tiled peak is independent of N "
          f"given fixed tiles (plus the N x d output, which naive also needs)")
    assert st["peak_elems"] < 6 * N * d            # O(N*d) bound, comfortably
    assert st["peak_elems"] * 4 < naive_peak       # far below the N^2 buffers
    # peak must not grow with N at fixed tile size (pure O(1) inner state):
    N2 = 2 * N
    Q2, K2, V2 = (rng.standard_normal((N2, d)) for _ in range(3))
    _, _, st2 = flash_forward(Q2, K2, V2, 64, 64)
    assert st2["peak_elems"] == st["peak_elems"], "inner-loop state grew with N"
    print(f"    doubling N to {N2}: tiled peak unchanged at {st2['peak_elems']:,} elements; "
          f"naive would need {2 * N2 * N2:,}")

    # (d) K/V HBM reads vs tile size: predicted = ceil(N/Br) * N * 2d
    print("\n(d) K/V read accounting (N=257, d=64):  reads = ceil(N/Br) * N * 2d")
    print(f"    {'Br':>4} {'measured':>12} {'predicted':>12} {'vs one pass over K,V':>22}")
    for Br in (16, 32, 64, 128, 257):
        _, _, st = flash_forward(Q, K, V, Br, 64)
        Tr = -(-N // Br)                           # ceil
        pred = Tr * N * 2 * d
        assert st["kv_read_elems"] == pred, (Br, st["kv_read_elems"], pred)
        print(f"    {Br:>4} {st['kv_read_elems']:>12,} {pred:>12,} {Tr:>20}x")
    print("    reads scale as 1/Br exactly: bigger query tiles (more SRAM) => fewer "
          "passes over K,V. With Br ~ M/d this is the O(N^2 d^2 / M) of Dao et al. 2022.")

    # cross-check against torch SDPA if available
    try:
        import torch
    except ImportError:
        torch = None
    if torch is not None:
        ref = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            torch.from_numpy(Q)[None], torch.from_numpy(K)[None], torch.from_numpy(V)[None]
        )[0].numpy()
        O, _, _ = flash_forward(Q, K, V, 64, 64)
        err = np.abs(O - ref).max()
        assert err < 1e-6
        print(f"\ncross-check vs torch SDPA: max|diff| = {err:.2e}")
    else:
        print("\n[skipped: torch not installed]")
    print("\nall assertions passed")

Running this prints, in about two seconds: online-vs-batch softmax worst discrepancy $4.44\times 10^{-16}$ over five chunkings; tiled-vs-naive worst error $1.22\times10^{-15}$ over seven tilings (assertion threshold $10^{-6}$, met with nine orders to spare, and a matching $7.77\times 10^{-16}$ against torch SDPA); a peak-allocation ratio of $132{,}098$ naive elements to $24{,}832$ tiled at $B_r{=}B_c{=}64$, with the tiled peak provably unchanged when $n$ doubles to 514; and the read-accounting table above, where measured K/V element reads match $\lceil n/B_r\rceil\, n\, 2d_k$ exactly at every tile size — 559,232 at $B_r{=}16$ down to 32,896 at $B_r{=}257$.

Under Encryption

This chapter's economics invert on ciphertext. Under CKKS the scarce resources are multiplicative depth and rotations, not bandwidth: the matmuls $QK^\top$ and $PV$ are the cheap part, while online softmax's running max is a comparison — non-polynomial, so each tile's $\max$ would burn depth on a high-degree polynomial approximation. Encrypted attention therefore drops max-stabilization entirely and bounds the input range instead, and the recompute-instead-of-store bargain of Section 31.4 stops paying: recomputing a tile re-spends depth that only expensive bootstrapping buys back, so storing ciphertexts wins. Chapters 38 and 39 take up softmax approximation in detail.

Key Takeaways
  • FlashAttention performs the same $4n^2 d_k$ attention matmul FLOPs as the naive algorithm (backward: more, via recomputation) — its entire speedup comes from cutting HBM accesses from $\Theta(n d_k + n^2)$ to $\Theta(n^2 d_k^2 / M)$ and its memory saving from never materializing $S$ or $P$. Certain
  • Online softmax is exactly batch softmax under any blocking of the row — the rescale factor $e^{m_{\text{old}}-m_{\text{new}}}$ makes the recurrence associative — and this associativity is the single identity underlying FlashAttention, split-KV decoding, and Ring Attention. Certain
  • The backward pass stores only the $O(n)$ logsumexp vector and recomputes score tiles, accepting a ~17% increase in attention matmul FLOPs per training step; on memory-bound hardware, recomputation is cheaper than remembering. Certain
  • FlashAttention-2's gains were pure scheduling — fewer non-matmul FLOPs, sequence-length parallelism, split-Q warp partitioning — for ~2$\times$ over FA-1 and up to 72% end-to-end MFU on A100; FlashAttention-3 rebuilt the pipeline around Hopper's TMA/WGMMA asynchrony plus FP8 with block quantization and incoherent processing, for 1.5–2$\times$ over FA-2, ~85% H100 utilization in BF16, and ~1.3 PFLOPs/s in FP8. Verify
  • A kernel is an algorithm plus a schedule, and the schedule is hardware-generation-specific: FA-1→2→3 rewrote the same mathematics three times as the bottleneck moved from I/O algorithm to occupancy to pipeline overlap — expect a fourth rewrite per new architecture. Likely
Chapter 32

Distributed Training

Learning Objectives
  • Derive the ring all-reduce communication volume $2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ per device and show it is bandwidth-optimal and (asymptotically) independent of worker count.
  • Derive the memory breakdown of mixed-precision Adam training — 16 bytes per parameter — and state exactly what each ZeRO stage shards and what it costs in communication.
  • Compute tensor-parallel communication volume per layer and explain why tensor parallelism stays within a node while data parallelism crosses nodes.
  • Derive the pipeline bubble fraction $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$ and explain the one-forward-one-backward and interleaved schedules.
  • Implement ring all-reduce and a parallelism planner in working code.
Read alongside — The HuggingFace Ultra-Scale Playbook is the single best companion: it walks the same parallelisms with profiler traces from real clusters. Stanford CS336 covers the systems half of this chapter as a graded assignment. Raschka shows the single-node DDP starting point in PyTorch.

Chapters 30 and 31 treated one GPU: the memory wall, kernel fusion, FlashAttention. But no frontier model fits on one device — a 70B-parameter model needs 1.12 TB just for training state, fourteen 80 GB accelerators before a single activation is stored. This chapter is about the four ways to split the work — data, tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism — and the central thesis is that they are not interchangeable. Each one trades a specific resource: data parallelism spends memory to save communication, ZeRO spends communication to save memory, tensor parallelism spends enormous bandwidth to shard compute, pipeline parallelism spends idle “bubble” time to shard depth. Matching the combination to your interconnect hierarchy is the most expensive decision in the field; getting it wrong can idle a cluster by an order of magnitude. Chapter 33 applies the same reasoning to inference; Chapter 22 supplied the mixture-of-experts models that Section 32.7 distributes.

32.1 Data Parallelism and Gradient All-Reduce

Data parallelism (DP) is the baseline: replicate all $N$ parameters on $P$ workers, give each worker a disjoint shard of the batch, and average gradients before the optimizer step. With per-worker batch $B/P$, worker $p$ computes $g_p = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta; x_p)$, and the update uses $\bar g = \frac{1}{P}\sum_p g_p$. Because every worker applies the same update to the same replica, synchronous DP computes exactly the same update as single-device training at batch $B$ — the parallelism changes throughput, not the optimization trajectory (up to summation order in floating point, see Chapter 5). Certain The batch-size and learning-rate consequences of growing $B$ with $P$ were Chapter 15's subject.

The cost is one gradient synchronization per step: an all-reduce of $S = N \cdot b$ bytes, where $b$ is the gradient dtype width (2 for bf16). For a 70B model that is 140 GB of gradient per step, every step. Two facts rescue DP. First, the all-reduce can overlap with the backward pass: gradients for layer $l$ are final as soon as backprop passes layer $l$, so frameworks bucket parameters (PyTorch DDP defaults to 25 MB buckets) and launch reductions on completed buckets while earlier layers are still differentiating. On a well-tuned setup, communication hides almost entirely behind the backward pass. Certain Second, the all-reduce itself can be done with per-worker traffic nearly independent of $P$ — that is Section 32.2.

Common Pitfall

Gradient accumulation without suppressing synchronization. If you accumulate over $k$ micro-batches by calling backward() $k$ times inside DDP, every call fires the bucketed all-reduce, multiplying communication by $k$ for identical results. PyTorch's model.no_sync() context exists precisely to skip the reduction on the first $k-1$ calls; forgetting it is invisible in the loss curve and can double or triple step time. The dual mistake: with no_sync, remember that accumulated gradients are a sum, so either scale the loss by $1/k$ or the learning rate accordingly — silently changing the effective step size is a classic source of “multi-node runs diverge” bugs.

32.2 Collective Primitives

Definition 32.1 (Collective operations)

Over $P$ workers each holding a tensor of $S$ bytes: broadcast copies one worker's tensor to all; reduce sums all tensors onto one worker; all-reduce leaves the sum on every worker; reduce-scatter leaves the $p$-th $1/P$-shard of the sum on worker $p$; all-gather starts from such shards and reassembles the full tensor everywhere; all-to-all transposes shards across workers ($P$ shards each, worker $p$ sends its $q$-th shard to worker $q$). The identity that organizes this chapter: all-reduce = reduce-scatter followed by all-gather.

The naive all-reduce — gather everything to a root, sum, broadcast back — moves $2(P-1)S$ bytes through the root's single link. The ring algorithm removes the bottleneck. Arrange workers in a cycle and split each tensor into $P$ chunks of $S/P$ bytes. Reduce-scatter phase, $P-1$ steps: at step $t$, worker $p$ sends chunk $(p-t) \bmod P$ to its right neighbor, which adds it into its own copy. Each chunk accumulates one contribution per hop; after $P-1$ steps, worker $p$ holds the complete sum of chunk $(p+1) \bmod P$. All-gather phase, $P-1$ more steps: each worker forwards the completed chunks around the ring, overwriting rather than adding. Every link carries exactly one chunk per step in each phase, in parallel.

Theorem 32.1 (Ring all-reduce is bandwidth-optimal)

Ring all-reduce completes with every worker sending (and receiving) exactly $2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ bytes, and no all-reduce whose messages are partial sums of input segments can beat this per-worker bound.

Proof. Achievability: each phase has $P-1$ steps and each worker transmits one chunk of $S/P$ bytes per step, giving $2(P-1)\cdot S/P$ — the artifact counts this exactly. For the lower bound (sketch, after Patarasuk–Yuan): any correct algorithm implicitly solves reduce-scatter and all-gather. In the gather direction, worker $p$ must end holding the $\frac{P-1}{P}S$ bytes of reduced output it did not itself finish, and since inputs are arbitrary these bytes are incompressible, so it receives at least $\frac{P-1}{P}S$. In the reduce direction, each worker's input must contribute to shards completed elsewhere; summing over workers, at least $\frac{P-1}{P}S$ additional bytes must leave each worker as (partial-sum) payloads. Summing the two requirements, per-worker traffic is at least $2\frac{P-1}{P}S$, which the ring meets. $\blacksquare$

The crucial reading: $2\frac{P-1}{P}S < 2S$ for every $P$, so per-device traffic is bounded by twice the tensor size no matter how many workers join. Scaling from 8 to 8{,}000 GPUs raises per-GPU all-reduce traffic by only $\frac{7999/8000}{7/8} - 1 \approx 14\%$. What does grow with $P$ is the latency term: $2(P-1)$ sequential steps, each paying link latency $\alpha$. In the $\alpha$–$\beta$ cost model, ring all-reduce costs $2(P-1)\alpha + 2\frac{P-1}{P}S\beta$, where $\beta$ is seconds per byte. For large tensors the $\beta$ term dominates and rings win; for small tensors (or huge $P$) the $\alpha$ term dominates, which is why NCCL switches to tree algorithms — $O(\log P)$ latency at the price of constant-factor bandwidth — below a size threshold, and why DDP buckets gradients into ~25 MB messages rather than reducing per-tensor. Certain

Example 32.1 (Counting the ring, $P=4$)

Four workers, $S = 128$ bytes (sixteen fp64 values, four chunks of 32 bytes). Reduce-scatter: 3 steps × 32 bytes sent per worker = 96 bytes. All-gather: 3 steps × 32 = 96 bytes. Total per worker: $192 = 2\cdot\frac{3}{4}\cdot 128$ bytes, matching the formula exactly — the artifact asserts this equality for $P \in \{2,4,5,8,16\}$. The naive gather-broadcast pushes $2(P-1)S = 768$ bytes through the root's link: $P$ times worse, and the gap is exactly $P$× for every configuration tested.

32.3 ZeRO and FSDP

DP's memory problem is that every replica stores the full training state. For mixed-precision Adam (Chapters 5 and 13), the per-parameter cost is:

$$\underbrace{2}_{\text{bf16 weights}} + \underbrace{2}_{\text{bf16 grads}} + \underbrace{4}_{\text{fp32 master}} + \underbrace{4}_{\text{fp32 } m} + \underbrace{4}_{\text{fp32 } v} = 16 \text{ bytes/parameter.}$$

The fp32 master copy exists because bf16's 8-bit mantissa cannot absorb updates of relative size $\sim\eta\cdot 10^{-3}$ without stagnating (Chapter 5); $m$ and $v$ are Adam's moments. So a 7B model needs 112 GB and a 70B model 1.12 TB — before activations, which add a batch-dependent amount on top. Certain

Example 32.2 (Hand count on a 46-parameter MLP)

Take an MLP $8\to4\to2$ with biases: $8\cdot4+4+4\cdot2+2 = 46$ parameters. Materialize the six tensors: bf16 weights $2\cdot46=92$ B, bf16 grads 92 B, fp32 master $4\cdot46=184$ B, $m$ 184 B, $v$ 184 B. Total $736 = 16 \times 46$ bytes. The artifact allocates exactly these arrays, sums their nbytes, and asserts 736; a torch cross-check confirms torch.optim.Adam really keeps two fp32 state tensors per parameter (92 state elements for the 46 parameters).

ZeRO's observation is that in DP these 16 bytes are replicated $P$ times, yet the optimizer state is only ever used elementwise — worker $p$ can own the state for $1/P$ of the parameters and update only those. The stages shard progressively:

StageShardsBytes/param/deviceComm volume per step (per device)
DP (ZeRO-0)nothing$16$$2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ (grad all-reduce)
ZeRO-1optimizer state$4 + 12/P$$2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ (reduce-scatter grads + all-gather params)
ZeRO-2+ gradients$2 + 14/P$$2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ — unchanged
ZeRO-3+ parameters$16/P$$3\frac{P-1}{P}S$ — 1.5× DP

Stages 1 and 2 are nearly free: the all-reduce decomposes as reduce-scatter + all-gather anyway (Definition 32.1), and ZeRO merely inserts the sharded optimizer step between the two halves — reduce-scatter the gradients, update your shard, all-gather the updated bf16 weights. Same $2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ on the wire. ZeRO-3 additionally shards the weights themselves, so each layer's parameters must be all-gathered just-in-time in the forward pass, again in the backward pass, then freed — hence the extra $\frac{P-1}{P}S$ and, in practice, sensitivity to the $\alpha$ term because the gathers are per-layer-sized and sit on the critical path unless prefetched. Certain PyTorch FSDP is the native implementation: FULL_SHARD corresponds to ZeRO-3 and SHARD_GRAD_OP to ZeRO-2, with wrapping granularity (usually one transformer block) setting the gather size. Verify against current FSDP docs; the API has churned (FSDP2 shards per-parameter on DTensor).

The planner in the artifact turns the table into decisions: at $P=8$ on 80 GB devices, a 7B model is infeasible under plain DP (112 GB) but fits under ZeRO-1 at 38.5 GB; a 70B model needs ZeRO-3 and $P \ge 64$ (17.5 GB at $P=64$, versus 140 GB at $P=8$). Sharding only pays down the $12N$ or $14N$ replicated bytes across $P$ — the $2$–$4$ bytes/param that remain replicated set a floor that only ZeRO-3, tensor, or pipeline parallelism can breach.

32.4 Tensor Parallelism

Tensor parallelism (TP) shards individual weight matrices across $t$ devices so that even one layer's compute and parameters are split. The Megatron scheme pairs a matmul sharded along its output dimension with one sharded along its input dimension (Megatron calls these “column-” and “row-parallel”, named in its $y = xA$ convention — transposed relative to this book's $y=Wx$) so that only a single synchronization is needed per pair. For the transformer MLP $Y = W_2\,\phi(W_1 x)$ with $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{4d\times d}$ split by rows across $t$ devices (each holds $W_1^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{(4d/t)\times d}$) and $W_2$ split by columns to match: each device computes $\phi(W_1^{(i)}x)$ with no communication — the nonlinearity applies elementwise to a complete shard — then $W_2^{(i)}\phi(\cdot)$ produces a partial sum of the full output, and one all-reduce over the $B\,n\,d$-element activation finishes the layer. Attention shards by heads with the same pattern: QKV projections column-split (each device owns $h/t$ heads, softmax is per-head so it never crosses devices), output projection row-split, one all-reduce. Per transformer layer: two all-reduces forward (attention, MLP) and two backward, each of $A = B\,n\,d\,b$ bytes. Certain

Per-device TP traffic per layer per micro-batch is therefore $4 \cdot 2\frac{t-1}{t} A \approx 8A$. Unlike DP's once-per-step gradient reduction, this sits inside the forward and backward of every layer, on the critical path, largely un-overlappable. Concretely: $d = 8192$, $n = 8192$, $B=1$, bf16 gives $A = 134$ MB; with $t=8$, that is $4 \times 1.75 \times 134\text{ MB} \approx 0.94$ GB per layer, or $\approx 75$ GB across 80 layers — per micro-batch. Over intra-node NVLink at $\sim$450 GB/s per direction (H100 Verify against vendor specs) that is $\sim$0.17 s; over a 400 Gb/s InfiniBand NIC ($\sim$50 GB/s Verify) it is $\sim$1.5 s — roughly a 9× penalty on communication that compute cannot hide. This single ratio is why the standard rule holds: TP degree $\le$ GPUs per node (typically 8), always inside the NVLink domain; DP and pipeline parallelism take the slow links. DP tolerates slow links because its volume is per-step and overlappable; TP does not because its volume is per-layer and blocking. Certain

32.5 Sequence and Context Parallelism

Two gaps remain in TP. First, inside a TP group the LayerNorm and dropout regions operate on replicated full activations — wasted memory $\times t$. Megatron-style sequence parallelism shards those regions along the sequence axis and replaces each TP all-reduce with an all-gather (entering the matmul region) plus a reduce-scatter (leaving it). Since an all-reduce is exactly that pair, total communication volume is unchanged, while the replicated activations shrink by $t$. It is a strict win and modern stacks enable it by default. Likely

Second, very long contexts make the $O(n)$ activations and $O(n^2)$ attention of a single device prohibitive even with TP. Context parallelism (Ring Attention) shards the sequence itself across $c$ devices: each holds $n/c$ queries permanently, while key/value blocks circulate around a ring, and each device accumulates its queries' attention output blockwise using the online-softmax rescaling of Chapter 31 — FlashAttention's tiling argument, lifted from SRAM tiles to devices. Communication per ring step is the $KV$ block ($2\cdot\frac{n}{c}\,d\,b$ bytes) and overlaps with the attention compute of the current block, so for long enough $n$ the ring is compute-bound. Causal masking makes late-position devices do more work than early ones; striped/zigzag sharding rebalances. Certain

32.6 Pipeline Parallelism and Bubbles

Pipeline parallelism (PP) cuts the model by depth: stage $i$ of $p$ holds layers $iL/p$ to $(i+1)L/p$ and forwards activations to stage $i+1$. Communication is tiny — one boundary activation of $B\,n\,d\,b$ bytes per micro-batch between adjacent stages, point-to-point, ideal for slow inter-node links. The cost is idleness: with one batch, stage $p-1$ waits for $p-1$ forward hops before doing anything, and stage 0 waits again during the backward sweep.

Split the batch into $m$ micro-batches, each taking $t_f + t_b$ per stage. Useful work per stage is $m(t_f+t_b)$; the pipeline drains and fills over $(p-1)(t_f+t_b)$ of unavoidable idle time, so total time is $(m+p-1)(t_f+t_b)$ and

$$\text{bubble fraction} \;=\; \frac{(p-1)(t_f+t_b)}{(m+p-1)(t_f+t_b)} \;=\; \frac{p-1}{m+p-1}.$$

Driving the bubble down means $m \gg p$ — but GPipe, which runs all $m$ forwards then all $m$ backwards, must hold activations for all $m$ in-flight micro-batches, and Chapter 30's arithmetic says activations are the scarce resource. The one-forward-one-backward (1F1B) schedule fixes memory, not the bubble: after warm-up, each stage alternates one forward with one backward, so a micro-batch's activations are freed as soon as its backward completes and at most $p$ micro-batches are ever in flight — peak activation memory drops from $O(m)$ to $O(p)$ while the bubble fraction stays exactly $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$. The interleaved schedule then attacks the bubble itself: give each device $v$ non-contiguous model chunks (device 0 holds layers 1–4 and 33–36, say), so a micro-batch clears each chunk in $t_f/v$, and fill/drain time shrinks by $v$: bubble $\approx \frac{p-1}{v\,m + p - 1}$, at the price of $v\times$ more inter-stage communication and a more intricate schedule. Zero-bubble schedules go further by splitting the backward pass into input-gradient and weight-gradient halves and using the latter as bubble filler, reaching near-zero bubble at matched memory. Likely

Example 32.3 (Bubble arithmetic)

$p = 8$ stages, $m = 32$ micro-batches: bubble $= 7/39 = 17.9\%$ — nearly a fifth of the cluster idle. Doubling to $m=64$: $7/71 = 9.9\%$. Interleaving with $v=4$ at $m=32$: $7/(4\cdot32+7) = 5.2\%$. To halve a bubble you double $m$ (needs batch size, hurts at fixed tokens-per-step) or double $v$ (needs communication); nothing is free.

32.7 Expert Parallelism

Mixture-of-experts layers (Chapter 22) add a fourth axis: place different experts on different devices (EP degree $e$), since each token activates only $k$ of $E$ experts. Routing turns a local matmul into communication: after the router picks top-$k$ experts per token, an all-to-all ships each token's $d$-vector to the devices owning its experts, the expert MLPs run, and a second all-to-all ships results back — two all-to-alls per MoE layer, each moving up to $k\,d\,b$ bytes outbound per locally held token. Unlike all-reduce, all-to-all traffic is data-dependent: a hot expert overflows its capacity buffer and tokens get dropped or rerouted, so the capacity factor is a real hyperparameter, and load-balancing losses (Chapter 22) are as much a systems necessity as a modeling one. EP composes naturally with DP (experts sharded where replicas once were) and prefers fast links for the same reason TP does: the all-to-all is on the critical path. Certain

32.8 Composing the Parallelisms

A frontier run uses several axes at once; the world size factors as $P_{\text{total}} = t \cdot p \cdot P_{\text{DP}}$ (times context and expert degrees where used). The composition rule follows directly from each axis's traffic pattern and the interconnect hierarchy:

AxisTrafficWhenPlacement
Tensor (+seq.)$\sim 8\frac{t-1}{t}A$ per layer, blockinglayer too big / activations too biginnermost, within NVLink node
Context$KV$ ring per attention, overlappablelong sequencesnode or adjacent nodes
Pipelineone activation per micro-batch, P2Pmodel depth exceeds a nodeacross nodes
Data / ZeRO$2$–$3\frac{P-1}{P}S$ per step, overlappablealways, for throughputoutermost, across nodes
Expert2 all-to-alls per MoE layerMoE modelsfast links preferred

Worked composition for a 70B dense model on 512 × 80 GB GPUs: $t=8$ (one node) cuts per-device weights+grads+state to 140 GB; $p=4$ brings it to 35 GB, leaving room for activations; $P_{\text{DP}} = 512/(8\cdot4) = 16$ replicas with ZeRO-1 sharding the remaining optimizer state. The alternative — no TP or PP, pure FSDP/ZeRO-3 — is also feasible: 64-way sharding already fits (17.5 GB/device by the artifact's planner), so on 512 GPUs one shards within groups of 64 and replicates 8-fold across groups (hybrid sharding); this route is often preferred below ~100B for its simplicity; above that, per-layer all-gathers on inter-node links start losing to PP's point-to-point trickle. Which wins is cluster-specific — the field genuinely splits, with Megatron-style 3D favored on InfiniBand-rich clusters and FSDP favored on Ethernet or smaller runs; a profile of your own interconnect settles it. Contested The one non-negotiable: never let TP cross the node boundary. Running $t=16$ across two nodes puts four blocking all-reduces per layer onto links $\sim$9× slower; that communication is exposed on the critical path, so once it dominates, step time degrades several-fold. Likely

32.9 Failures at Scale

Synchronous training has no partial credit: one failed worker stalls all $P$. Failure rates compound linearly, so if a single GPU-plus-links has mean time between failures $M_1$, the cluster fails every $M_1/P$. At $M_1 = 5$ years and $P = 16{,}384$, that is one failure every $\sim$2.7 hours. Meta's Llama 3 405B report is the public datapoint: 419 unexpected interruptions over 54 days of pretraining on 16K H100s — about one every 3 hours, ~78% attributed to hardware, GPUs and HBM leading. Verify against the Llama 3 paper's reliability section.

The defenses are checkpointing, redundancy, and detection. Checkpoint interval is an optimization, not a habit: writing costs $\delta$, and a crash loses on average half an interval $\tau$, so expected overhead per unit time is $\delta/\tau + \tau/(2M)$, minimized at the Young–Daly interval $\tau^{*} = \sqrt{2\delta M}$. With $\delta = 5$ min and $M = 3$ h, $\tau^{*} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 300 \cdot 10800}\,\text{s} \approx 42$ min. Fast distributed checkpointing (each rank writes its shard; asynchronous drain to remote storage) pushes $\delta$ down and with it the whole overhead curve. Beyond clean crashes lurk silent data corruptions — faulty ALUs that miscompute without raising errors, producing NaNs or, worse, quietly wrong gradients; detection requires redundant computation or algebraic checks, and large labs report SDC rates high enough to matter at $10^4$-GPU scale. Likely Straggler mitigation, spare-node hot-swap, and elastic restart round out the toolkit; every one is amortized bookkeeping against the $M/P$ clock.

Artifact 32.1 — Ring All-Reduce and a ZeRO Planner, From Scratch

The sandbox cannot launch multiple processes, so torch.distributed is out; instead the $P$ workers are $P$ numpy arrays in one process, and every byte that would cross a link is counted explicitly — the algorithm and the counts are exactly NCCL-ring's, only the transport is simulated. The module implements both ring phases with explicit chunk indices, asserts exact agreement with a direct sum (integer-valued data, so summation order cannot hide errors), asserts the per-worker wire count equals $2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ exactly for five $(P, S)$ pairs, and shows by counting that gather-then-broadcast moves $P\times$ more through the root's link. The planner then prices DP and ZeRO-1/2/3 per device, with the 16-bytes-per-parameter Adam breakdown asserted against a hand count on a 46-parameter MLP and cross-checked against torch.optim.Adam's actual state tensors.

"""Artifact 32.1 -- Ring all-reduce from scratch, plus a ZeRO parallelism planner.

torch.distributed cannot launch multiple processes in this sandbox, so the P
"workers" are simulated as P numpy arrays inside one process, and every byte
that would cross the wire is counted explicitly.  The algorithm and the byte
counts are exactly what NCCL's ring would do; only the transport is fake.
"""
import numpy as np

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None

# ----------------------------- ring all-reduce ------------------------------

def ring_allreduce(bufs):
    """All-reduce (sum) across P simulated workers arranged in a ring.

    bufs : list of P 1-D numpy arrays of equal length n, with P | n.
    Mutates bufs in place; afterwards every worker holds sum_p bufs[p].
    Returns sent[p] = bytes worker p transmitted on its outgoing link.
    """
    P, n = len(bufs), bufs[0].size
    assert n % P == 0, "pad the tensor so P divides its length"
    chunks = [np.split(b, P) for b in bufs]          # views into each buffer
    sent = [0] * P

    # Phase 1: reduce-scatter, P-1 steps.  At step t worker p sends chunk
    # (p - t) mod P to its right neighbour p+1, which adds it in.  After the
    # last step, worker p owns the fully reduced chunk (p + 1) mod P.
    for t in range(P - 1):
        msgs = []
        for p in range(P):
            c = (p - t) % P
            msgs.append(((p + 1) % P, c, chunks[p][c].copy()))
            sent[p] += chunks[p][c].nbytes
        for dst, c, payload in msgs:                 # deliver only after all send
            chunks[dst][c] += payload

    # Phase 2: all-gather, P-1 steps.  At step t worker p forwards the
    # completed chunk (p + 1 - t) mod P to its right neighbour, overwriting.
    for t in range(P - 1):
        msgs = []
        for p in range(P):
            c = (p + 1 - t) % P
            msgs.append(((p + 1) % P, c, chunks[p][c].copy()))
            sent[p] += chunks[p][c].nbytes
        for dst, c, payload in msgs:
            chunks[dst][c][:] = payload
    return sent


def naive_allreduce_root_bytes(P, nbytes):
    """Gather-to-root then broadcast: bytes crossing the ROOT's single link.

    Root receives (P-1) full tensors, then sends (P-1) full copies back out.
    That link is the bottleneck; everyone else moves only 2*nbytes.
    """
    return 2 * (P - 1) * nbytes


# --------------------------- ZeRO memory planner ----------------------------

# Mixed-precision Adam, bytes per parameter (fp16/bf16 compute, fp32 state):
#   2 (bf16 weights) + 2 (bf16 grads) + 4 (fp32 master) + 4 (m) + 4 (v) = 16.
W_LO, G_LO, OPT = 2, 2, 12          # OPT = fp32 master copy + m + v

def per_device_bytes(N, P, stage):
    """Per-device bytes for N params, DP degree P, ZeRO stage 0..3.
    Excludes activations, buffers, and framework overhead."""
    if stage == 0:  return N * (W_LO + G_LO + OPT)           # plain DP
    if stage == 1:  return N * (W_LO + G_LO + OPT / P)       # shard optimizer
    if stage == 2:  return N * (W_LO + (G_LO + OPT) / P)     # + shard grads
    if stage == 3:  return N * (W_LO + G_LO + OPT) / P       # + shard weights
    raise ValueError(stage)

def plan(N, P_list, budget_gb, label):
    print(f"\n--- planner: {label}, N = {N:.1e} params, budget {budget_gb} GB/device ---")
    print(f"{'DP':>5} | " + " | ".join(f"{s:>12}" for s in
          ["DP (ZeRO-0)", "ZeRO-1", "ZeRO-2", "ZeRO-3"]))
    for P in P_list:
        row = []
        for stage in range(4):
            gb = per_device_bytes(N, P, stage) / 1e9
            row.append(f"{gb:8.1f} {'ok ' if gb <= budget_gb else 'XXX'}")
        print(f"{P:>5} | " + " | ".join(f"{r:>12}" for r in row))


# --------------------------------- checks -----------------------------------

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

    # (a) exact correctness: integer-valued float64 so summation order is exact
    for P, n in [(2, 8), (4, 16), (5, 40), (8, 64), (16, 4096)]:
        data = [rng.integers(-1000, 1000, n).astype(np.float64) for _ in range(P)]
        truth = np.sum(data, axis=0)
        bufs = [d.copy() for d in data]
        sent = ring_allreduce(bufs)
        for b in bufs:
            assert np.array_equal(b, truth), "ring result != direct sum"

        # (b) bytes on wire per worker == 2*(P-1)/P * S, exactly, every worker
        S = data[0].nbytes
        expect = 2 * (P - 1) * S // P
        assert all(s == expect for s in sent), (sent, expect)

        # (c) gather+broadcast bottleneck moves strictly more than a ring worker
        naive = naive_allreduce_root_bytes(P, S)
        assert naive > expect and naive == P * expect
        print(f"P={P:>3} S={S:>6}B  ring/worker={expect:>6}B  "
              f"= 2(P-1)/P*S exactly; naive root link={naive:>7}B  ({P}x worse)")

    # (d) 16 bytes/param, hand-counted on a concrete 2-layer MLP (8->4->2):
    #     W1 8x4 + b1 4 + W2 4x2 + b2 2  ->  32+4+8+2 = 46 parameters.
    shapes = [(4, 8), (4,), (2, 4), (2,)]
    n_params = sum(int(np.prod(s)) for s in shapes)
    assert n_params == 46
    hand = 0
    for s in shapes:                       # materialize all six tensors and count
        hand += np.zeros(s, np.float16).nbytes      # bf16/fp16 weights
        hand += np.zeros(s, np.float16).nbytes      # low-precision grads
        hand += 3 * np.zeros(s, np.float32).nbytes  # fp32 master + m + v
    assert hand == 16 * n_params == per_device_bytes(n_params, 1, 0) == 736
    print(f"\nAdam mixed-precision hand count: {n_params} params -> {hand} bytes "
          f"= 16 x {n_params}  [exact]")
