    # torch cross-check: Adam really does keep two fp32 state tensors per param
    if torch is not None:
        tp = [torch.nn.Parameter(torch.randn(*s)) for s in shapes]
        opt = torch.optim.Adam(tp)
        sum((p ** 2).sum() for p in tp).backward()
        opt.step()
        st = sum(v[k].numel() for v in opt.state.values()
                 for k in ("exp_avg", "exp_avg_sq"))
        assert st == 2 * n_params
        print(f"torch.optim.Adam state elements: {st} = 2 x {n_params}  [matches]")
    else:
        print("[skipped: torch not installed]")

    # (e) the planner on two real model sizes, 80 GB devices (GB = 1e9 bytes)
    plan(7e9,  [8, 64, 512], 80, "7B model")
    plan(70e9, [8, 64, 512], 80, "70B model")
    print("\nAll assertions passed.")

Running it prints one line per configuration confirming the exact wire count — e.g. P= 8 S= 512B ring/worker= 896B = 2(P-1)/P*S exactly; naive root link= 7168B (8x worse) — then the Adam hand count (46 params -> 736 bytes = 16 x 46 [exact], torch state 92 = 2 x 46 [matches]), and the planner tables: for the 7B model, plain DP shows 112.0 XXX at every DP degree while ZeRO-1 at $P=8$ shows 38.5 ok; for the 70B model only ZeRO-3 at $P \ge 64$ is feasible (17.5 ok at 64, 2.2 ok at 512). It finishes with All assertions passed in about 3 s, most of it torch import.

Key Takeaways
  • Ring all-reduce moves exactly $2\frac{P-1}{P}S$ bytes per worker — bandwidth-optimal and under $2S$ for any worker count; only the $2(P-1)\alpha$ latency term grows with scale, which is why small messages get trees and gradients get bucketed. Certain
  • Mixed-precision Adam costs 16 bytes per parameter (2+2 low-precision weights/grads, 12 fp32 state); ZeRO-1/2 shard 12–14 of those bytes at zero extra communication, ZeRO-3 shards all 16 for 1.5× the wire volume. Certain
  • Tensor parallelism pays $\approx 8\frac{t-1}{t}\,B\,n\,d\,b$ bytes per layer of blocking traffic, so it lives inside the NVLink domain; data and pipeline parallelism, with per-step overlappable or point-to-point traffic, take the inter-node links. Certain
  • The pipeline bubble is $\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}$; 1F1B cuts activation memory from $O(m)$ to $O(p)$ without touching the bubble, interleaving with $v$ chunks divides the bubble by $\approx v$ for $v\times$ the communication. Certain
  • At $10^4$-GPU scale the cluster fails every few hours ($M_1/P$), so checkpoint at the Young–Daly interval $\sqrt{2\delta M}$ and expect silent data corruption to be a real line item, per public frontier-run reports. Verify
Chapter 33

Inference: Serving, Caching, and Speculative Decoding

Learning Objectives
  • Derive why prefill is compute-bound and decode memory-bandwidth-bound, and compute the KV-cache size $2 L\, n_{\text{kv}} d_h T b$ bytes for a given model configuration.
  • Explain paged KV-cache management and quantify the fragmentation it eliminates relative to contiguous max-length pre-allocation.
  • Explain continuous batching and chunked prefill, and predict their opposing effects on time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token.
  • Prove that speculative decoding preserves the target distribution exactly, and derive the expected tokens per verification cycle $(1-\alpha^{\gamma+1})/(1-\alpha)$ as a function of the acceptance rate $\alpha$.
  • Implement speculative decoding with a distributional-equivalence test, plus a paged KV allocator, in working code.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336's inference lectures are the closest course treatment of this chapter's roofline arguments and serving systems. Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), walks the generation loop and KV cache line by line, which makes the memory arithmetic here concrete.

Chapter 30 established the roofline: a GPU delivers its rated FLOP/s only when arithmetic intensity exceeds a ridge point of a few hundred FLOPs per byte. Training lives comfortably above that ridge. Autoregressive generation does not: producing one token requires streaming every weight and every cached key–value pair through the memory system to perform roughly two FLOPs per parameter. A single-user chat session therefore runs a multi-terabyte-per-second, near-petaflop machine at well under 1% arithmetic utilization. This chapter treats every major serving technique — KV caching, paged memory management, continuous batching, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, prefix caching — as one idea in different costumes: find something useful for the idle arithmetic units to do while the memory system is the bottleneck. Chapter 31's FlashAttention already made prefill fast; Chapter 34 shrinks the bytes themselves via quantization; Chapter 41 revisits this entire stack under encryption, where the KV cache becomes the central obstruction.

33.1 Prefill versus Decode

Generation has two phases with opposite performance characters. Prefill processes the $T$ prompt tokens in one forward pass; decode then emits output tokens one at a time, each conditioned on everything before it. Consider a weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ applied to a batch of $t$ token vectors: the GEMM costs $2td^2$ FLOPs and moves about $2d^2$ bytes of fp16 weights (activations are comparatively small), so its arithmetic intensity is roughly $t$ FLOPs per weight byte. In prefill, $t = T$ is hundreds or thousands — far above the ridge point, so prefill is compute-bound and runs near peak FLOP/s. In decode, $t = 1$: one FLOP per byte at fp16. On an H100 SXM the ridge sits near $989\ \text{TFLOP/s} / 3.35\ \text{TB/s} \approx 295$ FLOPs per byte Verify, so batch-1 decode sits two orders of magnitude below it. The arithmetic units are idle; the step time is set entirely by how fast HBM can stream the weights and KV cache.

Example 33.1 (The decode latency floor)

An 8-billion-parameter model in fp16 occupies $8\times 10^9 \times 2 = 16$ GB. Every decode step must read all of it. At 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth Verify, the step takes at least $16/3350 \approx 4.8$ ms, i.e. at most $\approx 209$ tokens/s for a single sequence — regardless of how many FLOP/s the chip has. The FLOPs actually performed are $2N \approx 16$ GFLOP per token, so the achieved rate is $209 \times 16\ \text{GFLOP} \approx 3.3$ TFLOP/s: about 0.3% of the machine. The other 99.7% is the budget every technique in this chapter spends.

Two consequences follow immediately. First, decode latency is bought with bandwidth and bytes, not FLOPs — which is why weight quantization (Chapter 34) speeds up decode roughly in proportion to the byte reduction. Second, batching $B$ concurrent sequences reuses the same weight read for $B$ tokens, multiplying throughput nearly for free until intensity approaches the ridge, around $B \approx 300$ at fp16 on the hardware above. The caveat: KV-cache reads do not amortize, because each sequence attends to its own cache. Writing $W$ for weight bytes and $K(T)$ for one sequence's KV bytes at length $T$, the bandwidth-bound step time is

$$t_{\text{step}} \;\approx\; \frac{W + B\,K(T)}{\text{BW}}, \qquad \text{throughput} \;\approx\; \frac{B\cdot\text{BW}}{W + B\,K(T)}.$$

Throughput grows almost linearly in $B$ while $BK(T) \ll W$, then saturates at $\text{BW}/K(T)$ once cache traffic dominates. The crossover $B^{*} = W/K(T)$ is small at long context: for the 8B model below, $W = 16$ GB and $K(8192) = 1$ GiB give $B^{*} \approx 15$. Beyond that, adding users buys little — the attention portion of decode stays bandwidth-bound even when the MLP portion has become compute-bound, which is precisely why shrinking $K(T)$ (GQA, cache quantization, paging) is a throughput optimization and not merely a capacity one. Certain

33.2 The KV Cache

Attention at decode step $t$ needs the keys and values of all previous positions (Chapter 18). Recomputing them each step would make step $t$ cost a full forward pass over $t$ tokens, $\approx 2Nt$ FLOPs, for a total of $\sum_{t=1}^{T} 2Nt \approx NT^2$ FLOPs to generate $T$ tokens — quadratic in $T$ where caching gives $2NT$, linear. So every serving system stores K and V per layer, per head, per position. The price is memory:

$$\text{KV bytes} \;=\; \underbrace{2}_{\text{K and V}} \;\times\; L \;\times\; n_{\text{kv}} \;\times\; d_h \;\times\; T \;\times\; b,$$

where $L$ is layer count, $n_{\text{kv}}$ the number of KV heads (equal to attention heads for vanilla multi-head attention; smaller under GQA/MQA, Chapter 18), $d_h$ the head dimension, $T$ the current sequence length, and $b$ bytes per element.

Example 33.2 (KV cache for a Llama-3-8B-class model)

Take $L=32$, $n_{\text{kv}}=8$ (GQA), $d_h=128$, fp16 ($b=2$) Verify. Per token: $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes $= 128$ KiB. At $T = 8192$: $128\ \text{KiB} \times 8192 = 1$ GiB per sequence. On an 80 GB card holding 16 GB of weights, the remaining $\sim$60 GiB caps concurrency at about 60 such sequences — and without GQA ($n_{\text{kv}}=32$) at about 15. The KV cache, not the weights, is what limits batch size, and Section 33.1 showed batch size is what buys throughput.

Every factor in the formula is a lever, and they compose multiplicatively:

Layout ($L=32$, $d_h=128$)$n_{\text{kv}}$$b$Bytes/tokenSequences at 8K in 60 GiB
MHA, fp16322524,28815
GQA, fp1682131,07260
GQA, int8 cache8165,536120
MQA, int8 cache118,192960

This is why GQA and MQA exist, why KV-cache quantization to 8 or 4 bits is standard practice (Chapter 34 covers its accuracy cost), and why long-context serving (Chapter 19) is primarily a memory problem. Note also that the cache grows during generation: a request's memory footprint at admission time is unknown, because you do not know how long its output will be. That uncertainty is the subject of the next section.

33.3 Paged Attention and Fragmentation

Early serving systems allocated each request's KV cache as one contiguous tensor sized to the maximum possible length — the only safe choice when the final length is unknown and tensors cannot grow in place. The waste is enormous: a request that generates 300 tokens against a 2048-token reservation strands 85% of its allocation as internal fragmentation, and differently-sized reservations churn the heap into unusable gaps (external fragmentation) besides. The vLLM authors reported that prior systems wasted 60–80% of KV memory this way Verify.

PagedAttention imports the operating-system fix wholesale: virtual memory. Physical KV memory is divided into fixed-size blocks of $B_{\text{blk}}$ tokens (16 is typical); each request holds a block table mapping logical position $i$ to physical block $\lfloor i/B_{\text{blk}}\rfloor$'s address plus offset. Blocks are allocated on demand from a free list as the sequence grows and returned on completion. Waste per request drops to at most $B_{\text{blk}}-1$ slots — the unfilled tail of the last block — and external fragmentation vanishes because all blocks are interchangeable. The attention kernel pays a small price: one level of indirection to gather K/V through the block table, a few percent of kernel time in practice Likely.

The improvement is predictable in closed form. With request lengths $T$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,T_{\max}\}$, contiguous reservation wastes an expected fraction $1 - \mathbb{E}[T]/T_{\max} = 1 - (T_{\max}+1)/(2T_{\max}) \approx 50\%$. Paging allocates $\lceil T/B_{\text{blk}}\rceil B_{\text{blk}}$ slots, an expected overhead of $(B_{\text{blk}}-1)/2$ slots per request, for a waste fraction of roughly $\frac{(B_{\text{blk}}-1)/2}{\mathbb{E}[T] + (B_{\text{blk}}-1)/2}$ — with $B_{\text{blk}}=16$ and $T_{\max}=2048$, about $7.5/1032 \approx 0.73\%$. Artifact 33.1 measures exactly this setup over 1,000 requests: contiguous reservation wastes 48.36% of allocated slots, paged allocation 0.694% — both in line with the closed forms, a $70\times$ reduction. Shrinking $B_{\text{blk}}$ further trims the tail waste but grows the block table and worsens gather locality; 16–32 tokens is the practical sweet spot Likely.

Paging buys more than density. Because a block is referenced through a table, two requests can share physical blocks: beam-search candidates share their common prefix with copy-on-write, and identical system prompts across users share cached blocks outright — the mechanism behind prefix caching (Section 33.7).

33.4 Continuous Batching and Chunked Prefill

Definition 33.1 (TTFT and TPOT)

Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is the delay from request arrival to the first output token — dominated by queueing plus prefill. Time-per-output-token (TPOT) is the average interval between subsequent tokens — dominated by decode step time. A serving system's latency contract is typically stated as percentile bounds on both.

Static batching — assemble $B$ requests, run all to completion, repeat — wastes capacity twice: finished sequences idle their slots until the longest one ends, and arriving requests wait for the next batch to form. Continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling, introduced by Orca) reschedules at every decode step: completed sequences exit the batch immediately and waiting requests join mid-flight, keeping the batch full and both queueing and slot waste near zero. This is the single largest throughput lever in modern serving — multiples, not percentages, over static batching under realistic arrival processes Likely.

It creates a scheduling tension, though. When a new request joins, its prefill must run. Prefill is compute-bound and long; decode steps are bandwidth-bound and short. If the scheduler runs a 4,000-token prefill as one unit, every co-resident decoding sequence stalls for the duration — a TPOT spike (“generation stall”) visible to users as the stream freezing. Prioritizing decode instead starves prefill and inflates TTFT. Chunked prefill (Sarathi-Serve) dissolves the tension: split each prefill into chunks of a few hundred tokens and build every iteration's batch as one chunk plus all pending decode tokens. Each iteration does enough prefill work to be compute-efficient, yet no iteration is much longer than a decode step, so TPOT stays smooth. The cost is a modest TTFT increase for the chunked request — its prefill now interleaves rather than monopolizes — plus a small overhead because each chunk re-reads the KV cache of prior chunks. The TTFT/TPOT trade-off becomes a tunable chunk-size knob rather than a hard choice. Certain

33.5 Speculative Decoding

Batching converts idle FLOPs into throughput across users. Speculative decoding converts them into latency for a single user — the one case batching cannot help. The observation: because decode is bandwidth-bound, a forward pass that scores $\gamma+1$ token positions costs nearly the same wall-clock as one that scores a single position — the weights stream through HBM either way. If we could guess the next $\gamma$ tokens, one target-model pass could verify all guesses at once. A cheap draft distribution $q$ proposes; the expensive target $p$ verifies. The subtlety is doing this without changing the output distribution — naive “accept if the target agrees” schemes bias sampling. The modified rejection rule of Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. does it exactly.

Definition 33.2 (Speculative sampling rule)

Given draft distribution $q$ and target distribution $p$ over the vocabulary at some position, sample $x \sim q$ and accept it with probability $\min(1,\, p(x)/q(x))$. On rejection, resample from the residual distribution $p'(x) = \max(0,\, p(x)-q(x)) / \sum_z \max(0,\, p(z)-q(z))$. One cycle drafts $\gamma$ tokens from $q$ autoregressively, verifies them left to right under $p$ (all $\gamma+1$ needed distributions come from a single target forward pass), stops at the first rejection with a residual resample, and — if all $\gamma$ are accepted — draws one bonus token from the target's $(\gamma+1)$-th distribution. Every cycle thus emits between $1$ and $\gamma+1$ tokens for one target pass.

Why is verification nearly free? A target pass over $\gamma+1$ positions is a tiny prefill: it moves the same $W$ weight bytes as a single decode step while performing $(\gamma+1)\times$ the FLOPs, so for small $\gamma$ its bandwidth-bound wall-clock is essentially unchanged — the verification FLOPs come out of the 99% idle budget of Example 33.1. Note also the greedy special case: if the target decodes by argmax, take $p$ to be a point mass; the acceptance test $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$ then reduces to “accept iff the draft equals the target's argmax,” and the residual resample is just the target's token — speculative decoding degenerates to exact-match verification, which is how it is often first implemented.

33.5.1 The Rejection-Sampling Proof
Theorem 33.1 (Exactness of speculative sampling)

The token emitted at any position by the rule of Definition 33.2 is distributed exactly according to $p$. Moreover the acceptance probability is $\alpha = \sum_x \min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 - D_{\mathrm{TV}}(p, q)$.

Proof. Fix a position and let $X$ be the emitted token. Acceptance of a drafted $x$ occurs with probability $q(x)\min(1, p(x)/q(x)) = \min(p(x), q(x))$, so the total acceptance probability is $\alpha = \sum_x \min(p(x), q(x))$; the identity $\min(a,b) = \tfrac{1}{2}(a+b-|a-b|)$ gives $\alpha = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_x |p(x)-q(x)| = 1 - D_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)$. The residual weights sum to $\sum_x (p(x)-q(x))^+ = 1-\alpha$, so $p'$ is a valid distribution. Then for any token $x$:

$$\Pr[X = x] \;=\; \underbrace{\min(p(x), q(x))}_{\text{drafted and accepted}} \;+\; \underbrace{(1-\alpha)\cdot \frac{(p(x)-q(x))^+}{1-\alpha}}_{\text{rejected, residual resample}} \;=\; \min(p(x),q(x)) + (p(x)-q(x))^+ \;=\; p(x),$$

using $\min(a,b) + (a-b)^+ = a$. Exactness at later positions in a cycle follows by the same computation applied to the conditional distributions given the (correctly distributed) prefix, and the bonus token is drawn from $p$ directly. $\blacksquare$

The theorem is unconditional: it holds for any draft distribution, including a terrible one — a bad draft costs speed, never correctness. Quality enters only through $\alpha$: the closer $q$ is to $p$ in total variation, the more drafts survive.

Theorem 33.2 (Expected tokens per verification cycle)

If each draft is accepted independently with probability $\alpha$, a cycle with $\gamma$ drafts emits on average $$\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens}] \;=\; \frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}$$ tokens (and $\gamma+1$ exactly when $\alpha = 1$).

Proof. Let $A$ be the number of accepted drafts, so tokens emitted $= A + 1$ (the final token is either the residual resample or the bonus draw). Since $A \ge k$ iff the first $k$ drafts all pass, $\Pr[A \ge k] = \alpha^k$ for $k \le \gamma$, and $\mathbb{E}[A] = \sum_{k=1}^{\gamma} \alpha^k = \frac{\alpha(1-\alpha^\gamma)}{1-\alpha}$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[A+1] = \frac{1-\alpha+\alpha-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha} = \frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}$. $\blacksquare$

If a draft token costs a fraction $c$ of a target step and verification costs one target step, the wall-clock speedup of a cycle is $\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{(1-\alpha)(\gamma c + 1)}$. The i.i.d.-acceptance assumption is an idealization — in real language models $\alpha$ varies by position, and the formula is the standard first-order model rather than an exact law Likely. In the artifact's controlled setting the assumption holds exactly, and the measured 1.8778 tokens/cycle matches the formula's 1.8805 to under 0.15%.

Example 33.3 (Speedup arithmetic)

Take $\alpha = 0.8$, $\gamma = 4$, draft cost $c = 0.05$. Expected tokens per cycle: $(1 - 0.8^5)/(1-0.8) = (1 - 0.32768)/0.2 = 3.3616$. Cycle cost: $4 \times 0.05 + 1 = 1.2$ target-step equivalents. Speedup: $3.3616 / 1.2 \approx 2.8\times$. Doubling $\gamma$ to 8 raises expected tokens only to $(1-0.8^9)/0.2 = 4.329$ while cost grows to $1.4$ — $3.1\times$. The geometric decay $\alpha^k$ means long drafts add little: past a few tokens, the marginal draft is probably wasted.

Common Pitfall

Applying sampling transforms inconsistently between draft and target. Theorem 33.1 holds for the distributions actually used in the ratio test — so temperature, top-$k$, and top-$p$ warping must be applied to both $p$ and $q$ before computing $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$ and the residual. A common bug is verifying against the raw target softmax while the production sampler uses temperature-0.7 top-p-0.9: the emitted stream then matches neither distribution, and the corruption is invisible to spot checks because every individual token still “looks plausible.” The distributional test in Artifact 33.1 — chi-square against the exact target over hundreds of thousands of tokens — is precisely the regression test that catches this class of bug.

33.6 Draft Models, Medusa, EAGLE

Where does $q$ come from? Three generations of answers. Separate draft models — a 1B model drafting for a 70B target — are simple and were the original proposal, but the draft runs autoregressively (adding $\gamma$ sequential small-model steps of cost $c$ each), must be trained and version-matched to the target's tokenizer, and its distributional mismatch caps $\alpha$. Medusa deletes the separate model: it bolts $k$ lightweight heads onto the target's last hidden state, head $j$ predicting the token $j$ positions ahead in a single non-autoregressive shot. Because independent heads are individually uncertain, Medusa drafts a tree of candidate continuations and verifies the whole tree in one target pass using a tree-structured attention mask — another purchase made with idle FLOPs. EAGLE improves the draft by autoregressing at the feature level: a single small transformer layer predicts the target's next hidden state from the current hidden state and sampled token, then reuses the target's own LM head. Hidden states carry far more information than sampled tokens, so acceptance rates rise substantially; EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3 add dynamically grown draft trees. Reported end-to-end speedups are roughly $2\times$ for classic two-model drafting, $2$–$3\times$ for Medusa, and $3$–$4\times$ for EAGLE-2/3 on standard benchmarks Verify.

One boundary condition: speculative decoding spends surplus FLOPs, so it helps most at small batch. As batch size approaches the ridge point (Section 33.1) the surplus vanishes, and verification passes compete with other users' work — at high server load, speculation can reduce total throughput even while it still cuts single-stream latency. Production schedulers increasingly toggle speculation based on load. Likely

33.7 Prefix Caching

Chatbots and agents (Chapter 36) resend nearly identical context every turn: system prompt, tool definitions, conversation so far. Since keys and values at position $i$ depend only on tokens $\le i$ (with the positional caveats of Chapter 19), the KV cache of a shared prefix is identical across requests and reusable. Paged storage makes this cheap: hash each full block of tokens (chained with its prefix's hash) and look up incoming requests' prefixes block by block, or keep a radix tree over cached token sequences as SGLang does; matched blocks are reference-counted and shared, and prefill runs only on the unmatched suffix. TTFT for a hit drops roughly in proportion to the cached fraction — for a 4,000-token system prompt ahead of a 100-token question, about $40\times$ less prefill compute. Commercial APIs expose the same mechanism as discounted “cached input token” pricing, roughly $2$–$10\times$ cheaper than uncached input depending on provider Verify. The eviction policy is LRU over blocks; the capacity spent on cache is capacity taken from batch, so the knob is workload-dependent.

33.8 Cost per Token

The economics compress into one line: $\text{cost/token} = \frac{\text{GPU-\$/s}}{\text{tokens/s}}$, and everything in this chapter is a tokens/s lever. The roofline yields a usable first-order cost model. Prefill throughput is compute-limited: $\approx P_{\text{peak}}/2N$ input tokens per second at full utilization. Decode throughput is bandwidth-limited: $\approx B \cdot \text{BW}/(\text{weight bytes} + B\cdot\text{KV bytes})$, growing with $B$ until either the ridge or — more often — KV memory (Example 33.2) caps it. For the 8B model of Example 33.1, prefill peaks near $989\ \text{TFLOP/s}/16\ \text{GFLOP} \approx 60{,}000$ tokens/s while batch-1 decode manages 209: a $\sim 300\times$ gap in marginal cost between input and output tokens at the extremes. Real serving closes much of that gap with batching, but an output token remains several times more expensive to produce than an input token, which is exactly the shape of commercial pricing — output rates commonly $3$–$5\times$ input rates Verify. To put dollars on it (spec-sheet arithmetic, not a measurement): at \$2/GPU-hour Verify, batch-1 decode at 209 tokens/s costs $\frac{2/3600}{209} \approx \$2.7$ per million output tokens, while the same model batched to $B=64$ at $T=2048$ ($K(T)=0.27$ GB per sequence, so $t_{\text{step}} \approx (16+17.2)/3350\ \text{s} \approx 9.9$ ms and $\approx 6{,}500$ tokens/s aggregate) costs about \$0.09 per million — a $30\times$ spread from batching alone, before speculation or caching. The full lever stack: quantization divides the bytes (Chapter 34), GQA and paging multiply feasible $B$, continuous batching keeps $B$ full, chunked prefill protects the latency contract while doing it, and speculation plus prefix caching recycle FLOPs and prefill work that would otherwise be wasted. Each attacks a different denominator term; a modern serving stack is simply all of them composed.

Artifact 33.1 — Speculative Decoding and Paged Allocation, Verified

Speculative decoding needs no language model to be understood or tested: it is a claim about sampling. The artifact fixes explicit target and draft distributions $p, q$ over a 32-token vocabulary (so $\alpha$, the output law, and tokens-per-cycle all have closed forms), runs 200,000 verification cycles of Definition 33.2 vectorized in NumPy, and asserts (a) the emitted stream matches $p$ by total variation and chi-square, (b) the measured acceptance rate matches $\sum_x \min(p,q)$, (c) measured tokens/cycle matches Theorem 33.2, with a torch.multinomial sampler as an independent cross-check. Part two implements a free-list paged KV allocator (block size 16) fed token-by-token by 1,000 requests of uniform random length up to 2,048, and compares its waste against contiguous max-length reservation.

"""Artifact 33.1 -- Speculative decoding from scratch + a paged KV allocator.

Speculative decoding is a statement about SAMPLING, not about language models:
given a target distribution p and a cheap draft distribution q over a vocabulary,
the modified rejection rule emits tokens whose distribution is EXACTLY p while
letting q do most of the proposing.  We use fixed (context-independent) discrete
distributions so every quantity has a closed form to assert against:
  * output distribution == p          (chi-square + total-variation test)
  * acceptance rate     == sum_x min(p(x), q(x)) = 1 - TV(p, q)
  * tokens/verification == (1 - alpha^(gamma+1)) / (1 - alpha)
Part 2 is a block-granular ("paged") KV allocator measured against contiguous
max-length pre-allocation on random-length requests.
"""
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1: speculative decoding over explicit distributions
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def sample(cdf, u):
    """Inverse-CDF sampling: map uniforms u in [0,1) to vocabulary indices."""
    return np.searchsorted(cdf, u, side="right")


def spec_decode(p, q, gamma, n_cycles, rng):
    """Run n_cycles of speculative decoding, vectorized over cycles.

    Each cycle: q proposes gamma tokens; the target verifies them left to
    right, accepting draft x with prob min(1, p(x)/q(x)); on first rejection
    it resamples from the residual max(0, p-q)/(1-alpha) and the cycle ends;
    if all gamma are accepted it draws one bonus token directly from p.
    Returns (token counts, #accepted drafts, #examined drafts, #tokens).
    """
    V = p.size
    q_cdf, p_cdf = np.cumsum(q), np.cumsum(p)
    residual = np.maximum(p - q, 0.0)
    residual /= residual.sum()                       # = (p-q)^+ / (1-alpha)
    r_cdf = np.cumsum(residual)

    drafts = sample(q_cdf, rng.random((n_cycles, gamma)))       # proposals ~ q
    accept_p = np.minimum(1.0, p[drafts] / q[drafts])           # min(1, p/q)
    acc = rng.random((n_cycles, gamma)) < accept_p
    # position of first rejection in each cycle; gamma if none
    first_rej = np.where(acc.all(axis=1), gamma, acc.argmin(axis=1))

    keep = np.arange(gamma)[None, :] < first_rej[:, None]       # accepted prefix
    kept_tokens = drafts[keep]
    # last token of the cycle: residual resample on rejection, else bonus ~ p
    u = rng.random(n_cycles)
    final = np.where(first_rej < gamma, sample(r_cdf, u), sample(p_cdf, u))

    counts = np.bincount(kept_tokens, minlength=V) + np.bincount(final, minlength=V)
    accepted = int(keep.sum())
    examined = accepted + int((first_rej < gamma).sum())  # verify stops at 1st reject
    return counts, accepted, examined, accepted + n_cycles


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 2: paged KV allocator vs contiguous pre-allocation
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
class PagedKVAllocator:
    """vLLM-style block allocator: KV slots are handed out in fixed-size
    blocks from a free list; a request's 'block table' maps its logical
    token positions to physical blocks.  A request of length T holds
    ceil(T/B) blocks, so waste is < B slots per request."""

    def __init__(self, n_blocks, block_size):
        self.B = block_size
        self.free = list(range(n_blocks))
        self.tables = {}                      # request id -> list of block ids
        self.lens = {}                        # request id -> tokens written

    def append_token(self, rid):
        n = self.lens.get(rid, 0)
        if n % self.B == 0:                   # current block full (or first token)
            self.tables.setdefault(rid, []).append(self.free.pop())
        self.lens[rid] = n + 1

    def allocated_slots(self):
        return sum(len(t) for t in self.tables.values()) * self.B


def fragmentation_experiment(rng, n_req=1000, max_len=2048, block=16):
    """All requests resident concurrently; lengths ~ Uniform{1..max_len}.
    Contiguous serving reserves max_len slots per request up front (it cannot
    know the final length); paging allocates blocks on demand."""
    lengths = rng.integers(1, max_len + 1, size=n_req)
    alloc = PagedKVAllocator(n_blocks=(n_req * (max_len // block + 1)), block_size=block)
    for rid, T in enumerate(lengths):        # feed tokens one at a time
        for _ in range(int(T)):
            alloc.append_token(rid)
    used = int(lengths.sum())
    paged_alloc = alloc.allocated_slots()
    # cross-check the allocator against the closed form ceil(T/B)*B
    assert paged_alloc == int((np.ceil(lengths / block) * block).sum())
    contig_alloc = n_req * max_len
    return used, paged_alloc, contig_alloc


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    V, gamma, n_cycles = 32, 4, 200_000
    p = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(V))                     # target distribution
    q = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(V))                     # draft distribution
    alpha = np.minimum(p, q).sum()                    # analytic acceptance rate

    counts, accepted, examined, n_tok = spec_decode(p, q, gamma, n_cycles, rng)

    # (a) output distribution == target, tested two ways
    emp = counts / n_tok
    tv = 0.5 * np.abs(emp - p).sum()
    chi2, pval = stats.chisquare(counts, f_exp=n_tok * p)
    print(f"[a] tokens={n_tok}  TV(empirical, p)={tv:.5f}  "
          f"chi2={chi2:.1f} (df={V-1})  p-value={pval:.3f}")
    # reference: direct i.i.d. sampling from p at the same sample size
    direct = np.bincount(sample(np.cumsum(p), rng.random(n_tok)), minlength=V)
    tv_direct = 0.5 * np.abs(direct / n_tok - p).sum()
    print(f"    reference TV for direct target sampling, same n: {tv_direct:.5f}")
    assert tv < 0.01, "speculative output drifted from target distribution"
    assert pval > 1e-3, "chi-square rejects distributional equivalence"

    # (b) measured acceptance rate vs analytic sum min(p, q)
    meas_alpha = accepted / examined
    print(f"[b] acceptance: measured={meas_alpha:.5f}  analytic={alpha:.5f}  "
          f"|diff|={abs(meas_alpha - alpha):.5f}")
    assert abs(meas_alpha - alpha) < 5e-3

    # (c) tokens per verification cycle vs (1 - a^(g+1)) / (1 - a)
    meas_tok = n_tok / n_cycles
    exp_tok = (1 - alpha ** (gamma + 1)) / (1 - alpha)
    print(f"[c] tokens/cycle: measured={meas_tok:.4f}  analytic={exp_tok:.4f}  "
          f"|diff|={abs(meas_tok - exp_tok):.4f}")
    assert abs(meas_tok - exp_tok) < 0.02

    # cross-check (a) with torch.multinomial as an independent sampler
    if torch is not None:
        tt = torch.multinomial(torch.from_numpy(p), n_tok, replacement=True,
                               generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
        tv_torch = 0.5 * np.abs(np.bincount(tt.numpy(), minlength=V) / n_tok - p).sum()
        print(f"    torch.multinomial cross-check TV: {tv_torch:.5f}")
        assert tv_torch < 0.01
    else:
        print("    [skipped: torch not installed]")

    # (d) paged allocator vs contiguous pre-allocation
    used, paged_alloc, contig_alloc = fragmentation_experiment(rng)
    frag_paged = 100 * (1 - used / paged_alloc)
    frag_contig = 100 * (1 - used / contig_alloc)
    print(f"[d] KV slots used={used}  paged alloc={paged_alloc}  "
          f"contiguous alloc={contig_alloc}")
    print(f"    fragmentation: contiguous={frag_contig:.2f}%  "
          f"paged (B=16)={frag_paged:.3f}%")
    assert frag_paged < frag_contig / 10, "paging should cut waste >10x here"

    print("All assertions passed.")

Running it (2.6 s on CPU) prints, for 375,567 emitted tokens: total variation from the target $0.00343$ against $0.00271$ for direct sampling from $p$ at the same sample size — statistically indistinguishable, confirmed by chi-square $34.3$ on 31 degrees of freedom ($p = 0.314$). Measured acceptance is $0.48116$ against the analytic $\alpha = 0.48208$; measured tokens/cycle $1.8778$ against the analytic $1.8805$. The allocator experiment reports contiguous fragmentation $48.36\%$ versus $0.694\%$ paged, with the allocator's block count matching the closed form $\lceil T/B\rceil B$ exactly.

Under Encryption

The KV cache is the precise reason encrypted autoregressive generation is qualitatively harder than encrypted single-pass inference. Everything in this chapter treats the cache as cheap, elastic memory — append 128 KiB per token, repack blocks, share prefixes by pointer. Under CKKS none of that is free: each cached key and value lives inside packed ciphertexts whose slot layout is fixed at encryption time, so “appending a token” means either wasteful one-token ciphertexts or expensive rotation-and-mask surgery to insert into existing slots, and every decode step's attention must touch a ciphertext cache that grows without bound while consuming multiplicative depth. This is why most published encrypted-transformer results report a single forward pass — effectively prefill — rather than open-ended generation. Chapter 41 works out the memory blow-up and rotation counts in detail.

Key Takeaways
  • Prefill is compute-bound (arithmetic intensity $\approx T$ FLOPs per weight byte); batch-1 decode is bandwidth-bound at $\approx 1$, leaving well over 99% of peak FLOP/s idle — the surplus every serving technique spends. Certain
  • KV cache size is $2 L\, n_{\text{kv}} d_h T b$ bytes — 128 KiB/token, 1 GiB at 8K context for an 8B GQA model — and it, not the weights, usually caps batch size and hence throughput. Certain
  • Paged allocation with 16-token blocks cut measured KV fragmentation from 48.36% (contiguous max-length reservation) to 0.694% on uniform random lengths, and its block indirection is what enables prefix sharing and copy-on-write. Certain
  • Speculative decoding is exactly distribution-preserving for any draft (Theorem 33.1), with acceptance rate $1 - D_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)$ and expected $(1-\alpha^{\gamma+1})/(1-\alpha)$ tokens per target pass — both verified empirically in Artifact 33.1 to within $3\times 10^{-3}$. Certain
  • Continuous batching plus chunked prefill trades a small TTFT increase for smooth TPOT and multiple-times higher throughput; speculation helps latency at small batch but can cost throughput near the compute roofline, so schedulers should gate it on load. Likely
Chapter 34

Quantization, Distillation, and Compression

Learning Objectives
  • Derive symmetric and asymmetric affine quantization and per-tensor versus per-group scaling, and compute the exact memory footprint of each setting in bits per weight.
  • Explain the emergent-outlier phenomenon in large-model activations and how mixed-precision decomposition and activation-aware scaling each address it.
  • Derive the GPTQ layerwise update from the optimal brain quantization framework and explain why it beats round-to-nearest.
  • Explain quantization-aware training, the straight-through estimator, and what ternary models have and have not demonstrated.
  • Implement GPTQ from scratch in working code, including the Cholesky-form inverse-Hessian error propagation.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 covers inference-time quantization in its systems lectures and is the closest course treatment of this chapter. The HuggingFace Ultra-Scale Playbook is the best practical reference for mixed-precision and FP8 training mechanics.

Chapter 30 established that decoding is bandwidth-bound: every generated token streams the full parameter set through HBM, so latency is bytes divided by bandwidth. Chapter 33 attacked the problem by batching and caching; this chapter attacks the bytes. Cutting weights from 16 bits to 4 cuts decode latency by nearly 4× before any kernel cleverness, which is why weight-only 4-bit quantization is the most deployed inference optimization in existence. The central claim: 4-bit weights are nearly free, 2-bit weights are not, and activation quantization is harder than weight quantization despite using more bits — and all three facts have the same cause, a handful of high-magnitude outlier feature channels that emerge in large transformers. We build the standard fixes (GPTQ, AWQ, rotations), then treat training-time quantization (QAT, FP8, ternary models), KV-cache quantization, and the two non-quantization compression axes, distillation and pruning. Part VIII, especially Chapter 40, returns to quantization as an enabler for encrypted inference.

34.1 Quantization Fundamentals

Definition 34.1 (Affine quantization)

A $b$-bit affine quantizer maps a real $w$ to an integer code $q \in \{0,\dots,2^b-1\}$ via a scale $s>0$ and zero-point $z$: $$q = \mathrm{clip}\!\left(\mathrm{round}(w/s) + z,\; 0,\; 2^b-1\right), \qquad \hat w = s\,(q - z).$$ The quantizer is symmetric when $z$ is fixed at the midpoint (equivalently, signed codes with $\hat w = s\,q$, $q \in \{-2^{b-1},\dots,2^{b-1}-1\}$) and asymmetric when $z$ is fit to the data. For a tensor with values in $[w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$, the standard asymmetric fit is $s = (w_{\max}-w_{\min})/(2^b-1)$, $z = \mathrm{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$; the symmetric fit is $s = \max|w| / (2^{b-1}-1)$.

Rounding to the nearest grid point bounds the elementwise error by $s/2$, so everything reduces to making $s$ small over the values that matter. Under the standard model of rounding error as uniform over a step, error variance is $s^2/12$ — decent for weights, badly wrong for activations (Section 34.2). Symmetric quantization wastes grid on skewed data; asymmetric costs a zero-point per unit and a subtraction per dequantize. Weights are near-symmetric, so both are used; post-SiLU activations are skewed, so asymmetric wins there.

The remaining design axis is granularity: how many elements share one $(s,z)$ pair. Storing scale and zero-point each in FP16 (32 bits of metadata per unit), the exact footprint per weight is:

GranularityScales storedEffective bits/weight4-bit example
Per-tensor1$b + o(1)$4.00
Per-channel (row of $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}$)$d_{\text{out}}$$b + 32/d_{\text{in}}$4.008 at $d_{\text{in}}{=}4096$
Per-group, size $g$ along $d_{\text{in}}$$d_{\text{out}} d_{\text{in}}/g$$b + 32/g$4.25 at $g{=}128$

Per-group at $g=128$ is the deployed default (GPTQ and AWQ checkpoints both use it): 4.25 effective bits shrinks a 7B-parameter model from 14 GB in FP16 to about 3.7 GB, a 3.76× reduction in the bytes every decode step must move. Certain The reason finer granularity helps so much is that one scale must span the whole range of its unit; a single large value inside the unit stretches $s$ and coarsens the grid for everyone else. That is the outlier problem in miniature.

Example 34.1 (One outlier stretches the grid)

Quantize $w = (0.1, -0.2, 0.5, 3.2)$ to $b=4$ bits, asymmetric, one shared scale. Range $= 3.4$, so $s = 3.4/15 = 0.2267$, $z = \mathrm{round}(0.2/s) = 1$. Codes: $0.1 \to \mathrm{round}(0.441)+1 = 1 \to \hat w = 0$; $-0.2 \to 0 \to -0.227$; $0.5 \to 3 \to 0.453$; $3.2 \to 15 \to 3.173$. Errors: $(0.100, 0.027, 0.047, 0.027)$ — the small weight takes the largest error. Drop the outlier and requantize the remaining three: $s = 0.7/15 = 0.0467$, max possible error $s/2 = 0.023$, and $0.1 \to 0.093$ (error $0.0067$, 15× smaller). One value in the unit degraded every other value by roughly the ratio of ranges, $3.4/0.7 \approx 4.9$. Groups bound the blast radius of an outlier to $g$ elements.

34.2 Outlier Features

Weights of trained transformers are well-behaved: approximately Gaussian per channel, range a few standard deviations, no heavy tail. Activations are not. Dettmers et al. (2022, LLM.int8()) documented that beyond roughly 6.7B parameters, transformer residual streams develop a small set of feature channels — the same coordinate indices across tokens and layers — with magnitudes up to ~20× the typical scale, and that these channels are functionally load-bearing: zeroing them collapses perplexity. Likely (the phenomenon replicates across model families; the sharp "emergence at 6.7B" threshold is softer in later measurements, which tie outliers to attention sinks and LayerNorm dynamics rather than scale per se). By Example 34.1's arithmetic, a 20× outlier channel inside a per-tensor activation scale destroys the effective resolution of every other channel — which is why naive W8A8 INT8 inference works up to a few billion parameters and then abruptly stops working, while 4-bit weight-only quantization keeps working: the outliers live in the activations, which weight-only schemes leave in FP16.

Two families of fixes:

Mixed-precision decomposition. LLM.int8() splits the GEMM by column: the ~0.1% of channels whose activation magnitude exceeds a threshold are computed in FP16, the rest in INT8, and the partial products are summed. Exact where it matters, but the scatter/gather is slow in practice — the paper itself reports small-batch overhead — and serving stacks largely abandoned this route. Verify

Scale migration. Since $Wx = (W\,\mathrm{diag}(s))(\mathrm{diag}(s)^{-1}x)$ for any positive per-channel scale $s$, difficulty can be moved between activations and weights without changing the function. SmoothQuant picks $s_j = \max|x_j|^{\alpha} / \max|w_{\cdot j}|^{1-\alpha}$ to shave activation outliers down into the (well-behaved, easy to absorb) weights, enabling W8A8. AWQ (Section 34.3) exploits the same identity for weight-only quantization — scaling salient weight columns up so the quantization grid resolves them finely. The artifact measures this directly: with 4 of 256 activation channels scaled 50×, those channels carry 97.6% of the layer's weight-quantization output error energy, and a per-channel scale with $\alpha=0.25$ cuts output MSE 3.9×.

Common Pitfall

Per-tensor symmetric absmax calibration on activations. The scale $s = \max|x|/127$ is set by the single largest outlier in the calibration batch; with a 20× outlier channel, typical activations land in the bottom ~6 of 127 levels and many round to exactly zero. The failure is silent — no NaNs, no errors, just a model that generates fluent garbage. Symptoms: INT8 works on the small model and fails on the big one from the same codebase. Fixes, in increasing order of effort: per-token or per-channel scales, percentile clipping instead of absmax, scale migration, rotations.

34.3 Weight-Only PTQ: RTN, GPTQ, AWQ

Post-training quantization (PTQ) takes a trained checkpoint and a few hundred calibration sequences; no gradients, no labels. The baseline is round-to-nearest (RTN): fit a grid per group, round every weight independently. RTN at 4 bits with $g=128$ is already close to lossless on models above ~7B (typically a few tenths of a point of perplexity): everything fancier is fighting for the remaining gap, and for the 3- and 2-bit regimes where RTN falls apart. Likely

RTN's error is suboptimal for a reason you can state exactly: it minimizes weight-space error $\|W - \hat W\|_F^2$, but the quantity that matters is layer-output error $\|WX - \hat W X\|_F^2$ over the actual input distribution, and inputs are correlated. Rounding error committed on one weight can be partially cancelled by adjusting other weights that multiply correlated inputs. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) is the algorithm that does this cancellation exactly, one column at a time, and it descends from optimal brain damage/surgeon via optimal brain quantization (OBQ).

34.3.1 The optimal update

Fix a row $w \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}}$ of $W$ and calibration inputs $X \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}} \times n}$. Perturbing $w$ by $\delta$ changes the layerwise loss by exactly $\delta^\top H \delta$ with $H = XX^\top$ (half the true Hessian $2XX^\top$; the factor cancels in everything below) — the loss is quadratic, so this is not a Taylor approximation. Quantizing coordinate $j$ forces $\delta_j = \hat w_j - w_j$; the question is how to set the other coordinates.

Theorem 34.1 (OBQ compensation step)

Let $H \succ 0$ and fix $\delta_j = \varepsilon$. The minimizer of $\delta^\top H \delta$ subject to that constraint is $$\delta^\star = \frac{\varepsilon}{[H^{-1}]_{jj}}\, H^{-1} e_j, \qquad \text{with cost} \qquad \delta^{\star\top} H \delta^\star = \frac{\varepsilon^2}{[H^{-1}]_{jj}}.$$

Proof. Lagrangian $\mathcal{L} = \delta^\top H \delta - 2\lambda(e_j^\top \delta - \varepsilon)$. Stationarity gives $H\delta = \lambda e_j$, so $\delta = \lambda H^{-1} e_j$. The constraint $e_j^\top \delta = \lambda [H^{-1}]_{jj} = \varepsilon$ fixes $\lambda = \varepsilon/[H^{-1}]_{jj}$. Substituting, $\delta^\top H \delta = \lambda^2 e_j^\top H^{-1} H H^{-1} e_j = \lambda^2 [H^{-1}]_{jj} = \varepsilon^2/[H^{-1}]_{jj}$. $\blacksquare$

So the optimal move is: commit the rounding error $\varepsilon$ on coordinate $j$, then spread a compensating update $\varepsilon\,[H^{-1}]_{F,j}/[H^{-1}]_{jj}$ across the not-yet-quantized coordinates $F$. The cost formula also says which coordinate to quantize next (the one minimizing $\varepsilon_j^2/[H^{-1}]_{jj}$) — that greedy ordering is OBQ, and it is $O(d_{\text{in}}^3)$ per row, hopeless for $d_{\text{in}} = 12{,}288$.

34.3.2 GPTQ's three simplifications

GPTQ makes OBQ linear-algebra-cheap with three observations. First, quantize columns in a fixed left-to-right order for all rows: empirically the greedy order buys little on large layers, and a fixed order means every row does the same sequence of Schur complements. Second, since $H = XX^\top$ is shared by all $d_{\text{out}}$ rows, the compensation directions can be precomputed once: taking the Cholesky factorization $H^{-1} = T^\top T$ with $T$ upper-triangular, row $j$ of $T$ is exactly the (rescaled) inverse-Hessian row needed at step $j$ after coordinates $1,\dots,j-1$ have been eliminated — the sequence of Schur-complement inverses, packaged in one $O(d_{\text{in}}^3)$ factorization. The update becomes: for each column $j$, quantize, then $$W_{:,\,j+1:} \;\mathrel{-}=\; \frac{(w_j - \hat w_j)}{T_{jj}}\; T_{j,\,j+1:},$$ applied to all rows at once as a rank-1 GEMM. Third, batch the rank-1 updates into blocks of 128 columns so the work is GEMM-bound rather than bandwidth-bound. Total cost is $O(d^3)$ per layer; the paper quantizes OPT-175B in about 4 GPU-hours on a single A100. Verify A practical necessity: $H$ is near-singular whenever calibration is thin or inputs are low-rank, so implementations add damping $H \mathrel{+}= \lambda\,\mathrm{mean}(\mathrm{diag}\,H)\,I$ with $\lambda \approx 0.01$ before the Cholesky; skip it and the factorization fails or the propagated updates explode.

Why does this beat RTN? Not by choosing better grids — GPTQ uses the same grid RTN would. It wins purely through propagation: each rounding error is partially refunded by later columns. The artifact isolates exactly this by running GPTQ with the update step disabled (identical grid, identical order) and measuring layer-output MSE on correlated calibration data: at 4/3/2 bits GPTQ achieves 0.67×/0.68×/0.68× the RTN error, while the no-propagation ablation is bit-for-bit identical to RTN. The relative gain is strikingly stable across bit widths; the absolute stakes are not, which is why GPTQ-vs-RTN matters little at 4 bits and enormously at 2.

34.3.3 AWQ

AWQ (Lin et al., 2023) starts from a measurement: protecting the ~1% of weight channels with the largest average activation magnitude (keeping them FP16) recovers most of RTN's quality loss, but mixed precision is hardware-hostile. The fix is the scale-migration identity from Section 34.2, deployed to protect weights rather than to smooth activations: multiply salient input-channel columns of $W$ by $s_j = \mathbb{E}[|x_j|]^{\alpha}$ (with $\alpha$ grid-searched per layer against reconstruction error), divide the activations correspondingly — in practice folded into the previous layer — and quantize the scaled weights. Scaled-up columns occupy more of the grid's dynamic range and get finer effective resolution precisely where the layer's output is most sensitive. No Hessian, no iterative solve, no backward pass; and because it never fits per-column updates to calibration data, AWQ generalizes somewhat better across domains on some evals. GPTQ and AWQ together are the deployed standard: the bulk of quantized open-model checkpoints on HuggingFace ship in one of the two formats (or GGUF's closely related k-quants). Verify against current HF download stats.

34.4 Rotation-Based Methods

Grouping bounds outlier damage; scaling migrates it; rotations dissolve it. For any orthogonal $Q$, replacing $W \to WQ$ and $x \to Q^\top x$ leaves every layer output unchanged, and in pre-norm transformers with RMSNorm the rotation commutes with the normalization (RMSNorm is rotation-equivariant once its diagonal gain is folded into the adjacent weights), so $Q$ can be absorbed into weight matrices offline at zero inference cost. A random or Walsh–Hadamard rotation mixes every coordinate into every other, so a residual stream with a few huge channels becomes, in the rotated basis, near-Gaussian with no heavy coordinates — formally, the rotation makes weights and activations incoherent, bounding $\max_{ij}$ entries relative to the Frobenius norm. QuIP established the incoherence framing; QuIP# added Hadamard-based incoherence processing plus E8-lattice vector codebooks and is among the strongest published results at 2–3 bits; QuaRot applied fused rotations to make weights, activations, and KV cache all INT4; SpinQuant learns the rotation matrices (optimizing over the orthogonal manifold via Cayley SGD) rather than fixing them randomly, and reports closing the W4A4KV4 zero-shot gap on LLaMA-2 7B to 2.9 points, where LLM-QAT under identical settings left a 22.0-point gap. Verify — these numbers are paper-reported, not remeasured here. Rotations are the reason "4-bit activations" stopped being absurd: the outliers were never information-theoretically necessary, they were a basis artifact.

34.5 Activation Quantization and FP8

Weight-only quantization accelerates memory-bound decode but leaves compute in FP16; compute-bound phases (prefill, training, large-batch serving) need both operands of the GEMM in low precision to use the fast tensor-core paths. Activations must then be quantized on the fly, per token — scales computed at runtime from data that includes the outliers, which is why W8A8 needed SmoothQuant-style migration and W4A4 needed rotations.

FP8 changes the trade rather than solving the problem: an 8-bit float (E4M3: 4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits; or E5M2) spends bits on dynamic range instead of resolution, tolerating outliers far better than INT8 at the same width. DeepSeek-V3 is the landmark at-scale validation: a 671B-parameter MoE pretrained with FP8 GEMMs throughout, using E4M3 for all tensors (not the earlier E4M3-forward/E5M2-backward convention), fine-grained scaling — $1\times128$ tiles for activations, $128\times128$ blocks for weights, the training-side echo of per-group weight quantization — and promotion of partial sums from tensor cores to FP32 CUDA-core accumulators every 128 multiply-accumulates, working around the H800's limited-precision internal accumulation. The reported relative loss error versus a BF16 baseline stays under 0.25%. Verify against the DeepSeek-V3 technical report (arXiv:2412.19437). The through-line from Section 34.1 is exact: even with floating-point formats, the winning move was finer scaling granularity.

34.6 QAT and the Straight-Through Estimator

PTQ repairs a frozen model; quantization-aware training (QAT) lets the model adapt. The forward pass applies "fake quantization" $\hat w = s(\mathrm{clip}(\mathrm{round}(w/s)+z) - z)$ while keeping an FP32 shadow copy of $w$; the backward pass faces the problem that $\mathrm{round}(\cdot)$ has zero derivative almost everywhere.

Definition 34.2 (Straight-through estimator)

The STE replaces the true Jacobian of the quantizer with the identity on the unclipped region: $$\frac{\partial \hat w}{\partial w} := \mathbb{1}\!\left[\,0 \le \mathrm{round}(w/s)+z \le 2^b - 1\,\right],$$ i.e., gradients pass through rounding unchanged and are zeroed where the value clipped. Updates accumulate in the FP32 shadow weights; the quantized value changes only when the shadow crosses a grid boundary.

The STE is a biased estimator of a gradient that does not exist, and it works anyway; the honest theoretical account is that fake-quantized training approximately minimizes the loss of the quantized network as long as steps are small relative to grid spacing, with the shadow weights doing a dithered search over grid assignments. Zeroing the gradient outside the clip range matters — pass gradients there too and weights drift arbitrarily far past the representable range. Refinements treat $s$ itself as a learnable parameter with its own STE-derived gradient (LSQ). The cost profile fixes the division of labor: QAT needs data, training infrastructure, and some percent of pretraining compute, so it is reserved for regimes PTQ cannot reach — sub-4-bit weights, aggressive activation formats, edge deployment — while 4-bit weight-only stays PTQ. Likely

34.7 Ternary Models

The extreme of QAT is training with weights constrained to $\{-1, 0, +1\}$ from step zero — 1.58 bits ($\log_2 3$) per weight, with a per-tensor FP scale, 8-bit activations, and FP32 shadow weights during training. BitNet b1.58 (Microsoft, 2024) claimed parity with FP16 LLaMA-architecture baselines at 3B parameters; BitNet b1.58 2B4T (2025) is the strongest public evidence: a 2B-parameter ternary model trained on 4T tokens that the technical report places within 1–2 points of similarly sized full-precision open models (Qwen2.5-1.5B, MiniCPM, Gemma-3 1B class) on MMLU, GSM8K, and commonsense suites, with ~0.4 GB weight memory and genuinely fast CPU inference via bitnet.cpp. Verify against arXiv:2504.12285.

What ternary models have not demonstrated is the claim the headlines imply. Contested The comparisons are against models trained on different data with different recipes, so "parity" is confounded; no ternary model has been shown competitive at 7B–70B+ against an equally resourced full-precision twin; and the fair baseline question is unsettled — at matched memory (a ternary 10B versus an FP4-quantized ~3B, say) or matched training compute, it is not established that ternary wins, and PTQ-to-4-bit of a strong FP model remains the better accuracy-per-byte trade at every scale where both exist. Our position: BitNet-class results are real evidence that extreme weight precision is not fundamental at the ~2B scale, and are not yet evidence that frontier training should be ternary. What would settle it: one controlled scaling study, identical data and tokens, ternary versus BF16 versus FP4-PTQ, crossing 7B. Note the asymmetry with Section 34.5: FP8 training is production reality at 671B; ternary's largest public validation is ~2B.

34.8 KV-Cache Quantization

Chapter 33 computed the KV cache at $2 \cdot L \cdot n \cdot d_{\text{kv}}$ elements per sequence; at long context it, not the weights, is the memory bound, and at large batch it is also the bandwidth bound for attention. The cache is activation data, so Section 34.2's pathology applies with a twist that has a clean empirical signature: keys exhibit strong per-channel outliers (specific $d_k$ coordinates are large across all positions, a structure RoPE further imprints), while values show no such channel structure. The deployed recipe follows directly: quantize keys per-channel and values per-token — the KIVI observation — which pushes both to 2 bits given a short FP16 window of recent tokens (rounding recent keys hurts most: their attention logits are largest, and $\mathrm{softmax}$ amplifies logit error exponentially). Likely In practice INT8 KV is near-free, 4-bit is the standard aggressive setting (llama.cpp, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM all ship it), and 2-bit degrades long-context retrieval first — needle-style evals are the right smoke test. Verify against current vLLM/TensorRT-LLM documentation.

34.9 Distillation and Pruning

Quantization shrinks bits per parameter; distillation shrinks the parameter count by training a small student against a large teacher's distribution rather than one-hot data. The classic loss (Hinton et al., 2015) softens both with temperature $\tau$: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}} = \tau^2 \cdot \mathrm{KL}\!\left(\mathrm{softmax}(z_t/\tau)\,\|\,\mathrm{softmax}(z_s/\tau)\right),$$ the $\tau^2$ keeping gradient magnitude comparable across temperatures. The teacher's soft targets carry the "dark knowledge" one-hot labels destroy — which wrong answers are nearly right — and act as a per-example regularizer. For autoregressive LLMs, token-level KL on teacher logits is often replaced by sequence-level KD: generate from the teacher, fine-tune the student on the outputs. DeepSeek-R1's distilled 1.5B–70B models — Qwen and Llama checkpoints fine-tuned on ~800K teacher-generated reasoning traces — are the most consequential recent example, transferring much of the reasoning behavior at a fraction of the size; on-policy (generalized) KD on student-generated sequences further reduces the train–inference mismatch. Verify specifics against the R1 report.

Pruning zeroes weights outright. Unstructured magnitude pruning compresses storage but not dense-GEMM time; hardware-realizable gains need structure, e.g. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity (two zeros per four consecutive weights), which NVIDIA tensor cores execute at up to a nominal 2× — realized end-to-end gains are substantially smaller. Verify The best PTQ pruning method is this chapter's math wearing a different constraint: SparseGPT solves the same layerwise objective $\|WX - \hat W X\|_F^2$ with the same Hessian $XX^\top$ and the same OBQ compensation of Theorem 34.1, except the "quantizer" sets weights to zero; Wanda then showed that for LLMs the selection criterion $|w_{ij}| \cdot \|x_j\|_2$ alone — salience again, as in AWQ — gets most of the way with no update step at all. One Hessian, three compressions.

Artifact 34.1 — GPTQ from Scratch with the Ablations That Matter

A layer $y = Wx$ with $256\times256$ weights and 2,048 correlated calibration vectors (power-law covariance — propagation only matters when $H$ has off-diagonal mass); affine grids at all three granularities; RTN; Cholesky-form GPTQ per Theorem 34.1. Asserted: (a) GPTQ beats RTN on layer-output MSE at 4, 3, 2 bits; (b) disabling only the propagation step collapses GPTQ to RTN exactly; (c) per-group(32) beats per-tensor at 4 bits; (d) injected outlier channels concentrate the error, and an AWQ-style grid-searched channel scale reduces it.

"""Artifact 34.1 -- GPTQ from scratch, with the error-propagation ablation,
per-group vs per-tensor scaling, and an AWQ-style outlier demonstration.

Pure NumPy. torch appears only as a cross-check on the output-MSE computation.
Everything asserted is measured here; nothing is quoted from a paper.
"""
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Setup: a "layer" y = W x with correlated calibration activations.
# X is (d_in, n): n calibration vectors as columns.  The layerwise
# objective GPTQ minimizes is ||W X - W_q X||_F^2, whose Hessian w.r.t.
# each row of W is H = 2 X X^T -- shared across rows.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
d_in, d_out, n = 256, 256, 2048
# Controlled covariance: decaying spectrum + random rotation, so H has
# strong off-diagonal structure (propagation only matters if it does).
U, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.standard_normal((d_in, d_in)))
spec = (np.arange(1, d_in + 1) ** -0.7)            # power-law eigenvalues
A = U * np.sqrt(spec)                               # Sigma^(1/2) up to rotation
X = A @ rng.standard_normal((d_in, n))              # cov(X) ~ U diag(spec) U^T
W = rng.standard_normal((d_out, d_in)) / np.sqrt(d_in)
Y_ref = W @ X                                       # exact layer output


def out_mse(Wq, Xc=X):
    """Layer-output MSE: mean squared error of (W - Wq) Xc."""
    D = (W - Wq) @ Xc
    return float(np.mean(D * D))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Quantization grids.  Asymmetric affine: q = clip(round(w/s) + z, 0, 2^b-1),
# w_hat = s (q - z).  Scales/zeros are per-row ("per-channel"), per-group
# (contiguous input-dim blocks), or one pair for the whole tensor.
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def make_grid(Wm, bits, granularity="channel", group=32):
    qmax = 2 ** bits - 1
    if granularity == "tensor":
        lo, hi = Wm.min(), Wm.max()
        s = np.maximum((hi - lo) / qmax, 1e-12); z = np.round(-lo / s)
        return np.full((Wm.shape[0], Wm.shape[1]), s), np.full(Wm.shape, z)
    if granularity == "channel":
        lo = Wm.min(axis=1, keepdims=True); hi = Wm.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        s = np.maximum((hi - lo) / qmax, 1e-12); z = np.round(-lo / s)
        return np.broadcast_to(s, Wm.shape).copy(), np.broadcast_to(z, Wm.shape).copy()
    # per-group: independent (s, z) for each row x each block of `group` cols
    s = np.empty_like(Wm); z = np.empty_like(Wm)
    for g0 in range(0, Wm.shape[1], group):
        blk = Wm[:, g0:g0 + group]
        lo = blk.min(axis=1, keepdims=True); hi = blk.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        sg = np.maximum((hi - lo) / qmax, 1e-12)
        s[:, g0:g0 + group] = sg; z[:, g0:g0 + group] = np.round(-lo / sg)
    return s, z


def quant(Wm, s, z, bits):
    q = np.clip(np.round(Wm / s) + z, 0, 2 ** bits - 1)
    return s * (q - z)


def rtn(Wm, bits, granularity="channel", group=32):
    s, z = make_grid(Wm, bits, granularity, group)
    return quant(Wm, s, z, bits)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# GPTQ, Cholesky form.  H = 2 X X^T + damping.  Let T = chol(H^{-1})
# (upper).  Quantize columns left to right; after fixing column j, subtract
# (w_j - q_j)/T_jj * T_{j,j+1:} from the not-yet-quantized columns -- the
# exact OBQ update, batched via the Cholesky factor.
# `propagate=False` uses the identical grid but skips the update:
# that is column-wise RTN on the same grid (ablation (b)).
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def gptq(Wm, Xc, bits, granularity="channel", group=32, propagate=True):
    H = 2.0 * (Xc @ Xc.T)
    H[np.diag_indices_from(H)] += 0.01 * np.mean(np.diag(H))  # damping
    Hinv = np.linalg.inv(H)
    T = np.linalg.cholesky(Hinv, upper=True)   # upper-triangular factor
    Wk = Wm.copy()
    s, z = make_grid(Wm, bits, granularity, group)  # grid fixed up front
    Q = np.empty_like(Wm)
    for j in range(Wm.shape[1]):
        w = Wk[:, j]
        Q[:, j] = quant(w, s[:, j], z[:, j], bits)
        if propagate and j + 1 < Wm.shape[1]:
            err = (w - Q[:, j]) / T[j, j]                 # scaled residual
            Wk[:, j + 1:] -= np.outer(err, T[j, j + 1:])  # push into the future
    return Q


# ======================================================================
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ---------- (a) + (b): GPTQ vs RTN vs GPTQ-without-propagation ----
    print("bits |    RTN MSE   |  no-prop MSE |   GPTQ MSE   | GPTQ/RTN")
    for bits in (4, 3, 2):
        m_rtn = out_mse(rtn(W, bits))
        m_nop = out_mse(gptq(W, X, bits, propagate=False))
        m_gptq = out_mse(gptq(W, X, bits))
        print(f"  {bits}  | {m_rtn:.6e} | {m_nop:.6e} | {m_gptq:.6e} | {m_gptq/m_rtn:6.3f}")
        assert m_gptq < m_rtn,  f"(a) GPTQ !< RTN at {bits} bits"
        assert m_gptq < m_nop,  f"(b) propagation did not help at {bits} bits"
    # sanity: same grid, no propagation == plain per-channel RTN
    assert np.allclose(gptq(W, X, 4, propagate=False), rtn(W, 4))

    # ---------- (c): per-group vs per-tensor at 4 bits (RTN) ----------
    m_tensor = out_mse(rtn(W, 4, "tensor"))
    m_group = out_mse(rtn(W, 4, "group", 32))
    print(f"\n4-bit RTN  per-tensor MSE {m_tensor:.6e}  vs  per-group(32) "
          f"{m_group:.6e}  ({m_tensor/m_group:.2f}x better)")
    assert m_group < m_tensor, "(c) per-group !< per-tensor"

    # ---------- (d): outlier channels + AWQ-style rescue --------------
    Xo = X.copy()
    out_idx = rng.choice(d_in, 4, replace=False)
    Xo[out_idx] *= 50.0                       # 4 emergent-outlier channels
    Y_o = W @ Xo
    dW = W - rtn(W, 3)                        # 3-bit RTN weight error
    # per-input-channel share of output error energy: ||dW_col_j||^2 E[x_j^2]
    energy = (dW ** 2).sum(0) * (Xo ** 2).mean(1)
    frac = energy[out_idx].sum() / energy.sum()
    print(f"\n4/{d_in} channels are outliers (x50); they carry "
          f"{100*frac:.1f}% of weight-quantization output error energy")
    assert frac > 0.5, "(d) error did not concentrate on outlier channels"

    base = float(np.mean(((W - rtn(W, 3)) @ Xo) ** 2))
    best = (None, np.inf)
    for alpha in (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0):      # AWQ grid search on the scale
        s_ch = np.abs(Xo).mean(1) ** alpha    # per-channel activation scale
        s_ch /= s_ch.mean()
        Wq = rtn(W * s_ch, 3)                 # quantize scaled weights
        m = float(np.mean(((W * s_ch - Wq) @ (Xo / s_ch[:, None])) ** 2))
        if m < best[1]:
            best = (alpha, m)
    print(f"3-bit RTN output MSE on outlier data: {base:.6e} -> "
          f"{best[1]:.6e} with AWQ scale (alpha={best[0]}), "
          f"{base/best[1]:.1f}x reduction")
    assert best[1] < base, "(d) AWQ scaling did not reduce error"

    # ---------- torch cross-check on the MSE computation --------------
    try:
        import torch
    except ImportError:
        torch = None
    if torch is not None:
        Wq4 = gptq(W, X, 4)
        ref = torch.mean(((torch.from_numpy(W) - torch.from_numpy(Wq4))
                          @ torch.from_numpy(X)) ** 2).item()
        np_val = out_mse(Wq4)
        print(f"\ntorch cross-check: |MSE_np - MSE_torch| = {abs(ref-np_val):.2e}")
        assert abs(ref - np_val) < 1e-10
    else:
        print("[skipped: torch not installed]")
    print("\nAll assertions passed.")

Running it prints: at 4 bits, RTN output MSE 6.98e-4 versus GPTQ 4.69e-4 (ratio 0.672); at 2 bits, 1.73e-2 versus 1.18e-2 (0.684); the no-propagation column equals RTN to machine precision at every width, so the entire gain is the Theorem 34.1 update. Per-group(32) beats per-tensor 4-bit RTN by 4.29×; the four outlier channels carry 97.6% of error energy; the AWQ scale at $\alpha=0.25$ cuts outlier-data MSE 3.9× (1.33e-1 to 3.44e-2). Wall time ~3 s on CPU.

Under Encryption

Under homomorphic encryption, quantization stops being an optimization and becomes an enabler — and the direction of help depends on the scheme. TFHE-style schemes evaluate arbitrary functions as programmable-bootstrap lookup tables over small integer domains, with cost exponential-ish in the bit width of the table input; aggressive 4–8-bit quantization is therefore what makes encrypted inference expressible at all, not a compression nicety. This is exactly the design point of Concrete-ML, which pairs quantization-aware training with compilation of the resulting integer network into TFHE circuits. CKKS is the opposite case: it computes on approximate reals natively, carrying ~30–50 bits of scale per level, so quantizing weights to 4 bits buys essentially no precision headroom — the noise floor is set by the encryption parameters, not the plaintext — though packing quantized weights does shrink plaintext/ciphertext count and thus memory and key-switching traffic. The scheme choice and the quantization decision are therefore one decision, not two: choosing TFHE is choosing low-bit integer inference, and choosing CKKS makes this chapter's machinery mostly moot. Chapter 40 returns to this when comparing private-inference systems.

Key Takeaways
  • Affine quantization error is bounded by half the scale, and the scale is set by the range of its unit — so granularity (per-tensor → per-channel → per-group) is the first lever, costing exactly $32/g$ extra bits per weight for group size $g$ with FP16 scale and zero-point. Certain
  • Large transformers develop a few outlier activation channels that dominate quantization error; the artifact measures 4/256 injected outlier channels carrying 97.6% of layer output error energy, and an AWQ-style channel scale cutting it 3.9×. Certain
  • GPTQ is exact OBQ compensation (Theorem 34.1) run column-wise with a shared Cholesky-factored inverse Hessian; on identical grids it beat RTN by ~1.5× in output MSE at 4, 3, and 2 bits in our measurement, entirely via error propagation. Certain
  • Rotation methods (QuIP#, QuaRot, SpinQuant) exploit the model's orthogonal invariance to dissolve outliers in a rotated basis, making 4-bit activations and KV cache viable; FP8 training with fine-grained tile scaling is production-validated at 671B by DeepSeek-V3 at <0.25% reported relative loss error. Verify
  • Ternary (BitNet-class) models show extreme weight precision is not fundamental at ~2B scale, but have not demonstrated frontier-scale parity under controlled comparisons; matched-memory and matched-compute baselines remain the unsettled crux. Contested
Part VII

The Frontier

This part covers what is genuinely unsettled: generative modelling beyond autoregression, agents that act over long horizons, and the interpretability work that is the field's only route to knowing what these systems compute. It is written to be replaced. Every claim carries a date, and the Key Takeaways lean hard on the Contested tag.
Chapter 35

Diffusion, Flow Matching, and Non-Autoregressive Generation

Learning Objectives
  • Derive the forward noising process, its closed-form marginal $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$, and the simplified noise-prediction loss, and connect it to denoising score matching via Tweedie's formula.
  • State the probability-flow ODE and explain why it shares every marginal $p_t$ with the reverse SDE, with deterministic (DDIM-style) sampling as its discretization.
  • Derive conditional flow matching and rectified flow, and explain why a straighter probability path permits fewer sampling steps at fixed discretization error.
  • Explain classifier-free guidance as score extrapolation and quantify its quality–diversity trade.
  • Implement DDPM and conditional flow matching in working code on an analytic 2D target, verifying the learned score and velocity against closed forms.
Read alongside — Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: Advanced Topics, for the full measure-theoretic treatment of diffusion, score matching, and SDE samplers; Prince, Understanding Deep Learning, whose diffusion diagrams are the best visual companion to the algebra below.

Everything before this chapter generated data one token at a time under the autoregressive factorization of Chapter 23, paying the serial-decoding costs itemized in Chapter 33. This chapter develops the alternative: generate everything at once, badly, then spend iterations refining it. Diffusion models (Sections 35.2–35.4) implement this as learned denoising; flow matching (Section 35.5) implements it as learned transport along a chosen probability path. The central claim, argued in Section 35.5 and tested empirically in Artifact 35.1, is that these are the same object under reparameterization — flow matching displaced diffusion in frontier image models because its default path is straighter, so ODE solvers need fewer steps, not because the theory changed. The latent-variable machinery comes from Chapter 9, the backbone architectures from Chapters 18 and 20, and the few-step frontier (Section 35.9) is this decade's answer to the inference economics of Chapter 33.

35.1 From Autoencoders to Diffusion

The VAE of Chapter 9 asks a decoder to map a low-dimensional Gaussian latent to a data sample in one function evaluation, and its Gaussian likelihood averages over everything the latent fails to specify — hence blurry samples. GANs sharpen this with an adversarial objective at the price of an unstable min-max game with no monitorable loss. Diffusion's move is to decompose one impossible inverse problem into a thousand trivial ones: corrupt data with a fixed, known noising process until it is indistinguishable from a Gaussian, then learn only the tiny conditional denoising step at each noise level. Each step is a regression with an analytically known target, so training inherits the stability of supervised learning — a mean-squared error that goes down — while sampling composes hundreds of steps into an expressive map. That trade — stable training, expensive sampling — is the defining economics of this model family, and Sections 35.4, 35.5, and 35.9 are all, at bottom, attacks on the sampling bill. Certain

35.2 The Forward Process

Definition 35.1 (Variance-preserving forward process)

Fix a schedule $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_T \in (0,1)$. The forward (noising) Markov chain on data $x_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}$ is $$x_k = \sqrt{1-\beta_k}\,x_{k-1} + \sqrt{\beta_k}\,\epsilon_k, \qquad \epsilon_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),$$ i.e. $q(x_k \mid x_{k-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(\sqrt{1-\beta_k}\,x_{k-1},\, \beta_k I\big)$. Write $\alpha_k = 1-\beta_k$ and $\bar\alpha_k = \prod_{j\le k}\alpha_j$.

The shrink factor $\sqrt{1-\beta_k}$ is what makes the process variance-preserving: if $\mathrm{Var}[x_{k-1}] = I$ then $\mathrm{Var}[x_k] = (1-\beta_k)I + \beta_k I = I$, so activations neither explode nor vanish across a thousand steps — the same signal-propagation discipline as Chapter 12, applied to a stochastic process. The practical payoff of this specific chain is that the $k$-step marginal collapses to a single Gaussian:

Theorem 35.1 (Closed-form marginal)

$q(x_k \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,x_0,\; (1-\bar\alpha_k) I\big)$, equivalently $x_k = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$.

Proof. Induction on $k$. Trivial at $k=0$. Assume $x_{k-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{k-1}}\,\epsilon'$. Then $x_k = \sqrt{\alpha_k \bar\alpha_{k-1}}\,x_0 + \sqrt{\alpha_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}\,\epsilon' + \sqrt{\beta_k}\,\epsilon_k$. The two independent Gaussian terms sum to a Gaussian with variance $\alpha_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1}) + \beta_k = \alpha_k - \alpha_k\bar\alpha_{k-1} + 1 - \alpha_k = 1 - \bar\alpha_k$ per coordinate. $\blacksquare$

This is the single most load-bearing formula in the chapter: training never simulates the chain. It samples $k$ uniformly, jumps straight to $x_k$ in one line, and regresses. The signal-to-noise ratio $\mathrm{SNR}(k) = \bar\alpha_k/(1-\bar\alpha_k)$ decreases monotonically from $\approx 10^4$ to $\approx 4\times 10^{-5}$ under the standard linear schedule $\beta_k \in [10^{-4}, 0.02]$, $T=1000$, so by $k=T$ the marginal is numerically indistinguishable from $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and sampling can start from pure noise. Schedule design (linear, cosine, log-SNR-uniform) is exactly the choice of how to allocate model capacity across noise levels. Certain

35.3 Score Matching and the Reverse Process

To generate, we must reverse the chain, and the reversal is governed by the score $\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$ of each noised marginal. The bridge between "predict the noise" and "know the score" is a conditional-expectation identity often called Tweedie's formula:

Theorem 35.2 (Denoising score matching / Tweedie)

Let $p_t$ be the marginal of $x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon$ with $x_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}$, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ independent. Then $$\nabla_x \log p_t(x) \;=\; -\frac{\mathbb{E}[\epsilon \mid x_t = x]}{\sigma_t},$$ and consequently the minimizer of the noise-prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0,\epsilon,t}\big[\|\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t) - \epsilon\|_2^2\big]$ satisfies $\epsilon_{\theta^*}(x,t) = \mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid x_t=x]$, so $s_{\theta^*}(x,t) = -\epsilon_{\theta^*}(x,t)/\sigma_t$ is the exact score.

Proof. $p_t(x) = \int p_{\text{data}}(x_0)\, \mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_t x_0, \sigma_t^2 I)\, dx_0$. Differentiating under the integral, $\nabla_x \mathcal{N}(x;\alpha_t x_0,\sigma_t^2 I) = \frac{\alpha_t x_0 - x}{\sigma_t^2}\,\mathcal{N}(\cdot)$, so $\nabla_x \log p_t(x) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\alpha_t x_0 - x}{\sigma_t^2} \,\Big|\, x_t = x\right] = -\frac{\mathbb{E}[\epsilon \mid x_t=x]}{\sigma_t}$, using $x = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t\epsilon$. The second claim is the standard fact that the $L^2$-optimal predictor of $\epsilon$ given $x_t$ is the conditional mean (Chapter 6). $\blacksquare$

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}}$ is the loss of Ho et al.'s DDPM; it is a fixed reweighting of the variational bound one would derive Chapter-9-style, and the reweighting empirically helps perceptual quality by not over-weighting near-zero noise levels. Certain With the score in hand, Anderson's time-reversal theorem gives the generative dynamics: if the forward process is the SDE $dx = f(x,t)\,dt + g(t)\,dw$, the reverse-time process $$dx = \big[f(x,t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)\big]dt + g(t)\,d\bar w$$ has the same marginals traversed backward.
