DDPM's ancestral sampler — at each step, form $\hat x_0 = (x_k - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon_\theta)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$, then sample the Gaussian posterior step toward $k' \lt k$ — is precisely an Euler–Maruyama-style discretization of this reverse SDE. Certain

Example 35.1 (Score and optimal noise prediction by hand)

Take 1D data $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(2, 0.25)$ and a step with $\bar\alpha = 0.64$, so $\sqrt{\bar\alpha} = 0.8$, $\sigma^2 = 0.36$, $\sigma = 0.6$. By Theorem 35.1 the marginal is $\mathcal{N}(0.8\cdot 2,\; 0.64\cdot 0.25 + 0.36) = \mathcal{N}(1.6,\, 0.52)$. At $x = 2.5$: score $= -(2.5-1.6)/0.52 = -1.7308$; optimal noise prediction $\epsilon^* = -\sigma \cdot \text{score} = 0.6 \times 1.7308 = 1.0385$. Cross-check via the posterior over clean data: $\mathbb{E}[x_0\mid x] = 2 + \frac{0.8\cdot 0.25}{0.52}(2.5-1.6) = 2.3462$, and indeed $0.8 \times 2.3462 + 0.6 \times 1.0385 = 1.8769 + 0.6231 = 2.5 = x$: the denoised mean and the predicted noise reassemble the observation exactly.

35.4 The Probability-Flow ODE and Deterministic Samplers

Theorem 35.3 (Probability-flow ODE)

The deterministic ODE $$\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x,t) - \tfrac{1}{2}g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)$$ has the same time-$t$ marginals $p_t$ as the forward SDE $dx = f\,dt + g\,dw$ (and hence as the reverse SDE).

Proof sketch. The SDE's marginals obey the Fokker–Planck equation $\partial_t p = -\nabla\!\cdot\!(f p) + \tfrac{1}{2}g^2 \Delta p$. Rewrite the diffusion term as a transport term: $\tfrac{1}{2}g^2\Delta p = \nabla\!\cdot\!\big(\tfrac{1}{2}g^2 p\, \nabla \log p\big)$, using $\nabla p = p\nabla\log p$. Then $\partial_t p = -\nabla\!\cdot\!\big[(f - \tfrac{1}{2}g^2\nabla\log p)\,p\big]$, which is the continuity equation of the stated ODE: a deterministic velocity field transporting exactly the same density. $\blacksquare$

The consequence is practical, not decorative. The same trained network $\epsilon_\theta$ can be sampled stochastically (reverse SDE; DDPM ancestral) or deterministically (probability-flow ODE; DDIM with $\eta=0$ is its discretization — both live in one sampler with a noise-injection knob $\eta$, as in Artifact 35.1). Determinism buys three things: fewer steps for a given accuracy, because ODE solvers of higher order exist and there is no injected noise to average away; an invertible map, so real images can be encoded to noise and edited; and a well-defined notion of a sample's trajectory, which few-step distillation (Section 35.9) needs as a training target. The cost of every sampler, stochastic or not, is measured in NFE — number of function evaluations of the network — and the discretization error of any solver is controlled by the curvature of the trajectories it integrates. That observation is the entire motivation for the next section. Certain

35.5 Flow Matching and Rectified Flow

Flow matching starts from the continuity equation directly: pick any path of densities $p_t$ from noise ($t{=}0$) to data ($t{=}1$), realized by a velocity field $u_t$, and regress a network $v_\theta$ onto $u_t$. The marginal field $u_t$ is intractable — it involves an expectation over the whole dataset — but a conditional construction sidesteps this exactly as Theorem 35.2 sidestepped the intractable score:

Definition 35.2 (Conditional flow matching, linear path)

Draw $x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ (noise), $x_1 \sim p_{\text{data}}$, $t \sim \mathrm{U}[0,1]$, and set $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$. The conditional target velocity is the constant $u_t(x_t \mid x_0, x_1) = x_1 - x_0$, and the CFM loss is $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x_0, x_1, t}\big[\|v_\theta(x_t, t) - (x_1 - x_0)\|_2^2\big].$$

Theorem 35.4 (CFM trains the marginal field)

$\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}} = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}$ where $\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_t \sim p_t}\|v_\theta(x_t,t) - u_t(x_t)\|_2^2$ and $u_t(x) = \mathbb{E}[x_1 - x_0 \mid x_t = x]$ is the marginal velocity generating $p_t$.

Proof. Expand both squares. The $\|v_\theta\|^2$ terms are identical in distribution. The cross terms agree by the tower rule: $\mathbb{E}\langle v_\theta(x_t,t), x_1 - x_0\rangle = \mathbb{E}\big\langle v_\theta(x_t,t), \mathbb{E}[x_1-x_0 \mid x_t]\big\rangle = \mathbb{E}\langle v_\theta, u_t(x_t)\rangle$. The remaining terms ($\|x_1-x_0\|^2$ vs. $\|u_t\|^2$) are $\theta$-independent constants. So the two losses differ by a constant — the conditional variance of the target — and share gradients. $\blacksquare$

That constant matters for reading loss curves: the CFM loss plateaus at the irreducible conditional variance of $x_1 - x_0$ given $x_t$, not at zero (1.886 in Artifact 35.1's run, against a noise-prediction plateau of 0.253 — both are floors, not failures). Sampling is a forward-Euler (or higher-order) integration of $dx/dt = v_\theta(x,t)$ from Gaussian noise.

35.5.1 The equivalence, and why straightness wins

Now the chapter's thesis. For a Gaussian path $x_t = a_t x_1 + b_t x_0$, the marginal velocity, the score, and the noise/data predictions are all affine functions of one another at each $t$: $u_t(x) = \frac{\dot a_t}{a_t}x + b_t\big(\frac{\dot a_t b_t}{a_t} - \dot b_t\big)\nabla_x \log p_t(x)$, and each is recoverable from $\mathbb{E}[x_1 \mid x_t]$. A diffusion model and a flow-matching model trained on the same data learn the same conditional expectation in different clothes; the choices that remain are the schedule $(a_t, b_t)$, the prediction target (which sets the loss weighting across $t$), and the sampler. Certain What flow matching changed in practice is the default path: the linear interpolant's conditional trajectories are straight lines, and its marginal trajectories are far straighter than the strongly curved variance-preserving spirals of DDPM. Straightness is the whole game for step count: forward Euler on a trajectory with constant velocity is exact in one step, and its global error otherwise scales with the trajectory's curvature. Rectified flow makes this quantitative and iterable: define straightness as $S = \int_0^1 \mathbb{E}\|x_1 - x_0 - v(x_t,t)\|_2^2\,dt$; after training, re-pair each noise sample with the data point its ODE actually reaches ("reflow") and retrain on the new coupling. Each reflow round provably does not increase transport cost and empirically slashes curvature, which is why one or two rounds enable few-step sampling. Likely Frontier image and video systems — Stable Diffusion 3's rectified-flow transformer and Flux among them — train with this objective. Verify The theory did not change; the parameterization with the smaller discretization error won.

Common Pitfall

Convention collisions between the two formalisms produce code that runs and silently generates garbage. DDPM indexes time so that $k{=}0$ is data ($\bar\alpha_0 = 1$); the linear-path flow matching above puts noise at $t{=}0$. Port a sampler between the two without flipping time and you integrate toward the prior, collapsing every sample to a fuzzy blob near the origin. Two adjacent bugs from the same family: converting noise prediction to score with the wrong sign or scale (it is $s = -\epsilon_\theta/\sigma_t$, not $-\epsilon_\theta/\sigma_t^2$ — the $\sigma_t^2$ variant comes from treating $\epsilon_\theta$ as the raw residual $x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$ when it predicts the standardized one), and evaluating the flow-matching conditional expectation at $t{=}1$ exactly, where the $1/(1-t)$ in $\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t]$ divides by zero — hence the $t \sim \mathrm{U}[10^{-3}, 1-10^{-3}]$ clamp in Artifact 35.1.

35.6 Classifier-Free Guidance

Conditional generation trains $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c)$ on (data, condition) pairs, randomly dropping $c$ (10–20% of batches) so the same network also learns the unconditional score. At sampling time, classifier-free guidance extrapolates: $$\tilde\epsilon_w = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + w\big(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)\big), \qquad w \ge 1.$$ In score terms, $\tilde s = s(x\mid c) + (w-1)\nabla_x \log p_t(c \mid x)$ by Bayes' rule — guidance adds a push up the gradient of an implicit classifier's confidence, which is why it needs no separately trained classifier. The trade is explicit in the formula: $w$ sharpens the conditional distribution toward high-likelihood-under-$c$ regions, raising fidelity and prompt adherence while shrinking diversity, and large $w$ (typical text-to-image defaults sit near $w \approx 5$–$8$ Verify) produces the familiar oversaturated, contrast-crushed look. Two working caveats. First, the guided field is generally not the score of any normalized distribution along the whole trajectory, so "sampling from $p(x\mid c)^w p(x)^{1-w}$" is a heuristic description, not a theorem. Likely Second, guidance doubles NFE (two forward passes per step) unless distilled into the student network — which is standard in few-step systems. The same extrapolation applies verbatim to velocity fields: replace $\epsilon$ with $v$ everywhere. Certain

35.7 Architectures: U-Net to DiT

The denoiser is architecture-agnostic in principle — it is a map $(x_t, t, c) \mapsto \mathbb{R}^{\dim x}$ — and the field has used two. The U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer & Brox, 2015, from Chapter 16's convolutional lineage) processes the image at multiple resolutions with skip connections between mirrored down/up stages and self-attention at coarse resolutions; timestep and condition enter via added embeddings and cross-attention. The Diffusion Transformer (DiT) discards this entirely: patchify the (latent) image as in Chapter 20's ViT, run a plain transformer, and inject $t$ and $c$ through adaLN-Zero — a conditioning MLP that regresses per-block scale/shift/gate parameters, with gates initialized to zero so every block starts as identity (the Chapter 12 signal-propagation trick, again). DiT's decisive property is that sample quality tracks total forward FLOPs across depth/width/patch-size trades, reproducing transformer scaling behavior (Chapter 24) in a domain U-Nets never exhibited cleanly; DiT-XL/2 reached FID 2.27 on class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 with guidance. Verify Current frontier text-to-image stacks (SD3, Flux) use multimodal DiT variants in which text and image tokens share attention. Verify

35.8 Latent Diffusion

Running a thousand denoiser evaluations at 1024×1024×3 is economically absurd, and perceptually most of those bits are texture the decoder can hallucinate. Latent diffusion therefore trains a VAE-style autoencoder (Chapter 9, upgraded with perceptual and adversarial losses so reconstructions stay sharp) and runs the entire diffusion in its latent space. Stable Diffusion's original recipe compresses 512×512×3 to 64×64×4 — a factor-8 spatial downsampling, 48× fewer elements — before any denoising happens; later systems widened the latent channel count (e.g. 16) to raise the reconstruction ceiling. Verify For a DiT backbone the leverage is quadratic-plus: token count falls 64× with the spatial factor, and attention cost falls with its square (Chapter 18). The division of labor is clean and worth internalizing: the autoencoder owns imperceptible high-frequency detail; diffusion owns semantic composition. The same pattern — do the hard generative work in a learned compressed space — recurs in video models and in the discrete-token systems of Section 35.10. Certain

35.9 Few-Step Generation

Between 2022 and today the sampling bill fell from ~1000 NFE to 1–4 with modest quality loss, through three overlapping strategies. Trajectory distillation: progressive distillation halves step count repeatedly by teaching a student to jump two teacher ODE steps at once; adversarial distillation (SDXL-Turbo lineage) adds a discriminator to sharpen 1–4-step outputs. Consistency models train a network mapping any point on a probability-flow trajectory directly to its endpoint, enforcing self-consistency between adjacent trajectory points — usable as distillation or trained from scratch; simplified continuous-time variants (sCM) closed most of the gap to full samplers at 2 NFE. Verify Direct few-step objectives: MeanFlow (2025) reparameterizes the target as the average velocity over an interval rather than the instantaneous velocity, satisfying an identity that links the two, and reached FID 3.43 on ImageNet 256×256 in a single NFE trained from scratch — no teacher, no distillation. Verify Successors refining the MeanFlow objective pushed 1-NFE FID to the mid-2s by early 2026, at which point one-step generation stopped being a stunt and became a design point. Verify The conceptual through-line: every one of these methods presupposes the deterministic trajectory structure of Section 35.4 — you cannot distill or shortcut a trajectory that is not well-defined — and every one benefits from the straighter paths of Section 35.5. The frontier question is no longer "can we sample in one step" but how much mode coverage one step silently sacrifices, which standard FID measures poorly. Contested Matched-compute evaluations with coverage-sensitive metrics (recall, per-mode statistics as in Artifact 35.1) would settle it; today's evidence says the gap is real but shrinking.

35.10 Diffusion Language Models

Text lives on a discrete alphabet, so Gaussian corruption does not apply directly; the dominant discrete corruption is masking: the forward process replaces tokens with [MASK] at a rate increasing in $t$, and the model learns to unmask — a time-indexed generalization of BERT-style infilling whose reverse process fills in many positions per step, in parallel, with revision of earlier choices. The pitch against Chapter 23's autoregression is throughput and bidirectional editing; the cost is that exact likelihood factorization is lost and per-step parallel predictions ignore within-step dependencies. The field moved fast: LLaDA showed 8B-parameter masked diffusion approaching comparable autoregressive models; Mercury Coder (Feb 2025) shipped commercially at ~1,100 tokens/s on H100; Gemini Diffusion (May 2025) reported 1,479 tokens/s with coding scores matching its AR counterpart (HumanEval 89.6% vs. 90.2%); Seed Diffusion (Aug 2025) reported 2,146 tokens/s on H20 GPUs for code at competitive quality. All of these are vendor-reported speeds on vendor-chosen hardware. Verify The consolidating recipe in early 2026 is to initialize from a pretrained AR model and continue training with the diffusion objective, plus block-wise hybrids that are AR across blocks and diffusion within them — recovering KV-cache-style reuse (Chapter 33) that pure diffusion forfeits. Likely Whether diffusion displaces autoregression for general-purpose LLMs is genuinely contested: the pro case is a 5–10× latency advantage exactly where inference economics bind, the con case is that AR still holds the quality lead at matched scale and enjoys a decade of tooling. Contested Our position: diffusion wins niches where parallel decoding and infilling dominate (code, editing, constrained generation) while AR remains the general-purpose default; a public, matched-compute scaling-law comparison (Chapter 24 methodology) would settle it, and none exists yet.

Artifact 35.1 — DDPM and Flow Matching on an Analytic Target

Both generative families, built from scratch in NumPy — the MLPs, backprop, Adam, and samplers — on a 3-mode 2D Gaussian mixture chosen because the exact score of every noised marginal and the exact flow-matching velocity field have closed forms (Gaussian mixtures stay Gaussian mixtures under both paths). The DDPM side trains $\epsilon_\theta$ against Theorem 35.1's one-line marginal and samples through a unified DDIM sampler whose $\eta$ knob interpolates ancestral SDE sampling ($\eta{=}1$) and the probability-flow ODE ($\eta{=}0$) of Theorem 35.3. The flow-matching side trains $v_\theta$ on Definition 35.2's linear path and integrates with forward Euler. Hard assertions: (a) the learned score and velocity match the analytic fields on a density-weighted grid; (b) sample means, covariances, and mode weights match the target; (c) flow matching crosses a fixed energy-distance threshold in at least 2× fewer NFE than ancestral DDPM; (d) the hand-written backprop matches torch autograd.

"""Artifact 35.1 -- DDPM and conditional flow matching from scratch on an
analytic 2D Gaussian-mixture target.

Everything is plain NumPy: the MLPs, the backprop, the Adam updates, the
samplers. The target is a 3-component isotropic Gaussian mixture, chosen
because BOTH the exact score of every noised marginal AND the exact
flow-matching velocity field are available in closed form, so the learned
networks can be checked against ground truth -- not against a vibe.

Self-checks (hard assertions):
  (a) learned score (from eps-prediction) matches the analytic score on a
      density-weighted grid at two noise levels, rel. error < 0.15; same
      for the learned FM velocity at t=0.5.
  (b) samples from both methods match the target's mean, covariance
      (Frobenius rel. error < 0.15) and mode weights (abs error < 0.06).
  (c) FM crosses a fixed energy-distance threshold in >=2x fewer function
      evaluations than ancestral DDPM, and beats DDPM head-to-head at 2
      and 4 NFE. Full NFE table printed.
  (d) NumPy backprop gradients match torch autograd to < 1e-5 (cross-check).
"""
import os, time
for _v in ("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS", "MKL_NUM_THREADS"):
    os.environ.setdefault(_v, "1")   # tiny matmuls: BLAS threads only spin
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t0 = time.time()

# ---------------- target: 3-mode isotropic Gaussian mixture ----------------
W  = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.2])                       # mode weights
MU = np.array([[-2.5, 0.0], [2.5, 1.5], [1.0, -2.5]])  # mode means
S2 = np.array([0.45, 0.55, 0.35]) ** 2               # per-mode variances (iso)

def sample_target(n, rg):
    k = rg.choice(3, size=n, p=W)
    return MU[k] + np.sqrt(S2[k])[:, None] * rg.standard_normal((n, 2))

def resp(x, m, v):        # posterior mode responsibilities under N(m_k, v_k I)
    lg = -np.sum((x[:, None, :] - m[None]) ** 2, -1) / (2 * v) - np.log(v)
    lg = lg + np.log(W); lg -= lg.max(1, keepdims=True)
    r = np.exp(lg); return r / r.sum(1, keepdims=True)

def mixture_score(x, m, v):   # exact grad log p for mixture N(m_k, v_k I)
    r = resp(x, m, v)
    return np.einsum('nk,nkd->nd', r / v, m[None] - x[:, None, :])

def mixture_logdens(x, m, v):  # log p_t up to const, for grid weighting
    lg = -np.sum((x[:, None, :] - m[None]) ** 2, -1) / (2 * v) - np.log(v)
    return np.log(np.exp(lg + np.log(W)).sum(1))

def fm_marginal_velocity(x, t):
    """Exact E[x1 - x0 | x_t] for path x_t=(1-t)x0 + t x1, x0~N(0,I), x1~mix."""
    c = t * t * S2 + (1 - t) ** 2                    # per-mode marginal var
    r = resp(x, t * MU, c)
    Ex1 = MU[None] + (t * S2 / c)[:, None] * (x[:, None, :] - t * MU[None])
    Ex0 = (x[:, None, :] - t * Ex1) / (1 - t)                       # E[x0|x,k]
    return np.einsum('nk,nkd->nd', r, Ex1 - Ex0)

# ---------------- tiny MLP + manual backprop + Adam ----------------
def timefeat(t):              # Fourier features of scalar time in [0,1]
    c = 2 * np.pi * t[:, None] * np.array([1., 2., 4., 8.])
    return np.concatenate([t[:, None], np.sin(c), np.cos(c)], 1)   # 9 feats

class MLP:                    # 11 -> 64 -> 64 -> 2, tanh hidden, linear out
    def __init__(self, rg, sizes=(11, 64, 64, 2)):
        self.Ws = [rg.standard_normal((a, b)) * np.sqrt(1.0 / a)
                   for a, b in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:])]
        self.bs = [np.zeros(b) for b in sizes[1:]]
        self.m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in self.Ws + self.bs]
        self.v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in self.Ws + self.bs]
        self.step = 0

    def forward(self, X):
        self.hs = [X]
        for i, (Wt, b) in enumerate(zip(self.Ws, self.bs)):
            X = X @ Wt + b
            if i < len(self.Ws) - 1: X = np.tanh(X)
            self.hs.append(X)
        return X

    def train_batch(self, X, Y, lr):        # MSE loss; returns loss value
        out = self.forward(X); n = len(X)
        g = 2 * (out - Y) / n                       # dL/dout
        gW, gb = [None] * len(self.Ws), [None] * len(self.bs)
        for i in reversed(range(len(self.Ws))):
            gW[i] = self.hs[i].T @ g; gb[i] = g.sum(0)
            if i: g = (g @ self.Ws[i].T) * (1 - self.hs[i] ** 2)
        self.step += 1; b1, b2 = 0.9, 0.999          # Adam
        for j, (p, gr) in enumerate(zip(self.Ws + self.bs, gW + gb)):
            self.m[j] = b1 * self.m[j] + (1 - b1) * gr
            self.v[j] = b2 * self.v[j] + (1 - b2) * gr ** 2
            mh = self.m[j] / (1 - b1 ** self.step)
            vh = self.v[j] / (1 - b2 ** self.step)
            p -= lr * mh / (np.sqrt(vh) + 1e-8)
        return np.mean((out - Y) ** 2)

# ---------------- DDPM: schedule, training, ancestral/DDIM sampler ---------
T = 1000
beta = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)
abar = np.concatenate([[1.0], np.cumprod(1 - beta)])   # abar[k], k=0..T

net_eps, net_v = MLP(rng), MLP(rng)
ITERS = 4000
lr_at = lambda it: 3e-3 if it < 2000 else (1e-3 if it < 3200 else 3e-4)
def main():
    for it in range(ITERS):                                 # DDPM training
        x0 = sample_target(512, rng)
        k = rng.integers(1, T + 1, 512)
        eps = rng.standard_normal((512, 2))
        a = abar[k][:, None]
        xt = np.sqrt(a) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - a) * eps         # closed-form marginal
        loss_d = net_eps.train_batch(np.concatenate([xt, timefeat(k / T)], 1),
                                     eps, lr_at(it))
    for it in range(ITERS):                                 # flow-matching training
        x1 = sample_target(512, rng)
        x0 = rng.standard_normal((512, 2))
        t = rng.uniform(1e-3, 1 - 1e-3, 512)[:, None]
        xt = (1 - t) * x0 + t * x1                          # linear (rectified) path
        loss_f = net_v.train_batch(np.concatenate([xt, timefeat(t[:, 0])], 1),
                                   x1 - x0, lr_at(it))
    print(f"final losses  DDPM eps-MSE {loss_d:.4f} | FM velocity-MSE {loss_f:.4f}")

    def ddim_sample(n, nfe, eta, rg):       # eta=1: ancestral DDPM; eta=0: PF-ODE
        x = rg.standard_normal((n, 2))
        seq = np.linspace(T, 0, nfe + 1).astype(int)
        for k, kp in zip(seq[:-1], seq[1:]):
            a, ap = abar[k], abar[kp]
            e = net_eps.forward(np.concatenate([x, timefeat(np.full(n, k / T))], 1))
            x0h = (x - np.sqrt(1 - a) * e) / np.sqrt(a)
            s2 = (eta ** 2) * (1 - ap) / (1 - a) * (1 - a / ap) if kp else 0.0
            x = (np.sqrt(ap) * x0h + np.sqrt(max(1 - ap - s2, 0.0)) * e
                 + np.sqrt(s2) * rg.standard_normal((n, 2)))
        return x

    def fm_sample(n, nfe, rg):              # forward-Euler on dx/dt = v_theta(x,t)
        x, dt = rg.standard_normal((n, 2)), 1.0 / nfe
        for i in range(nfe):
            t = np.full(n, i * dt + dt / 2)      # midpoint time label, still 1 NFE
            x += dt * net_v.forward(np.concatenate([x, timefeat(t)], 1))
        return x

    # ---------------- (a) learned score / velocity vs analytic -----------------
    g1 = np.linspace(-4, 4, 41)
    grid = np.stack(np.meshgrid(g1, g1), -1).reshape(-1, 2)

    def wrel(err_vec, ref_vec, logw):       # density-weighted relative L2 error
        w = np.exp(logw - logw.max())
        num = np.sum(w * np.sum(err_vec ** 2, 1))
        den = np.sum(w * np.sum(ref_vec ** 2, 1))
        return np.sqrt(num / den)

    print("\n(a) learned vs analytic fields (density-weighted rel. L2 on grid)")
    for k in (int(0.25 * T), int(0.55 * T)):
        a = abar[k]
        m_t, v_t = np.sqrt(a) * MU, a * S2 + (1 - a)
        s_true = mixture_score(grid, m_t, v_t)
        e = net_eps.forward(np.concatenate([grid, timefeat(np.full(len(grid), k / T))], 1))
        s_hat = -e / np.sqrt(1 - a)                     # score from eps-prediction
        r = wrel(s_hat - s_true, s_true, mixture_logdens(grid, m_t, v_t))
        print(f"  DDPM score, abar={a:.3f}: rel err {r:.4f}")
        assert r < 0.15, f"score mismatch {r}"
    tv = 0.5
    v_true = fm_marginal_velocity(grid, tv)
    v_hat = net_v.forward(np.concatenate([grid, timefeat(np.full(len(grid), tv))], 1))
    lw = mixture_logdens(grid, tv * MU, tv * tv * S2 + (1 - tv) ** 2)
    rv = wrel(v_hat - v_true, v_true, lw)
    print(f"  FM velocity, t=0.5   : rel err {rv:.4f}")
    assert rv < 0.15, f"velocity mismatch {rv}"

    # ---------------- (b) sample statistics vs target --------------------------
    mean_true = W @ MU
    cov_true = (np.einsum('k,kd,ke->de', W, MU, MU)
                + (W @ S2) * np.eye(2) - np.outer(mean_true, mean_true))
    def check_stats(x, name):
        dm = np.abs(x.mean(0) - mean_true).max()
        C = np.cov(x.T)
        dc = np.linalg.norm(C - cov_true) / np.linalg.norm(cov_true)
        hit = np.argmin(np.sum((x[:, None, :] - MU[None]) ** 2, -1), 1)
        dw = np.abs(np.bincount(hit, minlength=3) / len(x) - W).max()
        print(f"  {name}: |dmean| {dm:.3f}  cov rel-F {dc:.3f}  |dweights| {dw:.3f}")
        assert dm < 0.15 and dc < 0.15 and dw < 0.06, name
    print("\n(b) sample moments vs target (4096 samples each)")
    check_stats(ddim_sample(4096, 200, 1.0, rng), "DDPM 200-step ancestral")
    check_stats(fm_sample(4096, 32, rng), "FM   32-step Euler     ")

    # ---------------- (c) energy distance vs NFE -------------------------------
    def energy_dist(x, y):                  # sqrt(2E|X-Y| - E|X-X'| - E|Y-Y'|)
        d = lambda a, b: np.sqrt(((a[:, None, :] - b[None]) ** 2).sum(-1) + 1e-12)
        return np.sqrt(max(2 * d(x, y).mean() - d(x, x).mean() - d(y, y).mean(), 0))

    ref = sample_target(2048, rng)
    floor = energy_dist(sample_target(2048, rng), ref)     # sampling-noise floor
    print(f"\n(c) energy distance to 2048 target samples (floor ~{floor:.4f})")
    print("  NFE | DDPM ancestral | DDPM PF-ODE(DDIM) | flow matching")
    ed, NFES = {}, (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 50, 200)
    for nfe in NFES:
        ed[('d', nfe)] = energy_dist(ddim_sample(2048, nfe, 1.0, rng), ref)
        ed[('o', nfe)] = energy_dist(ddim_sample(2048, nfe, 0.0, rng), ref)
        ed[('f', nfe)] = energy_dist(fm_sample(2048, nfe, rng), ref)
        print(f"  {nfe:3d} |     {ed[('d', nfe)]:.4f}     |      {ed[('o', nfe)]:.4f}"
              f"       |    {ed[('f', nfe)]:.4f}")
    thr = 0.2                       # quality threshold ~ a few times the floor
    first = lambda tag: next(n for n in NFES if ed[(tag, n)] < thr)
    nf, nd = first('f'), first('d')
    print(f"  => energy distance < {thr}: FM at {nf} NFE, ancestral DDPM at {nd}")
    assert ed[('f', 2)] < ed[('d', 2)] and ed[('f', 4)] < ed[('d', 4)], "low-NFE"
    assert 2 * nf <= nd, "FM should need materially (>=2x) fewer NFE"

    # ---------------- (d) cross-check NumPy backprop against torch -------------
    try:
        import torch
        X = rng.standard_normal((16, 11)); Y = rng.standard_normal((16, 2))
        net = MLP(np.random.default_rng(7))
        tW = [torch.tensor(w, requires_grad=True) for w in net.Ws]
        tb = [torch.tensor(b, requires_grad=True) for b in net.bs]
        h = torch.tensor(X)
        for i in range(3):
            h = h @ tW[i] + tb[i]
            if i < 2: h = torch.tanh(h)
        (((h - torch.tensor(Y)) ** 2).sum() / 16).backward()  # match manual scaling
        out = net.forward(X); g = 2 * (out - Y) / 16     # replicate manual backward
        gW = [None] * 3
        for i in reversed(range(3)):
            gW[i] = net.hs[i].T @ g
            if i: g = (g @ net.Ws[i].T) * (1 - net.hs[i] ** 2)
        r = max(np.abs(gW[i] - tW[i].grad.numpy()).max() for i in range(3))
        print(f"\n(d) max |NumPy grad - torch grad| = {r:.2e}"); assert r < 1e-5
    except ImportError:
        print("\n(d) [skipped: torch not installed]")

    print(f"\nall assertions passed  ({time.time() - t0:.1f}s total)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Running it takes about 30 s on a single CPU core and prints the full verification: learned-vs-analytic relative errors of 0.080 and 0.041 for the DDPM score at $\bar\alpha = 0.524$ and $0.046$, and 0.058 for the flow-matching velocity at $t{=}0.5$ — both networks recover the true fields to a few percent. Sample moments land within tolerance for both samplers (covariance Frobenius error 0.031 for 200-step DDPM, 0.009 for 32-step Euler). The NFE table is the chapter's thesis in numbers: at 2 NFE, flow matching reaches energy distance 0.162 while ancestral DDPM sits at 0.805; DDPM needs 8 steps to cross the 0.2 threshold that flow matching crosses at 2. At 16+ NFE the methods converge toward the 0.033 sampling-noise floor — same model class, same data, same endpoint; the straight path just gets there 4× sooner. The torch gradient check agrees to 2.2×10−16.

Under Encryption

Iterative sampling is the worst case for FHE: the steps compose sequentially, so a 50-step sampler multiplies the denoiser's multiplicative depth by 50, and under CKKS that forces bootstrapping between essentially every step — the matrix multiplications inside each step are the one cheap part. Few-step generation (Section 35.9) is therefore not a latency nicety under encryption but the difference between feasible and absurd: a distilled one-step model leaves a single forward pass whose non-polynomial activations are the remaining obstacle. Chapter 39 takes up that approximation problem in detail.

Key Takeaways
  • The forward chain's closed-form marginal $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$ makes training a one-line regression, and Tweedie's formula makes the trained noise predictor an exact score estimator: $s = -\epsilon_\theta/\sigma_t$. Certain
  • The probability-flow ODE shares every marginal with the reverse SDE (a two-line Fokker–Planck rewrite), giving deterministic sampling, invertible encoding, and the trajectory structure all few-step methods rely on. Certain
  • Diffusion and flow matching learn the same conditional expectation under different parameterizations; flow matching's linear path wins on step count because Euler error scales with trajectory curvature — measured here as 2 vs. 8 NFE to equal sample quality. Certain
  • Classifier-free guidance is score extrapolation through an implicit classifier; it buys fidelity and prompt adherence at a measurable cost in diversity, and it is a heuristic field, not the score of a normalized distribution. Likely
  • The frontier has moved to 1–4-step generation (consistency models, MeanFlow-family objectives) and to diffusion language models decoding at 1,000–2,000+ tokens/s in vendor reports; whether the latter displace autoregression beyond code and editing niches remains open. Verify
Chapter 36

Agents, Tool Use, and Long-Horizon Training

Learning Objectives
  • Model task success as per-step reliability compounded over horizon length, compute the per-step accuracy $p = s^{1/H}$ required for end-to-end success $s$, and state where the independence assumption fails in both directions.
  • Explain tool calling as constrained generation and identify the training data that makes it reliable.
  • Explain reinforcement learning for multi-turn agents: credit assignment over trajectories, and why verifiable environments dominate current results.
  • Explain context management for long horizons — compaction, memory, sub-agents — and their measured failure modes.
  • Implement an agent loop with horizon-scaling measurement in working code.
Read alongside — Stanford CS336 for the post-training and RL infrastructure that agent training sits on; Chakraborty, Introduction to Large Language Models, for the NLP-side framing of tool-augmented generation; Géron for the end-to-end evaluation discipline that agent systems need more than any other ML artifact.

An agent is a language model in a loop: emit an action, observe the result, repeat. That single change — from one forward pass to a sequence of dependent decisions — replaces the question "how accurate is the model?" with "how does accuracy compound?" This chapter is organized around one piece of arithmetic: if each step succeeds with probability $p$ and a task needs $H$ steps, success is roughly $p^H$, which collapses fast. Every real intervention either raises $p$ (better training, Sections 36.3–36.6) or breaks $H$ into verifiable segments with retry (Sections 36.2, 36.5); prompt scaffolding that does neither moves nothing. The training machinery comes from Chapters 27 and 28 (GRPO, test-time compute); the measurement crisis of Chapter 29 returns here in aggravated form; long-context limits from Chapter 19 become the mechanism of a specific failure mode. Chapter 37 takes up what agents mean for safety.

36.1 What an Agent Is

Definition 36.1 (LLM agent)

An LLM agent is a policy $\pi_\theta(a_t \mid h_t)$ where the action $a_t$ is a generated token sequence parsed into either a tool call or a final answer, the environment executes tool calls and returns an observation $o_t$, and the context evolves as $h_{t+1} = h_t \oplus (a_t, o_t)$. The scaffold is the surrounding code: the parser, the tool implementations, and the rule for constructing $h_t$ from the history. Formally this is a partially observed MDP in which the model's context window is the (truncated) state estimate.

What distinguishes this from chat is that environment state persists and actions are consequential: a wrong file write at step 3 is still on disk at step 40. The scaffold is not neutral plumbing — the choice of what enters $h_t$ is a choice of policy class, which is why "context management" (Section 36.4) is an architectural decision, not an implementation detail.

Theorem 36.1 (Horizon compounding and geometric retry)

Let a task require $H$ sequential steps, each succeeding independently with probability $p$, with the task succeeding iff every step succeeds. Then (i) end-to-end success is $S(H) = p^H$; (ii) achieving $S(H) \ge s$ requires $p \ge s^{1/H} = e^{\ln s / H} \approx 1 + \frac{\ln s}{H}$; (iii) if a sound verifier checks each step and failed steps are retried with independent attempts, up to $r$ retries, the task succeeds with probability $\big(1-(1-p)^{r+1}\big)^H$.

Proof. (i) is a product of independent events. (ii) follows by monotonicity of $x \mapsto x^H$ and taking logarithms; the approximation is the first-order expansion of $e^{\ln s/H}$. (iii) A step now fails only if all $r+1$ independent attempts fail, probability $(1-p)^{r+1}$; apply (i) with the effective per-step success $q = 1-(1-p)^{r+1}$. $\blacksquare$

The continuous version: a constant failure hazard $\lambda$ per unit of task length gives $S(T) = e^{-\lambda T}$, and the task length at which success is 50% is $T_{50} = \ln 2/\lambda$. This is not just a toy: METR reports that measured agent success versus human task duration is well fit by exactly this exponential decay ($R^2 \approx 0.83$) Likely, which licenses reading their horizon measurements (Section 36.7) through Theorem 36.1: doubling the horizon is the same event as halving the per-minute hazard.

Example 36.1 (Reliability arithmetic)

A 99%-reliable step over 50 steps: $0.99^{50} = e^{50\ln 0.99} = e^{-0.5025} \approx 0.605$. Sixty percent — from a step accuracy that would look superb in isolation. Required accuracy for 90% success at $H=64$: $p = 0.9^{1/64}$, and $\ln 0.9 = -0.10536$, so $p = e^{-0.10536/64} = e^{-0.001646} \approx 0.99836$. With retry: $p=0.9$, $r=2$ gives $q = 1 - 0.1^3 = 0.999$ and $q^{64} = e^{64 \ln 0.999} = e^{-0.0640} \approx 0.938$. Artifact 36.1 validates the governing formulas $p^H$ and $q^H$ by Monte Carlo and prints the required-accuracy table, including the 0.99836.

36.1.1 Where independence fails, in both directions

The model $p^H$ assumes each step is a fresh coin flip. It fails pessimistically — real agents do better than $\bar p^H$ computed from the average observed per-step error rate — for two reasons: errors cluster in already-doomed trajectories, so the marginal step-error rate double-counts failures; and models increasingly notice and repair their own mistakes within a step, which is an implicit retry loop. METR attributes much of the measured horizon growth precisely to "increased reliability and ability to adapt to mistakes" Likely. It fails optimistically when errors corrupt persistent state: a wrong value written to disk, a polluted context, a stale assumption — these raise the hazard of every subsequent step, so success falls below $p^H$ even when the per-step error rate measured on fresh state equals $p$. Artifact 36.1 measures both directions in one sandbox: the corrupted-state regime lands 7–8 pooled standard errors below $p^H$, while the naive per-line accuracy of that same regime under-predicts its success by five orders of magnitude.

36.2 ReAct, Planning, Reflection

ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) interleaves free-text reasoning with actions, so each tool call conditions on an explicit deliberation; it beat act-only baselines on the 2022-era question-answering and text-game tasks it was proposed on Certain. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) adds verbal self-critique persisted across episode attempts — literally the retry branch of Theorem 36.1 with the model itself as a weak verifier. Plan-and-execute scaffolds decompose the task up front, then execute the pieces.

Run these through the compounding lens and the accounting is short. A scaffold helps iff it (a) raises per-step $p$ — reasoning-before-acting did, for models that had never been trained to deliberate — or (b) inserts verification that converts one $H$-step episode into segments with independent retry. Scaffolds that do neither — role prompts, restated plans, reflection with no new information — leave the curve where it was. And the (a)-type gains are being absorbed into the policy: models RL-trained to reason (Chapter 28) internalized the ReAct trick, and elaborate prompt scaffolds buy progressively less on top of them Likely. Reflection without ground truth can even hurt: without external feedback, models are more likely to talk themselves out of correct answers than into them (Huang et al., 2023) Likely. The durable residue of this literature is not the prompts; it is the loop structure — act, observe, verify — which survives as scaffolding's legitimate job: exposing verifiable segment boundaries.

36.3 Tool Calling and Structured Output

A tool call is a structured emission: the model must produce a tool name and arguments conforming to a schema. Constrained decoding makes the syntax exact: compile the JSON schema (or any context-free grammar) into a state machine, and at each decoding step mask the logits of tokens that cannot continue a valid string. Invalid output becomes impossible by construction, at negligible cost. What masking cannot buy is semantics: the right tool, the right arguments, the decision to call a tool at all. Constraints can even hurt content — forcing generation into a rigid format measurably degrades reasoning performance on some tasks (Tam et al., 2024) Likely — which is why production systems let the model reason freely, then constrain only the emission.

36.3.1 The training data that makes it reliable

Semantic reliability comes from data. Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) bootstrapped it self-supervised: insert candidate API calls into pretraining text, keep the ones whose results reduce the model's perplexity on subsequent tokens. Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) trained on API documentation paired with generated calls. Current practice is synthetic at scale: thousands of simulated tools and rubric- or execution-filtered multi-turn trajectories, including simulated users — Kimi K2's report describes an agentic-data pipeline of this shape Verify. Three data properties matter most: schema diversity (so the model binds to the schema in context rather than memorized APIs), error-recovery traces (a model shown only successful calls has never learned what to do with a stack trace), and negative examples of when not to call a tool. Function-calling accuracy is tracked publicly by the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard; treat any specific score as perishable Verify.

Common Pitfall

Retry without independence. Theorem 36.1(iii) requires the $r+1$ attempts to be independent. A loop that catches a failed tool call and re-issues the same request with unchanged context at temperature 0 produces perfectly correlated attempts: the effective per-step success stays $p$, not $1-(1-p)^{r+1}$, and the retry code is dead weight that merely multiplies latency. The same bug in softer form: swallowing the tool's error message, so the retried attempt cannot condition on what failed. Working retries change something — sample at $\tau > 0$, feed the error text into context, or escalate to a different plan — and Artifact 36.1's verifier branch matches the geometric prediction only because its attempts are independent draws.

36.4 Retrieval and Its Limits

An agent has three places to keep knowledge: in weights, in context, and in the environment (retrievable on demand). Retrieval-as-a-tool handles the knowledge side well — facts, docs, code search — but it does not solve the harder problem, which is state: what the agent has done, decided, and committed to so far. Two measured limits shape everything here. First, models use long contexts unevenly: retrieval accuracy over in-context documents is strongly position-dependent, best at the edges and worst in the middle (Liu et al., 2023) Certain. Second, effective per-step accuracy degrades as context grows and fills with stale tool output — which is exactly the rising-hazard regime of Section 36.1.1: long-context degradation is how state corruption manifests in practice.

The three context-management responses, with their failure modes: Compaction summarizes old turns to bound $|h_t|$; its measured failure is silent constraint loss — a requirement stated once, early, is summarized away and later actions violate it, with no error signal at the moment of loss. Memory tools move state out of context into the environment (files, notes, databases), trading recall cost for durability — state in the environment can be re-read and checked; state in a summary cannot. Sub-agents give each subtask a fresh, short context (Section 36.8), at the price of a lossy hand-off in each direction. The long-horizon benchmark literature measures the aggregate effect: agents on multi-hundred-step tasks with 200k+ token trajectories fall far below humans (UltraHorizon), and iterated-change benchmarks report agents degrading within a handful of sequential revision requests unless an external feedback signal (a test suite) re-anchors them, which the StaminaBench authors report improves performance up to twelvefold Verify. The pattern is consistent: externalized, checkable state beats remembered state.

36.5 Environments and Verifiable Rewards

Definition 36.2 (Verifiable environment)

A training or evaluation environment is verifiable if the reward is computed by a programmatic oracle $R(\tau) \in \{0,1\}$ — unit tests, exact-match answers, a compiler, a checkable game state — whose satisfaction is (ideally) achievable only by actually solving the task. Verifiability is a property of the checker, not the task: the same coding task is verifiable under a hidden test suite and gameable under "does the diff look right to a reward model."

Chapter 27 explained why learned reward models buckle under optimization pressure; agents make it worse, because a multi-turn policy explores an enormous trajectory space and will find the reward's blind spots. This is measured, not hypothetical: long-horizon coding evaluations report reward hacking in a nontrivial fraction of rollouts — the SWE-Marathon authors report 13.8% Verify — and SpecBench reports that the gap between visible-test and held-out-test pass rates grows with task size, by roughly 28 percentage points per tenfold increase in code volume Verify. Hence the shape of current results: the tasks where agent RL demonstrably works — competition math, code against test suites (DeepSeek-R1's GRPO training, Chapter 28), SWE-bench-style repair — are exactly the verifiable ones Certain. Environment engineering has consequently become a core discipline: containerized repos with hidden tests, simulated users with policy rubrics (τ-bench style). The scarce resource is tasks that are simultaneously hard, diverse, and checkable; and even "verifiable" checkers leak — visible partial-credit tests invite hardcoding, which is why held-out tests are non-negotiable.

36.6 Multi-Turn Credit Assignment

Write a trajectory $\tau = (h_1, a_1, o_1, \ldots, a_H, o_H)$ and recall the policy gradient $\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}\big[\sum_t A_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid h_t)\big]$. With outcome-only reward, every token in every turn receives the same advantage $A_t = R(\tau) - b$: one scalar spread over $10^4$–$10^5$ token-level decisions. The estimator is unbiased but its variance grows with the number of decisions sharing that scalar — which tool call earned the reward is statistically unidentifiable from a single rollout. GRPO (Chapter 27) attacks the variance with a group baseline: $b$ is the mean return of $G$ rollouts of the same task, so the gradient weights within-task relative success. The alternative — dense per-turn credit from a learned value function or process reward model (Chapter 28) — trades variance for bias, and the bias is adversarial: a learned dense reward is one more thing for the policy to hack. The honest summary of results through 2025: outcome-only verifiable reward plus group baselines plus a lot of rollouts is what has produced every headline agent-RL result; the field pays the variance cost in compute rather than the bias cost in corruption Likely.

Two structural subtleties are specific to long horizons. First, credit must flow across context boundaries: by the time reward arrives, the decisive action may have been compacted out of context, so the policy is being trained to act through its own summaries. Second, exploration: at long $H$ most rollouts fail, and an all-zero reward group carries zero gradient. The standard remedy is a horizon curriculum — and the compounding law says where to sit. Reward variance for a Bernoulli return is $S(1-S)$, maximized at $S = \tfrac12$: the most informative training tasks are those at the model's current 50% horizon, $H \approx \ln 2/\lambda$. Train at the frontier of the horizon curve and move it outward Likely.

36.7 Horizon Length as the Capability Axis

Definition 36.3 (50% time horizon)

The 50% time horizon $T_{50}$ of a model is the human task duration at which its success rate is 50%, obtained by fitting success against log human-completion-time across a task suite. The 80% horizon $T_{80}$ is defined analogously and is substantially shorter, since success decays continuously in task length.

The METR measurement (Kwa et al., 2025) is the cleanest quantitative statement of agent progress we have. On a suite of ~170 software and research tasks with human baseline times from seconds to many hours, frontier-model 50% horizons grew from seconds in 2019 to roughly 50 minutes by early 2025 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet), doubling approximately every seven months across that period, with signs of acceleration in 2024–2025 Certain. Success versus task duration follows the exponential decay of Section 36.1 ($R^2 \approx 0.83$), so via $T_{50} = \ln 2/\lambda$ the finding is a reliability finding: each doubling of the horizon is a halving of the per-minute failure hazard. Subsequent METR updates report faster recent doubling — on the order of three to four months from 2024 onward — with measured horizons now in the hours and estimates beyond the suite's calibrated range explicitly flagged as unreliable; these numbers move quickly and should be checked against metr.org/time-horizons before quoting Verify.

The caveats are part of the result. The suite is software-weighted, containerized, and cleanly specified; METR reports lower success on tasks scored higher for real-world "messiness," so horizons on messy work are shorter than the headline Likely. Human baseline times are noisy, and the 80% horizon — arguably the deployment-relevant one — is several times shorter than the 50% figure everyone quotes Likely. And benchmark horizon is not delivered value: METR's own randomized controlled trial found experienced open-source developers were 19% slower when allowed early-2025 AI tools on their own repositories, while estimating they had been sped up (Becker et al., 2025) Certain. The horizon curve measures what models can do unattended on well-posed tasks; it does not yet measure what they save you.

36.8 Multi-Agent Systems, Honestly

The arithmetic first: splitting $H$ steps among $k$ agents does not reduce the number of steps, and it adds communication steps that are themselves fallible. A multi-agent system can win only through three concrete mechanisms: context isolation (each worker gets a fresh, short context, raising its per-step $p$ relative to one agent dragging a long degrading context — Section 36.4); parallelism (wall-clock, not reliability); and cross-checking (one agent verifying another approximates the verifier of Theorem 36.1(iii)). Anything sold beyond these three is narrative.

The evidence is genuinely split Contested. In favor: Anthropic reports an orchestrator-plus-parallel-subagents research system outperforming a single-agent baseline by 90.2% on an internal research evaluation — at roughly 15× the token cost of chat, and on read-heavy, parallelizable work Verify. Against: Cognition's position is that for shared-state work like coding, sub-agents fork state and return conflicting decisions, so context should be unified in one agent; and the MAST taxonomy (Cemri et al., 2025), built from 200+ execution traces across seven frameworks, catalogs 14 recurring failure modes in three classes — specification failures, inter-agent misalignment, and weak verification — most attributable to system design rather than model capability Likely. My reading: multi-agent is a context-management technique, not a capability multiplier — it wins on parallelizable read-heavy tasks with cheap merging, loses on write-heavy shared-state tasks. What would settle it is matched-token-budget comparisons on public benchmarks; vendor evidence at unmatched budgets settles nothing.

36.9 Evaluating Agents

Distinguish two metrics over $k$ attempts: pass@$k$ = $\mathbb{E}[1-(1-p_{\text{task}})^k]$ credits any success and rises with $k$; pass$^k$ = $\mathbb{E}[p_{\text{task}}^k]$ demands all $k$ succeed and falls with $k$. The second is Theorem 36.1 applied across episodes, and it is the deployment-relevant one: τ-bench introduced it and reports GPT-4o falling from roughly 60% pass$^1$ to below 25% pass$^8$ on its retail domain Likely — a "60%-capable" agent that can be relied on for one in four repeated workflows.

The current landscape, briefly: SWE-bench Verified (500 human-screened GitHub issue repairs; the de facto coding-agent standard, with frontier scores now high enough that contamination and scaffold effects dominate the leaderboard's top — treat any current number as perishable Verify); τ/τ²-bench (tool + simulated user + policy adherence); OSWorld (desktop computer use); WebArena (browser tasks; GPT-4 scored 14.4% against a 78.2% human baseline at 2023 release, a gap since largely closed Likely); GAIA (tool-using assistant questions); Terminal-Bench; and a newer generation of deliberately long-horizon suites — SWE-bench Pro, marathon- and repository-scale benchmarks — built because the older ones saturate, on which their authors report frontier success rates below 30–40% Verify.

Chapter 29's measurement crisis applies here with interest: a reported score is a property of model plus scaffold plus harness; single-run reporting of a high-variance quantity is common; harnesses themselves get reward-hacked. The prescription follows from this chapter's thesis. Report the success-versus-horizon curve, not a scalar. Report pass$^k$. And fit the $p^H$ model to your own agent: where measured success sits above the fit, self-correction is working; where it sits below, state corruption is accumulating — the deviation is a diagnostic, and Artifact 36.1 is the template for measuring it.

Artifact 36.1 — Horizon Compounding in a Sandbox Agent Loop

A deterministic agent loop over three in-process tools (calculator, key-value store, append-only file) driven by a scripted policy with an injectable per-step error rate — no LLM calls, because the object of study is the reliability arithmetic itself. The task is to maintain a running sum and log it each step; success is judged by comparing the final file to ground truth through the environment. Three regimes are measured over 3,000 episodes at each of nine horizons spanning $H = 1$ to $64$: independent errors, persistent state corruption (glitches leave junk keys that raise the later read hazard), and a per-step verifier with up to two independent retries. Assertions check that regime one tracks $p^H$ within binomial tolerance, regime two is significantly worse, and regime three matches the geometric-retry prediction $q^H$.

"""Artifact 36.1 -- Horizon compounding in a deterministic sandbox agent loop.

A tiny agent environment with three in-process tools (calculator, key-value
store, append-only file) driven by a SCRIPTED policy with an injectable
per-step error rate.  No LLM calls anywhere: the point is the reliability
arithmetic, measured through the environment rather than assumed.

Task: maintain a running sum acc_t = sum_{i<=t} (2i+1) = t^2 + 2t and log
"t:acc_t" to the file each step.  An episode of horizon H succeeds iff the
final file equals the ground-truth log exactly.

Three regimes:
  (a) independent  -- each step re-derives its value from the plan; an injected
      error corrupts only that step's line.  Prediction: success = p^H.
  (b) corrupt      -- the policy reads the accumulator back from the KV store,
      and glitches leave junk keys that persist; the more junk, the likelier a
      later read grabs junk (state corruption raising the later hazard).
      Prediction: success measurably WORSE than p^H at the same injected rate.
  (c) verify       -- like (a), plus a per-step verifier (a unit test for the
      segment) that catches a bad step and retries it up to r times.
      Prediction: success = q^H with q = 1-(1-p)^(r+1) (geometric retry).
"""
import numpy as np

# ------------------------------ sandbox tools -------------------------------
class Calculator:                                   # pure, deterministic
    def apply(self, op, a, b):
        if op == "add": return a + b
        if op == "mul": return a * b
        raise ValueError(op)

class KVStore:                                      # mutable state that persists
    def __init__(self): self.d = {}
    def set(self, k, v): self.d[k] = v
    def get(self, k, default=None): return self.d.get(k, default)
    def junk_count(self): return sum(1 for k in self.d if k.startswith("tmp"))

class FileTool:                                     # append-only log
    def __init__(self): self.lines = []
    def append(self, line): self.lines.append(line)

def truth_lines(H):
    return [f"{t}:{t * t + 2 * t}" for t in range(1, H + 1)]

# ------------------------------ one episode ---------------------------------
def run_episode(H, p, rng, mode, truth, retries=0, glitch_p=0.10, snag_p=0.05):
    calc, kv, log = Calculator(), KVStore(), FileTool()
    for t in range(1, H + 1):
        if mode == "independent":
            # Stateless re-derivation: acc_t = t*t + 2t computed fresh from the
            # plan, so an error here cannot propagate to later steps.
            acc = calc.apply("add", calc.apply("mul", t, t), 2 * t)
            if rng.random() > p:                    # injected action error
                acc += int(rng.integers(1, 10))
        elif mode == "corrupt":
            # Stateful accumulation: read acc back from the store.  Each junk
            # key snags the read with prob snag_p (independently), so the
            # per-step hazard grows with accumulated corruption.
            j = kv.junk_count()
            prev = kv.get("acc", 0)
            if j and rng.random() > (1.0 - snag_p) ** j:
                prev = 999_983                      # grabbed a junk entry
            acc = calc.apply("add", prev, 2 * t + 1)
            if rng.random() > p:                    # same injected rate as (a)
                acc += int(rng.integers(1, 10))
            if rng.random() < glitch_p:             # glitch leaves junk behind
                kv.set(f"tmp{t}", 999_983)
        elif mode == "verify":
            # Verifiable segment: the environment can unit-test each step's
            # output; a failed check rolls the step back and retries.
            expected = t * t + 2 * t
            for _ in range(retries + 1):
                acc = calc.apply("add", calc.apply("mul", t, t), 2 * t)
                if rng.random() > p:
                    acc += int(rng.integers(1, 10))
                if acc == expected:
                    break                           # verifier accepts
        kv.set("acc", acc)
        log.append(f"{t}:{acc}")
    ok_lines = sum(a == b for a, b in zip(log.lines, truth))
    return log.lines == truth, ok_lines            # success judged via the env

def simulate(H, p, n, rng, mode, retries=0):
    truth = truth_lines(H)
    wins = tot_ok = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        w, ok = run_episode(H, p, rng, mode, truth, retries)
        wins += w; tot_ok += ok
    return wins / n, tot_ok / (n * H)              # success rate, line accuracy

# --------------------------------- driver -----------------------------------
if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng  = np.random.default_rng(0)
    p, r, N = 0.90, 2, 3000                        # per-step accuracy, retries, episodes
    q    = 1.0 - (1.0 - p) ** (r + 1)              # geometric-retry effective accuracy
    grid = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64]
    sd   = lambda s: (max(s * (1 - s), 1e-12) / N) ** 0.5

    print(f"p = {p}  retries = {r}  q = 1-(1-p)^{r+1} = {q:.6f}  N = {N} episodes/point")
    print(f"{'H':>3} {'p^H':>8} {'indep':>8} {'corrupt':>8} {'verify':>8} {'q^H':>8}")
    res = {}
    for H in grid:
        sA, lA = simulate(H, p, N, rng, "independent")
        sB, lB = simulate(H, p, N, rng, "corrupt")
        sC, lC = simulate(H, p, N, rng, "verify", retries=r)
        res[H] = (sA, lA, sB, lB, sC)
        print(f"{H:>3} {p**H:>8.4f} {sA:>8.4f} {sB:>8.4f} {sC:>8.4f} {q**H:>8.4f}")

    # (a) independent errors track p^H within binomial tolerance at every H
    worst = max(abs(res[H][0] - p ** H) - 4.5 * sd(p ** H) for H in grid)
    print(f"\n[a] max (|indep - p^H| - 4.5*sigma) over H grid: {worst:+.4f}  (<= 0.004 required)")
    for H in grid:
        assert abs(res[H][0] - p ** H) <= 4.5 * sd(p ** H) + 0.004, f"(a) fails at H={H}"
    phatA = res[16][1]                              # measured per-step accuracy, mode (a)
    print(f"[a] measured per-step line accuracy at H=16: {phatA:.4f} (injected p = {p})")
    assert abs(phatA - p) < 0.01

    # (b) persistent corruption: worse than p^H, by >3 pooled-sigma at H=16,32
    for H in (16, 32):
        sA, _, sB, _, _ = res[H]
        gap  = p ** H - sB
        pool = ((p**H * (1 - p**H) + sB * (1 - sB)) / N) ** 0.5
        print(f"[b] H={H}: p^H - corrupt = {gap:.4f}  ({gap/pool:.1f} pooled sigma)")
        assert gap > 3 * pool, f"(b) not separated at H={H}"
    sB16, lB16 = res[16][2], res[16][3]             # independence fails both ways:
    print(f"[b] H=16 marginal line accuracy {lB16:.4f}: naive {lB16:.3f}^16 = "
          f"{lB16**16:.2e} << measured success {sB16:.4f} < p^16 = {p**16:.4f}")
    assert lB16 ** 16 < sB16 < p ** 16              # under- and over-prediction

    # (c) verifier+retry matches the geometric prediction q^H and beats (a)
    worst = max(abs(res[H][4] - q ** H) - 4.5 * sd(q ** H) for H in grid)
    print(f"[c] max (|verify - q^H| - 4.5*sigma) over H grid: {worst:+.4f}  (<= 0.004 required)")
    for H in grid:
        assert abs(res[H][4] - q ** H) <= 4.5 * sd(q ** H) + 0.004, f"(c) fails at H={H}"
        if H >= 8:
            assert res[H][4] - res[H][0] > 0.2, f"(c) no lift at H={H}"
    print(f"[c] lift at H=64: verify {res[64][4]:.4f} vs indep {res[64][0]:.4f} "
          f"(analytic {q**64:.4f} vs {p**64:.4f})")

    # required per-step accuracy for 90% end-to-end success
    req = ", ".join(f"H={H}:{0.9 ** (1.0 / H):.5f}" for H in (8, 16, 32, 64))
    print(f"\nper-step accuracy required for 90% end-to-end success: {req}")
    print("ALL ASSERTIONS PASSED")

With $p=0.9$: at $H=16$ the independent regime measures 0.1833 against $p^{16}=0.1853$, and the worst deviation across the whole grid stays inside 4.5 binomial standard errors (max slack $-0.0027$). The corrupted-state regime measures 0.1180 at $H=16$ — 7.3 pooled standard errors below $p^H$ — while its naive per-line accuracy of 0.415 would predict $0.415^{16} \approx 7.7\times 10^{-7}$, five orders of magnitude too pessimistic: independence fails in both directions in the same data. The verifier regime holds 0.9470 at $H=64$ against the analytic $q^{64}=0.9380$, versus 0.0013 without it. Total runtime: about 3 s on CPU.

Under Encryption

An agent loop is data-dependent control flow — which tool to call, with what arguments, whether to halt — and that is the one construct FHE cannot hide cheaply. Branching on a ciphertext requires either decrypting the decision (leaking the trajectory) or evaluating every branch obliviously, multiplying cost by the branching factor at each step and burning comparison depth that CKKS must bootstrap back; and tool calls produce plaintext side effects in the environment anyway, so an encrypted model whose trajectory leaks through tool I/O protects little. This is why the private-inference systems of Chapter 40 target single forward passes, not loops; Chapter 38 makes the control-flow barrier precise.

Key Takeaways
  • Under independent errors, end-to-end success is $p^H$: 90% success at $H=64$ requires per-step accuracy 0.99836. Per-step reliability is the whole game; measured success tracks the formula to within binomial noise in Artifact 36.1. Certain
  • A sound verifier with $r$ independent retries lifts per-step success to $1-(1-p)^{r+1}$; in the artifact this turns 0.13% end-to-end success at $H=64$ into 94.7%, matching the analytic prediction. Correlated retries (same context, temperature 0) buy nothing. Certain
  • Constrained decoding guarantees tool-call syntax; only training data — diverse schemas, error-recovery traces, negative examples — buys tool-call semantics. Likely
  • Agent RL that works today is outcome-only reward in verifiable environments with group baselines; dense learned rewards trade variance for a bias the policy learns to exploit, and reward hacking is measured to grow with task size. Likely
  • METR's 50% time horizon doubled roughly every seven months from 2019 to early 2025, faster since; because success decays exponentially in task length, horizon growth is per-step hazard reduction — the capability axis is a reliability axis. Current horizon figures move monthly; check before quoting. Verify
Chapter 37

Interpretability, Safety, and Open Problems

Learning Objectives
  • State the superposition hypothesis and give the near-orthogonality argument for why $d$ dimensions can carry $e^{O(\epsilon^2 d)}$ features at interference $\epsilon$.
  • Derive the sparse-autoencoder objective, trace the sparsity–fidelity frontier it induces, and name the documented failure modes: shrinkage, dead latents, feature splitting, and feature absorption.
  • Explain circuit-level interpretability — the logit lens, activation patching, induction heads, and attribution graphs — and what each can and cannot establish causally.
  • Distinguish alignment failures with empirical demonstrations from those that remain speculative, citing the specific experiment for each empirical claim.
  • Implement a toy superposition model, a TopK sparse autoencoder with verified feature recovery, and a causal steering test in working code.
Read alongside — No textbook in our list covers this material; the field publishes on transformer-circuits.pub, arXiv, and the Alignment Forum, and Section 37.8 tells you how to read those. For the substrate being dissected: Karpathy's nanoGPT is the standard small transformer on which to replicate induction-head and patching experiments, and Raschka's Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) gives you the activation-extraction plumbing an SAE needs.

Every prior chapter treated the trained network as a function to be improved; this one treats it as an object to be explained. The residual stream of Chapter 18 turns out to be a compressed encoding — more concepts than dimensions — which is why staring at neurons fails and why the field's main tool is a dictionary-learning method, the sparse autoencoder, whose objective is a cousin of Chapter 9's PCA and whose failure modes are now better documented than its successes. We then climb from features to circuits (the algorithms connecting them), show that steering a model is easier than explaining it, and audit which alignment failures have actual experiments behind them — material that motivated the oversight problems of Chapters 27, 28, and 36. The chapter closes Part VII honestly: with open problems. Part VIII then changes the threat model entirely, protecting the computation itself with encryption.

37.1 Why Neurons Are Polysemantic

Look at almost any single neuron in a trained language model and you find it fires on an incoherent grab-bag: one documented unit responds to a mixture of academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests, and Korean text (Bricken et al., Towards Monosemanticity, 2023). This polysemanticity is not sloppy training; it is the optimal use of limited dimensions, and the argument is geometric. The working assumption of the field is the linear representation hypothesis: a model's "features" — interpretable properties of the input like is-Python-code or refers-to-the-Golden-Gate-Bridge — are encoded as directions in activation space, with the feature's strength as the coefficient. Likely There is strong evidence for many linearly represented features (Section 37.5 steers with them), and known counterexamples such as circular representations of days-of-week, so the hypothesis is a good default rather than a law. Likely

Definition 37.1 (Superposition hypothesis)

A layer with activation dimension $d$ represents $m \gg d$ features as directions $\{f_i\}_{i=1}^m \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ that are not mutually orthogonal, tolerating interference $\langle f_i, f_j\rangle \neq 0$ because features are sparse: few are active on any one input, so interference is rare and small. The network is then a lossy simulation of a much larger network with one dimension per feature (Elhage et al., Toy Models of Superposition, 2022). Certain (as a demonstrated phenomenon in toy models; its prevalence in frontier models is inferred).

Why can $d$ dimensions hold far more than $d$ almost-orthogonal directions? Exact orthogonality caps you at $d$, but relaxing to near-orthogonality changes the count from linear to exponential — the same concentration phenomenon behind the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.

Theorem 37.1 (Near-orthogonal packing)

For any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ there exist $K \geq e^{d\epsilon^2/4}$ unit vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $|\langle f_i, f_j\rangle| \leq \epsilon$ for all $i \neq j$.

Proof sketch. Draw $K$ vectors uniformly from the sphere. For a fixed pair, the inner product concentrates: $\Pr[|\langle f_i,f_j\rangle| > \epsilon] \leq 2e^{-d\epsilon^2/2}$ (Lévy concentration of measure; the inner product with a fixed unit vector has variance $1/d$). A union bound over the $\binom{K}{2} < K^2/2$ pairs gives failure probability below $K^2 e^{-d\epsilon^2/2}$, which is under $1$ when $K \leq e^{d\epsilon^2/4}$, so a valid configuration exists. $\blacksquare$

The numbers are what matter. A random pair of unit vectors in $d = 4096$ (a mid-sized residual stream) has typical cosine $1/\sqrt{d} \approx 0.016$. At tolerance $\epsilon = 0.1$, Theorem 37.1 guarantees $e^{4096 \cdot 0.01/4} = e^{10.24} \approx 2.8 \times 10^4$ directions, and the bound is loose; tighter spherical-code bounds and empirical dictionary sizes suggest far more. This is why a neuron basis fails: features get distributed across near-orthogonal directions that have no reason to align with coordinate axes, so each axis (neuron) receives projections of many features — polysemanticity is the shadow of superposition on the standard basis. Certain

37.2 Superposition in a Toy Model

Elhage et al. (2022) made this trainable and quantitative with a model small enough to fully analyze, and Artifact 37.1 reproduces it. Data: $x \in \mathbb{R}^m$ with $m$ features, each independently active with probability $p$ (value uniform on $[0,1]$, else $0$), with importance weights $I_i = 0.9^i$. Model: compress to $d \ll m$ dimensions and reconstruct through a ReLU, $$\hat{x} = \mathrm{ReLU}(W^\top W x + b), \qquad W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times m}, \qquad \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_i I_i (x_i - \hat{x}_i)^2\Big].$$ Column $W_i$ is the direction assigned to feature $i$; $\|W_i\| \approx 0$ means the feature is dropped. The result is a phase transition in $p$. Dense features ($p = 1$): the model keeps almost exactly the $d$ most important features orthogonally and drops the rest, like PCA. Sparse features ($p \ll 1$): it packs far more than $d$ features as non-orthogonal directions, in striking geometric arrangements (antipodal pairs, pentagons, tetrahedra) that trade interference against coverage. In our run ($d=5$, $m=20$), the dense model keeps exactly $5/20$ features while the sparse model at $p = 0.05$ keeps $15/20$ at relative loss $0.226$ — well below the $0.534$ importance mass forfeited by any model that keeps $5$ features and reconstructs zero for the rest. Certain (measured; Artifact 37.1).

Example 37.1 (Three features in two dimensions)

Why the ReLU is essential: place three unit feature directions at $120^\circ$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$: $f_1 = (1,0)$, $f_2 = (-\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, $f_3 = (-\tfrac12, -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, so every pair has $\langle f_i, f_j\rangle = -\tfrac12$. Take $b = 0$. Encode $x = (1,0,0)$: $h = f_1$, and the reconstruction is $\hat{x}_i = \mathrm{ReLU}(\langle f_i, h\rangle)$, i.e. $\hat{x} = (\mathrm{ReLU}(1), \mathrm{ReLU}(-\tfrac12), \mathrm{ReLU}(-\tfrac12)) = (1,0,0)$ — exact, because the interference is negative and the ReLU clips it. Now activate two features, $x = (1,1,0)$: $h = f_1 + f_2 = (\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, giving $\hat{x}_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(1 - \tfrac12) = \tfrac12$, $\hat{x}_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-\tfrac12 + 1) = \tfrac12$, $\hat{x}_3 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-\tfrac12 - \tfrac12) = 0$, so the squared error is $(\tfrac12)^2 + (\tfrac12)^2 = \tfrac12$. Superposition stores 3 features in 2 dimensions perfectly when one is active and pays $\tfrac12$ when two co-occur — a good trade exactly when co-occurrence is rare. That is the whole hypothesis in four lines of arithmetic.

37.3 Sparse Autoencoders

If activations $a \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are sparse combinations of directions from an unknown dictionary, recovering that dictionary is classical sparse coding (Olshausen & Field, 1996), scaled up. A sparse autoencoder learns an overcomplete dictionary $W_{\mathrm{dec}} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$, $m \gg d$, and a sparse code $z \in \mathbb{R}^m_{\geq 0}$ per activation:

Definition 37.2 (Sparse autoencoder)

Encoder $z = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_{\mathrm{enc}}(a - b_{\mathrm{dec}}) + b_{\mathrm{enc}})$, decoder $\hat{a} = W_{\mathrm{dec}}^\top z + b_{\mathrm{dec}}$, trained on $$\mathcal{L} = \|a - \hat{a}\|_2^2 + \lambda \|z\|_1,$$ the $\ell_1$ term being the convex surrogate for the intractable $\|z\|_0$ (the same relaxation as the lasso, Chapter 14). Rows of $W_{\mathrm{dec}}$ are constrained to unit norm; the candidate "features" are those rows, and a latent's activations over a corpus are what you inspect to label it. TopK variants replace the $\ell_1$ term by keeping only the $k$ largest pre-activations per input (Gao et al., 2024), fixing $\|z\|_0 = k$ exactly. Certain

The $\ell_1$ penalty causes shrinkage: it pays $\lambda$ per unit of magnitude even on correctly-active latents, biasing $z$ low and reconstruction short. TopK, JumpReLU (Rajamanoharan et al., DeepMind 2024), and gated encoders exist mainly to remove this bias. Scaled up, the method produced the field's most visible results: Anthropic trained SAEs with up to 34M latents on Claude 3 Sonnet activations, finding features for sycophancy, security vulnerabilities, and the Golden Gate Bridge (Templeton et al., Scaling Monosemanticity, 2024), and OpenAI trained a 16M-latent TopK SAE on GPT-4 (Gao et al., 2024). Verify (latent counts; check the two papers).

Common Pitfall

Training an $\ell_1$ SAE without constraining decoder row norms. The penalty is on $\|z\|_1$ but the reconstruction only sees $W_{\mathrm{dec}}^\top z$, so gradient descent scales $z$ down by $c$ and $W_{\mathrm{dec}}$ up by $c$, driving the sparsity penalty toward zero without any actual sparsity — the loss curve looks great and the dictionary is garbage. Renormalize decoder rows every step (as Artifact 37.1 does) or project the gradient. A second real bug: dead latents. In large SAEs a substantial fraction of latents can stop firing entirely mid-training, silently shrinking your dictionary; production runs monitor firing frequency and resample or ghost-grad dead latents.

37.3.1 The Sparsity–Fidelity Frontier

Sweeping $\lambda$ (or $k$) traces a frontier between $L_0 = \|z\|_0$ and reconstruction error, usually reported as fraction of variance unexplained. You cannot read quality off either axis alone, and Artifact 37.1's frontier on planted data shows why. With true sparsity $3$: at $k=1$ the SAE is starved (normalized MSE $0.48$, recovers $21/32$ planted features); at $k=3$ it is exact (MSE $1.7\times 10^{-9}$, $32/32$ recovered); at $k=6$ and $k=12$ reconstruction stays essentially perfect ($10^{-8}$–$10^{-7}$) while recovery collapses to $24/32$ and then $2/32$. An over-budgeted SAE reconstructs perfectly using a wrong dictionary — distributing each true feature across several latents. On real models there is no planted ground truth, so a low-MSE point on the frontier is not evidence the dictionary is right; mis-set sparsity yields confidently wrong features (Chanin & Garriga-Alonso, Sparse but Wrong, 2025). Certain (the measured frontier); Likely (the transfer of this diagnosis to LLM SAEs).

37.3.2 Failure Modes

Beyond shrinkage and dead latents, two failure modes are structural. Feature splitting: as $m$ grows, a "math" latent splits into "algebra" and "geometry" latents, with no principled level at which to stop — the dictionary is resolution-dependent, which undermines the claim that latents are the model's units. Feature absorption (Chanin et al., 2024, arXiv:2409.14507): with hierarchical features (starts-with-S $\supset$ short), sparsity is minimized by having the specific latent absorb the general one, so the "starts with S" latent mysteriously fails to fire on "short" — a gerrymandered latent that looks monosemantic on top activations and lies about its own extension. Varying size or sparsity does not fix it. Certain (both are empirically documented across hundreds of SAEs).

Then came the walk-backs. In March 2025 Google DeepMind's mechanistic interpretability team published negative results — on the downstream task it tested, detecting harmful intent out of distribution, SAE-based probes failed to beat simple linear probes — and announced it was deprioritizing SAE research. Certain (the announcement is public). Follow-up work converged on a narrower positive claim: SAEs are useful for discovering unknown concepts (hypothesis generation, unsupervised audits), not for acting on known concepts, where a supervised probe trained on labels is cheaper and better (arXiv:2506.23845, 2025). Likely The honest summary: SAEs demonstrably find human-interpretable directions, and it is not demonstrated that those directions are the units the model itself computes with — there is no ground truth to check against, which is precisely why Artifact 37.1 plants one. Contested — optimists read absorption and splitting as engineering problems (fixable with better priors), skeptics as evidence the "true features" framing is wrong. A decisive test would be an SAE-derived circuit that predicts model behavior out of distribution better than behavioral baselines; nothing published clears that bar as of this writing.

37.4 Circuits and Patching

Features are nouns; circuits are the verbs connecting them. Three tools, in increasing causal strength. The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the final unembedding to intermediate residual streams, reading each layer's "current best guess" of the output; it shows predictions refining layer by layer but is purely correlational and fails on models whose intermediate bases drift (the tuned lens of Belrose et al., 2023, patches this with per-layer affine maps). Activation patching is the causal upgrade: run the model on a clean prompt and a corrupted prompt, splice one activation from the clean run into the corrupted run, and measure how much of the correct behavior is restored. Components whose patching restores behavior are causally implicated; this is causal mediation analysis (Vig et al., 2020) and the "causal tracing" behind the ROME editing work (Meng et al., 2022). It localizes computation without explaining it, and results are sensitive to the choice of corruption and metric — a documented source of interpretability illusions. Certain

The canonical discovered circuit is the induction head (Olsson et al., 2022). On a sequence containing $\ldots A\,B \ldots A$, an induction circuit predicts $B$: a first-layer "previous-token" head writes each token's predecessor into its residual position; a second-layer head then queries for positions whose previous token matches the current token and copies what followed. Two heads, composing across layers, implement "find the last time this happened and repeat what came next" — a primitive of in-context learning. The circuit appears abruptly during training as a visible loss-curve bump, and its formation co-occurs with the jump in in-context learning ability; in attention-only 2-layer models the mechanism is fully verified, while in large models the same co-occurrence is strong but the causal story is coarser. Certain (small models) / Likely (large ones).

The current frontier is attribution graphs (Anthropic, March 2025: Circuit Tracing and On the Biology of a Large Language Model). Cross-layer transcoders — SAE-like sparse replacements trained to imitate the MLPs — make the whole forward pass approximately a sparse linear graph from input tokens through features to logits, for one prompt at a time. On Claude 3.5 Haiku this surfaced multi-step internal reasoning ("Dallas" $\to$ Texas $\to$ "Austin"), forward planning of rhyme words in poetry before the line is written, and cases where the model's chain-of-thought explanation provably does not match its internal computation — motivated reasoning, mechanistically caught. Certain (the papers' claims about studied prompts).
