# ---------------- HARD ASSERTIONS: sourcing discipline ----------------
def check(db):
    names = {s.name for s in db}
    assert len(db) >= 7 and {"BOLT", "BumbleBee", "NEXUS", "SHAFT"} <= names, \
        "coverage: need >=7 systems incl. BOLT/BumbleBee/NEXUS/SHAFT"
    for s in db:
        # 1. non-interactive claims must not carry per-layer client rounds
        assert not (not s.interactive and "per-protocol" in s.client_rounds), \
            f"{s.name}: non-interactive yet charges per-protocol client rounds"
        assert not (("non-interactive" in s.family) and s.interactive), \
            f"{s.name}: family/interactive flag contradiction"
        # 2. any latency claim must state exclusions (even 'none stated')
        if s.latency != NR:
            assert s.exclusions not in ("", NR), f"{s.name}: latency without exclusions"
        # 3. every record is sourced
        assert s.venue not in ("", NR) and s.provenance not in ("", NR), \
            f"{s.name}: missing venue/provenance"
        # 4. no empty fields: every field is a claim or an explicit n/r
        for k, v in asdict(s).items():
            assert v != "" and v is not None, f"{s.name}.{k}: empty field"
    return len(db)

def row(cols, widths):
    return " | ".join(str(c)[:w].ljust(w) for c, w in zip(cols, widths))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    n = check(DB)
    fams = []
    for s in DB:
        if s.family not in fams:
            fams.append(s.family)
    print(f"ALL ASSERTIONS PASSED: {n} systems, {len(fams)} protocol families, "
          f"{sum(1 for s in DB if s.latency != NR)} latency claims each with an "
          f"exclusions note, {sum(asdict(s)[k] == NR for s in DB for k in asdict(s))} "
          f"fields honestly marked n/r\n")
    W1 = (11, 34, 38, 40)
    print("TABLE 1 -- strategies, grouped by protocol family")
    print(row(("system", "softmax strategy", "activation strategy", "venue"), W1))
    print("-" * (sum(W1) + 9))
    for f in fams:
        print(f"[{f}]")
        for s in DB:
            if s.family == f:
                print(row((s.name, s.softmax, s.activation, s.venue), W1))
    W2 = (11, 26, 12, 24, 48)
    print("\nTABLE 2 -- why the latency column is NOT comparable")
    print(row(("system", "benchmark model", "seq len", "hardware", "reported latency"), W2))
    print("-" * (sum(W2) + 12))
    for s in DB:
        if s.latency != NR:
            print(row((s.name, s.model, s.seq_len, s.hardware, s.latency), W2))
    print("\nEvery row above measures a DIFFERENT model, sequence length, hardware "
          "platform,\nand threat model, and each excludes different setup costs; "
          "the column must never\nbe read as a ranking. Consistency spot-check from "
          "the papers' own claims:")
    bolt_over_bb_via_nexus = 372.5 / 53.6   # NEXUS: bandwidth vs BOLT / vs BumbleBee
    print(f"  NEXUS implies BOLT uses {bolt_over_bb_via_nexus:.2f}x BumbleBee's "
          f"bandwidth; BumbleBee itself claims 10x --")
    print("  both are 'true' because they measured different configurations. QED.")

Running it prints ALL ASSERTIONS PASSED: 10 systems, 5 protocol families, 9 latency claims each with an exclusions note, 17 fields honestly marked n/r, then the two tables. Table 2 lists the nine sourced latency claims side by side — BumbleBee's ≈8 min/token on CPUs against NEXUS's 37.3 s on GPU against Bifrost's projected ratios — and closes with the printed spot-check: NEXUS implies BOLT uses 6.95x BumbleBee's bandwidth; BumbleBee itself claims 10x, the Example 40.1 arithmetic reproduced from code.

Key Takeaways
  • The literature splits into three protocol families — 2PC with HE subprotocols, non-interactive FHE, and TEE hybrids — that answer different questions under different threat models; no family dominates, and cross-family comparison of headline numbers is a category error. Certain
  • Every system's innovation budget goes to the same three operators — softmax, normalization, activation — and the strategies form a spectrum from faithful protocol-level approximation (Iron, BOLT, NEXUS, THOR), through distribution-aware low-degree fitting that leaves the model frozen (Nimbus), to model surgery that trains the non-linearity away (Powerformer). Certain
  • Interactive designs pay in bandwidth and rounds to keep multiplicative depth nearly free; non-interactive designs pay in depth and bootstrapping to collapse communication to two ciphertexts — packing is optimized against opposite objectives in the two families. Certain
  • A latency claim is only meaningful as the tuple (threat model, model, sequence length, hardware, network emulation, exclusions, accuracy cost); cross-paper reconstructions disagree by ~1.5× even between honest papers, which is the measurement noise floor of the field. Likely
  • What is deployed today is trusted hardware for transformer inference (Apple's Private Cloud Compute) and homomorphic encryption only for shallow retrieval workloads (Live Caller ID Lookup, Enhanced Visual Search); no FHE transformer serves production traffic as of this writing. Verify
Chapter 41

Encrypted LLM Serving at Scale

Learning Objectives
  • Compute the ciphertext count and memory footprint of an encrypted KV cache as a function of sequence position $t$, packing density, and RNS precision.
  • Derive the rotation and repacking cost of appending one generation step to a packed cache, and the cost of attending over it.
  • Place bootstrapping inside the generation loop and derive tokens-per-bootstrap $B/d_{\text{tok}}$ for a given level budget $B$.
  • Compare the effective precision of a CKKS pipeline against fp16's 11-bit significand at matched settings, and state what accuracy evidence exists beyond single-pass classification.
  • Implement an encrypted-generation cost model — op counts, bootstrap accounting, and a bootstrap-dominance crossover — in working code.
Read alongside — Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), for the plaintext KV cache implemented line by line: you need the plaintext loop cold before encrypting it. Stanford CS336 for the serving-side framing (prefill versus decode, cache economics) that this chapter re-derives under encryption.

Chapter 40 surveyed private transformer inference systems and Chapter 39 built their polynomial cores; nearly every number in those chapters describes one forward pass. This chapter asks what those systems have mostly not: what happens when you decode autoregressively, so that the KV cache of Chapter 33 becomes a growing set of ciphertexts. Three costs that a single-pass benchmark never exercises — cache memory blow-up, per-step repacking, and bootstrapping in a loop whose depth grows without bound — turn out to dominate. We derive each, verify the closed forms against a counting model in Artifact 41.1, and end with the number the field least likes to print: an honest end-to-end accounting of one generated token. Chapter 42 uses the gaps identified here as a map of where a research contribution fits.

41.1 One Forward Pass Is Not Generation

The CKKS facts this chapter consumes, stated once (for the constructions themselves see a dedicated source — Cheon et al.'s original CKKS and CKKS-bootstrapping papers, or the edited volume Lauter, Dai & Laine, Protecting Privacy through Homomorphic Encryption (Springer, 2021)): a ciphertext over ring degree $N$ carries $N/2$ complex slots; each ciphertext–ciphertext or masking multiplication consumes one level from a finite ladder, with a rescaling after each; slot permutations are rotations, each costing a key-switch comparable to a multiplication; and when levels run out, bootstrapping refreshes them at a cost two to three orders of magnitude above a multiplication, itself consuming part of the ladder and capping output precision. Certain

The benchmark culture of Chapter 40 is single-pass: encrypt an input, run the circuit once, decrypt one output. NEXUS (Zhang et al., NDSS 2025) reports BERT-base inference in 37.3 s at 164 MB of bandwidth — the GPU figure, a 42.3× speedup over its own CPU implementation (SEAL with HEXL, FHE-MP-CNN for bootstrapping), exactly as Chapter 40 prices it; THOR (CCS 2025) and MOAI (ePrint 2025/991) report CKKS transformer inference in the same single-pass shape, with MOAI's paper reporting an extension of its pipeline to a LLaMA-3-8B forward pass. These are classification- or prefill-shaped workloads: depth is fixed at compile time, every ciphertext's level schedule is known in advance, and the circuit runs once.

Generation breaks all three properties. Decoding $T$ tokens is $T$ sequential forward passes: total multiplicative depth grows linearly in $T$, so no fixed ladder survives and bootstrapping is not an occasional refresh but a metronome. The cache that makes plaintext decoding cheap — $O(td)$ attention per step instead of $O(t^2 d)$ recompute — must itself live in ciphertext, and its slot layout is frozen at encryption time. And the argmax/sampling step between passes is a comparison, the operation CKKS does worst (Chapter 39). NEXUS's secure argmax primitive was built for a different purpose — returning an encrypted classification label instead of the full logit vector — but generation needs the same machinery for a harder reason: the emitted token must be selected and re-embedded without ever leaving ciphertext.

How thin is the actual generation literature? As of this writing: PUMA (Dong et al., 2023) reports generating one token of LLaMA-7B in around five minutes — under three-party MPC, a different threat model from FHE, with per-token cost roughly flat because MPC has no depth budget. On the FHE side, the first systems to integrate a genuinely encrypted KV cache appear in 2026 preprints: Cachemir (arXiv 2602.11470) reports FHE packing algorithms designed around the cache, an "augmented bootstrapping placement" strategy, speedups of 48.83× over MOAI and 67.16× over THOR on CPU, and under 100 s per generated token for LLaMA-3-8B on GPU; CryptoGen (arXiv 2602.08798) reports a hybrid HE/secret-sharing design with persistent encrypted KV-cache reuse, near-linear per-token scaling, and 4.4–7.6× lower per-token latency than discriminative secure-inference systems adapted to decoding, at input lengths of 128–512 tokens, evaluated on GPT-2-scale models trained on WikiText-2, PTB, and LAMBADA. Verify What has not been demonstrated, in any published system we could find: multi-hundred-token generations from a modern LLM under FHE with reported output quality; interactive (sub-second) per-token latency under any encrypted threat model at LLM scale; or batch-one decode economics that close within even two orders of magnitude of plaintext. That absence is the subject of this chapter, not an aside. Likely

41.2 The Encrypted KV Cache

Plaintext first (Chapter 33): after $t$ steps, the cache holds $2Ltd$ scalars — keys and values, per layer — and at fp16 costs $4Ltd$ bytes. Under CKKS the unit of storage is the ciphertext, and the accounting changes twice: once because slots quantize storage, and again because each slot costs far more than two bytes.

Definition 41.1 (Packing density of a cached step)

Fix ring degree $N$ with $s = N/2$ slots. A packing assigns the $d$-dimensional key (or value) vector of each cached step to slots. Its density $g$ is the number of steps stored per ciphertext, $1 \le g \le \lfloor s/d \rfloor$. The compact packing takes $g = \lfloor s/d \rfloor$; the one-ciphertext-per-step packing takes $g = 1$. After $t$ steps a layer's key cache occupies $m(t) = \lceil t/g \rceil$ ciphertexts, and the full cache $2L\,m(t)$.

Memory per ciphertext is set by the RNS representation: two polynomials of $N$ coefficients over $\ell$ limbs of $w$ bytes each, i.e. $2N\ell w$ bytes at level $\ell$. The bytes-per-cached-scalar of a compact packing is therefore $2N\ell w / (gd) \approx 2N\ell w/s = 4\ell w$, independent of the model: at $\ell = 12$ limbs and $w = 8$ bytes, 384 bytes per scalar against fp16's two — a $\sim$192× expansion before any slack from $\lceil\cdot\rceil$ effects. Certain

Example 41.1 (Cache memory at $t=1024$, GPT-2-small geometry)

Take $L=12$, $d=768$, $N=2^{16}$ (so $s=32{,}768$, $g=\lfloor 32768/768\rfloor = 42$), cache held at $\ell=12$ limbs. One ciphertext: $2 \times 65536 \times 12 \times 8 = 12{,}582{,}912$ bytes $= 12.0$ MiB. At $t=1024$: $m = \lceil 1024/42 \rceil = 25$, so $2 \times 12 \times 25 = 600$ ciphertexts $= 7.03$ GiB. The fp16 plaintext cache is $4 \times 12 \times 1024 \times 768 = 36$ MiB — a 200× blow-up. The $g=1$ packing needs $2 \times 12 \times 1024 = 24{,}576$ ciphertexts $= 288$ GiB, 8192× fp16. Both figures are printed by Artifact 41.1.

So a single stream's encrypted cache at modest length occupies what a plaintext server spends on the weights of a 3B-parameter model. Two consequences follow. First, the batching that makes plaintext serving economical (Chapter 33) is nearly foreclosed: CKKS batching packs many independent inputs into slots, but a compact cache already spends its slots on cache steps, and every client's cache is encrypted under a different key. Second, the choice of $g$ is a genuine trade, not an optimization detail: $g=1$ makes appending free (the new step simply becomes a fresh ciphertext) but makes memory and attention cost scale with $t$ ciphertexts; compact packing divides both by $g$ but makes appending a slot-surgery problem — the subject of the next section.

41.3 Appending, Attending, Repacking

Slots are positional and immutable-in-place: to write step $t$'s key vector into slot block $(t \bmod g)$ of the current cache ciphertext, the server must (i) rotate the freshly computed key ciphertext by $(t \bmod g)\,d$ slots, (ii) multiply by a 0/1 mask plaintext to zero everything else, and (iii) add into the cache ciphertext. Step (ii) is a real multiplication: it consumes a level. Appending is never free under compact packing — per token it costs, across $K$ and $V$ and all layers, $2L$ rotations, $2L$ masking multiplications, and one level of depth on the cache lane. This is the repacking tax, and it recurs every token for the life of the stream.

41.3.1 Attending over the packed cache

With head dimension $d_k$ and heads interleaved in slots, computing scores $q \cdot k_i$ for the $g$ steps inside one cache ciphertext costs one ciphertext–ciphertext multiplication (the replicated query against the packed keys) plus $\lceil \log_2 d_k \rceil$ rotations for the rotate-and-sum inner product; the weighted-value accumulation costs one more multiplication plus $\lceil \log_2 g \rceil$ rotations per value ciphertext. Cross-ciphertext combination is slot-aligned addition, which is free in this accounting. Per token, the cache-dependent cost is therefore

$$A(t) = L\, m(t)\,\big(2\,c_{\times} + (\lceil \log_2 d_k \rceil + \lceil \log_2 g \rceil)\, c_{\mathrm{rot}}\big), \qquad m(t) = \lceil t/g \rceil,$$

which is a staircase, flat within a ciphertext and jumping by $b = L(2 + \lceil \log_2 d_k\rceil + \lceil \log_2 g \rceil)$ multiplication-equivalents every $g$ tokens (weighting rotations and ct-mults equally at $c_\times = c_{\mathrm{rot}} = 1$, key-switch-dominated ops being comparable). For the Example 41.1 geometry, $b = 12(2+6+6) = 168$; Artifact 41.1's least-squares fit of its simulated staircase recovers slope $168.000000$ with maximum residual $1.8\times 10^{-12}$. Under $g=1$ the same derivation gives $\lceil\log_2 g\rceil = 0$ and $m(t)=t$, so per-token cost is linear in $t$ with slope $L(2+\lceil\log_2 d_k\rceil) = 96$ against the compact packing's effective $b/g = 4$ — $24\times$ steeper. The two packings trade append cost against attend cost, and neither escapes growth in $t$. The assertion the artifact enforces is the chapter's first claim in executable form: per-token cost grows with cache length under any fixed packing. Certain

Cachemir's contribution is a better point on this trade surface: the paper reports an "interleaved replicated" packing for the vector–matrix multiplications that KV-cache-driven decoding produces in the transformer's linear layers, chosen to keep slot utilization high where a naive packing would waste most of the ciphertext. Verify It does not repeal the staircase; it lowers $b$.

Common Pitfall

Level misalignment in the cache. The key written at step 10 has consumed a different number of levels than the key written at step 400 — each passed through a different number of bootstrap cycles before being cached. CKKS addition requires operands at the same level, so a naive implementation either crashes at the add-into-cache step or silently mod-switches the entire cache ciphertext down to the newest entry's level, ratcheting the whole cache toward level zero and forcing a full-cache bootstrap. The fix is a write-time contract: mod-switch every fresh $K$/$V$ to a fixed resident level $\ell_{\text{cache}}$ chosen at compile time, and budget the masking multiplication below it. Every FHE KV-cache design must state $\ell_{\text{cache}}$ somewhere; if a paper doesn't, its memory numbers are not reproducible, because $\ell$ is a factor in every byte count.

41.4 Bootstrapping Placement

Each decoded token consumes a fixed depth $d_{\text{tok}} = L\, d_{\text{layer}}$: attention scores, the softmax polynomial, the value mix, projections, LayerNorm inverse-square-root and activation polynomials, plus the append mask (§41.3). Depth per token is constant in $t$ — longer caches add rotations and multiplications, not levels — but it accrues across tokens without bound, so bootstrapping enters the loop as a fixed per-token toll rather than a rare event.

Theorem 41.1 (Greedy bootstrap count)

Model the residual stream as one serial lane consuming $D$ levels in total, starting with a fresh budget of $B$ usable levels and bootstrapping (restoring $B$) exactly when the budget is exhausted and more depth is needed. The number of bootstraps is $\lceil D/B \rceil - 1$, and no schedule that only bootstraps (never wastes levels) does better.

Proof. After $k$ bootstraps the total usable depth supplied is $(k+1)B$; greedy bootstraps only when forced, so it runs to completion at the least integer $k$ with $(k+1)B \ge D$, i.e. $k = \lceil D/B - 1\rceil = \lceil D/B \rceil - 1$, the last equality because shifting by an integer commutes with $\lceil\cdot\rceil$. Optimality: any schedule with $k$ bootstraps supplies at most $(k+1)B$ levels, so every schedule needs $k \ge D/B - 1$. $\blacksquare$

The serial-lane model is the honest simplification to state loudly: a real circuit has parallel lanes at different levels, and production placement (as in the FHE compilers of Chapter 40, and the "augmented" cache-aware placement Cachemir's paper reports) exploits that slack. But it changes constants, not the structure: steady-state tokens per bootstrap is $B / d_{\text{tok}}$, and for every realistic transformer this is far below one — you bootstrap many times per token, not the reverse.

Example 41.2 (Tokens per bootstrap)

With $d_{\text{layer}} = 21$ levels (1 QKV, 1 append mask, 1 scores, 6 softmax, 1 value mix, 1 output projection, $2\times 2$ LayerNorm, 1+4+1 MLP with activation) and $L = 12$: $d_{\text{tok}} = 252$. With $B = 18$ usable levels: $252/18 = 14$ bootstraps per token, i.e. $0.0714$ tokens per bootstrap. Over $T = 1024$ tokens, $D = 258{,}048$ and Theorem 41.1 gives $\lceil 258048/18\rceil - 1 = 14{,}335$; Artifact 41.1's step-by-step level simulation counts exactly $14{,}335$ (13 for the first token, whose fresh budget is free, then 14 every token thereafter).

Placement freedom that generation adds and single-pass circuits lack: the cache itself. Cache ciphertexts sit at the fixed resident level and lose one level per append-mask; refreshing them can be batched (bootstrap $2L$ cache lanes together, amortizing key-switch keys and memory traffic) and scheduled off the token's critical path, since step $t{+}1$ needs the cache only at its attention layer. Overlapping cache refresh with the MLP of the previous layer is the FHE analogue of the prefetching tricks of Chapter 33 — reported as a design element in the 2026 cache papers, not yet standard. Likely

41.5 Effective Precision: CKKS versus fp16

fp16 carries an 11-bit significand (10 stored, one implicit). A CKKS slot's effective precision is $\log_2(\Delta / \lVert e \rVert)$: scale over noise. Fresh encryptions at $\Delta = 2^{40}$ typically start near 30 bits; each level consumed costs a model-dependent fraction of a bit (rescaling rounding plus approximation error); and bootstrapping does not restore fresh precision — it caps it, with reported CKKS bootstrapping output precision in the high-teens to low-20s of bits at practical parameters. Verify The steady-state pipeline therefore lives on a sawtooth: precision $p_{\text{boot}}$ after each bootstrap, decaying by $\lambda$ bits per level for $B$ levels. The floor is $p_{\text{boot}} - \lambda B$, and it — not the fresh-encryption headline — is the number to compare against fp16. At Artifact 41.1's stated parameters ($p_{\text{boot}} = 20$, $\lambda = 0.5$, $B = 18$) the floor is exactly $11.0$ bits: fp16 parity with zero margin, and the model's implied maximum budget for fp16 parity is $B_{\max} = \lfloor (p_{\text{boot}} - 11)/\lambda \rfloor = 18$. This is a parameterized model, not a measurement — but it exposes the real coupling: raising $B$ to bootstrap less often lowers worst-case precision. Depth budget and precision budget are the same budget spent twice.

What accuracy evidence exists beyond single-pass classification? Very little. The single-pass systems of Chapter 40 report small degradations on GLUE-style classification — a task family where a half-bit of logit error rarely flips an argmax. Generation is harsher in one way and gentler in another, and the field genuinely disagrees on which wins. Contested The pessimistic position: approximation error compounds across $T$ sequential passes — each token is sampled from perturbed logits and then conditions all later steps, so quality should degrade with length, and perplexity-style evaluation under encryption over long horizons has not been published for any modern LLM. The optimistic position: greedy decoding snaps to a discrete token, which is an error-erasing nonlinearity — if the perturbation doesn't flip the argmax, the emitted prefix is exactly the plaintext one and nothing compounds. Both are right in their regimes (peaked versus flat next-token distributions). What would settle it is cheap to state and expensive to run: token-level agreement curves between encrypted and plaintext decoding versus generation length, at matched sampling settings, on a model people care about. CryptoGen's paper is the closest published step — it reports perplexity for GPT-2-scale models on WikiText-2/PTB/LAMBADA nearly identical to plaintext inference — but that is aggregate perplexity at GPT-2 scale, not token-level agreement at LLaMA scale, and no result of the latter kind exists as of this writing. Verify

41.6 GPU-Accelerated FHE

Everything above counts operations; GPUs change the constant per operation. CKKS's inner loops — NTTs and base conversions over $N=2^{16}$ rings — are memory-bandwidth-bound, which is exactly the regime GPUs win (Chapter 30). The landmark is Jung et al. (TCHES 2021), the first GPU CKKS bootstrapping: the paper reports 0.423 μs amortized bootstrapping time per bit and a 257× speedup over a single-threaded CPU baseline, achieved by memory-centric kernel fusion rather than FLOP tricks. Since then:

SystemWhat the paper/repo reportsBootstrapping?
Jung et al. (TCHES 2021)0.423 μs/bit amortized bootstrap; 257× vs 1-thread CPUYes (first on GPU)
Phantom (ePrint 2023/049)CUDA BFV/BGV/CKKS libraryNo
HEonGPU (ePrint 2024/1543)Repo reports slim bootstrapping, $N=2^{16}$, in 99.12 ms on an RTX 4090 VerifyYes (CKKS, BFV, TFHE)
FIDESlib (arXiv 2507.04775, 2025)Reports up to 227.8× over OpenFHE and 74.4× over AVX-optimized OpenFHE for bootstrappingYes
Cheddar (ASPLOS 2026; arXiv 2407.13055)ASPLOS version reports 2.18–4.45× over state-of-the-art GPU implementations; the 2024 preprint reported 2.9–25.6× against the then-current baselines VerifyYes
NEXUS-GPU (NDSS 2025)Reports 42.3× over its own CPU versionYes (via FHE-MP-CNN port)

These rows are not mutually comparable: they differ in GPU generation, ring degree, bootstrapping variant (slim versus full-slot), target precision, and what is excluded from timing (key generation, host–device transfer), so read each as a claim about one system, never as a ranking. For the practitioner in OpenFHE, the directly relevant row is FIDESlib, which is built to be interoperable with client-side OpenFHE and reports its speedups against that CPU baseline. The structural point is that a $\sim$100 ms-class GPU bootstrap moves the bootstrap-to-multiplication ratio $R$ from the $\sim\!10^3$ of CPU pipelines toward $\sim\!10^2$ — which matters because, as §41.7 shows, $R$ is the single knob that decides whether the generation loop is bootstrap-bound. What GPU acceleration does not change: the staircase in $t$, the tokens-per-bootstrap arithmetic, and the 200× cache memory expansion — 7 GiB per stream at $t=1024$ now competes with model weights for HBM. Certain

41.7 An Honest Cost of One Token

Assemble the pieces at the Example 41.1 geometry, from Artifact 41.1's run. Decoding one token at $t=1$ costs 19,149.6 multiplication-equivalents in the counting model; at $t=1024$, 23,181.6, with the cache-attention share growing from 0.9% to 18.1%. Bootstrapping adds $14 \times R$ equivalents per token; at the [Verify]-tagged $R=100$ that is 1,400 — 6.8% of modeled time at $t=1$, diluting to 5.7% at $t=1024$. The crossover where the growing attention staircase overtakes the fixed bootstrap toll has the closed form $t^{*} = \lfloor d_{\text{tok}} R / (B\,b) \rfloor \cdot g + 1 = 337$, and the simulation's op-by-op scan finds exactly $t=337$. On a CPU pipeline with $R \sim 10^3$, the same closed form pushes $t^{*}$ past 3,000: bootstrap-bound for any realistic chat turn. That inversion is worth stating plainly: GPU bootstrapping does not remove the bootstrap problem; it relocates the bottleneck to cache traffic, which is the harder one to fix because it is bandwidth, not compute. Likely

To anchor against published wall-clock: Cachemir's paper reports under 100 s per generated token for LLaMA-3-8B on GPU; PUMA's paper reports about five minutes per LLaMA-7B token under three-party MPC. These two numbers come from different threat models, hardware, and timing boundaries and must not be compared to each other or to plaintext serving numbers; read separately, they place the published state of the art somewhere in the range of one to five minutes per token for 7–8B models under cryptographic protection. Verify A plaintext A100 serves the same model at tens of milliseconds per token — three to four orders of magnitude. The honest sentence, then: encrypted generation exists as a demonstrated capability at the scale of single tokens and short sequences, and does not yet exist as a demonstrated service. The distance is measured in exactly the three quantities this chapter derived — bytes per cached scalar ($4\ell w$), the staircase slope $b$, and tokens per bootstrap ($B/d_{\text{tok}}$) — and Chapter 42 treats each as an open problem with a research surface attached.

Artifact 41.1 — An Encrypted-Generation Cost Model

This module extends Artifact 38.1's op counter to autoregressive decoding: it simulates $T=1024$ tokens with a growing KV cache under the compact packing of Definition 41.1, counting rotations, ciphertext multiplications, masking multiplications, and bootstraps under greedy level accounting. It is a counting model — no FHE library runs, and the only wall-clock-flavored input is the [Verify]-tagged ratio $R$. It asserts the chapter's three closed forms against the simulation: staircase growth with fitted slope equal to $b$, Theorem 41.1's bootstrap count, and the crossover $t^{*}$; it also evaluates the parameterized precision model of §41.5.

"""Artifact 41.1 -- Encrypted-generation cost model (extends Artifact 38.1's op counter).

COUNTING MODEL ONLY. No FHE library is invoked; nothing here is a measurement.
We count homomorphic operations (rotations, ct-ct multiplies, pt-ct multiplies,
fresh ciphertexts, bootstraps) for autoregressive decoding with a growing
encrypted KV cache under one explicitly stated packing.  Wall-clock enters only
through a single [Verify]-tagged ratio R_BOOT = bootstrap cost / ct-ct-mult
cost; effective precision is a parameterized model, not a measurement.
"""
import math
import numpy as np

# ---------------- model geometry (GPT-2-small-like; all stated, not measured) --
L, d, H, dk, dff = 12, 768, 12, 64, 3072   # layers, width, heads, head dim, FF
N = 1 << 16                                 # CKKS ring degree
SLOTS = N // 2                              # 32768 complex slots
G = SLOTS // d                              # cache steps packed per ciphertext (compact packing)
LIMB_BYTES = 8                              # one RNS limb coefficient = 8 bytes
ELL_CACHE = 12                              # limbs at which cache ciphertexts are held (stated)

# unit costs, in "ct-ct multiply equivalents" (keyswitch-bearing ops ~ 1)
W_ROT, W_CTMULT, W_PTMULT = 1.0, 1.0, 0.1

# depth (levels consumed) per layer per generated token -- stated component model:
# qkv proj 1, cache append masks 1, scores 1, softmax poly 6, AV 1, out proj 1,
# LN approx 2+2, MLP in 1, activation poly 4, MLP out 1  => 21
D_LAYER = 21
D_TOK = L * D_LAYER          # levels consumed per generated token (residual stream)
B_LEVELS = 18                # usable multiplicative budget between bootstraps
R_BOOT = 100.0               # [Verify] bootstrap / ct-mult cost ratio; HEonGPU's README
                             # reports ~99 ms slim bootstrapping (N=2^16, RTX 4090) vs
                             # ~1 ms-scale GPU ct-mults => order 1e2. Re-check per system.


def per_token_cost(t):
    """Op counts to decode ONE token when the cache already holds t-1 steps
    (so it holds t after the append).  Explicit loops over cache ciphertexts --
    the closed forms in the chapter are checked AGAINST this, not derived from it."""
    rot = ctm = ptm = 0.0
    m = math.ceil(t / G)                     # live cache ciphertexts per layer per K (and V)
    for _ in range(L):
        # -- cache-independent core (Halevi-Shoup/BSGS matvecs on one token vector)
        rot += 4 * 2 * math.ceil(math.sqrt(d));   ptm += 4 * d        # Wq,Wk,Wv,Wo
        rot += 2 * 2 * math.ceil(math.sqrt(dff)); ptm += 2 * dff     # MLP up/down
        ctm += H * (6 + 8)                       # softmax: exp poly + inverse poly, per head
        ctm += 6                                 # activation polynomial on FF ciphertext
        ctm += 2 * 8; rot += 2 * math.ceil(math.log2(d))  # 2 LayerNorm inv-sqrt approx
        # -- appending this step's K,V into the packed cache: rotate into slot + mask
        rot += 2; ptm += 2                       # one rotation + one mask mult, for K and V
        # -- attending over the packed cache: per cache ciphertext,
        #    scores: 1 ct-mult + log2(dk) rotations; AV: 1 ct-mult + log2(G) rotations
        for _ in range(m):
            ctm += 1; rot += math.ceil(math.log2(dk))
            ctm += 1; rot += math.ceil(math.log2(G))
    total = W_ROT * rot + W_CTMULT * ctm + W_PTMULT * ptm
    attend = L * m * (2 * W_CTMULT + W_ROT * (math.ceil(math.log2(dk)) + math.ceil(math.log2(G))))
    return dict(rot=rot, ctmult=ctm, ptmul=ptm, total=total, attend=attend, m=m)


def simulate(T):
    """Decode T tokens from an empty cache; greedy level accounting on the
    residual stream: bootstrap exactly when the budget is exhausted."""
    per_tok = np.zeros(T); attend = np.zeros(T); boots = np.zeros(T, dtype=int)
    levels, nboot = B_LEVELS, 0
    for i in range(T):
        c = per_token_cost(i + 1)
        per_tok[i], attend[i] = c["total"], c["attend"]
        b0 = nboot
        for _ in range(D_TOK):                # consume one level per depth unit
            if levels == 0:
                nboot += 1; levels = B_LEVELS  # bootstrap refreshes the budget
            levels -= 1
        boots[i] = nboot - b0
    return per_tok, attend, boots, nboot


if __name__ == "__main__":
    T = 1024
    per_tok, attend, boots, nboot = simulate(T)
    base = per_tok - attend                    # cache-independent share

    print("=== Artifact 41.1: encrypted-generation cost model (counting model) ===")
    print(f"geometry: L={L} d={d} H={H} dk={dk} | slots={SLOTS} G={G} steps/ct "
          f"| depth/token={D_TOK} budget={B_LEVELS} R_BOOT={R_BOOT} [Verify]")

    # ---- (1) per-token cost grows with cache length under this packing --------
    print("\n[1] per-token cost curve (ct-mult equivalents):")
    for t in [1, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]:
        print(f"    t={t:5d}  total={per_tok[t-1]:9.1f}  attend={attend[t-1]:7.1f} "
              f"({100*attend[t-1]/per_tok[t-1]:4.1f}%)  cache cts m={math.ceil(t/G)}")
    diffs = np.diff(per_tok)
    assert (diffs >= -1e-9).all() and per_tok[-1] > per_tok[0], "cost must grow with t"
    # cross-check: attend cost is exactly linear in m; fit and print the residual
    ms = np.array([math.ceil(t / G) for t in range(1, T + 1)], float)
    slope, icept = np.polyfit(ms, attend, 1)
    resid = float(np.abs(np.polyval([slope, icept], ms) - attend).max())
    b_analytic = L * (2 + math.ceil(math.log2(dk)) + math.ceil(math.log2(G)))
    print(f"    fitted slope/cache-ct = {slope:.6f} vs analytic b = {b_analytic} "
          f"(max fit residual {resid:.2e})")
    assert abs(slope - b_analytic) < 1e-6 and resid < 1e-6

    # ---- (2) bootstraps match the analytic ceil accounting --------------------
    total_depth = T * D_TOK
    analytic = math.ceil(total_depth / B_LEVELS) - 1   # start fresh; none after last op
    nb_tok = D_TOK / B_LEVELS
    print(f"\n[2] bootstraps over T={T} tokens: simulated={nboot}  "
          f"analytic ceil({total_depth}/{B_LEVELS})-1={analytic}  "
          f"(={nb_tok:.1f}/token; tokens/bootstrap={1/nb_tok:.4f})")
    assert nboot == analytic, (nboot, analytic)
    # steady state is exactly D_TOK/B per token (B | D_TOK); token 1 gets the
    # fresh budget for free and needs one fewer
    assert (boots[1:] == int(nb_tok)).all() and boots[0] == int(nb_tok) - 1

    # ---- (3) crossover: growing attention cost overtakes bootstrap cost -------
    boot_cost = nb_tok * R_BOOT                 # per-token, constant in t (depth is)
    scan = next(t for t in range(1, T + 1) if attend[t - 1] > boot_cost)
    m_star = math.floor(boot_cost / b_analytic) + 1
    closed = (m_star - 1) * G + 1
    print(f"\n[3] per-token bootstrap cost = {boot_cost:.0f} mult-equivs; "
          f"attention overtakes it at t={scan} (closed form: m*={m_star}, t*={closed})")
    assert scan == closed, (scan, closed)
    print(f"    below t={closed}: bootstrapping outweighs cache attention; above: cache wins")
    print(f"    bootstrap share of total modeled time at t=1: "
          f"{100*boot_cost/(per_tok[0]+boot_cost):.1f}%  at t={T}: "
          f"{100*boot_cost/(per_tok[-1]+boot_cost):.1f}%")

    # ---- (4) encrypted KV-cache memory at t=1024 (both packings) --------------
    ct_mib = 2 * N * ELL_CACHE * LIMB_BYTES / 2**20   # binary units throughout
    m = math.ceil(T / G)
    compact_cts, naive_cts = 2 * L * m, 2 * L * T
    plain_mib = 2 * L * T * d * 2 / 2**20      # fp16 plaintext KV cache
    print(f"\n[4] KV cache at t={T} ({ELL_CACHE} limbs, {ct_mib:.1f} MiB/ct):")
    print(f"    compact packing : {compact_cts:6d} cts = {compact_cts*ct_mib/1024:8.2f} GiB "
          f"({compact_cts*ct_mib/plain_mib:7.0f}x fp16)")
    print(f"    one-ct-per-step : {naive_cts:6d} cts = {naive_cts*ct_mib/1024:8.2f} GiB "
          f"({naive_cts*ct_mib/plain_mib:7.0f}x fp16)  [fp16 plaintext: {plain_mib:.1f} MiB]")

    # ---- (5) CKKS effective precision vs fp16 (parameterized model, NOT measured)
    P_FRESH, LOSS, P_BOOT, FP16 = 30.0, 0.5, 20.0, 11  # bits; P_BOOT is [Verify]
    prec = P_BOOT                                       # steady state: post-bootstrap
    seg = [prec := prec - LOSS for _ in range(B_LEVELS)]  # one inter-bootstrap segment
    floor_sim, floor_closed = min(seg), P_BOOT - LOSS * B_LEVELS
    b_max = math.floor((P_BOOT - FP16) / LOSS)
    print(f"\n[5] precision model: fresh {P_FRESH} bits, {LOSS} bit/level loss, "
          f"bootstrap output {P_BOOT} bits [Verify]")
    print(f"    worst-case bits in a {B_LEVELS}-level segment: simulated={floor_sim:.1f} "
          f"closed form={floor_closed:.1f}  | fp16 significand = {FP16} bits")
    print(f"    largest budget keeping >= fp16 precision: {b_max} levels "
          f"(chosen B_LEVELS={B_LEVELS})")
    assert abs(floor_sim - floor_closed) < 1e-12
    assert floor_closed >= FP16 - 1e-9, "budget exceeds the fp16-parity envelope"
    print("\nAll assertions passed. Counting model only -- no FHE library was run.")

Running it takes 0.15 s and prints the staircase (19,149.6 → 23,181.6 mult-equivalents per token from $t{=}1$ to $t{=}1024$, attention share 0.9% → 18.1%), the fitted slope 168.000000 against the analytic $b=168$ with residual $1.8\times 10^{-12}$, the bootstrap count 14,335 matching $\lceil 258048/18 \rceil - 1$ exactly, the crossover at $t=337$ matching the closed form ($m^{*}=9$), the 7.03 GiB versus 288 GiB cache footprints (200× and 8192× fp16), and the precision floor of 11.0 bits against fp16's 11 — then All assertions passed. Change one geometry constant and every downstream number moves consistently; that, not the specific values, is what the artifact is for.

Key Takeaways
  • Single-pass benchmarks structurally understate encrypted serving: decoding $T$ tokens multiplies depth by $T$, forces a ciphertext-resident KV cache, and inserts a secure argmax between every pair of passes. Certain
  • An encrypted KV cache costs $\approx 4\ell w$ bytes per cached scalar — a $\sim$200× expansion over fp16 at typical parameters — and appending under compact packing burns rotations, masks, and one level every token. Certain
  • Tokens per bootstrap is $B/d_{\text{tok}}$, which is $\ll 1$ for any realistic transformer (0.07 at the chapter's geometry); Theorem 41.1's $\lceil D/B\rceil - 1$ accounting matches the artifact's simulation exactly. Certain
  • The bootstrap-versus-cache crossover $t^{*} = \lfloor d_{\text{tok}}R/(Bb)\rfloor g + 1$ says GPU bootstrapping ($R\sim 10^2$) relocates the bottleneck to cache traffic rather than eliminating it; the constituent cost ratios drift with every library release. Verify
  • Published encrypted generation results are one-token-scale (PUMA's paper reports ~5 min/token for LLaMA-7B under MPC; Cachemir's reports <100 s/token for LLaMA-3-8B under FHE on GPU — different threat models, not comparable); long-horizon output quality under encryption is undemonstrated, and whether approximation error compounds across steps or is erased by argmax snapping remains genuinely unsettled. Contested
Chapter 42

The Research Frontier: Where a Contribution Fits

Learning Objectives
  • Apply a fixed nine-point extraction template to any paper in the encrypted-inference literature, and say what each point is protecting you from.
  • Name the five claims this literature routinely overstates, and state the experiment that would settle each one.
  • Derive the depth-and-rotation comparison between an attention block and a selective state-space block under CKKS at matched width, and locate the crossover in $T$.
  • Map the open problems — encrypted SSMs, encrypted MoE routing, scheme switching, encrypted PEFT, generation at depth — onto the chapters that equip you for each.
  • Implement the attention-versus-SSM encrypted-cost comparison in working code, with the crossover computed and asserted rather than argued by hand.
Read alongside — there is no textbook for this chapter. Two systematizations are the closest thing to a map: SoK: Private LLM Inference using Approximate Homomorphic Encryption (Al Badawi, Alexandru, Polyakov, Vaikuntanathan; ePrint 2026/935), written by OpenFHE maintainers and therefore unusually honest about parameter-level constraints, and SoK: Private Transformer-Based Model Inference (ePrint 2026/491). For the state-space side, Chapter 21's sources remain the only complete treatment. Read surveys for taxonomy, never for numbers.

Chapters 38 through 41 built a complete price list: what CKKS charges (38), how to approximate what it cannot evaluate (39), what the published systems actually did (40), and why generation is a different problem from a forward pass (41). This chapter is about what to do next with that price list. Its method is deliberately unromantic: the open problems in encrypted machine learning are not exotic cryptography, they are the places where two chapters of this book collide and nobody has done the arithmetic across the seam. Section 42.1 gives a fixed template for reading a paper here; 42.2 names what the literature overstates; 42.3 does one such piece of arithmetic in full, comparing an attention block against a selective state-space block under encryption; 42.4 maps the remaining collisions to chapters; 42.5 picks three problems a single researcher could finish; 42.6 closes the book.

42.1 How to Read This Literature

Section 40.5's five-point latency checklist is a special case. The general problem is that a paper here makes claims in three currencies at once — cryptographic, systems, machine-learning — and a reviewer strong in one is routinely weak in the other two, which is why Section 42.2's overclaims survive peer review. Extract the following before forming any opinion, in an order chosen so the earliest points invalidate the most papers.

Definition 42.1 (The nine-point extraction)

For any private-inference paper, record: (1) Threat model — who is hidden from whom, who must stay online, and whether the model weights are plaintext at the server. (2) The function actually evaluated — the architecture after surgery, not the one in the title; a distilled, softmax-free, LayerNorm-linearized network is a different function from the checkpoint it is named after. (3) Depth ledger — levels per block, bootstraps per inference, and whether either is reported at all. (4) Packing and slot utilization — what fraction of the $N/2$ slots carry live data at the narrowest point of the circuit. (5) The baseline — which system, rerun by whom, at whose parameters. (6) The timing boundary — key generation, weight encoding, client compute, and network time are each either inside or outside; papers differ. (7) The accuracy bill — task, metric, and the plaintext reference it is measured against. (8) Amortization convention — per input, or per slot-batch of inputs that no real deployment can assemble. (9) Reproducibility — library and version, ring dimension, level budget, and claimed security level with the estimator used.

Points 3 and 4 are the ones a machine-learning reader skips and should not. A paper reporting end-to-end latency but no depth ledger has made its central design decision — where to bootstrap — unauditable. Point 4 catches the most common silent inefficiency: a system that packs activations into ciphertexts of $N/2 = 32{,}768$ slots and then evaluates a per-head operation touching $d_k = 64$ slots at a time runs at $0.2\%$ utilization, and its rotation counts will be enormous for reasons unrelated to the idea being proposed. Likely

Point 9 is where cryptographic and machine-learning norms genuinely conflict. CKKS is an approximate scheme, and Li and Micciancio (EUROCRYPT 2021; ePrint 2020/1533) showed the standard IND-CPA notion is insufficient for it: decryption returns an approximation whose error is key-dependent, so an adversary seeing decryptions of known computations can recover the secret key — demonstrated in practice against HEAAN, SEAL, HElib, and PALISADE. The repaired notion is IND-CPA$^{\mathrm{D}}$; the countermeasure is flooding the decryption output with key-independent noise. Certain The systems consequence is concrete: flooding costs precision, precision costs polynomial degree, degree costs depth — so a latency number measured without the countermeasure is measuring a cheaper scheme. Few machine-learning-venue papers here state which side of that line they are on.

Common Pitfall

Comparing your system's accuracy against the original checkpoint's published GLUE score rather than against your own plaintext run of your own modified architecture. The failure is not subtle: if you replace softmax with a degree-15 polynomial and LayerNorm with a learned affine map, you must report the plaintext accuracy of that network as the reference, and separately report the encrypted-versus-plaintext gap of the same network. Papers that conflate the two attribute architectural damage to the cryptography, or — far more often — hide architectural damage inside a claim of "no accuracy loss under encryption." Both numbers are needed; either alone is uninterpretable.

42.2 What Is Routinely Overclaimed

Five claims recur, in rough order of how often they appear.

"Private." Unquantified, it almost always means "the input tensor is not sent in the clear." It rarely means the output distribution, the sequence length (ciphertext counts reveal it), or the architecture is hidden, or that a client-aided decryption step leaks nothing — the criticism Chapter 38 recorded against client-aided designs. The settling experiment: a simulation-based leakage statement, exhibiting a simulator that produces the server's view from public parameters and input shape alone; failing that, an empirical attack reconstructing inputs from what the server does observe.

Speedup factors. Every headline "$k\times$ faster" is against a baseline the authors reran, at parameters they chose, on hardware the baseline's authors never used; Example 40.1 put the resulting noise floor near $1.5\times$. The settling experiment: a shared artifact benchmark — fixed model, sequence length, ring dimension and level budget, one machine, all systems rerun by a third party. The field has none, which makes it the most valuable unglamorous contribution available. Likely

"Accuracy is preserved." Usually established on sentence classification at sequence length 128, where a two-class boundary tolerates enormous representational damage. The settling experiment: perplexity of the polynomial surrogate on a held-out corpus, same tokenizer, reported beside the plaintext base — Chapter 29's discipline applied to encrypted models. Losing $0.3\%$ on SST-2 and four points of perplexity is not accuracy preservation.

"Scales to a 7B/8B model." Chapter 41 took this apart: one forward pass over an 8-token prompt is not generation, and per-token cost under a growing encrypted cache is a staircase. The settling experiment: generate 128 tokens; report the latency curve and the text.

Security-level claims. "128-bit security" attached to a parameter set chosen for depth rather than checked against a current lattice estimator, silent on IND-CPA$^{\mathrm{D}}$. The settling experiment: print the estimator output and the flooding parameter. Certain

None of this makes the literature dishonest; it makes it young. The venues that would enforce measurement conventions (security) and those that understand the models (machine learning) are disjoint.

42.3 The SSM Opportunity: Depth Arithmetic

Chapter 21 built selective state-space models: linear-in-$T$ compute, constant state at inference, quality competitive with attention at moderate scale. Chapter 38 built the encrypted price list: multiplications cost depth, non-polynomials cost far more, and softmax is the worst offender in the block. Put them together and a question falls out that neither chapter asks. Under encryption, is a selective SSM block cheaper than an attention block?

The answer turns on one structural fact. Attention's depth is independent of $T$ — the score matrix costs one ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication however many tokens it holds — but it pays for softmax on the critical path. A selective SSM has no softmax at all, but its recurrence is sequential in $T$, and a sequential recurrence of length $T$ has depth $T$, which is fatal. The escape is the one Chapter 21 used to make Mamba trainable: the recurrence is linear in the state, so step composition is associative, so a parallel scan replaces the sequential chain.

Theorem 42.1 (Depth of an encrypted selective scan)

Let the discretized recurrence be $h_t = \bar{A}_t h_{t-1} + \bar{B}_t x_t$ with $\bar A_t$ diagonal, and write $b_t = \bar B_t x_t$. Suppose $\bar A_t$ and $b_t$ are available as ciphertexts at level $\ell_0$, laid out across slots along the sequence axis. Then all $h_t$, $0 \le t < T$, can be computed at multiplicative depth exactly $\lceil \log_2 T\rceil$ below $\ell_0$, using $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ rotations in each of the two lanes — $2\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ in total — and no non-polynomial operation.

Proof. The affine maps $h \mapsto A h + b$ form a monoid under composition, with $(A_1,b_1)\star(A_2,b_2) = (A_2A_1,\;A_2b_1+b_2)$ — $\star$ meaning “apply the first, then the second” — and identity $(1,0)$; associativity is associativity of function composition. The Kogge–Stone inclusive scan performs $\lceil \log_2 T\rceil$ rounds, round $j$ combining each slot with the slot $2^j$ positions earlier, after which every slot holds the composition over a window of length $2^{j+1}$; after $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ rounds every prefix is complete. Each round is one slot rotation per lane ($A$ and $b$) followed by one ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication in each lane, and the two lanes are evaluated in parallel — so one level per round, $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ in total. Rotations cost zero levels by Chapter 38's convention. $\blacksquare$

Two remarks, both bearing on whether the theorem is usable. First, the scan algorithm choice inverts under encryption. Blelloch's work-efficient scan performs $O(T)$ operations across an up-sweep and down-sweep, $2\lceil\log_2 T\rceil - 1$ rounds; Kogge–Stone performs $O(T\log T)$ operations in $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ rounds. On a GPU, where work is the constraint, Blelloch wins. Under CKKS the extra work happens inside slots of the same ciphertext and is free, while every extra round is a level off the forty Chapter 38 allowed itself. Minimizing depth beats minimizing work, decisively. Certain

Second, the rotation is cyclic, so round $j$ wraps the last $2^j$ slots to the front and corrupts them. The standard repair is a plaintext 0/1 mask — and a mask is a multiplication, costing a level, doubling scan depth to $2\lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ and, as the artifact prints, destroying the result. The depth-free repair is to pad the slot array to $2T$ with the monoid identity $(1,0)$, so the cyclic wrap brings in identities. The price is $2\times$ the slot footprint, paid in rotations and memory rather than levels.

Common Pitfall

Charging the scan a masking multiplication per round. With $\texttt{scan\_mask\_levels}=1$ the artifact reports the selective block at depth 51 at $T=2048$ against attention's 44, and the crossover collapses from $T=32{,}768$ to $T=128$ — the architecture's entire advantage, deleted by one implementation detail that a plaintext programmer would never think about. Identity padding, not masking, is what makes Theorem 42.1 true in practice.

With the scan priced, the block comparison is mechanical. Artifact 42.1 rebuilds Chapter 38's ledger as a directed acyclic graph, charging parallel branches $\max(\text{parents}) + \text{cost}$ rather than summing — necessary because both blocks have parallel branches (Q/K/V; the SSM gate path) that a linear ledger misprices.

Example 42.1 (Block depth at $d=768$, twelve heads)

A Mamba-style block replaces attention and the MLP, so the honest comparison is one SSM block against attention-plus-MLP. Walking the SSM critical path at four Goldschmidt iterations and degree-15 gating polynomials: RMSNorm $1 + 8 + 1 = 10$; input projection $11$; depthwise causal convolution (plaintext kernel) $12$; SiLU $+4 = 16$; the $\Delta$ projection $17$; softplus $+4 = 21$; $\Delta \odot \mathrm{diag}(A)$ $22$; the discretizing exponential $+4 = 26$; the scan $26 + \lceil\log_2 T\rceil$; the $C$ contraction $27 + \lceil\log_2 T\rceil$; the output gate $28 + \lceil\log_2 T\rceil$; the output projection $29 + \lceil\log_2 T\rceil$. So the closed form is $29 + \lceil\log_2 T\rceil$ against attention's flat $44$. At $T = 128$: $36$ versus $44$. At $T = 8192$: $42$ versus $44$. The crossover is $\lceil\log_2 T\rceil = 15$, i.e. $T = 32{,}768$ — the SSM block is shallower at every context length anyone currently serves under encryption. Of attention's 28 critical-path levels, 13 are softmax (exp 4, Goldschmidt reciprocal 8, normalize 1); the SSM block spends zero.

The rotation side is more lopsided still: attention's ciphertext-ciphertext products need rotate-and-sum reductions scaling with $H \cdot T$, while the scan's rotations scale with the activation-ciphertext count times $\log_2 T$. The artifact reports 41,880 rotations per attention block against 528 per SSM block at $T=128$, and 3,859,968 against 36,096 at $T=8192$ — roughly $79\times$ and $107\times$. These are counts under one packing convention; a better attention packing would narrow them, so the direction is the claim, not the factor. Likely

State the conclusion with its dependence intact. The crossover moves with the softmax budget: at a degree-3 exponential and two Goldschmidt iterations — the aggressive end of Chapter 39's frontier — the artifact reports attention at depth 38 and a crossover at $T=512$; at degree 63 and six iterations, depth 50 and a crossover past $10^6$. Contested This book's position: on current practice (degree 15–31, three to five Goldschmidt iterations, because lower degrees have not been shown to hold accuracy generatively), the SSM block is shallower at every practical $T$, and the eight-level gap at $T{=}128$ is two-thirds of a bootstrap per layer at Chapter 38's twelve levels reclaimed per refresh. A demonstrated degree-3-class softmax holding perplexity on a generative benchmark would overturn it.

42.3.1 What has actually been published

The claim "nobody has built it" needs narrowing to survive contact with the literature, so here is the honest status as of writing. Verify: this is the fastest-moving corner of the area; re-run the search before writing an introduction.

Encrypted state-space inference does exist. Brito's Public-Decay Homomorphic State Space Models for Private Sequence Inference (arXiv 2605.16647) is what its title says: a state-space block under FHE whose carried state is updated by ciphertext-plaintext decay, pushing ciphertext-ciphertext multiplication onto a local write path. The paper reports encrypted classifications matching plaintext exactly on full Rotten Tomatoes and SST-2 validation splits, at 0.7505 and 0.7420 accuracy over frozen fastText features, and roughly $5\times$ the speed of HE-friendly polynomial attention on the same workloads. The decisive word is public: the decay is input-independent, so this is an S4-class time-invariant system, not Chapter 21's selective one. Its framing is candid about why — input-dependent encrypted gates multiplying the encrypted carried state make the carry path consume depth through time, the problem Theorem 42.1 solves and that paper sidesteps.

Selective Mamba exists under a different threat model: MPCMamba (Journal of Information Security and Applications, vol. 93, 2025) runs Mamba inference under secure multi-party computation, reporting accuracy and latency improvements over MPCViT on CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet. Under MPC there is no fixed depth budget — depth costs communication rounds, not a bootstrap — so this section's calculus does not apply — which is why the FHE side is still open.

So the contribution-shaped hole is narrower and more defensible than "encrypted SSMs": a selective, input-dependent state-space block evaluated non-interactively under CKKS at language-model scale, with a reported depth ledger, a bootstrapping schedule, and generative quality against a plaintext reference. Every piece is in this book — Chapter 21 the recurrence and scan, Chapter 39 softplus, SiLU and the exponential as polynomials on bounded intervals, Chapter 38 the packing and ledger, Chapter 41 the generation-time accounting. And there the SSM's second advantage appears, larger than the first: its state is $O(1)$ in $T$, so Example 41.1's 200$\times$ encrypted-KV-cache blow-up does not occur. What replaces it is a state ciphertext losing one level per token, bootstrapped on a metronome. That trade — unbounded cache growth versus per-token bootstrapping of a small state — is the most under-examined question in encrypted serving. Likely

The same exercise, compressed, for the other four collisions.

Encrypted selective SSMs21, 38, 39, 41Public-decay HSSM published (arXiv 2605.16647); selective Mamba under MPC (MPCMamba, 2025). Gap: input-dependent gating under non-interactive CKKS, benchmarked generatively.

(arXiv 2505.07329, Zama) give an interactive HE-LoRA protocol on Llama-3.2-1B; SHE-LoRA (arXiv 2505.21051) encrypts sensitivity-selected LoRA parameters federated, the paper reporting ~94.9% less communication and ~99.8% less encryption compute.
