C.5 Artifact Conventions

Five rules hold across all 42, and they are why the chapters’ numbers can be trusted.

Executed before written, re-run during fact-checking. Each artifact was written to a file, run to completion, and iterated until clean; only then was the source pasted into the chapter, and the paragraph following each listing quotes measured output from that run. Every artifact was then independently re-executed during fact-checking, from the extracted listing rather than the working copy. Wall-clock figures are tagged Verify, because timings are the one class of number a different machine will legitimately contradict.

Optional imports are guarded. The core of every artifact is NumPy. Cross-check libraries are imported inside try/except ImportError and the fallback prints a skip line rather than raising:

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    torch = None
    print("[skipped: torch not installed]")

35 of the 42 files contain at least one such skip path. Certain A missing library costs you a cross-check, never a run. The six SciPy hard dependencies above are the honest exception: SciPy does load-bearing work there — an L-BFGS-B fit, an inverse normal CDF — rather than confirming a result already computed.

One seed, stated explicitly. Randomness enters through np.random.default_rng with a literal integer seed, never the legacy global np.random.seed and never unseeded. Forty of the 42 artifacts draw random numbers, and every one of the forty constructs np.random.default_rng(0). Certain Eight of them open further streams with other small literal seeds where two experiments in the same file must not share one — Chapter 17 uses 0 through 6 across its decay sweep, Chapter 14 uses 1, 2 and 3 for its three exact-identity checks and 11 for its torch cross-check — and Chapter 14’s five ablation arms are instead averaged over the shared seeds 0, 1, 2, so the arms differ by regularizer and nothing else. Chapters 40 and 41 draw none at all. Reproducibility is bit-level on pure-NumPy paths and float64-rounding-level through BLAS, where thread count changes summation order.

Assertions print residuals, not verdicts. The 42 artifacts contain 300 assert statements. Verify A check that prints only OK hides how much room was left; every check here prints the measured quantity beside its threshold, which is what lets a chapter say a gradient matched torch to $4.4\times10^{-16}$ rather than merely that it passed at $10^{-6}$ — the difference between an exact derivation and one that is close enough today.

Self-verification is always against something external. No artifact checks itself against itself. Every assertion resolves to one of four independent references:

Reference classWhat it meansRepresentative artifacts
Finite differencesAn analytic derivative against a central difference quotient of the objective it differentiates6 (gradient and Hessian), 10, 11, 12, 15, 18, 20, 27
Brute forceA fast algorithm against an exhaustive enumeration too slow to ship, small enough to run1 (rank-$k$ search), 8 (all split candidates), 14 (all $2^{12}$ masks), 24 (400,001 allocations), 25 (all pairs), 42 (all DAG paths)
Closed formA simulation or fit against an analytic answer, the problem chosen so one exists2, 4, 5, 21, 27 ($\pi^\ast$), 28 (pass@$k$), 33, 35 (the exact score), 36, 38, 41
Reference implementationA from-scratch implementation against a mature library’s, weights transplanted so the comparison is of arithmetic5, 13, 16, 17, 18 (torch); 7, 8, 9 (scikit-learn); 29 (both)

The ordering matters. A closed form beats a reference implementation, because a library can be wrong and frequently changes; where neither exists, brute force beats a plausibility check. A reference implementation is the weakest of the four and is the sole check in none of the 42. Likely That is why several artifacts construct their problem so that an exact answer exists at all — Chapter 27’s 6-armed bandit and Chapter 35’s Gaussian-mixture target are chosen precisely so the thing being learned has a formula.

C.6 The Companion Ladder: ml-foundations/

Alongside the book sits ml-foundations/, an exercise ladder of 17 standalone files across seven tiers — tier0_math/ through tier6_encrypted/ — running from matrix calculus and floating point up to polynomial approximation and depth budgeting under encryption. Verify Tier 0 maps onto Parts I–II (Chapters 1, 2, 4, 5, 6), tier 1 onto Part III, tiers 2–3 onto Part IV, tier 4 onto Part V, tier 5 onto Part VI, tier 6 onto Part VIII. Run all of it, or one tier:

python3 check.py
python3 check.py tier0_math

The ladder follows the same dependency discipline — optional imports guarded, tiers 0–3 fully usable with NumPy alone — and uses the book’s confidence markers: TenSEAL and OpenFHE surfaces in tier 6 carry Verify, because those APIs move faster than any book.

The two are not redundant, because their intent is opposite. An artifact is a demonstration: complete, commented, runnable the moment you paste it, built to make a chapter’s claim checkable. You read it, run it, see that the residual against finite differences really is $10^{-10}$, and move on. Reading it is the point. A ladder exercise is a specification with a reference solution attached, and its README tells you to delete the function body, replace it with pass, and write it again from the docstring and the assertions below. The assertions are the specification; the reference implementation exists so you can check yourself, not so you can read it.

Reading an implementation and writing one are different skills, and only the second transfers. An artifact read carefully leaves you able to recognize the construct; an exercise reimplemented from an empty file leaves you able to build it. The ladder’s standard is the right one: an exercise is finished when you can delete it, wait a week, and write it again from the docstring. Likely None of the 42 artifacts is designed for that. Use them to verify what you have read; use the ladder to find out what you can write.

Appendix D

Sources and Further Reading

Where this book and a source disagree, the source wins. That convention is stated in the book’s own writing contract and it is not modesty. This book compresses: it takes a result that a paper established over twenty pages with ablations and error bars and states it in one sentence with a number attached. Compression loses the conditions under which the number holds. Every claim here that matters enough to act on — a scaling exponent, a latency, a depth budget, a security level — should be checked against the entry below that owns it before you build on it. This appendix is therefore evaluative rather than bibliographic: each entry says what the source is actually good for, and, where the book takes a different line, says so. Sections D.1 through D.7 are organized by what you are trying to learn; D.8 is about the harder problem of not falling behind. Volatile facts — editions, course offerings, preprint numbers that may acquire venues — carry a Verify tag.

D.1 Foundational Textbooks and Courses

Five books are the ones a reader is most likely to already own, and the ones whose attributions are easiest to get wrong; they are given here in full. Appendix E maps these and eight further sources chapter by chapter.

Aurélien Géron, Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch: Concepts, Tools, and Techniques to Build Intelligent Systems. O’Reilly, 2 December 2025; ISBN 9798341607989. Verify This is the PyTorch edition, which replaces the earlier TensorFlow/Keras editions rather than supplementing them — if your copy says “Keras” on the cover, its second half no longer matches current practice. Best for: end-to-end project discipline, the scikit-learn API surface behind Part II, image pipelines and transfer learning for Chapter 20, and the practitioner’s account of automatic mixed precision that Chapter 5 derives from first principles. Where it differs from us: Géron treats the framework as the object of study; this book treats PyTorch as a cross-check against NumPy code you wrote yourself. Read him for the API, us for what the API is hiding.

Sebastian Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch). Manning, October 2024; ISBN 9781633437166; code at github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch. The closest text in existence to Chapters 18, 19, 23, 26 and 33: tokenizer, dataloader, causal multi-head attention, KV cache, instruction templating with loss masking, and a generation loop, all written out line by line. Part VIII leans on it in a way that is easy to miss — Chapters 38 and 41 re-price exactly the plaintext block and the plaintext KV cache that Raschka builds, so having his code cold is a genuine prerequisite for the encrypted material, not a nicety.

Andrew W. Trask, Grokking Deep Learning. Manning, 2019. Backpropagation by hand, on scalars, before any framework exists. It is the right companion to Chapters 10 and 11 and the best available antidote to treating loss.backward() as magic. It stops well short of modern architectures; that is the correct scope for what it does.

Luis G. Serrano, Grokking Machine Learning. Manning, December 2021. The gentlest treatment of the classical algorithms that is still correct — no hand-waving that would have to be unlearned. Use it as a ramp into Part II. Its deliberate avoidance of linear algebra means it cannot reach the SVD-basis view of ridge regression in Chapter 6 or the spectral account of PCA in Chapter 9; for those, go to ESL and Bishop.

Tanmoy Chakraborty, Introduction to Large Language Models (Wiley India, 2025) Verify and NPTEL course 106102576, “Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs)”. The course is taught by Prof. Tanmoy Chakraborty (IIT Delhi) with Prof. Soumen Chakrabarti (IIT Bombay); lectures are free on YouTube and the syllabus is public at nptel.ac.in/courses/106102576. This is the NLP-side framing of everything in Part V: it comes at language models from problems in natural language processing rather than from optimization, which makes it the best available second angle on Chapters 17, 24, 26, 29 and 36. Its historical framing of the Kaplan-to-Chinchilla arc is more careful than most.

Attribution, Stated Once, Correctly

NPTEL 106102576 is Prof. Tanmoy Chakraborty’s course, co-taught with Prof. Soumen Chakrabarti. An earlier draft of this project attributed it to the wrong person, and misattributions of Indian academic courses propagate quickly through secondary listings because the same course runs under multiple SWAYAM offering codes each term. If you cite it, cite the NPTEL course page, not a course-aggregator card.

Beyond the crosswalk, six reference texts carry most of the load.

Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016; free at deeplearningbook.org) remains canonical for Parts I–III: the linear-algebra and numerical-computation preliminaries behind Chapters 1 and 5, the information-theoretic derivation behind Chapter 2, BPTT and the vanishing-gradient analysis behind Chapter 17. Read its regularization chapter knowing that Chapter 14 disputes its organizing assumption — that capacity control is the binding constraint — for the large-data regime.

Simon J. D. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning (MIT Press, December 2023; ISBN 9780262048644; free PDF at udlbook.github.io). Verify The best diagrams in print, and this book carries none: Prince’s pictures of ReLU networks folding input space, of variance decay through depth, of momentum trajectories on ill-conditioned losses, and of the diffusion forward process are the visual complement to Chapters 10, 12, 13 and 35 respectively.

Kevin P. Murphy, Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction (MIT Press, 2022) and Advanced Topics (MIT Press, 2023). Advanced Topics is the probabilistic lookup volume for this book: the measure-theoretic statements Chapter 2 makes informally, the variational machinery behind the ELBO in Chapter 9, the Gaussian-process side of Chapter 7, the policy-gradient derivations under Chapter 27, and the full SDE treatment of diffusion behind Chapter 35. It is a reference, not a read-through.

Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Springer, 2006; a free PDF is distributed by the author Verify) and Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2009; free PDF from Stanford). Part II canon. Bishop owns the probabilistic derivations — logistic regression via IRLS, kernels and the SVM dual, PCA and EM. ESL owns shrinkage, the lasso path, CART and cost-complexity pruning, and Friedman’s original gradient boosting. ESL’s bias–variance chapter is also the strongest statement of exactly the picture Chapter 3 attacks; read it first, then read Chapter 3 as a rebuttal.

Three non-book sources matter more than most books. Stanford CS336, “Language Modeling from Scratch” (Percy Liang and Tatsunori Hashimoto; Spring 2025 lectures on YouTube, materials at cs336.stanford.edu) Verify is the closest course to Parts V and VI, and it is the assignments rather than the lectures that do the work: a byte-level BPE tokenizer trained at scale, a rotary cache you then break at long context, a Triton FlashAttention exercise, and a distributed-training assignment. Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero, with micrograd, nanoGPT and minbpe, is the from-scratch pedagogy standard; the “makemore” episodes plot per-layer activation and gradient histograms and re-derive the Kaiming gain on screen, which is Chapter 12’s artifact in interactive form, and nanoGPT is the standard substrate for replicating the interpretability experiments in Chapter 37. The Ultra-Scale Playbook: Training LLMs on GPU Clusters (Hugging Face / nanotron, 2025) is the practical companion to all of Part VI, worked on real clusters with profiler traces rather than on paper. Verify

D.2 Architectures

The classical foundations. Five papers own the material of Parts II and III, and this book teaches all five in depth while citing them only in passing; they are collected here. Rosenblatt, The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain (Psychological Review 65(6), 1958), is the linear classifier Chapter 10.1 starts from and Minsky & Papert's Perceptrons (MIT Press, 1969) is the XOR objection that motivates depth. Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors (Nature 323, 1986), is Chapter 11's subject; read it knowing that Linnainmaa (1970) has mathematical priority and that the Nature paper's contribution was attaching reverse-mode differentiation to representation learning, which is the framing Chapter 11 keeps. Cortes & Vapnik, Support-Vector Networks (Machine Learning 20(3), 1995), is the soft-margin formulation Chapter 7.3 derives; Platt's SMO technical report (Microsoft Research, 1998) is the solver Artifact 7.1 implements. Breiman, Random Forests (Machine Learning 45(1), 2001), and Friedman, Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine (Annals of Statistics 29(5), 2001), are the two ensemble papers behind Chapter 8, and Chen & Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System (KDD 2016), is the second-order reformulation Chapter 8.4 derives. Chapter 8 argues these still win on tabular data; the papers do not make that argument and the evidence for it is in Grinsztajn, Oyallon & Varoquaux (NeurIPS 2022) instead.

The convolutional line. Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (AlexNet, NeurIPS 2012), is the result that started the current era, and its interest now is archaeological rather than architectural — the row it occupies in Chapter 16.6's table is the honest summary. Simonyan & Zisserman, Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition (VGG, ICLR 2015), is the source for the stacked-$3\times3$ argument of Chapter 16.5 and for the dense-layer parameter blowup that global average pooling later removed. Ronneberger, Fischer & Brox, U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation (MICCAI 2015), matters here not for segmentation — which this book does not cover — but because its encoder–decoder-with-skips shape became the default diffusion denoiser of Chapter 35.7. Ioffe & Szegedy, Batch Normalization (ICML 2015), is the normalization paper of Chapter 12.4, and it should be read together with Santurkar et al., How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization? (NeurIPS 2018), which refutes its stated mechanism while confirming the effect — Chapter 12.4 follows the second paper, and this is the clearest example in the book of a technique outliving its own explanation.

Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (NeurIPS 2017), is short and still worth reading in the original, but be aware that Chapter 18 does not follow it: the paper puts LayerNorm after the residual add, and every model trained since roughly 2019 puts it before. Read the paper for the idea and Chapter 18.5 for the block that people actually build.

He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (CVPR 2016), is the single most consequential architecture paper for Part III, and its argument is about optimization, not representation. Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, Long Short-Term Memory (Neural Computation 9(8), 1997), remains the correct source for the gating argument in Chapter 17; the constant-error-carousel motivation is clearer in the original than in any retelling.

For position: Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (arXiv 2104.09864; Neurocomputing, 2024), for the derivation Chapter 19.4 follows; Press, Smith & Lewis, Train Short, Test Long (ALiBi, ICLR 2022); and Peng et al., YaRN (ICLR 2024), for context extension. Chapter 19.6 takes a harder line than any of these on base-frequency changes: the papers report what worked, not the failure modes.

Vision and multimodal: Dosovitskiy et al., An Image Is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT, ICLR 2021); Touvron et al., DeiT (ICML 2021); Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models from Natural Language Supervision (CLIP, ICML 2021); and Zhai et al., Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training (SigLIP, ICCV 2023, pp. 11975–11986). Those four are the ones Chapter 20 singles out as unusually readable primary sources, and they are — this is a corner of the literature where the papers beat the surveys. Liu et al., Swin Transformer (ICCV 2021), is the separate source for the hierarchical, windowed design of Section 20.7.

State space models: Gu, Goel & Ré, Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces (S4, ICLR 2022); Gu & Dao, Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces (COLM 2024); Dao & Gu, Transformers Are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality (ICML 2024). Chapter 21 says flatly that the primary papers are the only complete treatment, and adds Albert Gu’s Goomba Lab blog series as the clearest exposition of the semiseparable-matrix argument. This is also the corner of Part IV that Chapter 42.3 identifies as the most under-exploited opportunity under encryption.

Conditional computation: Shazeer et al., Outrageously Large Neural Networks (ICLR 2017), and Fedus, Zoph & Shazeer, Switch Transformers (JMLR 2022). Neither anticipates the shared-expert and fine-grained-expert designs of Chapter 22.5; for those the current model reports are the sources.

D.3 Training, Scaling, and Post-Training

The pretraining papers the book uses as vocabulary. Four names appear throughout Part V as though they need no introduction, and they are cited here once properly. Devlin et al., BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding (NAACL 2019), introduced the masked-language-model objective — which this book treats only obliquely, as one of the classical latent-variable objectives recovered in Chapter 9.6, since Part V commits to next-token prediction throughout. BERT earns its place here for a different reason: encrypted-inference papers overwhelmingly benchmark on BERT-base at sequence length 128, which makes it the de facto unit of Chapters 38 through 42, and Chapter 40.5 shows what goes wrong when a number measured on that encoder is set against one measured on a decoder’s generation step. The encoder-only design it established is now confined to embedding and reranking models. Radford et al., Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (OpenAI technical report, 2018) and Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2, OpenAI technical report, 2019), are the decoder-only counter-line, and the second is the origin of the zero-shot framing that Chapter 29 now has to evaluate around. Neither was peer-reviewed, which is worth noticing about a field this consequential. Liu et al., RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (arXiv 1907.11692, 2019), is the ablation that matters more than its modest headline: it showed BERT was substantially undertrained, and it is the earliest clean demonstration of the recipe-over-architecture principle that Chapters 24 and 25 both rest on. Raffel et al., Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5, JMLR 21(140), 2020), contributed the text-to-text framing and, in its systematic ablation grid, the closest thing the pre-scaling-law era had to a controlled study; the C4 corpus it released is also the ancestor of the filtering pipelines in Chapter 25.2.

Optimization: Kingma & Ba, Adam (ICLR 2015), and Loshchilov & Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (ICLR 2019), which is the AdamW correction Chapter 13.4 derives. For the matrix-preconditioning line ending in Chapter 13.6, Liu et al., Muon Is Scalable for LLM Training (arXiv 2502.16982, 2025), is the first paper to report Muon at a scale where the claim can be assessed; Keller Jordan’s original blog post is the clearer derivation and the paper is the better evidence. Verify

Hyperparameter transfer: Yang et al., Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer (arXiv 2203.03466; NeurIPS 2021), is the muP source for Chapter 15. Read it for the coordinate-check methodology in particular — Section 15.4 exists because the parametrization is easy to get subtly wrong and the check is the only thing that catches it. McCandlish et al., An Empirical Model of Large-Batch Training (arXiv 1812.06162), owns the gradient-noise-scale argument behind Chapter 15.7.

Scaling laws: Kaplan et al., Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (arXiv 2001.08361, 2020), and Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla, NeurIPS 2022). Chapter 24 treats these as a pair whose disagreement is the point, and it insists on two follow-ups that most secondary accounts omit: Besiroglu et al.’s replication of the Chinchilla fit (arXiv 2404.10102), which corrects the published parametric estimates, and Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models (arXiv 2305.16264; NeurIPS 2023), which is the source for the repeated-data regime in Chapter 24.6. If you quote a Chinchilla exponent, quote it from the replication.

Tokenization: Sennrich, Haddow & Birch, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units (ACL 2016), for BPE, and Kudo, Subword Regularization (ACL 2018), for the unigram model. Both predate the pathologies catalogued in Chapter 23.6, which have no canonical paper and are documented mostly in issue trackers.

Post-training: Ouyang et al., Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT, NeurIPS 2022), for the three-stage recipe; Schulman et al., Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms (arXiv 1707.06347, 2017), for the clipped surrogate and the value critic that Chapter 27.4 derives — note that it is a continuous-control paper and that everything specific to language models in Chapter 27 was bolted on afterwards, which is much of why DPO and GRPO exist; Rafailov et al., Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model (NeurIPS 2023), for the derivation Chapter 27.5 reproduces and for the assumptions it makes silently; Shao et al., DeepSeekMath (arXiv 2402.03300, 2024), for GRPO. Parameter-efficient adaptation: Hu et al., LoRA (ICLR 2022), and Dettmers et al., QLoRA (NeurIPS 2023), the latter also being the reference for NF4 and paged optimizers in Chapter 26.5.

D.4 Systems and Efficiency

The FlashAttention line is short and readable end to end: Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra & Ré (NeurIPS 2022); Dao, FlashAttention-2 (ICLR 2024); Shah et al., FlashAttention-3 (NeurIPS 2024). Read them in order — each one changes what the bottleneck is, and reading only the third leaves you unable to say why. Milakov & Gimelshein, Online Normalizer Calculation for Softmax (arXiv 1805.02867, 2018), is the short prerequisite for all three and is the actual content of Chapter 31.2.

Serving: Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (SOSP 2023), is the vLLM paper and the source for Chapter 33.3; Leviathan, Kalman & Matias, Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (ICML 2023), for Chapter 33.5, where the acceptance-rate arithmetic is what matters and the wall-clock numbers are hardware-bound.

Distributed training: Rajbhandari et al., ZeRO (SC 2020); Shoeybi et al., Megatron-LM (arXiv 1909.08053); Huang et al., GPipe (NeurIPS 2019). These three define the vocabulary of Chapter 32, but none of them composes the parallelisms the way current practice does; the Ultra-Scale Playbook is better on composition and on the failure modes of Chapter 32.9.

Quantization: Dettmers et al., LLM.int8() (NeurIPS 2022), for outlier features; Frantar et al., GPTQ (ICLR 2023); Lin et al., AWQ (MLSys 2024). Quantization is the one topic in Part VI whose numbers move fastest, and it is also where the plaintext and encrypted halves of the book meet: Chapter 34 and Chapter 39 are solving the same problem — how much precision can you give up before the model changes behavior — against completely different cost models.

For hardware primitives, the vendor documentation is the source and there is no substitute: the NVIDIA CUDA C++ Programming Guide for the execution model of Chapter 30, and the Triton documentation for Chapter 31.8. Both are versioned and both drift; check the version against your toolkit. Verify

D.5 Generative Modeling

Kingma & Welling, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (ICLR 2014), is where Chapter 35.1 starts. Ho, Jain & Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (NeurIPS 2020), is the paper that made the discrete formulation work; Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling Through Stochastic Differential Equations (ICLR 2021), is the continuous-time unification that Chapter 35.3 and 35.4 follow, and it is the one to read if you only read one. Lipman et al., Flow Matching for Generative Modeling (ICLR 2023), and Liu, Gong & Liu, Rectified Flow (ICLR 2023), give the straight-path reformulation of Chapter 35.5; the two papers arrive at nearly the same object from different directions, which is itself instructive.

Ho & Salimans, Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance (NeurIPS 2021 Workshop on Deep Generative Models and Downstream Applications; extended version arXiv 2207.12598, 2022), is short and explains the single most load-bearing trick in practical image generation. Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (CVPR 2022), and Peebles & Xie, Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (DiT, ICCV 2023), cover the architectural half of Chapter 35.7 and 35.8. Chapter 35.10 on diffusion language models is the section most likely to date; treat its citations as a snapshot.

D.6 Evaluation, Interpretability, and Safety

Chapter 37 says plainly that no textbook in the book’s list covers interpretability, and that remains true. The field publishes on transformer-circuits.pub, on arXiv, and on the Alignment Forum, in that order of density. The four papers Chapter 37 is built on are Elhage et al., Toy Models of Superposition (2022), which is the source of the phase-transition picture in Section 37.2; Olsson et al., In-Context Learning and Induction Heads (2022); Bricken et al., Towards Monosemanticity (2023); and Templeton et al., Scaling Monosemanticity (2024). All four are web-native publications with interactive figures, and the figures carry argument that the text does not — do not read them as PDFs.

Evaluation has one genuinely contested pair, and Chapter 29.5 presents both sides: Wei et al., Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models (TMLR 2022), against Schaeffer, Miranda & Koyejo, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage? (NeurIPS 2023). The dispute is about whether discontinuity is a property of the model or of the metric, and it is settled empirically by re-scoring the same checkpoints under a continuous metric — which is what the second paper does and what you should do before repeating either claim. Contested

For benchmark infrastructure: Liang et al., Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM, TMLR 2023), for the multi-metric framing; Hendrycks et al., Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU, ICLR 2021), still the most-cited and most-contaminated benchmark in the field; Chiang et al., Chatbot Arena (ICML 2024), for the pairwise-ranking methodology and its documented biases. EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness is the reference implementation of the scoring protocols in Chapter 29.2, and reading its code is the fastest way to understand why the same benchmark yields different numbers in different papers.

D.7 Encrypted Machine Learning

Part VIII is the half of this book with no textbook. Everything below is a primary source, and the field’s norms make that unusually workable: cryptography publishes preprints on the IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive with stable identifiers, and most of these papers ship artifacts.

The scheme. Cheon, Kim, Kim & Song, Homomorphic Encryption for Arithmetic of Approximate Numbers (ASIACRYPT 2017, pp. 409–437), is CKKS, and Chapter 38 deliberately does not re-derive it. Cheon, Han, Kim, Kim & Song, Bootstrapping for Approximate Homomorphic Encryption (EUROCRYPT 2018; ePrint 2018/153), is the refresh procedure whose cost dominates every budget in Chapters 38.6 and 41.4.

Parameters and security. Chapter 38 cites the Homomorphic Encryption Standard v1.1 (homomorphicencryption.org, November 2018) for parameter tables. Use it, but know that it has been effectively superseded: Bossuat et al., Security Guidelines for Implementing Homomorphic Encryption (IACR Communications in Cryptology 1(4), January 2025; ePrint 2024/463), carries updated security tables and functional parameter sets for all common schemes, and is the document to check a concrete parameter choice against today. Verify Li & Micciancio, On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers (EUROCRYPT 2021; ePrint 2020/1533), is the paper that showed plain IND-CPA is insufficient for approximate schemes; Chapter 42 treats the resulting IND-CPA-D notion as a live constraint on deployment, not a footnote.

Approximation. Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice, Extended Edition (SIAM; ISBN 9781611975932) Verify is the source for Chebyshev interpolation, equioscillation and Remez done properly, and it is a genuinely enjoyable book. For comparison and sign specifically — the machinery every CKKS system now ships and which Chapter 39.5 builds — the two sources are Cheon, Kim, Kim, Lee & Lee, Numerical Method for Comparison on Homomorphically Encrypted Numbers (ASIACRYPT 2019, pp. 415–445; ePrint 2019/417), and Cheon, Kim & Kim, Efficient Homomorphic Comparison Methods with Optimal Complexity (ASIACRYPT 2020, LNCS 12492, pp. 221–256). Both are short.

Systems. Chapter 40 splits these into an interactive and a non-interactive line, and the split is the right way to read them.

SystemVenue / identifierWhat it is the reference for

GPU acceleration. Phantom (ePrint 2023/049), HEonGPU (ePrint 2024/1543), Cheddar (ASPLOS 2026; arXiv 2407.13055) and FIDESlib (arXiv 2507.04775) are the four Chapter 41.6 works with. Read their kernel-level accounting rather than their headline speedups: the speedups are stated against different CPU baselines and are not comparable across papers.

Systematizations. Two SoKs are the closest thing to a map of this field: Al Badawi, Alexandru, Polyakov & Vaikuntanathan, SoK: Private LLM Inference Using Approximate Homomorphic Encryption (ePrint 2026/935), written by OpenFHE maintainers and consequently unusually honest about what parameter selection actually constrains, and SoK: Private Transformer-Based Model Inference (ePrint 2026/491). Two broader surveys exist (arXiv 2412.08145 and arXiv 2505.10315). Verify

Surveys for Taxonomy, Never for Numbers

Chapters 40 and 42 both state this rule and it is the single most useful habit in this literature. A survey’s comparison table flattens away the model, the sequence length, the threat model, the hardware, and whether the reported latency includes setup and key generation. Every one of those changes the number by an order of magnitude. Take the taxonomy from the survey; take the number from the paper, and take it with the configuration attached.

Libraries. OpenFHE is the most complete and the best documented, and its documentation is a legitimate source for what a production library exposes. Microsoft SEAL, Lattigo (Go), HEaaN, and Zama’s Concrete/Concrete-ML round out the set; TenSEAL is the easiest entry point for a first encrypted tensor. Library APIs move faster than papers — check any call signature against the version you have installed rather than against a tutorial.

D.8 How to Keep Current

The half-life of Parts V through VIII is roughly eighteen months. Likely Parts I through III will not move in your lifetime. Budget your reading accordingly: the foundations reward depth once, the frontier rewards a cheap recurring habit.

The habit that works is venue-based rather than feed-based, because feeds select for novelty and venues select for having survived review.

VenueCoversCadence
NeurIPS, ICML, ICLRCore ML; Parts I–VIAnnual; proceedings open-access
COLMLanguage models specifically; Part VAnnual, since 2024
ACL, EMNLPNLP-side evaluation and analysis; Chapters 23, 29Annual
MLSys, ASPLOS, SOSP/OSDISystems; Part VI and Chapter 41.6Annual
CRYPTO, EUROCRYPT, ASIACRYPTScheme-level cryptography; Chapters 38–39Annual, IACR
IEEE S&P, ACM CCS, USENIX Security, NDSS, PETSPrivate inference systems; Chapters 40–42Annual
IACR ePrint ArchiveEverything cryptographic, months earlierContinuous
arXiv cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CREverything else, months earlierContinuous

Four practices are worth more than any reading list. Read the artifact before the abstract. If a paper ships code, the code answers questions the paper does not: what the baseline actually was, which numbers are measured and which are extrapolated, and what the configuration was. Chapter 40.5 is an entire section on reading a latency claim, and its method is to look for the configuration, not the headline. Reproduce one number. Not the whole paper — one number, on the smallest configuration the code supports. The gap between what you get and what is reported is the paper’s real error bar. Track the correction, not just the claim. Chinchilla’s published fit was corrected by a replication; emergence was reframed by a rebuttal; the 2018 HE parameter tables were superseded by the 2025 security guidelines. In each case the correction is less cited than the original and more correct. Prefer the source that states its own limits. The SoK written by library maintainers is more honest about parameter constraints than the survey written from abstracts, for the same reason a paper with an artifact is more honest than one without: someone had to make it run.

Finally, on this book’s own numbers. Every claim tagged Verify is a claim that was correct when measured and is expected to drift — hardware bandwidths, model versions, prices, library APIs, preprint venues. Appendix F collects the dated reference numbers in one place precisely so that they can be re-measured rather than trusted. When one of them disagrees with a source you have checked, the source wins, and the book is what needs updating.

Appendix E

Reading Crosswalk

The front matter’s instruction — “read the fundamentals in at least two of them” — is worthless without a table saying which two. This appendix supplies one: a row for each of the book’s 42 chapters naming a source for the derivation and a second for the intuition or the working implementation, and marking plainly where no second source exists. Every chapter number and title below was extracted mechanically from the assembled book, not recalled. One rule governs the citations: they name topics, never chapter numbers in other books. Editions repaginate, courses renumber lectures between offerings, and a free PDF revised twice a year does not hold its section numbers still. A pointer to “Goodfellow’s numerical-computation material” survives that; a numbered pointer would be a guess dressed as a citation.

E.1 How to Read Two Sources at Once

Parallel reading fails when both sources are asked to do the same job: two textbook derivations of gradient descent give you one derivation and a wasted afternoon. The method that works assigns each source a distinct role before you open it.

E.1.1 Three roles, three sources

The derivation source proves the thing: assumptions explicit, theorem in a form you could cite, no skipped step. For Parts I–III this is almost always Goodfellow, Bishop, Hastie et al., or Murphy; for Parts V–VI there is frequently no book at all, and the role falls to CS336 or to a primary paper in Appendix D.

The intuition source makes it picturable. Prince is strongest here in print — this book carries no diagrams by design, and Prince’s are the ones to hold in your head. Trask covers anything with a backward pass, Serrano the classical algorithms of Part II, Karpathy anything you will eventually type.

The book’s artifact is the arbiter. When the two appear to disagree you do not adjudicate by authority or publication date: you run the chapter’s artifact, instrument the disputed quantity, and read the number. Appendix C indexes all 42 by what each verifies itself against, which is also an index of what each is competent to arbitrate.

E.1.2 Most disagreements are notational

Before treating a conflict as substantive, apply one test: does the numeric prediction differ? If it does not, you have found a convention, not a contradiction. The usual suspects are row versus column vectors (this book fixes column vectors and $y = Wx$; several sources use $x^{\top}W$), the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in a squared loss, natural log versus $\log_2$ in every information-theoretic quantity, whether a fused multiply–add counts as one FLOP or two (Chapter 1 counts two, giving $2mnk$; sources that count one report half this book’s FLOPs everywhere), and whether a regularizer carries $\lambda$ or $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}$. Appendix A fixes the book’s conventions; check there before believing a source is wrong.

Real disagreements exist and this book names them. Chapter 3 argues directly against the capacity-control framing that Goodfellow presents as doctrine and Hastie et al. in its strongest classical form; read those as the position being attacked, not as background. Chapter 8 marks the tabular-data question contested, Chapter 5 the cost of non-deterministic reduction order. Each states which measurement would settle it, and the artifact runs whatever part of it fits on a CPU in thirty seconds.

Common Pitfall

Parallel reading degrades into serial skimming: you read three accounts of backpropagation, feel fluent, and cannot write the backward pass for a matmul from an empty file. Two sources plus one implementation beats five sources plus none, every time. Time-box the second source — it exists to unstick you on one step, not to be read cover to cover — and treat a chapter as unfinished until the artifact runs and you can explain the residual it prints.

E.2 The Sources, and the Role Each Plays

SourceRole it plays best
Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, Deep Learning (2016)Derivation, Parts I–III. Mathematical preliminaries, optimization vocabulary, backprop on general graphs, the regularization catalogue. Pre-2017 on generalization and architectures.
Prince, Understanding Deep Learning (2023)Intuition. The best diagrams available for variance propagation, loss geometry, linear regions, receptive fields, attention maps, diffusion. Free PDF. Verify

E.7 The Gaps, Stated Plainly

Seven chapters have no adequate companion among the sources catalogued in Section E.2, and padding those rows would have been the easiest dishonesty in this book: Chapter 21, Chapter 37, and all five of Part VIII, with Chapters 28 and 36 close behind. Chapter 39 is the mildest case — its companion, Trefethen on approximation theory, exists but sits outside that list; the other six have nothing book-length at all. Likely The pattern is not random. A textbook enters this crosswalk when a topic has stabilized enough that someone would spend two years writing about it; the gaps are where that has not happened. Part VIII is worse than merely new — it sits between two literatures, and the cryptography texts covering CKKS correctly do not discuss transformers while the ML texts covering transformers do not discuss ciphertext.

The substitution protocol has three steps. First, read the primary paper in Appendix D for its assumptions rather than its results table — Section 40.5 demonstrates at length how much of a latency claim lives in its assumptions. Second, use an adjacent in-book chapter as the derivation source: Chapter 17 and Section 18.7 stand in for the background of Chapter 21; Chapters 33, 38 and 39 compose into Chapter 41; Chapter 5 is the numerical grounding under Chapter 34. Third, run the artifact and change a parameter the paper held fixed. A gap chapter’s artifact does double duty as the only cross-check you have, and Appendix C states exactly what each verifies itself against.

Common Pitfall

Substituting a survey for the missing textbook. Surveys are useful as taxonomies and dangerous as sources of numbers: they copy latency and accuracy figures across papers using different sequence lengths, security parameters and hardware, and provenance is lost by the second citation. Chapters 40 and 42 both say so outright. Use a survey to find which papers exist, take the number from the paper, and record the conditions alongside it — the discipline Artifact 40.1 enforces mechanically.

E.8 Using the Crosswalk

Three ways this table earns its keep. As a prerequisite check: if a chapter’s derivation column names a source you have never opened, that is a signal about the chapter, not the source. Chapter 7 is hard without Bishop on the dual; Chapter 32 is hard without having seen a profiler trace of the kind the Ultra-Scale Playbook reproduces. As triage when you are stuck: being stuck on a derivation and on an implementation are different failures with different remedies, and the two columns separate them — if you cannot see why the algebra works, go left; if the algebra is clear and your code prints the wrong number, go right and diff against the implementation named there. As a reading order: the crosswalk thins from dense in Part I to nothing by Part VIII, a fair description of how much scaffolding exists at each depth. Read Parts I–III with a companion open, Part IV with Prince and Raschka open, Parts V–VI with CS336 and the Ultra-Scale Playbook open, and Part VIII with the papers open and the artifacts running, because there is nothing else.

Two standing cautions. Volatile entries are tagged: course offerings change their assignments between years, the Ultra-Scale Playbook is revised continuously, and Géron’s 2025 PyTorch edition replaced the earlier TensorFlow and Keras editions, so an older copy on your shelf will not match the API discussion cited here. Verify Check any dated entry against Appendix F before citing it. And one ordering rule governs conflicts: where a named source and this book disagree on a fact, the source wins, and the response is to correct the book rather than reconcile the two in your head. Where they disagree on a measurement, run the artifact.

Appendix F

Reference Numbers (dated)

Compiled August 2026. Every volatile number the book leans on is collected here so that the book ages in one appendix rather than in forty-two chapters. Sections F.1 through F.4 hold numbers that drift — accelerator specifications, model cards, prices, benchmark scores. Section F.5 holds the formulas, which do not, and F.6 says how to rebuild the rest. That separation is the point of the appendix: when a chapter says an H100 executes about 295 bf16 FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic, the durable content is the definition of machine balance $B^{*} = \pi/\beta$ from Section 30.3, and the 295 is a perishable input. Re-derive, do not re-read. Where a number here disagrees with a chapter, this appendix is the later measurement and wins; one such disagreement is flagged explicitly in F.1.

Common Pitfall

Do not cite this appendix. Cite the source it names. Accelerator datasheets are revised silently, model cards are edited after release, API prices in this table have moved within a single week, and benchmark leaderboards are re-scored under new harnesses. Every row below carries a Verify tag and names where to check it. A row without a source is a row that was omitted — several were. An incomplete honest table beats a complete invented one, and the failure mode this appendix exists to prevent is a reader quoting a 2026 price in 2028 because it was typeset in a book.

All throughput figures are dense bf16 tensor-core peaks. Vendor marketing routinely quotes the structured-sparsity number, which is exactly twice the dense number and unreachable on ordinary weights; the H100's widely repeated “1,979 TFLOP/s” is the sparse figure and the dense one is 989. Divide any quoted tensor-core peak by two if you cannot tell which you are looking at.

F.1.1 The derived machine balance point

The final column is not a specification. It is $B^{*} = \pi/\beta$, peak dense bf16 FLOP/s divided by HBM bytes per second — Definition 30.2. It is the only number in the table that matters directly to a kernel author, because by Theorem 30.1 an operation with arithmetic intensity $I < B^{*}$ cannot reach peak no matter how the kernel is written. Worked once, for the H100: $989 \times 10^{12} / (3.35 \times 10^{12}) = 295.2$.

Discrepancy with Chapter 30. The hardware table in Section 30.8 lists the B200 at “180–192 GB” and “$\sim$8 TB/s”, giving $B^{*} \approx 281$. Re-verification for this appendix returns 180 GB at 7.7 TB/s, so $2250/7.7 = 292$. The chapter's arithmetic is right for its input; the input conflated two SKUs — the HGX B200 board is 180 GB at 7.7 TB/s, while the 8 TB/s figure belongs to the GB200 NVL package at 186 GB. Use 292 for a B200. Verify This is precisely the drift the appendix exists to absorb, and it is worth noticing how small it is: a 4% error in a bandwidth spec moved the balance point by 4% and changed no conclusion in the chapter. The conclusions that depend on $B^{*}$ — that batch-1 decode sits two to three orders of magnitude below it, that elementwise kernels never approach it — survive any plausible revision of these rows.

Two structural facts the table encodes are more durable than any cell in it. First, $B^{*}$ has stayed inside a band of roughly 150 to 320 across all five accelerators above and both vendors, because FLOP/s and bandwidth have scaled together by design; a hypothetical accelerator with $B^{*} = 30$ would make most of Part VI moot, and none exists. Second, the H200 is an H100 with a better memory system and an unchanged compute peak — it lowers $B^{*}$ from 295 to 206 and nothing else — which is the cleanest available evidence that decode is bandwidth-bound in the market's own judgement. Certain

Chapter 29 argues that the durable output of an evaluation is the protocol and the contamination audit, not the score; this section is a demonstration of why. Certain

F.5 Formulas that do not drift

Everything above expires. Nothing below does. These are the closed forms the book uses to convert hardware and model numbers into decisions, and each is stated with the caveat that makes it wrong when ignored.

F.5.1 Training compute: $C \approx 6ND$

Training a dense transformer of $N$ parameters on $D$ tokens costs approximately $C = 6ND$ FLOPs: two FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward multiply–accumulate, and about twice that again for the backward pass, which computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights. The neglected term is attention's score and value products: $4nd$ FLOPs per token per layer before masking, halved to about $2nd$ by causality since a token attends to $n/2$ positions on average, against the $24d^2$ of the parameter matrices — a ratio of $n/(12d)$, as Section 24.2.1 derives it. At $d = 4096$ the correction stays under 10% for $n$ below about 4,900 tokens and becomes the dominant term long before $n$ reaches a modern context window. Use $6ND$ for budget arithmetic and scaling-law fits as in Chapter 24; do not use it for long-context runs without adding the quadratic term. Certain

F.5.2 Inference compute: $2N$ per token

One forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token, the same multiply–accumulate count without the backward factor of three. For a mixture-of-experts model substitute the active parameter count: DeepSeek-V3 costs $2 \times 37\text{B} = 74$ GFLOP per token, not $2 \times 671$B. The memory system does not get the same discount — every expert must be resident because the next token may route anywhere — which is the whole content of Section 22.8 and the reason F.2 tabulates both columns. Combined with F.5.1, the inference-aware scaling objective of Section 24.5 is $6ND + 2ND_{\text{inf}}$, whose minimizer sits strictly left of Chinchilla's. Certain

F.5.3 KV-cache size

For $L$ layers, $n_{\text{kv}}$ key/value heads, head dimension $d_h$, and $b$ bytes per element, one sequence of length $T$ occupies $$K(T) \;=\; 2\,L\,n_{\text{kv}}\,d_h\,b\,T \ \text{bytes},$$ the leading 2 being keys plus values. Section 33.2's worked case — $L=32$, $n_{\text{kv}}=8$, $d_h=128$, fp16 — gives $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes per token, exactly 128 KiB, so an 8,192-token sequence carries 1 GiB of cache. Multi-query attention is $n_{\text{kv}} = 1$; multi-head is $n_{\text{kv}} = $ the query head count. The formula is exact for standard attention and does not apply to multi-head latent attention, which caches a compressed joint representation instead. Certain

F.5.4 Arithmetic intensity, machine balance, roofline

For an operation performing $C$ FLOPs while moving $Q$ bytes to and from the memory level under consideration, the arithmetic intensity is $I = C/Q$. Given peak throughput $\pi$ FLOP/s and bandwidth $\beta$ bytes/s, the machine balance is $B^{*} = \pi/\beta$ and the attainable rate is bounded by $$P \;\le\; \min(\pi,\ \beta I),$$ so the operation is memory-bound exactly when $I < B^{*}$. Two traps: $Q$ is traffic at a specified level, so an operation memory-bound against HBM may be compute-bound against L2; and $\pi$ must be the peak for the precision actually issued, which is why the dense-versus-sparse distinction in F.1 changes conclusions rather than decorating them. Square bf16 matmul has $I \approx n/3$, giving the compute-bound threshold $n \ge 3B^{*}$; batch-1 decode has $I \approx 1$ regardless of model size. Certain

F.5.5 Ring all-reduce volume

Over $P$ workers all-reducing $S$ bytes, the ring algorithm runs a reduce-scatter and an all-gather, each $P-1$ steps of $S/P$ bytes, so each worker transmits $$V \;=\; 2\,\frac{P-1}{P}\,S \ \text{bytes}, \qquad t \;=\; 2(P-1)\alpha \;+\; 2\,\frac{P-1}{P}\,S\beta$$ in the $\alpha$–$\beta$ model. This is bandwidth-optimal (Theorem 32.1). The bytes saturate at $2S$ as $P$ grows — going from $P=8$ to $P=8000$ increases per-worker traffic by about 14% — while the latency term grows linearly in $P$, which is why rings win on large tensors and lose on small ones, and why hierarchical and tree collectives exist. Certain

F.5.6 The pass@$k$ estimator

For an i.i.d. sampler with per-problem success probability $p$, $\text{pass@}k = 1 - (1-p)^k$. Given $n \ge k$ samples of which $c$ verify correct, the unbiased estimator (Chen et al., 2021) is $$\widehat{\text{pass@}k} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}} \;=\; 1 - \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{n-c-j}{n-j},$$ and the product form is the one to implement: the binomial coefficients overflow for the $n$ used in coverage studies. The plug-in alternative $1-(1-c/n)^k$ is biased downward — $1-(1-p)^k$ is concave in $p$, so Jensen's inequality puts $\mathbb{E}[1-(1-c/n)^k] \le 1-(1-p)^k$ — and the bias grows as $k$ approaches $n$: at $p = 0.05$, $n = 64$, $k = 32$ it is $-0.08$ against a true value of $0.81$, exactly the regime where pass@$k$ inversion claims between base and RL-tuned models are decided. Section 28.3 also insists on the interpretive point: pass@$k$ at large $k$ measures the sampler's support, not its reliability. Certain

F.5.7 CKKS depth accounting

Each ciphertext–ciphertext multiplication consumes one level from a fixed budget, so a circuit of multiplicative depth $d$ requires at least $d$ levels and refreshing the budget requires bootstrapping. Summing the per-layer ledger of Section 38.4 over $L$ layers gives the per-token depth $d_{\text{tok}}$; for the twelve-layer geometry of Section 41.4, twenty-one levels per block gives $d_{\text{tok}} = 252$, and with $B = 18$ usable levels that is $252/18 = 14$ bootstraps per token. Over $T$ tokens the total depth is $D = T\,d_{\text{tok}}$ and greedy scheduling performs $$\left\lceil \frac{D}{B} \right\rceil - 1 \ \text{bootstraps}$$ by Theorem 41.1 — $\lceil 258{,}048/18 \rceil - 1 = 14{,}335$ for $T = 1024$. Two companions. A ciphertext at level $\ell$ in RNS with $w$-byte limbs occupies $2N\ell w$ bytes, which is why an encrypted KV cache runs two orders of magnitude above its fp16 counterpart. And baby-step–giant-step reduces the Halevi–Shoup diagonal matvec from $d-1$ rotations to $n_1 + n_2 - 2 \approx 2\sqrt{d}$ — 4,095 down to 126 at $d = 4096$ (Theorem 38.1). Depth is the currency; rotations are the tax. Certain

F.6 Re-verifying this appendix

The tables above were built by fetching primary sources, not by recall. Rebuilding them takes under an hour. Fetch the vendor datasheets for F.1 and recompute $B^{*}$ yourself rather than trusting a quoted balance point; pull the model cards and technical reports named in F.2 by their arXiv identifiers; fetch the provider pricing pages for F.3 on the day you need them; and for F.4 read the protocol section of each paper before copying its number. A minimal harness:

mkdir -p refcheck && cd refcheck
printf '%s\n' 2407.21783 2401.04088 2412.19437 2508.10925 2503.19786 \
              2405.00332 2501.00656 2509.16941 \
  | xargs -I ID curl -sL -o ID.pdf https://arxiv.org/pdf/ID
python - <<'PY'
specs = {                       # (dense bf16 TFLOP/s, HBM TB/s)
    "H100 SXM": (989.0, 3.35),
    "H200 SXM": (989.0, 4.80),
    "B200 SXM": (2250.0, 7.70),
    "TPU v5p":  (459.0, 2.765),
    "TPU v7":   (2307.0, 7.37),
}
for name, (pi, beta) in specs.items():
    print(f"{name:10s} B* = {pi / beta:6.1f} FLOPs/byte")
PY

When a row changes, change it here and nowhere else. That is the contract this appendix is written under, and the reason Chapter 30 states a balance point in prose while this appendix states the bandwidth it came from.
